en: Salutations to Śrī Vāsudeva, the Supreme Brahman.
This is the *Śrī Vyāsa-Pāṇini-Bhāva-Nirṇaya*, [a work concerning] the embodiment of existence, consciousness, and bliss, resembling a water-laden cloud.
We worship Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the beloved of Ramā, the Lord of Īśa. || 1 ||

I bow for the purification of my intellect to Vyāsa—the noble lion among men, whose hand is adorned with the *jñānamudrā*, who is worshipped by the hands of Nṛsiṃha, and who is a celestial *mandāra* tree for those who seek his refuge. || 2 ||
I pay homage to Pāṇini and the other masters who initiated the science of grammar;
the well-spoken words of these great men heal the impurities of speech. (3)

I bow to the venerable teacher Śrī Subbarāya, who is a pitcher-born sage (Agastya) for the ocean of grammar, who is proficient in the systems of Gautama and Kaṇāda, and who is skilled in the two schools of Mīmāṃsā. 4.
Remembering their words, I, the wise one known as Śrī Setumādhava,
compose this determination of the intent of the two sages, Śrī Vyāsa and Pāṇini.
That Vāsudeva is the supreme reality—this Vyāsa and Pāṇini intend to convey; this is stated here in brief along with its authoritative evidence.

An Examination of the Cause for the Composition of the Treatise: That venerable great seer, the teacher Pāṇini, having obtained the traditional inventory of phonemes (*akṣarasamāmnāya*) from Maheśvara—who was propitiated by his long-term ascetic practice—sat down on pure ground facing the east with the sacred *darbha* grass in hand, as an authority for all. With great mental concentration, he composed the rules beginning with "vṛddhir ādaic" and ending with "a a," thereby shaking off the impurities of speech for men and generating the discernment that distinguishes correct words (*śabda*) from corrupt words (*apaśabda*). Salutations to that Pāṇini, who, having received the traditional enumeration of phonemes from Maheśvara, proclaimed the entire science of grammar.
"Salutation to that Pāṇini, by whom the darkness born of ignorance was shattered with the pure waters of words—the speech of men.

This is universally acknowledged. Such a grammar as this is useful for both sentences and sentence-meanings; it is the means for understanding words and word-meanings; and it is the primary auxiliary (*aṅga*) in the investigation of the meaning of the Veda, which is the cause for knowing the majesty of the Supreme Person, who is the means for achieving all human goals (*puruṣārtha*). For it is said in the *Paspaśāhnika* of the *Mahābhāṣya*: "And among the six auxiliaries, grammar is the most important."

No one of discernment would ever hastily utter words to claim that the grammatical derivation of words accomplished by Pāṇini through such a treatise is unreal, or that others—whether Vedic scholars or worldly linguists—who proceed with the investigation of the meanings of bases (*prakṛti*) and suffixes (*pratyaya*) under the impression that it is real, are mistaken.

The authors of works such as the *Pradīpa*, *Kaustubha*, *Vaiyākaraṇasiddhāntakārikā*, *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇa*, its *Sāra*, and the *Mañjūṣā*, however, maintain that the derivation of words which Pāṇini accomplished through this great treatise is not ultimate. This [derivation] serves as a means for the realization of the *sphoṭa*, which is the true referent of Brahman; for it is said that "standing upon the unreal path, one seeks the real," thus describing the unreal as a means for attaining the reality of things.

And therefore, the *sphoṭa* known as the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*) is the only one that is real; it alone is both the signified and the signifier. For those who find simplicity in the case of the capacity [to signify]—just as they do in the case of the capacity [to be signified]—let there be a distinction among the phonemes (*varṇa*) based on adventitious conditions (*aupādhika*), like the difference between high and low pitch.

Because of this statement, everything else consisting of name and form—the entire world—is unreal (illusory). Furthermore, those who engage in an analysis of the meanings of bases (*prakṛti*) and suffixes (*pratyaya*) with the intention that they possess real existence, while the grammatical system of Pāṇini itself is non-real, are mistaken. The *Śabdakaustubha* has been drawn from the ocean of the Bhāṣya spoken by the Serpent (Patañjali). The very meaning determined therein is here stated in brief.

Having thus promised, "This *Vaiyākaraṇasiddhāntamañjūṣā* is being composed," [the author] has thoroughly established [the doctrine] in his various works, preceded by examples from the *Mahābhāṣya*. Although many different varieties are found in these works, nevertheless, regarding the fact that the *sphoṭa* is the ultimate reality and everything else is not so, all of them are indeed of one voice.

Let it be that they have such an intention; what loss is there for others by that? For it is natural for authors to describe their own preferred doctrines within their respective works. True, do not speak so loudly, saying "there is no loss. Indeed, great harm could arise from hearing words of censure against the teachers.

Therefore, Manu—instructing one to perform acts such as covering the ears upon hearing an accidental censure of one's gurus—has made it known that one should simply not listen to the censure of one's teachers at all.
Wherever slander or even censure of the guru takes place, one should either cover one's ears or depart from that place to another. (2.200)
Thus, [the text states]:

"Hearing disparagement of the Teacher and so forth is a cause of misfortune; therefore, one must certainly provide a remedy"—this is the meaning. And providing such a remedy—namely, instructing all those who possess devotion to the Teacher that they must not speak thus when disparaging their Guru—is not easy for people of the present day, and such a response is fruitless.

However, contemporary scholars such as Nāgojībhaṭṭa and others—who, while defining in their own works meanings that were neither stated nor intended by the ancient masters (*ācāryas*), claim that "the masters spoke of meanings for *prakṛti* and so forth that are merely non-real"—it is precisely these who speak what is unreal, and not the masters Pāṇini and his predecessors; for it must be understood that the masters indeed taught only the real meaning. With this realization, [the author says] "of many births... (*bahūnāṃ janmanām*).

Our endeavor here is to inform the discerning and the non-believers that this is the nature of the supreme reality as intended by Vyāsa, the author of the Sūtras, and Pāṇini, and that this is their true intention, by means of elucidating the underlying purport of the words of the Blessed One.
Furthermore, it is to establish that the Mahābhārata, Rāmāyaṇa, and other such texts have Vāsudeva as their ultimate goal.

Now, one might ask: among the many verses in the *Gītā*, for what reason is the commentary on this particular verse being introduced? It is said in reply: here, in the *Mañjūṣā*, Nāgeśa states that the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of "I" and "mine" is itself ignorance (*avidyā*), because it is the direct opposite of the knowledge (*vidyā*) expressed in the statement "Vāsudeva is all. By declaring that the realization of the fact that everything has Vāsudeva as its essence is the correct knowledge that removes ignorance, he reveals the intended meaning of the *Gītā*’s words—that this alone is the ultimate purport of all the scriptures.

While elaborating upon this, he establishes the illusory (or false) nature of everything. This entire [work] is un-Pāṇinian, because it was not taught by him; furthermore, considering that it is understood to be unacceptable to the author of the Sūtras—who composed the two rules "vāsudevārjunābhyāṃ vun" (Pāṇini 4.3.95) and "a a" (Pāṇini 8.4.68)—I have determined that the following observation is now the appropriate occasion to present. Therefore, this verse first came to my mind, and as it is also relevant, I shall place it at the beginning.
Introduction: Following the explanation of the meaning of the verse, the intention of the author of the Sūtras, Pāṇini, will now be elucidated.

This verse occurs in the Mahābhārata, within the Bhīṣma-bhārata, specifically in the seventh chapter of the Gītā-parvan in the Bhīṣma-parvan. It is undisputed that this narrative of the Mahābhārata—a jewel of history containing the essence of all the Vedas and serving as a supplement to all the Śāstras—primarily expounds the majesty of the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva.

This very narrative was composed by the glorious Lord Nārāyaṇa, the abode of compassion, desiring to show grace to those men whose minds are deluded by association with the wicked and who suffer in *saṃsāra* due to the loss of knowledge over time. Having descended in the form of Vyāsa upon Satyavatī through Parāśara, he created it. Regarding this, it is said: "O bull among the Bharatas, in the Veda, in the meritorious Rāmāyaṇa, and in the Mahābhārata, Hari is sung everywhere—at the beginning, at the end, and in the middle."
The Blessed One Vāsudeva is celebrated here as the eternal;
for he is indeed truth and immortality, as well as purity and merit itself.
In the Bhārata (1.1.282), the Blessed Lord Ṛṣi has described the majesty of Vāsudeva, the truthfulness of the Pāṇḍavas, and the wicked conduct of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.

By stating "He who is distinct from all" (*bhārata* 1.1.76) and so forth, the Great Sage himself declared that it is Hari alone who is established as the subject of his own work. Furthermore, in the *Gītā*, Lord Vāsudeva—the Ancient Supreme Person, endowed with the attributes proclaimed by the authority of all the Vedas, Smṛtis, Itihāsas, and Purāṇas—speaks thus.
And that very reality which Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the son of Vasudeva, taught to Pārtha through seven hundred verses, that same reality Bādarāyaṇa has here composed in this *Bhārata*.

In that regard, desiring to describe briefly the majesty of the Blessed One which had been described at length in the *Mahābhārata* and other works, the venerable Vyāsa composed the jewel among Purāṇas called the *Śrīmad Bhāgavatam*, which abounds in the aesthetic flavor of devotion (*bhakti-rasa*) and is a mine of jewels consisting of the Lord’s qualities. And therein [he states]:
"O Arjuna, O scorcher of foes, it is only by means of unswerving devotion that I, who am of such a nature, can be known in truth, seen as I truly am, and entered into. (Gītā 11.54)

Having ascertained, according to the direction stated above, that devotion is the supreme means for the attainment of one's desired goal, he explains—with examples—that taking refuge at the lotus-feet of the Lord Nārāyaṇa, the Consort of Śrī, is the means for attaining all forms of happiness. To illustrate:
"O God, we bow to Your lotus-feet, which are a parasol that extinguishes the heat of distress for those who have sought refuge;
for the ascetics, whose banner is rooted in these feet, quickly cast far away the vast suffering of saṃsāra."

One should always meditate upon that which destroys all humiliation, which grants the desired fruit without fear, which is the abode of sacred pilgrimage sites, which is praised by Śiva and Viriñca, and which is the true refuge.
We bow to Your lotus feet, O Puruṣa, which destroy the suffering of Your servants and serve as a boat for those who have taken refuge from the ocean of worldly existence.
(Bhāgavata 11.5) Salutations, salutations to You, the thread of all-knowing consciousness, who remain steadfast while assuming a form of pure goodness.
"By good fortune, this one who torments the world has been slain; O Lord, through devotion to Your feet, we have attained peace.

(Bhāgavata 3.20). Modern teachers of that region also consider the nature of bhakti as defined by the mental state directed toward the Supreme Object—termed *anurāga* or "attachment"—to be appropriate, and thus they [describe] the essential nature of devotion to the Blessed One...
That attachment which is accompanied by deep respect is called constant devotion; that alone is the supreme instrument for the Lord.

Thus, according to the direction stated by the Blessed One elsewhere, the uninterrupted flow of love directed toward the Lord—preceded by the knowledge of His majesty, which is not shared by others—is what the scriptures describe when they employ such expressions as: "There is no deity other than Vāsudeva who is both the object of worship and the bestower of fruits," and "Meditation [should be performed] by way of [His] possessing qualities that are not shared by others. Having established the essential truth of the scriptures—that worship of the Lord through *ananya-bhakti* (exclusive devotion) is the means to the fruit—they instruct the virtuous in that very meaning of the scriptures.

This very devotion is not easily attainable by all; rather, it is accessible only to those who have purified their inner selves through the performance of their prescribed duties, whose sins have been destroyed, who are endowed with tranquility (*śama*) and other virtues, and who have studied the sacred knowledge.

As it is said: "A person devoted to his own respective duty attains perfection" (Gītā 3.45); "Having become tranquil, self-controlled, withdrawn from sense-objects, patient, and composed, one should see the Self in the self alone" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.4.22); "Having examined the worlds built of karma, let one seek the learned Brāhmaṇa who is firmly established in Brahman" (Īśāvāsya Upaniṣad 2.12); and "The man who has a teacher knows [Brahman]" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.14.2).

6.1.4.2) As stated in the Gītā and other scriptures: "Learn that by prostration, by inquiry, and by service" (Gītā 4.34), and "and likewise by worshiping the teacher" (Gītā 13.7). Among these, the first duty is the *saṃdhyā-vandana* (twilight prayer). By failing to perform it, one indeed lacks qualification for all ritual acts. "One who neglects the *saṃdhyā* is eternally impure and unfit for all rites;
whatever action he performs, he shall not partake of its fruit."
For this reason, Vijñāneśvara established [the rule] in the section on expiation (*prāyaścitta*) by introducing the topic of mindfulness (*smṛti*).

Thus, although the blessed Vyāsa had already performed such a service, he was supremely compassionate; and considering that the Vedas are infinite, the *Mahābhārata* consists of one hundred and twenty-five thousand verses, the *Śrīmad Bhāgavata* of eighteen thousand verses, and many other Purāṇas contain immeasurable texts—how could living beings of limited lifespan and little capacity be able to contemplate these daily and thereby keep the qualities of the Lord in mind? Having reflected thus, [he composed this work].

He composed the great treatise named *Brahmasūtra*, which is a compendium of the essence of all the Āgamas; it is characterized by various primary and secondary qualities such as the Lord’s authorship of the universe and other attributes that are imperishable and must be meditated upon. This title of his is truly significant: for "Brahma" refers to the supreme state of Śrīmat Nārāyaṇa, who is distinguished by infinite auspicious qualities—such as being the cause of the birth and so forth of the universe—as established by the Vedas and the Śrutis, Itihāsas, and Purāṇas that follow them; while "Sūtra" refers to a work that is concise in syllables, free from ambiguity, substantial, and comprehensive in its scope.
Those who know the Sūtras understand that a Sūtra is that which is free from redundancy and irreproachable.

Thus, it refers to the supreme scripture endowed with the characteristics defined by etymology (*nirukta*). Consequently, its meaning is that this *sūtra* establishes the Supreme Brahman, who is designated by such terms as Nārāyaṇa and Vāsudeva—terms which possess infinite qualities and are free from blemish, as established by an etymology not shared by any other. Alternatively, "Brahman" means the Veda; therefore, its meaning is what is to be grasped, and the *sūtra* is that which determines it. And the object of the Veda is Vāsudeva, characterized by the aforementioned qualities. Furthermore, there is the usage of the term "Vedānta-śāstra" for this work, and it is also conventionally referred to as the "Vedānta-sūtra."

The word *veda* refers to the meaning of the Vedas (*vedārtha*), and the word *anta* signifies "determination" (*nirṇaya*). This is because, in the passage "the end of both is seen" (*ubhayor api dṛṣṭo 'ntaḥ*, Gītā 2.17), all authorities accept that the word *anta* has the sense of determination. Consequently, the compound *vedānta* is a *bahuvrīhi*: that in which there is the end—the determination—of the Veda and its meaning. Then, through the words *śāstra* and *sūtra*, a *karmadhāraya* compound is formed. Thus, the meaning is: "the scripture that determines the meaning of the Vedas," and so forth. Furthermore, the meaning of the Vedas has been stated to be Vāsudeva alone.

All commentators and their followers declare that the scriptural passage beginning with "One should desire to know That" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1) and the aphorism "Then, therefore, the desire to know Brahman" (Brahma-sūtra 1.1.1) enjoin that one must seek to know this very Brahman, Vāsudeva. Śrīkaṇṭhācārya, however, maintains that Śiva is the object to be known.

Some, establishing the supreme excellence of Nārāyaṇa and his being propounded by all the scriptures such as the Brahma-sūtras, and asserting the authorship of Bādarāyaṇa and others, declare that this scripture is intent upon duality (*bhedapara*). Others, however, demonstrating with evidence that Nārāyaṇa is the presiding lord of all, the supreme deity, and the one propounded by all the scriptures beginning with this [Brahma-sūtra] as the cause of the entire universe and so forth, maintain that this scripture is intent upon duality.
Others, however, pointing to this or that particular subject matter, say that this scripture culminates in their own respective preferred views of difference, non-difference, and so forth.

Even in such a manner, this [scripture] is not capable of determining the meaning of the Veda without assistance; rather, it is only when accompanied by *upabṛṃhaṇa* (elaborative supplements). If one asks what those supplements are, they are the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas*. For it was said by the venerable Vyāsa:
"One should supplement the Veda with the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas*."
"The Veda fears one of little learning, thinking, 'He will deceive me'" (Mahābhārata 1.1.213).

For this very reason, the venerable Vyāsa composed many sūtras containing the word "Smṛti," such as "And because of Smṛti. Here, the mention of the "Veda" is illustrative, including this scripture which follows it. Consequently, the determination of its meaning must also be carried out by means of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas. For this reason, commentators such as the venerable Śaṅkarācārya cite passages from the Mahābhārata and other texts as corroborative evidence to determine the meaning of specific topical sections (*adhikaraṇa*).

In that regard, many Purāṇic citations have been quoted by Śrīmad Rāmānuja, Śrīmat Pūrṇaprajña, Vijñānabhikṣu, and Bhāskara Ācārya in their commentaries—both in the *Smṛtyadhikaraṇa* (Brahma-sūtra 2.1.1) of the venerable Śaṅkara-bhāṣya, and in other sections of that work.
[This section concerns] the determination of the reasons for the non-availability of those authoritative texts cited in the commentaries.

[Objection: But surely, among the Purāṇic passages cited by various commentators, some are found in the original sources while others are not; therefore, how can there be confidence in this matter? [Reply: It is said: what could the commentators do if the passage were not found in the source today?

However, those [scholars] rely solely on statements found in the Purāṇas and other texts from the past; their failure to find such passages now is rooted in the personal convictions of learned men who have gained authority in the work of writing and editing. Thinking that the statements existing here and there are not favorable to their own preferred doctrines, they exclude them and insert some fabricated statements that are indeed favorable.

In some places they omit what exists, and in others they add what is extra; in some places they omit what exists, and in others they add what is extra. For this very reason, in texts such as the *Mahābhārata* and the *Rāmāyaṇa*, one observes variations in readings in some instances, omissions of portions of the text in others, and additional readings in yet others. Therefore, it has been said by the learned: "In some places they insert texts, and in others they even omit them."

This is the first example here: in the second chapter of the Ādi Parvan of the Śrī Mahābhārata, within the summary of the Aśvamedhika Parvan, the reading is: "The Sudarśana, as well as the narrative and the Vaiṣṇava dharma. This is the reading found in the edition of the Bhārata printed at the Nirṇaya Sāgara Press by T. A. Kṛṣṇācārya, a resident of the city of Kumbhakoṇam. Furthermore, in that same book, regarding the indication of the number of chapters, it is stated: "One hundred and three chapters are proclaimed; there are three thousand verses and as many hundreds [three hundred] as well."
And twenty verses have likewise been enumerated by the seer of reality.

Thus, one and a half verses are seen [in the critical edition]. However, in that very same manuscript belonging to the Āśvamedhika Parvan, one hundred and eighteen chapters are observed. There are fifteen chapters more than the number specified in the Parvasaṃgraha. Furthermore, in another South Indian manuscript of the Mahābhārata printed in Devanāgarī script—containing the passages "The Maṇidarśana and likewise the narrative... and "In the Aśvamedha, the vision of the Maruts occurs right here..."—one hundred and thirty-three chapters are stated.
Forty thousand and as many hundreds.

Thus ends the summary of the subject matter, and verses indicating the number of chapters and so forth are also seen. Similarly, by Navanīta Kṛṣṇācārya, a resident of the village named Tirunāgeśvara near the town of Kumbhaghōṇa, it was stated that there ought to be one hundred and thirty-three chapters in the Āśvamedhika Parvan. However, because a complete manuscript of that Bhārata has not been obtained, the deficiency or excess of chapters is not demonstrated here.

In the Bhāratakośa, printed at the Gaṇapati Mudraṇālaya in Mumbai and accompanied by the Nīlakaṇṭhī commentary, the meaning of the verse beginning with "sadarśanam" is entirely absent; nor is there any other verse conveying this same sense. However, as in the first cited edition of the Mahābhārata, the one-and-a-half-verse beginning with "adhyāyānām" is present in the Parvasaṃgraha.

In the Āśvamedhika Parvan, however, the narrative portion extends up to the *Nakulopākhyāna*, wherein nineteen chapters (19) are observed; yet, according to the method of the half-verse summary (*adhyardhaśloka*) recited in the section on the compendium of the parvas within that very manuscript, it lacks eleven chapters. Now, as for the statement, "We say that that portion does not exist in that parva," it is not to be trusted; for the learned authorities cite the texts found therein as authoritative evidence.

Therefore, one should not conclude that [the Vedic texts] do not exist simply because they are not seen in the extant repositories (*ākara*) of the words cited by the author of the *Bhāṣya*. For this very reason, in the *Mahābhāṣya*, in the *Paribhāṣā-pāda* of the first *Āhnika*, after beginning with "For thus it is heard," and citing: "Bṛhaspati taught Indra for a thousand years the complete study of words (*śabdapārāyaṇa*) consisting of words explicitly mentioned word-for-word (*pratipadokta*), yet he did not reach the end," it is stated in that same work, under the sixth rule, "One [substitute] takes the place of both the preceding and the following" (*ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ*), that "A single word, when correctly understood..."

"When [speech] is accompanied by the science (śāstra) and well-employed, it becomes a cow of plenty (kāmadhuk) in the heavenly world. Furthermore, regarding the authority cited by Yāska—"Knowledge indeed came to the Brāhmaṇa, saying: 'Guard me; I am your treasure. Do not speak of me to one who is envious, nor to one who is dishonest, nor to one who is unrestrained; thus may I be potent'"—no wise person, even if doubting, asks, "Where is this authority? nor does he say, "This is not authoritative because it is not found in the original sources (ākara)."

If it be argued that we may conclude that great sages such as Patañjali and others, being possessed of vast knowledge, would not speak of what does not exist, then—alas!—let it be firmly concluded that the commentators on the *Brahmasūtra*, the crest-jewels among those who know the higher and lower principles and the most profoundly learned, having explained the spiritual science (*adhyātma-śāstra*) which is the means for attaining the fourfold goals of human life, and being instructors of the nature of the supreme reality, would likewise not speak of what does not exist. Enough of this digression.
Here follows the consensus of the teacher Ānandavardhana regarding the supremacy of Viṣṇu in the *Mahābhārata* and the *Rāmāyaṇa*.

We have stated previously that the *Mahābhārata* and the *Gītā* proclaim the majesty (*mahiman*) of Vāsudeva. This majesty is a unique power (*śakti*), not shared by any other, which is synonymous with the capacity for the creation, preservation, and so forth, of a manifold and most diverse phenomenal world (*prapañca*). Regarding this very [majesty] in the *Mahābhārata* and similar texts, certain moderns, following the path of *dhvani* (suggestive poetry), consider it to refer to something other than Vāsudeva.

Indeed, the ancient and most eminent scholars who established the path of *dhvani* maintain that its ultimate goal is *Vāsudeva*. Regarding this, the teacher Ānandavardhana stated with due reflection in the fourth chapter (*dyota*) of his *Dhvanyāloka*: "Furthermore, when a single primary sentiment (*rasa*) is presented as the dominant element throughout a literary composition (*prabandha*), it nourishes a specific excellence and an extraordinary splendor. This is seen, for example, in the *Rāmāyaṇa* or the *Mahābhārata*. In the *Rāmāyaṇa*, the sentiment of pathos (*karuṇa-rasa*) is the principal one."

In the Mahābhārata, the sentiment of tranquility (śānta-rasa) is the primary one; the human goal characterized by liberation (mokṣa) is the most important among all human goals; and the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva is the principal subject matter established throughout various sections of the Vāsudeva [portion].

Therefore, direct your cultivated minds toward that very Lord Vāsudeva, the Supreme Lord who transcends saṃsāra; do not fix them upon worldly powers which are devoid of essence. This point has been determined by those who know the true nature of the Word (Śabdatattva), by commentators, and by others as well, based on the statement: "The eternal Lord Vāsudeva is celebrated here."

The wise scholars of the past and those even more ancient than them—who possess knowledge of the reality signified by words—have established that Vāsudeva alone, as propounded by the Vedas and the scriptures following them, is the supreme reality; Ānandavardhana Ācārya indicates that this very same view is his own. Thus, while elaborating upon the essence of the Śrī Rāmāyaṇa and the Mahābhārata, this Ānandavardhana maintains that both of these works are Vaiṣṇava treatises on liberation (mokṣa-śāstra).

In this regard, the claim made by some of the most recent [scholars] that the *Rāmāyaṇa* and the *Mahābhārata* are, according to the principle of suggestion (*vyaṅgya*), primarily concerned with the supremacy of Śiva, is to be considered doubtful. This is because the status of Vāsudeva as the central subject was established by ancient scholars themselves, and because the Great Sage, the author of the *Mahābhārata*, himself stated: "Vāsudeva is the one who is expounded. Such is the summary.
As for the meaning of the verse beginning with "of many":
"At the end of many births, the man of knowledge attains Me."
"Vāsudeva is everything"—such a great soul is very difficult to find (Gītā 7.19).

In this regard, the venerable Bādarāyaṇa [states]: Regarding Kurukṣetra as a region suitable for battle, the Kauravas and Pāṇḍavas, desiring to fight, assembled there together with eighteen akṣauhiṇīs.

There, having ascertained who among those who had arrived were equals, who were unequals, or who were superior in merit—and likewise, among those previously rejected, who had come and who had not—Arjuna, desiring to see those assembled for the ease of preparing the appropriate materials for the battle, stationed his chariot between the two armies; standing right there, he beheld them all.

But seeing his teachers, kinsmen, maternal uncles, and others assembled there, he was overcome with compassion and overwhelmed by a sense of shame and affection for his relatives. Thinking, "How can I kill these kinsmen and others? What is the use of this battle, which results only in the slaughter of one's own kin, which is devoid of any desired fruit in this world or the next, and which is rooted in sin? Therefore, I do not wish to engage in this fruitless conflict," he spoke thus, cast aside his bow and arrows, and sat down in silence.

Then, although Dhanañjaya had been consoled by the Blessed One with words of reconciliation, he remained distressed due to affection for his kinsmen and was perplexed as to what ought to be done, saying: "I do not know dharma and adharma; yet I do not see this battle as a means to achieve the highest good. May you yourself instruct me in that which you perceive to be our welfare. For I am your disciple; I have taken refuge at your feet."

To the son of Pṛthā, who had thus spoken, who was surrendered, desirous of knowledge, and seeking the highest good, the Blessed One taught the ultimate meaning of all the scriptures in brief, beginning with: "You grieve for those who should not be grieved for" (Gītā 2.11), up to:
"Renouncing all duties, come to Me alone as your refuge."
"I shall liberate you from all sins; do not grieve" (Gītā 2.54–66). Thus concludes [the first section].

In this *Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā*, there are three groups of six chapters (*ṣaṭka*). Among them, in the first group of six, the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*), the two types of karma-yoga, and the yoga of meditation (*dhyānayoga*) which serves as a limb for the direct realization of the Lord are taught. In the second group of six, the yoga of devotion (*bhaktiyoga*) and the majesty of the Lord, which is its cause, are explained. In the third group of six, the subject matter of the preceding two groups of six is integrated, and the necessity of knowing the essential nature of categories—such as their being characterized by purity (*sāttvika*) and so forth—is established.

There too, having taught the yoga of knowledge through the passage beginning with "You grieve for those who should not be grieved for" (Gītā 2.11) and ending with "This wisdom has been declared to you according to Sāṃkhya" (Gītā 2.31), and having taught the two-fold karma-yoga— the external means of knowledge— in both brief and detailed forms from "But hear this regarding yoga" (Gītā 2.39) up to the conclusion of the fifth chapter,
[the Lord says]: "Knowing Me as the enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities, the Great Lord of all worlds, and the friend of all beings, one attains peace" (Gītā 5.29).

Thus, having taught in the final verse of the fifth chapter—by the statement "knowing Me, he attains peace" (*jñātvā māṃ śāntimṛcchati*)—that knowledge of the Supreme Self is the means for attaining liberation, the sixth chapter instructs on *dhyānayoga*, the internal auxiliary means to that knowledge. In its final verse, [the Lord says]: "Of all yogis as well, he who worships Me with his inner self absorbed in Me, full of faith, he is deemed by Me to be the most disciplined. (Gītā 6.47)

In this context, having commenced this sixth chapter for the purpose of establishing the greatness of the Lord—introduced as a limb of meditation through such statements as "with a mind absorbed in Me" and "possessing faith"—and having promised the instruction on both kinds of greatness in the seventh chapter, which is devoted to defining the Lord's majesty in its general and specific forms denoted by the terms *jñāna* and *vijñāna* with the words "I shall declare that knowledge to you along with realization" (Gītā 7.2), [the Lord speaks of] *jñāna* in the verse beginning "Among thousands of men... (Gītā 7.3).

Having praised [the Lord] with the four verses beginning with "Earth, water, fire, air" (Gītā 7.4) and ending with "There is nothing else higher than Me" (Gītā 7.7), He taught the greatness of the general [nature] denoted by the term *jñāna*; and having taught the greatness of the specific [nature] denoted by the term *vijñāna* with the five verses beginning with "I am the taste in the waters, O son of Kuntī" (Gītā 7.8) and ending with "And whatever states are characterized by goodness" (7.12), [He stated that] not all people are capable of attaining such knowledge.

They do not merely manifest power; rather, although the Supreme Self is the agent of effects consisting of the three *guṇas* and so forth, He is not bound by the three *guṇas*. Therefore, with the thought that He is the "Supreme Person" (*uttamaḥ puruṣaḥ*) and the refuge of all, they have gone for shelter to the feet of the Blessed One, [relying] on the grace of the Blessed One—just as in the world, when someone is the object of another's exceeding love, that person is fit to be designated as "I am he. This is shown by six verses beginning with "By the three states consisting of the *guṇas*" (Gītā 7.13) and "All these are indeed noble, but the man of knowledge... (Gītā 7.18).

Having taught through these verses, Lord Vāsudeva praises knowledge by way of praising the knower, [showing] that the grace of the Lord—which consists of the supreme Self and compassion and which is the cause for such designations—is not easily obtained by all. He says:
"Of many... The construction here is as follows: "Of many births"—from the age of four until the age of sixteen, actions are indeed performed with regularity.
He creates the causes for ten bodies at the very least.

Thus, for those who have established through valid means (*pramāṇa*) that they have undergone many births, in their final birth, [they realize]: "Vāsudeva is everything"—that is, the entire collection of the manifold world (*prapañca*) consisting of the moving and the unmoving is Vāsudeva, or rather, is dependent upon him; or else, "everything" refers to the full reality, which is Vāsudeva, Hari himself; or else, "everything" is the all-pervading Vāsudeva; or else, as it is said: "I am the father of this world, its mother, its supporter, and its grandfather" (Gītā 9.17).

9.17) Thus, Vāsudeva is one whose kinsmen and people are all [deities] as will be described; or, Vāsudeva is the source of the origin and dissolution of everything; or, Vāsudeva alone is "everything"—that is, every entity possessing knowledge directed toward all objects. One who possesses such knowledge—being thus endowed with knowledge and thereby fit for liberation—resorts to, that is, attains, Me, the Supreme Self, Nārāyaṇa, who is non-different from him. He is the possessor of such knowledge; this is a qualifying attribute containing a reason.

For this very reason, the Great-Souled One is worthy of worship; for it is said regarding the worshipfulness of the knower of the Self: "Whatever world a person of purified being contemplates in his mind, and whatever desires he desires—he conquers that world and those desires. Therefore, one who desires prosperity should honor the knower of the Self" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.10). Thus, because of the statement regarding the worshipfulness of the knower of the Self, [such a person] is extremely rare and is not easily found.

Here, because of the statement regarding its rarity, those possessing such knowledge of Brahma are indeed few; for this very reason it is said, "Someone knows Me in truth" (Gītā 7.3). Regarding the word *sarva* as signifying "complete," it is according to the commentary by the sage Pūrṇaprajña on the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "Because of its extreme proximity to Brahma, and because its qualities are entirely full, that [Vraja] is Brahma itself; and he who is Viṣṇu is directly from Brahma. Furthermore: "You pervade everything, therefore You are all" (Gītā 11.40).

(11.40) Thus, it should be understood that the word "all" (*sarva*) signifies all-pervasiveness, according to the direction that will be stated hereafter. Furthermore, in the commentary on the *Upaniṣad* passage, "That indeed is his this [state]" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 6.3.29), which is intended to explain the state of liberation, Ānandagiri explains Śrī Śaṅkara’s commentary—namely, "When he becomes distinguished from ignorance, then he attains oneness with all"—by stating, "'With all' means together with the full Supreme Self. From this, it is well-established that the word "all" also carries the sense of "full" (*pūrṇa*).

The meaning is this: knowledge, however, is accomplished through many births. And this has been explained by the Blessed One in the sixth chapter of the *Gītā* through a series of questions and answers, beginning with "one endowed with effort and faith" (*Gītā* 6.37) and ending with "perfected through many births" (*Gītā* 6.45); for it is established therein that the attainment of the fruit occurs even in another birth.

However, liberation attained through the Lord occurs at the very end of the body, provided there is no obstacle; but if such an obstacle exists, it occurs at another time. This very point was established by the author of the Sūtras in the two aphorisms: "In this life, [liberation occurs] when there is no obstacle to the burning away [of karma], because that is seen" (Brahma-sūtra 3.4.50), and "The uniformity of the fruit of liberation [is established] because its state is determined" (Brahma-sūtra 3.4.51).

For instance, when there is an absence of obstacles in the form of *prārabdha* (commenced karma), direct knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) arises even in this very life, provided there is the attainment of the means [to liberation], because such is observed and because it is stated in the Śruti, "having heard the Self," and so forth; this is the meaning of the first [verse]. The word "knowledge" is supplied by ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*). The purport is that when this obstacle is absent, the arising of knowledge occurs in this very birth, but when it is present, it occurs in another birth. This very same meaning has been described in the Śaṅkara Bhāṣya as well.

In this way, just as with knowledge, there is no fixed rule regarding the fruit of liberation; that is, even for the fruit of liberation, there is no certainty. Liberation occurs at the very moment of the arising of knowledge provided there is an absence of obstacles; if such obstacles exist, it occurs in another birth. And thus, according to Śaṅkara, liberation occurs in the very same birth in which knowledge arises.

In the *Śrībhāṣya* of Rāmānuja, however, the meaning of these two sūtras is explained as follows: "There is no rule that the fruit of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*), distinct from liberation (*mokṣa*), occurs only after its respective means have been completed; likewise, there is no rule that even the fruit of liberation occurs only after its means have been completed. Thus, there is no rule that wherever the means are perfected in a given birth and knowledge (*jñāna*) arises, knowledge and liberation must occur at the very end of that life; for *prārabdha* karma acts as an obstacle.

By describing the rarity of the man of knowledge (*jñānin*), it is shown that knowledge—which is the cause of the supreme delight of the Lord and the ground for designating [the self] as the Self—is exceedingly rare; thus, it is knowledge itself that is being praised. This concludes the section on the Gītā’s focus on non-duality.

One should not think that, by this, the designation "the knower is indeed the Self" and the statement "Vāsudeva is everything" intend to convey the non-difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (Īśvara), nor that they intend to convey that everything has the nature of Vāsudeva. For if that were the case, it would be impossible to speak of the relationship between the object of worship and the worshiper, as well as the relationship between the goal to be attained and the attainer, between Brahman and the individual soul—as expressed in such passages as "The man of knowledge takes refuge in Me" and "But those who constantly worship Me, they cross over this Māyā"—since those relationships depend upon their difference.

If it is argued that—since it is the experience of everyone that one's own self alone is dear to oneself and not another self, and therefore, if the Knower were different [from the object], He could not be an object of love, and thus His very statement implies the intention of their non-difference—it is replied: the designation "dear" refers to the fact that a particular, preeminent quality residing in each individual object captivates the mind of another; this is an experience witnessed by the hearts of all.
For an ordinary worldly quality does not attract the mind of the Blessed Lord.
"Neither by the study of the Vedas and sacrifices, nor by gifts, nor by rituals, nor by fierce austerities,
can I be seen in such a form in the world of men by anyone other than you, O hero among the Kurus.
But by unswerving devotion alone, O Arjuna, am I to be known in this manner."
To know and to see it in its true essence, and to enter into it, O scorcher of foes. (Gītā 11.54)

Thus, having refuted the idea that the study of the Vedas and other such means constitute the instruments for attaining knowledge, [the text] teaches that devotion alone is the instrument for that attainment. However, there are two unsurpassed qualities: knowledge established by the scriptures, which consists of the cognition of the Lord as possessing the attribute of being the "All-Knowing One" (*sarvajña*), and devotion, which is a continuous flow of supreme love toward Him as its object, rooted in that very knowledge. This is because of such scriptural statements as, "For I am exceedingly dear to the knower, and he is dear to Me," and "But by unswerving devotion. For this very reason, [it says], "Knowing Him thus..."

The Śruti passages such as "Ātmā vā are" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.5), "Athāto brahmajijñāsā" (Brahma-sūtra 1.1.1), and others, as well as the Sūtras, declare that knowledge is the means for attaining the goal of human life (*puruṣārtha*). Consequently, devotion (*bhakti*)—described as "He who possesses devotion is dear to Me"—is the cause of the Lord’s pleasure, as is the aforementioned distinctive knowledge; however, [the Self] is not the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the Self. The statement "the Self alone" is intended solely to demonstrate that the knower of the Self possesses this distinction from others, and not to indicate that [the Lord] is the essential nature of the Self.

Otherwise, since it has already been stated that one's own true nature (*svarūpa*) is indeed dear to oneself, teaching that [nature] would be fruitless. Furthermore, according to the view of Mañjūṣākṛt, who maintains the doctrine of the oneness of the Self (*ātmaikatvavādin*), the non-difference of all individual souls (*jīva*) from Brahman is self-evident; therefore, speaking of it specifically for the wise would be useless. Moreover, at the very beginning of this [work], it is said:
"You grieve for those who should not be grieved for, yet you speak words of wisdom.
The wise do not grieve for the dead or the living" (Gītā 2.11).
"But indeed, I was never non-existent, nor you, nor these lords of men;
and none of us shall ever cease to be hereafter" (Gītā 2.12).

By the use of the plural "these lords of men" (*janādhipāḥ*) in the phrase "those who are not to be grieved for," and by stating that they serve as examples for the self in the proof of its eternity, the plurality of selves is established; this is also evident in the conclusion:
Fix your mind on Me, be devoted to Me, sacrifice to Me, and bow down to Me;
thus you shall come to Me alone—this I promise you in truth, for you are dear to Me. (Gītā 18.65) Abandoning all duties, take refuge in Me alone.

By the two verses beginning with "I shall liberate you from all evils; do not grieve" (Gītā 18.66), Śrī Kṛṣṇa—known as the Supreme Brahman—is shown to be the object of worship, while Arjuna and all other human beings are shown to be the worshippers; thus, the fundamental distinction between the Self [of the Lord] and [the selves of] others is established. Therefore, in accordance with both these points, the meaning of the phrase "the Self alone" is rightly that which we have stated.

Therefore, those who are learned in the principles of *upakrama* (introduction) and other hermeneutical criteria (*nyāya*) state that both the description here of the Knower as being of the same nature as Vāsudeva, and the subsequent determination of the intent (*tātparya*) of the scriptures regarding the non-difference of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman based on that, are not logical.

If it is objected: "Since the difference established between the introduction and the conclusion is unreal (*apāramārthika*), it is improper to say 'in accordance with both of them' and so forth," we reply: No, because it is improper to state an unreal matter at the very beginning of a scripture. As it is said: "I am your disciple; teach me, who have taken refuge in you" (Gītā 2.7).

2.8) By this, it is understood that Pārtha has gone for refuge to the Blessed One out of a desire to know reality (*tattva*); therefore, since it is the primary duty of the teacher to produce correct knowledge by teaching that very same meaning at both the beginning and the end to a disciple who has surrendered, it is illogical that an unreal meaning would be taught in both instances.

By this, it should be understood that both of these points—the description of the purport of the verse "Everything has Vāsudeva as its essence" based on the claim that "the superimposition of 'I' and 'mine' is itself ignorance (*avidyā*), because it is the direct opposite of the knowledge that 'Vāsudeva is everything,'" and the repeated demonstration of the oneness of the Self—are unacceptable to both teachers. This is because, according to the direction already stated, the verse does not possess such a meaning; for [the Lord says]: "And whoever shall study this sacred dialogue of ours, by him I shall have been worshipped through the sacrifice of knowledge; such is my conviction. (Gītā 18.70)
"Even the man who merely hears this with faith and without malice,
he too, being liberated, shall attain the auspicious worlds of those who perform meritorious deeds" (Gītā 18.71).

By these two verses, since this scripture establishes that the attainment of the highest worlds is the very fruit for both the teachers and the listeners, it is understood that neither of these [worldly gains] was intended by the great sage Śrī Vyāsa.

Regarding the meaning of the *sūtra* "vāsudevādi" (*vāsudevārjunābhyāṃ vun*, Pāṇini 4.3.98), even for the teacher Pāṇini himself, who composed the *sūtra* "aa" (Pāṇini 8.4.68), there is a determination that the Blessed Vāsudeva is the Supreme Self and the universal supervisor; for this very reason, there is also a determination that he is the most venerable of all and distinct from everything else. This is understood because it is clear that [the author] does not accept [any other interpretation] of that [term]. Consequently, having first made the formal proposition "In the established doctrine of the Grammarians," it is improper to describe a meaning that is not accepted by him.

If it is asked, "But how is it determined that the intended meaning was stated by the composition of such a sūtra?", it is replied: we have already stated that among the six auxiliary sciences (ṣaḍaṅga), grammar (vyākaraṇa) is the most important and the very essence, as it is useful for determining the meaning of the Vedas through traditional lineage.

Just as this Sūtra teaches the correctness of words, so too its *ceṣṭita* (intentional action) establishes specific meanings; for here, the intention of the Teachers is understood through gestures, actions, winks, and extensive compositions of Sūtras. Thus, by stating the two rules "not when there is a *saṃprasāraṇa*" (Pāṇini 6.1.37) and "not after *mun*" (Pāṇini 8.2.3), the author of the Bhāṣya has established a systematic rule (*vyavasthā*).

*Ingita* is mental activity; *ceṣṭita* is physical activity, which in the present context refers to articulation; and *nimiṣita* is ocular activity. In that regard, in certain instances, the Teacher reveals his own intention through a specific rule (*sūtra*), as for example in the case of *yūnaḥ* and so forth, where there is the occurrence of two or more *yaṇ* vowels suitable for *saṃprasāraṇa*. In such a situation, he reveals his intention—namely, that the *saṃprasāraṇa* does not apply to the preceding *yaṇ*—by means of the specific statement "not [in the case of] *saṃpra*" (*na saṃpra*).

In some instances, however, he reveals his own intention by adopting as a cause (*nimitta*) some form of the word that has become an effect (*kārya*), such as in the rule "na mune. By this, taking the word *na*—established through the absence of *ā*—as the cause, he brings to mind his own view through the method of inference: that the non-ineffectiveness (*asiddhatvābhāva*) of the substitution of *m* for *n*, which is prescribed [by P. 8.2.3], does not remain ineffectual even when the absence of *ā* (the *nābhāva*) is relied upon as the cause for its application; thus, the substitution of *m* (*mutva*) is not *asiddha*.

If it were assumed in this way, then since the substitution of *mut* would be considered *asiddha* when the absence (*abhāva*) is to be effected, the very word *naḥ* would not exist, resulting in the non-establishment of the reason; thus, the Sūtra would become devoid of scope. Furthermore, in the present case as well, the fact that the word *Vāsudeva* is placed first (in the form of prior usage within a *dvandva* compound) indicates that the Teacher intends to convey that the referent of the term *Vāsudeva* is a specific deity who is distinct from all others, who is the most excellent of all, and for that very reason, the most venerable in every respect.

Otherwise, according to the rule established by Pāṇini himself—namely, that the word *arjuna* should have been placed first because it begins with a vowel (*ajādya*), ends in a short vowel (*adanta*), and has fewer syllables (*alpāctara*) under the rules "ajādyadantam" (Pā. Sū. 2.2.33) and "alpāctaram" (Pā. Sū. 2.2.34)—the prior use of the word *vāsudeva*, which does not possess those characteristics, would be unjustifiable. Therefore, we understand that there exists in Vāsudeva a quality such as being the Supreme Self (*paramātmatva*) which serves as the basis for his being more venerable; thus, his own philosophical position is indicated.

For this very reason, even setting aside his own established rule (*vyavasthā*), he first employed the word *vāsudeva*. It should be understood that among the qualities mentioned—such as being more venerable (*abhyarhitatva*) and so forth—each preceding one serves as the cause for each succeeding one. If it is objected: "It is logical to assume superiority and greater venerability in relation to the meanings of the words uttered in proximity [to one another], but such an assumption is not [universally] valid," we reply: This very point has been clearly demonstrated by both the Bhāṣya and Kaiyaṭa on this very sūtra.

For instance, the *Bhāṣya* states: "Or rather, this is not the designation 'Kṣatriya'; it is a technical name (*saṃjñā*) for the Blessed One (*bhagavat*) there. Kaiyaṭa explains: "'It is a technical name' means that here the term Vāsudeva refers to the eternal Supreme Self (*paramātman*), a specific deity. This is because in the *Bhāṣya*, the word *vāsudeva* is explained by the word *bhagavat*.
[As it is said: "Sovereignty, heroism, fame, splendor, as well as knowledge and discernment—the sixfold [collection] is called *bhaga*."
Knowledge, power, glory, sovereignty, valor, and splendor— these, in their entirety and devoid of all qualities to be abandoned, are what is denoted by the word "Bhagavat."

Thus, He possesses qualities such as the governance of the universe—which are unique to Him, not shared by others, and which coexist with the absence of all defects proven by valid means of knowledge.
Indeed, this much is sufficient to indicate His lack of equality or superiority through His attributes:
"For those who abandon all else and pray to Him, His sovereign power attends even upon the dust of His feet, though He desires it not. (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.8.20)

Moreover, who else in this world besides Mukunda could be called a true possessor of the title "Lord," when even the water used for the worship offered by Viriñca, once released from the tips of his toenails, purifies the entire universe including Śeṣa?
(Śrīmad Bhāgavatam 18.21) "I have been questioned by you, O Aryamanas; I shall declare to you the extent of my own realization in this matter.
Just as birds fly through the sky according to their own capacity, so do the wise attain the goal of Viṣṇu according to their own measure."

Thus, in the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* (18.23), that specific deity who is the Lord of Lakṣmī— who is designated by such terms as Viṣṇu and Mukunda, who is determined to be the referent of the word "Bhagavān," and who is worshipped by all the gods beginning with Brahmā and Īśāna— is [the Supreme].
This word "Bhagavān" and likewise the word "Puruṣa" [refer to Him].
Both of those two always abide in the eternal Vāsudeva.

Thus, by this authority, it is taught that Vāsudeva is to be understood as the primary denotation of the word *bhagavat*. Kaiyaṭa’s statement that it refers to “a particular deity” means “the supreme deity. Since the author of the Bhāṣya employs the term *bhagavat* instead of other terms such as *hari*, the aforementioned meaning is in accord with the Bhāṣya and other authorities; therefore, there is no room for any objection whatsoever.

Thus, in the Sūtra, the word *vāsudeva* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). Furthermore, when the word *vasu*—ending in the *aṇ* suffix derived by the *uṇādi* rules—is placed in a *karmadhāraya* compound with the word *deva*, it denotes Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Śrī, who is the support of all and the inner controller of all. As it is said: "All this is strung upon me, like clusters of gems on a thread" (Gītā 7.7); "The Lord of all beings" (Gītā 18.61); and: "Because He dwells everywhere and everything dwells in Him, therefore He is celebrated as Vāsudeva by the wise."
Because of your abiding [within all], you are Vāsudeva; the three worlds have been perfumed by you.
You are the dwelling place of all beings; O Vāsudeva, salutations be to you!
"I cover the entire world, having become like the sun with its rays;

I am Vāsudeva, the abode of all beings"—since such *smṛti* passages establish that He alone is characterized by the qualities of being the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of all and the substratum of all; and because Śaṅkarācārya himself, in his commentary on the scriptural passage "This is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 5.7), stated that the status of being the inner controller belongs to Nārāyaṇa alone.

Alternatively, this Pāṇinian utterance of the word *vāsudeva* in its earlier usage—namely, "May my sons eat rice with plenty of milk and ghee from a bronze vessel"—is pregnant with its full intended meaning, just like the speech of the old maiden mentioned in the commentary on the rule *na mu na*. Commentators explain that while the speech of the old maiden is pregnant with the desire for all possible prosperity such as a husband, sons, wealth, grain, and so forth, [this utterance is likewise pregnant with its full sense].

By making the non-inflected designation "a a" when one ought to have said "asya a," the venerable Pāṇini—acting in accordance with the suitability of the meaning for the purpose of phonetic refinement (*śabdasaṃskāra*)—has thereby performed that which must necessarily be done at the conclusion of a treatise: the repetition (*dvirvacana*) established by tradition as a sign of the completion of the work; as well as the auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) consisting of the remembrance of his chosen deity, which is established by the authority of the maxim "undertakings conclude with an auspicious rite" and is required as a duty at the end of a treatise; and furthermore...

He considers that everything has been accomplished: the invocation of the Lord to offer his own work to Him; the communication to the listeners of his own knowledge that Vāsudeva, the Blessed One, is his chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) and so forth, thereby generating such knowledge in them as well; and therein, the repetition (*abhyāsa*) is evident.

From the statement, "The letter 'A' is Vāsudeva; the letter 'A' is the Lord Viṣṇu," and from the Śruti, "A is Brahman" (Ai. Ā. 2.3.8), as well as from the traditional teaching that the word 'A', which denotes Vāsudeva, is employed at the end [of a work] for the sake of auspiciousness, it is established that there exists the recognition of Vāsudeva—the supreme being denoted by the word 'A'—as one's chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā).

Since the word "a" can be understood as ending in a vocative case, it serves to address the Lord for the purpose of surrendering one's own work to Him. In this interpretation, the repetition [of the vocative] is out of reverence; furthermore, it ensures that the listeners—by virtue of their firm conviction that the Teacher possesses the status of the most supreme among all deities regarding the Blessed Vāsudeva—will likewise possess such a conviction themselves and become His worshippers, and that they will remain firm in their resolve and practice accordingly. Thus, everything is entirely consistent.
The grace of the Blessed One has the power to remove ignorance (*avidyā*).

Furthermore, as for the claim that "I" and "mine" arise from ignorance (*avidyā*), that may be so; however, the argument that the knowledge "Vāsudeva is all"—meaning that everything has Vāsudeva as its essence—is the wisdom (*vidyā*) that contradicts this ignorance, is not tenable. For even this [knowledge] is a specific form of ignorance, just like "I" and "mine. We perceive no distinction whatsoever between the status of "I" and "mine" as ignorance and the status of "Vāsudeva is all" as wisdom.

"Non-apprehension of reality with respect to that which is not [that] is indeed ignorance (*avidyā*). And this is common to both cases. For that which is the remover of something is its opposite. In the world, regarding the false apprehension 'this is silver,' the subsequent sublating cognition 'this is not silver,' or the knowledge of the true nature of the substrate 'this is mother-of-pearl,' is the remover; however, learned men say that another form of ignorance such as 'this is a pot' or 'this is a cloth'—which shares the same status as the former—is not."
But the scripture, which is the grace of the Blessed One, declares that it removes the ignorance of "I" and "mine," which is the seed of saṃsāra:
"If that very Blessed One, the Infinite, should show compassion to those who have taken refuge in his feet with their whole being and without guile."
They indeed know and they transcend the divine illusion;
in them there is no thought of "mine" or "I" regarding what is to be eaten by dogs and jackals.
This divine illusion of Mine, consisting of the modes of nature, is difficult to overcome.
"Those who take refuge in Me alone cross over this illusion" (Gītā 7.14).
Those men who, free from passion and knowing the higher and the lower,
constantly remember Nārāyaṇa, the preceptor of the gods.
By means of that meditation, their sins having been destroyed, they do not drink the milk from their mother's breast again. (From the *Pāṇḍavagītā*)

But those who desire liberation, who have placed their trust in the words of the Teacher and the scriptures that the crossing over of saṃsāra is easily accomplished through the worship of the Blessed One alone; who correctly understand both the supreme and the non-supreme reality; who are free from longing for objects such as sons, friends, and wives; who constantly remember the Blessed One and serve Him with sincerity; whose hearts are intoxicated by tasting the nectar flowing from the lotus feet of the Blessed One; they become those who have taken refuge in the feet of the Blessed One.

The unbroken meaning of the conclusion of the scriptures (*śāstravinirṇaya*) is as follows: those who, through the grace of the Blessed One, have developed discrimination, have removed the seeds of *saṃsāra*, and are freed from the bonds of ignorance consisting of "I" and "mine," and whose merits and demerits—other than those already set in motion (*prārabdha*)—have ceased by their very nature, do not undergo rebirth. The Lord’s *māyā* consists of the three *guṇas* dependent upon the Supreme Self; it is delusive (an obstacle to the apprehension of the true nature of reality). He should show compassion—that is, He should exercise mercy—and favor them with His grace.

The suffix *liṅ* is used here after the root *kṛ*, which is derived from the noun *dayā* (compassion) with the causative suffix (*ṇic*). The phrase "in a body to be devoured by dogs and jackals" is an elliptical expression that includes all perishable objects of sense.

By the statement "they attain [the Lord] and cross over," the relationship of cause and effect between the attainment of the Lord’s feet and the crossing over of *māyā* is indicated; this is similar to the relationship between the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) and the act of teaching, as seen in such injunctions as, "One should marry a Brahmin boy of eight years and teach him."

The meaning of "vigata" and so forth is that they possess discernment regarding the higher and lower principles through detachment from sense objects. The meaning of "hatakilbiṣa" and so forth is that their defects, such as ignorance, have been destroyed by the grace of Hari; in other words, they are pure-souled. It follows that they become liberated, being devoid of birth caused by the drinking of mother's milk. The rest is clear.

By this, it should be understood that whatever has been asserted by Nāgeśa in the *Mañjūṣā*—and by other grammarians in their respective works—regarding the acceptance of an unprecedented category called *sphoṭa*, its status as Brahman, its being the material cause of the universe, and its being the sole reality, all of this is intended merely to produce delusion in the ignorant; for it is entirely contrary to the intention of the author of the Sūtras and the Bhāṣya.

The primary intent [of both works] is that Vāsudeva alone is the supreme reality, the Supreme Brahman, and that the mere remembrance of Him bestows the goals of human existence (*puruṣārtha*). Furthermore, since the status of *sphoṭa* as Brahman and so forth is nowhere stated even in the *Bhāṣya*, its underlying intention likewise conforms to the intent of Vyāsa and Pāṇini.
Thus, the intention of Vyāsa has been shown through the commentary on the meaning of the verses of the *Gītā*, and that of Pāṇini through the commentary on the sūtra beginning with "vāsudeve."

**The Resolution of the Contradiction Regarding Grammatical Coreferentiality:** Now, one might object: "Through coreferential designations such as 'The knower is indeed the Self' and 'Vāsudeva is everything,' a cognition of non-difference arises spontaneously, just as in cases like 'the blue pot. To this we reply: a coreferential designation is not capable of producing a cognition of identity of essence in all instances. For even when such designations are used in cases like 'the face is the moon,' 'the boy is a lion,' or 'the sacrificial post is the sun,' a cognition of non-difference does not arise."

Furthermore, among the four types of words distinguished by name (*saṃjñā*), genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*kriyā*), there occurs the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) of quality and action with the words for name and genus, as in "Sundara is a cook" (*sundaraḥ pācakaḥ*) or "Devadatta is a Brahmin" (*devadatto brāhmaṇaḥ*); of name and genus, as in "Devadatta is a Brahmin" (*devadatto brāhmaṇaḥ*); of quality and action, as in "Sundara is a cook" (*sundaraḥ pācakaḥ*); of two qualities, as in "Blue and beautiful" (*nīlaḥ sundaraḥ*); and of two actions, as in "A cook and a reciter" (*pācakaḥ pāṭhakaḥ*).

Co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) produces a cognition of non-difference (*abhedadhiy*) therein, because in all such cases it is possible for properties (*dharma*) to reside in a single substratum (*ekasminn adhikaraṇe*). However, this is not the case where there is co-utterance of two universals (*jāti*) or two names (*saṃjñā*) alone, as in "the Kṣatriya is a Brāhmaṇa" or "Devadatta is Yajñadatta. In these instances, since [the properties] such as Kṣatriyahood and Brāhmaṇahood are contradictory properties (*viruddhadharma*), their subsistence in a single substratum is impossible.

In the present context, however, because the statement "the knower is indeed the Self" is equivalent in usage to "Devadatta is Yajñadatta," there is no cognition of identity; for here the term "knower" [refers to one of the four types mentioned in]:
"O Arjuna, best of the Bharatas, four kinds of virtuous people worship Me:
the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the man of wisdom" (Gītā 7.16).

Thus, because it is impossible for the two terms to reside in a single substratum—since the word *ātman* refers here to the soul of the aforementioned special class of upāsakas who possess knowledge (as a secondary sense), whereas [the term *paramātman*] refers to the essential nature of the Lord—it follows that the understanding must be "one who is like the Self," just as in the case of expressions such as "the boy is fire. The properties that serve as the basis for this similarity are, first, being extremely dear, and second, being free from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*) and so forth; here, the former is explicitly mentioned, while the latter is not.

By this it should be understood that the term *jñānin* here refers to the class of knowers in general; therefore, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is established. Thus, as for the cause of such a distinct cognition, one should consult the omniscient Lord, who is the source of all instruments, or the learned and sensitive scholars (*sahṛdaya*) who know the true nature of the meaning of words.

If it is argued that, in this case, there ought to be a reference using the suffix *-vat*, as in *ātmavat* ("like the self"), we reply: no, because even without that suffix, the cognition of similarity is established through experience. Moreover, the fact that the meaning is conveyed without such a formal reference is established by the stylistic convention of the authors of technical treatises (*śāstra*). For this very reason, Pāṇini employed the forms *gāṅkuṭādibhyo’ñṇidṅti* (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.2.1) and *goto ṇit*.

Regarding those two very sūtras, the author of the Bhāṣya states—with an illustration—that the understanding of the meaning of the suffix *vati* occurs even without the suffix *vati*: "The transfer [of properties] is not understood without the suffix *vati*, yet the transfer of properties is understood even without the suffix *vati*. For example: 'This is Brahmadatta'; one says of someone who is not Brahmadatta, 'He is Brahmadatta'; we understand from this that 'he is like Brahmadatta. In the same way here as well, when one says 'that which has a marker *ṅ*' (*ṅit*) or 'that which has a marker *ṇ*' (*ṇit*), it is understood as 'like that which has *ṅ*' (*ṅidvat*) or 'like that which has *ṇ*' (*ṇidvat*). Thus, the author of the Bhāṣya declares that the comprehension of the sense of *vati* takes place even in the absence of the suffix *vati*.

Similarly, regarding the rule *bahugaṇavatuḍati saṃkhyā* (Pāṇini 1.1.23), even under the view of extended application (*atideśapakṣa*), they have stated—beginning with "if [the word] expresses a non-number as a number, then it is a number"—that by this very example, "even when 'number' (*saṃkhyā*) is mentioned, it is understood as 'like a number' (*saṃkhyāvat*). Such usage alone reveals the poet's skill in conveying the intended meaning, nourishes the beauty of the poetry, and delights the minds of connoisseurs.
For this very reason, the authors of the treatises point out numerous grounds for the justification of such usages.

In that regard, the authors of the Mahābhāṣya, while determining the reasons for the word *praṣṭha* being used in the feminine in the rule *puṃyogādākhyāyām* (Pāṇini 4.1.48), state four ways in which the expression "that [word] is applied to what is not that" (*atasmin sa*) occurs: through location (*tātsthyāt*), through shared attributes (*tāddharmyāt*), through proximity (*tatsāmīpyāt*), and through association (*tatsāhacaryāt*). They provide examples for these applications of a word to something other than its primary referent: "Mañca laughs" (*mañcā hasanti*), "Devadatta has matted hair" (*jaṭī devadattaḥ*), "A hamlet on the Ganges" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*), and "Bring in the spears" (*kuntān praveśaya*). These are the illustrative instances where a word is used for something else due to a specific cause.

Having raised the doubt as to how there can be a reference to letters (*varṇagrahaṇa*) in rules such as *igyaṇaḥ saṃprasāraṇasya* (Pāṇini 6.1.108), they have stated that just as one born from a crow is called a "crow," so too the word *saṃprasāraṇa* refers to the letters produced from the sentence [defining] the technical term *saṃprasāraṇa*; thus, even this state of being produced from that [sentence] serves as the basis for applying that word to what is not literally that.

Gautama also states in the *Nyāyasūtra*: "Metaphorical application (*upacāra*) of a term occurs—despite the absence of that [actual] identity—with respect to companionship, location, purpose, activity, measure, support, proximity, conjunction, instrumentality, and sovereignty; as in the cases of a Brahmin, a boy, a mat, a king, groats, sandalwood, the Gaṅgā, a cart, a cloth, food, and a person" (*Nyāyasūtra* 2.2.64). He thus sets forth the grounds for *lakṣaṇā* (indication). The author of its commentary (*bhāṣyakāra*) explains that this means the designation by a word of something that does not possess that [literal] meaning, by virtue of properties such as companionship and the rest.

Mañjūṣākāra, however, states the meaning of the Sūtra as follows: "Even in the absence of that property, there is the linguistic usage of that word; and that [usage] occurs through the superimposition of that property. Furthermore, the grounds for such superimposition are association and so forth. This is because he uses the expression "through superimposition" (*āropeṇa*). Although it appears from Nāgeśa’s commentary—specifically his restatement of the view of the *Nyāyavārtika* which says, "Having superimposed by means of inherence the universal inherent in the conjunction [with the staff] upon the Brahmin, one says 'the Brahmin is a stick'"—that superimposition exists according to the Vārtikakāra’s own view.

Nevertheless, it is the claim of many of their followers that there is no superimposition (*āropa*) in cases of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*); therefore, this point requires further investigation. Concomitance (*sahacaraṇa*) means inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*); location (*sthāna*) means the substratum (*āśraya*); purpose (*tādarthya*) means having that as one's motive; conduct (*vṛtta*) means behavior (*ācāra* or *vyāpāra*); measure (*māna*) means the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); support (*dhāraṇa*) means a specific locus; proximity (*sāmīpya*) means vicinity (*sannidhi*); instrument (*sādhana*) means the cause (*hetu*); sovereignty (*ādhipatya*) means lordship (*prabhutva*). Examples of these may be seen in the commentary on that [work].

Jaimini also [states] that in such cases as "The sacrificial grass-bundle (*prastara*) is the sacrificer," "Fire is indeed the Brahmin," and "The sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is the sun," since non-difference is sublated, the use of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) would be untenable; this being the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*), he establishes its validity by stating the grounds—namely, genus (*jāti*), similarity (*sārūpya*), and so forth—in the fourth quarter of the first chapter. And this is his summary verse: "By means of six factors—establishment of identity (*tatsiddhi*), genus (*jāti*), similarity (*sārūpya*), praise (*praśaṃsā*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and abundance (*bhūman*)—the figurative application (*gauṇī vṛtti*) of words is established everywhere."

And this [point] is stated in the *Śāstradīpikā* under the section on "liṅgasamavāya" (*Jaiminisūtra* 1.4.23): the authors of the *Brahmasūtras* also, by stating the example "and it may be so for one [word], like the word 'Brahman'" (*Brahmasūtra* 2.3.4)—that is, "like the word Brahman"—intend to show that while this word has its primary application in the Supreme Self, its usage elsewhere is secondary (*gauṇa*). Their view is that the basis for this is the possession of those attributes (*tāddharmya*) and so forth. The meaning of the sūtra is: the primary application of a single word to one object may have a secondary application to another object, just as the word "Brahman" [is used].

This meaning is accepted by the three commentaries. According to the systems of the Śaṅkara and Rāmānuja commentaries, this is a sūtra presenting the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position. In both of these two commentaries, the word *saṃbhūta* ("produced") from the scriptural passage "From the Self, space was produced" (*ātmana ākāśaḥ saṃbhūtaḥ*) serves as the illustrative example (*dārṣṭāntika*). However, according to the commentary of Pūrṇaprajña, it is the word *anādi* ("without beginning") from the scriptural passage "This space is indeed without beginning" (*anādir vā ayam ākāśaḥ*) that serves as the example.

In the passage "Austerity is Brahman" (*Taittirīya Upaniṣad* 3.2), all three commentators maintain that the word *brahman* is used figuratively (*gauṇa*) with respect to food and other such means of attaining knowledge of Brahman, as well as with respect to austerity itself (Śaṅkara); in the passage "Therefore, this [universe] has the name and form of Brahman" (*Ārtabhāga* 1.1.1), they hold that the word *brahman* is figurative with respect to the *pradhāna* (Rāmānuja); and in that same scripture, they assert that the word *brahman* is figurative with respect to the four-faced Brahmā, who is the effected Brahman (*kāryabrahman*) (Pūrṇaprajña). Thus, all three commentators agree on the following: that a word whose primary meaning is one thing is applied to something else, and that it is used in a grammatical construction of apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*).

They consider that the grounds [for such usage] are "being for the sake of that" (*tādarthya*) and "being dependent on that" (*tadadhīnatva*), and so forth. Having established that space (*ākāśa*) is an effect of Brahman, Śaṅkarācārya states in the *Viyanadhikaraṇa* (Brahma-sūtra 2.3.1–7), at the conclusion of the sūtra "As far as there is modification... (*yāvadvikāra-*), that the expression "Space is the Self" (*ākāśa ātmā*) is figurative (*gauṇa*). His intention is that the use of a coordinate construction (*samānādhikaraṇa-aprayoga*) occurs because of the possession of similar qualities or because of being produced from that [source].

By this, it is shown that the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) found in passages such as "I am the taste in the waters, O Kaunteya" (Gītā 7.8), "I am the resolve, I am the sacrifice" (Gītā 9.16), and "Among the Ādityas, I am Viṣṇu" (Gītā 10.21)—which occur within the section defining the Lord's manifestations (*vibhūti*)—does not intend to convey non-difference from taste and so forth. Rather, its purpose is to indicate that [the Lord] is the source of the essence of taste-ness and so on for tastes and the like, or that He bestows excellence upon those of the same class, or that He is the controller of the presiding deities (*abhimānidevatā*) of those things; for a quality belongs to whomsoever it is dependent upon.

According to the maxim, "He is designated by the qualities belonging to him," [the Lord] is denoted by such terms as *rasa* (flavor) and the like; thus, *rasa* means that which bestows the quality of flavor (*rasatva*) and so forth, or that which imparts excellence to flavor and the rest. Some maintain that because the Supreme Self is the indwelling body of all things, He is designated in such a manner by virtue of having flavor and the rest as His body.

For this very reason, conventional expressions based on distinctions—such as "All this is strung upon me like clusters of gems on a thread" (Gītā 7.7), "By which manifestations you abide pervading these worlds" (Gītā 10.13), "In what various beings may I meditate upon You, O Blessed One? (Gītā 10.17), "And I am seated in the heart of all; from Me come memory, knowledge, and their loss" (Gītā 15.15), "Abiding in the inner self of all beings" (Gītā 10.19), and "The Lord dwells, O Arjuna, in the heart of all beings" (Gītā 18.61)—are all logically consistent.

In this context, the phrase "all [is] in me" denotes merely a specific kind of conjunction consisting in being strung upon Hari, using the analogy of a thread and a gem; the phrase "by which" declares the Lord's pervasion throughout all worlds; and the phrase "in which ones?"—by way of a question regarding the substrata for meditation—explains that one should perform the worship of the Lord by postulating some substratum here or there.

For this very reason, Śaṅkarācārya has stated in various places that [the practice] is "like the worship of Hari at the Śālagrāma and so forth. The author of the Sūtras as well, in the aphorism *na pratīke na hi saḥ* (Brahma-sūtra 4.1.4), declares that one should not cultivate the notion of being the Self (i.e., the notion of non-difference between the symbol and Brahman) with respect to a symbol (*pratīka*) as a locus. By this, he reveals his intention that the notion of Brahman-ness should not be cultivated in all instances regarding the effects of Brahman.

The statement, "I am the Self, O Guḍākeśa, dwelling in the hearts of all beings," is Kṛṣṇa’s reply to Arjuna’s question, "In what, in what [beings]? It describes Hari’s abiding within the hearts of all living creatures. The word "of all" expresses that Hari resides within every heart and that He is the cause of memory and other such functions.
