Furthermore, the phrase "the Lord of all" establishes the Blessed One’s status as the controller of everything by virtue of His being the inner ruler (antaryāmī) of all.

If there were no difference between phenomenal manifestation (*prapañca*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), then all these worldly transactions would be untenable. By this, the claim that the statement "Vāsudeva is everything" expresses the fact that everything has Vāsudeva as its essence (i.e., its non-difference from him) is refuted; for it is impossible for the world—consisting of the moving and the unmoving, as indicated by the word "everything" in its unrestricted sense—and Vāsudeva to be identical in their essential nature (*svarūpa*).

Furthermore, if there were no difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*), [such statements as] "My devotees come to me too" (Gītā 7.23) and "He shall come to Me alone, without doubt" (Gītā 8.7) would be contradicted.

Having come to Me, the high-souled ones, having attained the supreme perfection, do not undergo rebirth, which is transient and an abode of suffering. (Gītā 8.15) Be intent on Me, be My devotee, sacrifice to Me, and bow down to Me.
"Thus, having disciplined yourself and making Me your supreme goal, you shall come to Me alone" (Gītā 9.34).

How could the relationship of worshiper and worshipped, established in passages such as "With Me as your mind... you are dear to Me" (Gītā 18.64), be logically consistent? For that relationship is based upon duality.
Furthermore—
"I am the origin and likewise the dissolution of the entire universe" (Gītā 7.6).
"I am the source of all; from me everything proceeds" (Gītā 10.5).

Thus, since the description of the manifestations (*vibhūti*) begins prior to the seventh and tenth chapters, and because in the ninth chapter—following the description of the manifestations in the statement, "I am the father of this world, the mother, the sustainer, and the grandfather" (Gītā 9.17)—there is also a mention of Hari as the cause of the world, this too indicates that the intent of the section on manifestations is not non-difference. For, since *rasa* and the other [tastes] are effects consisting of *ramā* (the goddess Lakṣmī), they are dependent upon her; and according to the maxim, "whatever is dependent on something else has its existence dependent on that," they possess an existence dependent on her. Therefore, just as one says, "The king is the kingdom," [the same applies here].

This indicates that the designation is made through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). The Blessed One would become angry and resentful toward those who explain the verse otherwise. For in the world, even an ordinary person whom someone has called "this man is like a stone" becomes angry and resentful when others speak of him in that way.
Furthermore:
"Or rather, what is the use of this extensive knowledge of yours, O Arjuna?"
"Supporting this entire universe with a single fraction, I remain as the world" (Gītā 10.42).

Since the Lord himself has established the purport of the section on manifestations (*vibhūti*) by declaring in this concluding verse of that section that his manifestation consists precisely in his omnipresence through supporting the entire world, you should consider that an interpretation of the Gītā-teacher’s intent as being directed toward identity with Him is not convincing.

In this context, "sustaining" (*dhārakatva*) refers to an activity conducive to the existence (*sattā*) inherent in each respective object, and this is included within "protection" (*pālana*), since protection consists of a collection of various activities such as maintaining stability and so forth. Consequently, it should be understood that the purport of the *Vibhūti-adhyāya* is that the existence of the *rasas* and other categories is dependent upon the Lord. Furthermore, the fact that the existence of all things is dependent on the Lord was stated by the Lord Himself: "I am not in them, but they are in Me" (*Gītā* 7.12).

"I am dependent on Him; all entities are in Me and dependent on Me"—this is the meaning, as explained by all the commentators and sub-commentators. The reality here is this: Viṣṇu and the others mentioned in the section on manifestations (*vibhūti*) are indeed forms of the Blessed Lord Himself, whereas taste and the other qualities, being distinct from Him, are His effects and thus dependent upon Him.

Regarding the scriptural passage, "All this, indeed, is Brahman; as from that, by that, and in that—let one meditate with a tranquil mind" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.1), it should be understood that even the designation of "all" as "Brahman" is due to everything being an effect of Brahman and being dependent upon it, just as one says "the king is the kingdom. As for the meaning of the scripture: "this"—that is, all this entire perceptible reality—"is indeed Brahman," meaning it is Brahman itself. To the question, "On what basis is the designation of 'Brahman-ness' applied? the text replies, "as from that" (tajja).

The logical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "from that [Brahman] it was born, into that it dissolves, and by that it is sustained (*rakṣyamāṇa*). The purport of the Śruti is that the designation of everything as Brahman is based on such grounds as being born from it and so forth. This very point has been explained in this same manner by Śaṅkarācārya in the *Chāndogya-bhāṣya*, as well as in the commentary on the Sūtra "On account of the teaching of what is well-known everywhere" (*sarvatra prasiddhopadeśāt*, Brahma-sūtra 1.1.1). The relevant commentary there states: "Because it is born from that, because it dissolves into that, and because it is sustained by that."

Pūrṇaprajña, however, explains the meaning of the Śruti as follows: "This is Brahman; all is full" (meaning that Brahman is full of all attributes). "He breathes in and moves within the waters" (meaning He reclines upon the ocean of dissolution or the milk-ocean). Knowing this, one should worship—becoming peaceful and endowed with qualities such as tranquility—and meditate upon Him through His fullness and other attributes. This is the interpretation of the Śruti.

Regarding the statements from the Chāndogya and Muṇḍaka Upaniṣads, namely "All this is indeed the Self" (Chā. 7.25.2) and "Brahman alone is all this, the universe" (Mu. 2.2.1), the intended meaning must be described as follows: although in both cases the cause for designating everything as the Self is taught through its all-pervasiveness—expressed as "The Self alone is below... in front... Brahman"—nevertheless, in that context, this [other] reason, namely being born from That (*tajjatva*) and so forth, is also to be combined with it.

This is what must be understood: wherever in the scriptures a reason is taught through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), there that reason—such as "being born from that" (*tajjatva*) and so forth—must also be combined with it. However, where [such a reason] is not taught, this very [reason of identity] is to be understood. This is because there is no reason to abandon a cause established by the Vedas and other authorities, and because such abandonment would be improper. Furthermore, one should not postulate a causal relationship (*tātkārya*) when there is non-difference in essential nature (*svarūpa-abheda*). And regarding this very point, there is a corroborating statement from the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*. For instance, therein:
The universe has arisen from Viṣṇu and remains within Him alone;
He is the author of the sustenance and withdrawal of the universe, and therefore the universe is He.

Thus it has been said: "The meaning of this is as follows: the world-expansion (*jagat-prapañca*) arose from Viṣṇu, that is, from Nārāyaṇa; it remains in that very Viṣṇu alone, and at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*), it is merged into him. And because he, Viṣṇu, is the agent of the maintenance and withdrawal (*saṃyama*) of the world-expansion—where 'withdrawal' (*saṃyama*) means dissolution, and this is also indicative of [his being] the agent of birth—he is the one upon whom the world depends."

Having established here that the birth and other states of the world proceed from Hari, it is clearly stated by means of the grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) in the expression "the world is He" (*jagacca sa*) that the cause for such usage is the world's being born from Him and so forth.

Some, however, maintain that the word *khalu* signifies negation, because in the sūtra "In the case of the prohibitions *alaṃ* and *khalu*, the suffix *ktvā* is used in the sense of the absolutive in common usage" (Pāṇini 3.4.18), the author of the sūtras states that its meaning is negation. The sense is as follows: all this is indeed Brahman, yet it is not [merely] Brahman. What then? To this he says: "tajjalān. That is, "born from that (*tajja*), dissolved in that (*tallaya*), and absorbed in that (*tadana*)."

This is the intended meaning: they say that one should worship Brahman as the cause of all, having become tranquil by abandoning the conceit of independence upon realizing that "all this is indeed the work of Brahman and not independent like Brahman; we are all included within the sphere of action and are thus dependent on Him."

On this basis, Kaiyaṭa’s interpretation of the Mahābhāṣya passage from the *Vaspaśāhnika*—which states, "Substance (*dravya*) is eternal, while form (*ākṛti*) is non-eternal," and explains that "the reality of Brahman delimited by unreal adjuncts is what is denoted by the word *dravya*; because the universal of 'cowness' (*gotvajāti*) is also non-existent from the perspective of the [ultimate] Brahman, it is non-eternal according to the Śruti 'The Self alone is all this' (*ātmaivedam')"—is to be considered doubtful. This is because that Śruti does not possess such a meaning.

This is because that [Bhāṣya] does not proceed with the intention of establishing the eternality of the former (the genus) and the unreality of the other (the individual). For instance, in the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "Now, what is the word in 'cow'?", among the four possibilities—genus and so forth—that are proposed as the meaning of a word, the analysis "in the word, the object, and the relation which are established" (*siddhe śabde arthe sambandhe*) is adopted by resorting to the view that "the genus is the word-meaning" (*jātiḥ padārthaḥ*), rather than by resorting to the view that "the individual is the word-meaning" (*vyaktiḥ padārthaḥ*). This is the question posed, and it is answered: "The genus is the word-meaning."

With the intention that "this word is based on a class (pakṣa)," it was stated that "it expresses the form (ākṛti)," and then it was said that "that [form] alone is eternal. Even when the view is held that "the referent of a word is the substance (dravya) itself," the eternality of the substance is easily established; thus, the Bhāṣya proceeds with the statement, "Or rather, the referent of a word is the substance itself."

In this view, finding no finality [in the previous argument], the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra), relying on the previously introduced position that "the universal (*jāti*) is the word-meaning," states: "Even with respect to the configuration (*ākṛti*. Having stated the definition of permanence as "that in which its true nature (*tattva*) is not destroyed" in response to the question of how its permanence is established, he proves the permanence of the configuration as well by stating: "Its being is its true nature; even in the case of the configuration, its true nature is not destroyed."

The meaning of this is as follows: the destruction of the substrate—the individual substance—is established by all direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), whereas the destruction of the qualities (*jāti*) residing therein is difficult to establish, because that [quality] continues to exist in another directly perceived substance. Although the word *ākṛti* denotes a specific configuration that manifests the universal (*jāti*), it should nevertheless be understood here as referring to the universal manifested by that configuration.

Having thus established both positions, [the opponent objects]: "What is achieved for us by this irrelevant inquiry? There is nothing to be accomplished here through the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities. We say that this analysis is based on whatever you consider to be eternal among the categories of genus (*jāti*) and substance (*dravya*). This intention is indicated by the *Bhāṣya* passage beginning with "Or rather, what [is the use]? which shows a lack of reliance on the previous argument; for in the *Bhāṣya*, there is no mention at all of Brahman and the world, as [the discussion concerns] "the reality of Brahman through the vision of Brahman."

The explanation beginning with "the genus such as 'cowness' (gotva) is impermanent because it is non-existent" is incorrect. Furthermore, the author of the Bhāṣya intends the permanence of the *ākṛti* (form/structure) in both the introduction and the conclusion; therefore, the statement regarding the impermanence of the genus (*jāti*) contradicts the Bhāṣya. Moreover, the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "Alternatively, the word-meaning is the substance itself" does not represent the final established position (*siddhānta*); hence, one must consider for what reason such an interpretation of that Bhāṣya was made.

Furthermore, if this [position] were accepted by the author of the Bhāṣya, then, according to Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on this Bhāṣya and other sources, one would have to say that its purpose is to establish the tenet accepted by the Siddhāntin—that Brahman alone is eternal. Consequently, with the thought, "What will proving the eternity or non-eternity of a particular entity have to do with our present subject? the subsequent Bhāṣya beginning with "What is the use of this?"—which was intended to indicate a lack of reliance on the preceding Bhāṣya—would fail to arise.

This is because it would be impossible to indicate a lack of reliance on the Bhāṣya which teaches the objects of knowledge according to the Siddhānta. Furthermore, according to Kaiyaṭa’s view, if everything other than Brahman were non-existent, then since the word and its relation would be as non-existent as a hare's horn, the relation of Brahman with a word would be difficult to establish; consequently, since the very relation between word and meaning would become impossible, even the inquiry based upon it would be devoid of any logical foundation. Thus, Kaiyaṭa’s commentary must indeed be considered contradictory to the Vārttika and the Bhāṣya.

Furthermore, since Kaiyaṭa and others, who maintain the doctrine that the *sphoṭa* is produced (*jāta-sphoṭa*), accept that the universal (*jāti*) is of the nature of Brahman, their assertion of its impermanence is untenable. Nāgeśa, however, holds from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-dṛṣṭi*) that everything is indeed unreal; yet, for as long as linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) persists, it is treated as real by virtue of its existence within that context.

And thus he states that the purport of the Bhāṣya is that conventional permanence would be lost for this [entity]; but that is not so, because no authority is found for such an assumption in either the Sūtra or the Bhāṣya, and because it is improper to establish the investigation of the subject matter, the acceptance of categories, and the system of the opponent's doctrine as the author of this treatise’s own established conclusion by resorting to the views of others.

It should be considered how this proponent of the theory of negation (*nañvādī*), intending to establish the conclusion that "the very nature of difference is difficult to define," can possibly postulate two distinct states—the ultimate (*pāramārthika*) and the conventional (*vyāvahārika*)—based upon difference.

Since it is established—on the basis of the *sūtra* and its *bhāṣya*, "The suffix *vuñ* [is added] after *vāsudeva* and *arjuna*," both of which intend to demonstrate that Vāsudeva is the supreme of all—that the conception of everything as having the nature of the Blessed Lord, or the conception of the Blessed Lord as having the form of everything, is improper, it follows that the doctrine of the non-existence (or falsity) of everything rooted therein contradicts the intention of the author of the *Sūtras* and others; therefore, Kaiyaṭa’s commentary is indeed to be disregarded.

To this we reply: the assumption that what was stated by Kaiyaṭa and others is the opinion of the Teacher (Pāṇini) on the basis of the maxim "what is not prohibited is approved" is a false assumption; for while Pāṇini intended to express Vāsudeva’s superiority, he certainly did not prohibit Vāsudeva’s being the Self of all—which would contradict his being the supreme of all—since the aforementioned maxim does not apply here.

Furthermore, according to the logic already stated, it is reasonable to assume that the system of Ācārya Pāṇini, or the system established by teachers prior to him, was accepted by the Teacher [Patañjali], but not a system established by a person of a later time. For this very reason, everything spoken by Vyāsa was acceptable to Pāṇini, because he preceded Vyāsa and did not refute what was spoken by him. This, however, is not the case regarding the system of Kātyāyana.

For this very reason, it is stated in the *Kaumudī* regarding the rule *na kvādeḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.59): "Even though, according to the view of the Sūtra itself, the opposite result would have been obtained. To assume the lack of authority for the statement of an earlier sage on the grounds that "the authority of the sages increases in descending order" serves no purpose other than as a mere diversion for the modern grammatical circles who seek to establish the authority of [their own] preferences and the like.

For this very reason, regarding the statements made by Kātyāyana, the commentators (*bhāṣyakāras*) cite various Vedic indicators (*sautra-jñāpaka*) found here and there, asserting that they show favor toward the authors of the *sūtras*. Thus, when there is a contradiction between the words of the sages, it should be understood that "a difference in philosophical perspective (*darśanabheda*) alone is the correct explanation.

By this, Nāgeśa’s statement in works such as the *Mañjūṣā*—that one must accept the mental modification (*vṛtti*) called "verbal cognition" (*śabdajñānānupātī*) defined in Patañjali’s *Yogasūtra* 1.9 as "conceptual construction devoid of a real object" (*vikalpa*), and that through this the falsity of the referent of a word is established—is refuted; for Patañjali was later than the teacher Pāṇini.

Nor should it be argued that by establishing that what was spoken by Vyāsa is approved by Pāṇini, it follows that all the subject matter (*prameya*) of the *Pātañjala* [Yoga] system is approved by Pāṇini, because the *Yogasūtrabhāṣya* was composed by Vyāsa; for in the view of Patañjali, the world is not illusory (*mithyātva*). Furthermore, the term "Vyāsa" is intended to refer specifically to the son of Parāśara, whereas the author of the *Yogasūtrabhāṣya*, Vyāsa, is distinct from that son of Parāśara.

The claim that Vyāsa, the son of Parāśara, is himself the author of the *Yogasūtrabhāṣya* is merely the prattle of the deluded. For this very reason, Patañjali did not cite anywhere in his *Mahābhāṣya* even those sūtras composed by himself. Consequently, the determination of the subject matter made in the *Śekhara* under the rule *aco 'ntyādi ṭi* (Pāṇini 1.1.64)—beginning with "in reality" (*vastutaḥ*) and citing the *Yogasūtra* "at the time of the knowledge of words" (*śabdajñāne*)—is to be regarded as questionable.

It should be understood that in cases where a composite whole (*samudāya*) does not exist, the designation *ṭi* occurs either by the principle of "behaving like what is designated" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*) or through the following application of the rule. As for that application: in the rule *antyādī*, the word *antya* is a separate term with its nominative case ending elided. [The meaning is: "that which begins with the final vowel among the vowels—that entire group, as well as that final phoneme itself—is designated as *ṭi*. In this way, in examples such as *śakandhu*, the designation *ṭi* is established even for the mere vowel *ā* following the letter *k* in *śaka*. We shall explain this further below. Furthermore, the non-difference between the Lord (*īśa*), the individual soul (*jīva*), and the insentient (*jaḍa*) is thereby established for him.
It has been stated that this is so even when there is a designation by way of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya).
Indeed, Vāsudeva alone is the subject of all scriptures;

for in both the Śruti and the Sūtra, it is Brahman that is propounded, and thus it has been stated by the learned: "The Vedāntins [hold] 'Brahman'. Furthermore, in the Gītā, Vāsudeva is explained in this very way by all the founders of philosophical systems.

If it is asked how it is established that Vāsudeva is the subject taught everywhere in the Śruti and other scriptures, they reply here: "When dharma was being overwhelmed by adharma and adharma was increasing, Viṣṇu—the primordial creator known as Nārāyaṇa—desiring to protect the stability of the world, indeed manifested as Kṛṣṇa through a portion of himself from Vasudeva in the womb of Devakī for the sake of protecting the status of the Bhāgavatas and the Brahminhood. This very Gītā-śāstra [is his teaching]."

"...the Gītā scripture reveals this two-fold Dharma, which is a compendium of the essence of the meaning of the entire Veda, as well as the ultimate reality (paramārthatattva) that has liberation as its purpose, namely the Supreme Brahman designated as Vāsudeva"—so says the introduction to the *Gītā-bhāṣya* by Śaṅkara. Furthermore, in the fifteenth chapter: "The entire meaning of the Gītā scripture is stated in summary in this chapter; not only the meaning of the Gītā scripture, but the meaning of the entire Veda is completed here—thus, O sinless one, this most secret scripture has been declared by me."
Having understood this, O Bhārata, one becomes wise and has accomplished all that was to be done. (Gītā 15.20)

Thus, by means of Śaṅkara’s commentary on the *Ślokavārttika*, by Śaṅkara’s commentary on the *Bhagavadgītā* which explains terms such as "Īśvara" as "Nārāyaṇa, Vāsudeva, Viṣṇu," by Śaṅkara’s commentary on the verse "Īśvaraḥ sarvabhūtānām" which explains the word "Īśvara" as "Nārāyaṇa, whose nature is to rule over all living beings," by the commentaries of his followers such as Madhusūdana Sarasvatī and others bearing such meanings, and by the commentaries and other works of other authoritative teachers;

It is universally accepted that Vāsudeva is propounded in the Gītā, and that the very meaning of the Gītā is the meaning of all the Vedas. Nor should it be asked how such a conclusion can be reached through mere commentary; for according to the maxim "the specific meaning is understood from the commentary," the commentaries of the great masters alone are the determiners of the true nature of the subject matter.

Furthermore, because the Blessed Vyāsa has designated that which is the subject matter of the *Gītā* by the word "Brahman" in such passages as the *Śaṅkara-bhāṣya* and others—"this [work] being a compendium of the essence of the meaning of all the Vedas"—and in the *Gītā* itself: "The single syllable 'Om' is Brahman" (8.13), "The supreme Brahman, the highest abode" (10.12), and "I am the beginningless, supreme Brahman" (13.12), as well as: "And by all the Vedas, I alone am to be known" (15.15).

And because of the statement by the Teacher of the Gītā [in 15.15], since Vāsudeva is non-different from Brahman, it is established that the Śruti, the Sūtras, and the Gītā have a single subject matter; thus, the truth that Nārāyaṇa, designated as Vāsudeva, is the subject of all scriptures is well-founded.

Furthermore, the author of the Sūtras, Bādarāyaṇa, considering that knowledge of Brahman—revealed by such scriptural passages as "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1), "Knowing Him thus, one becomes immortal here" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 13), and "The knower of the Self crosses over sorrow" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.1.3)—is the supreme means for the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*), [declares] in the *Brahma-mīmāṃsā* the necessity of undertaking the inquiry into Brahman, which consists in the investigation of the means for the direct realization of the Self that is the cause of the human goal: "Therefore, next, the inquiry into Brahman" (Brahma-sūtra 1.1.1).

Having established [Brahman] by means of the first aphorism, "Then, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman" (1.1.1), and desiring to make known its nature through its definition—since it is impossible to point it out by seizing it by the horn or the ear when there arises the inquiry into its essential form, "What is that Brahman?"—he states by means of the second aphorism, "From which the origin, etc., of this [world]" (Bra.Sū. 1.1.2), that Brahman is the cause of the world, in the sense that "Brahman is that from which the creation, sustenance, dissolution, and so forth, of this perceived, manifold world proceed."

Having stated that characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), [the author] addresses the objection that maintenance (*pālana*) cannot be a defining characteristic of Brahman, because maintenance consists of various activities such as protection, and thus includes the act of governing (*niyamana*); furthermore, because in the *Antaryāmibrāhmaṇa*—in passages such as "He who dwells in the earth" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 5.7.3)—this governing is heard to reside in the wind named Sūtra. To resolve this objection, [the author states]: "The Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*) is [Brahman], because His attributes are designated in relation to the gods and so forth" (*Brahma-sūtra* 1.2.18).

By the sūtra (1.2.18), it is established in the Siddhānta that the entity described in the Vājasaneyaka as the inner ruler (*antaryāmin*) of the earth and other elements is indeed Brahman, who is described as the cause of the world. According to the meaning of the sūtra: "But that [inner ruler] is Brahman alone, because of the designation of its attributes," for in the Śruti passage, "And this is the Self," the attribute of Brahman—namely, the governance of all—is stated. This should be understood: here, it is Brahman alone, determined as the cause, which is denoted by the word "Self" (*ātman*) occurring in the *Antaryāmibrāhmaṇa* passage.

Therefore, since protection culminates in Brahman, it constitutes its defining characteristic; thus, there is no fault whatsoever. In that Upaniṣad, by the word "Vāyu," the Self alone is expressed, because it is stated that the referent of the word "Vāyu" is the support of all worlds, and that is possible only for the Supreme Self and not for anything else—such is the intention of the author of the Sūtras.

For this very reason, all three commentators, citing the sentence "This is Your Self" (*eṣa ta ātmā*) as the subject matter of this section, speak with one voice that the author of the Sūtras has demonstrated that the Inner Controller (*antaryāmī*) mentioned in this context is none other than Brahman, the cause of the universe. Among them, Śaṅkarācārya, in his commentary on the Upaniṣad, explains the literal meaning of the scriptural text "This is Your Self" as: "This Self is Nārāyaṇa, the Inner Controller of me and of all."

Furthermore, regarding the sūtra *utpattyasaṃbhavāt* (Brahma-sūtra 2.2.42), Śaṅkarācārya stated: "The Blessed One alone, Vāsudeva, who is stainless and whose nature is knowledge, is the ultimate reality (*paramārthatattva*). In that regard, what they [the Pāñcarātras] say—that this Nārāyaṇa, who is well-known as the Supreme Self beyond the unmanifest—is not refuted."

Furthermore, when the first chapter established that the omniscient Blessed One, the Supreme Self, is the cause of the world by way of scriptural concordance (*samanvaya*), the second chapter was commenced to resolve the objections raised by the Śākyas and others who could not tolerate this. They contended that what was stated was inconsistent because it contradicts the *Smṛti* of Kapila and other traditions. To refute this, the first section (*pāda*) of the second chapter proceeds to counter the objection regarding the lack of scope for such *Smṛti*, beginning with: "If it be argued that there would be the fault of leaving no room for *Smṛti*, we say: no."

While commenting on the first section (*adhikaraṇa*) of the *Brahma-sūtras* with the words, "Because it would entail the fault of leaving no room for other [authoritative] Smṛtis" (BS 2.1.1), Śaṅkarācārya establishes the conclusion that Nārāyaṇa alone is the cause of the world, based on powerful Smṛtis that follow the Śruti. His commentary (*bhāṣya*) on that sūtra is as follows: "If Brahman were accepted as the sole cause, there would result the futility of the Smṛtis of Kapila and others, which—being composed primarily concerning the means to liberation and being devoted exclusively to that subject—are otherwise left without scope."

Therefore, the Vedānta passages must be interpreted in a manner that does not contradict them. For in that regard—where it is stated that *pradhāna* is the cause of the world, and where the Sāṃkhyas raise the objection that *pradhāna* alone is the creator of the world and not Brahman—the following is the resolution: that is not tenable, because it would entail the flaw of leaving no room for other Smṛtis. Many Smṛtis are found that follow the Śrutis and maintain that God is the cause; if *pradhāna* were the cause, those [Smṛtis] would result in being purposeless.
In the event of conflicting interpretations, only those [scriptures] that follow the Śruti are authoritative; we shall cite them:
"Therefore, listen to this summary: the ancient Nārāyaṇa is all this.
At the time of creation, he creates everything, and at the time of departure, he consumes it once again."
Thus it is stated in the Purāṇas and in the Gītā:
"I am the origin and likewise the dissolution of the entire world"; and Āpastamba also recites this, referring specifically to the Supreme Self:
"Therefore, all living beings arise from that; he is the root, he is eternal, he is the constant" (Dharmasūtra 1.8.13.2). Thus [it is said].

The essential purport of the commentary here is as follows: when there is doubt regarding the meaning of the Śruti, Sūtras, and so forth, that meaning must be determined in accordance with the Itihāsas and Purāṇas. Consequently, the statements of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas that follow the Śruti constitute a more powerful authority (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, passages such as "Therefore, [the Lord] is the summary" (*ataśca saṃkṣeparam*) are such authorities. And by the mention of "summary" (*saṃkṣepam*) here, the entire meaning of the scripture is encompassed. Therefore, the meaning of all the causal statements (*kāraṇavākya*) should be explained in conformity with this.

Consequently, the causal statements beginning with "From which indeed these [beings arise]" (*yato vā imāni*) have as their intended meaning that Nārāyaṇa alone is the cause of the entire universe. The terms *ātman*, *brahman*, and so forth occurring therein refer exclusively to Nārāyaṇa. The doctrine asserting the causality of *pradhāna* (primordial matter) and other such principles is contradicted by the Śrutis and other authorities. Therefore, Nārāyaṇa alone is the supreme reality (*paratattva*). Having all this in mind, the conclusion of the *Samanvaya-adhikaraṇa* was formulated in the commentary on Śaṅkara’s *Śārīrakabhāṣya* entitled *Sat-prabhā*: "The entire harmony of the Vedas resides in the supreme abode named Rāma."

There is no disagreement among Śeṣanāga Ācārya (the author of the *Paramārthasāra*), Vallabhācārya (the author of the *Aṇubhāṣya*), the venerable Śrī Rāmānuja Muni, and the eminent sage Śrī Pūrṇaprajña Muni that Vāsudeva alone is the supreme reality (*paratattva*) and the cause of the universe; this is their established doctrine (*siddhānta*).

The meaning of the verse beginning with "Therefore, [this is] the summary" (*ataśca saṃkṣepam*) is as follows: For these reasons—namely, because the scriptures are infinite and the lifespan of human beings is limited—the scripture is endless, that which is to be known is vast, one's own life is short, and obstacles are many.
That which is the essence should be cultivated, just as a swan extracts milk from water mixed together.

Because of this statement: "Listen [śṛṇudhvam]—the Vedic middle voice is used—[to] this summary (saṃkṣepam), which is a compendium of the essence of the meaning of all the scriptures, that is about to be spoken. Nārāyaṇa—the Lord of Śrī, the ancient (purāṇa) Primordial Person (ādipuruṣa)—lying upon a bed of the coils of the serpent in the midst of the Ocean of Milk: that Nārāyaṇa, at the time of creation (sarge), creates (karoti)—this term is also indicative of maintaining (sthiti)—this entire world (samastaṃ jagat) as it is currently perceived; and at the time of departure, that is, at the time of dissolution (pralaya).

It devours—that is, it destroys—all that entire created universe; "again," meaning once more, "thus" is the ellipsis, for it acts in this very same way at every kalpa, according to the Vedic revelation: "As the Creator fashioned it in the beginning" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 10.190.3). The intended meaning is quite clear. This should be understood: because the word "Smṛti" is used here and elsewhere in the Sūtras, and because Śaṅkara’s commentary cites Purāṇic statements, the intention of the authors of the Sūtras and their commentaries is that Purāṇic statements should be cited as corroborative evidence (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) for both the prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) of a topical discussion (*adhikaraṇa*).

Nor is it proper to introduce [the authority of] Smṛti in a Sūtra that does not contain the word "Smṛti," nor should it be argued that its introduction is improper in a Sūtra that lacks such a term; for this is done even in the Sūtra "But because the Word has the Veda as its source" (Brahma-sūtra 2.1.27), which does not contain the word "Smṛti. As the authors of the Purāṇas have said:
"Those entities which are indeed inconceivable should not be subjected to logical reasoning;
that which is beyond the primary material causes (prakṛtis) is the characteristic of the inconceivable."

Thus, because such a construction is untenable due to the citation of Purāṇic statements in Śaṅkara’s commentary; nor [is it so] because of the qualification of the fourth self as "Śiva" in the passage: "The fourth is without measure, indefinable, the cessation of phenomenal expansion, auspicious, non-dual; thus the syllable Om is indeed the Self; he who knows this enters the Self by means of the Self through the Self" (Māṇḍūkya 12), and because [the text continues]: "Neither inwardly cognitive, nor outwardly cognitive... [and so forth].

Furthermore, because of the statement "peaceful, auspicious, non-dual, the fourth" in the mantra (Māṇḍūkya 7), and because of the use of the word "śivam," one might think it is appropriate that Śiva alone is the subject of the scripture (*śāstra*). However, this is not tenable; for in the twelfth [Māṇḍūkya] mantra, the venerable Śaṅkarācārya explained the term "Śiva" as "the bringer of auspiciousness," and in the seventh [mantra], Ānandagiri explained "śivam" as "completely pure. Since these do not refer to Rudra, they lack the capacity to establish Śiva as the subject of the scripture.

Even the hearing of the statement "the divine form" (*aiśvaraṃ rūpam*) in the Viśvarūpa chapter of the Gītā does not prove that the Gītā and other such texts have Śiva as their ultimate subject. For instance: "Just as you have shown yourself to me, O Supreme Lord, so do I wish to see your divine form, O Supreme Person" (Gītā 11.3).

Thus, because Saṅkarācārya explained the phrase "the form of Īśvara" in the verse expressing the prayer for the vision of the universal form as "the Vaiṣṇava form endowed with knowledge, sovereignty, strength, power, valor, and splendor," it is established that the subject matter of the prayer is the desire to behold the Vaiṣṇava form.
Having spoken thus, [the Lord said]: "Then, O King, Hari, the great lord of yogis, showed him his supreme, sovereign form" (Gītā 11.9).

Thus, in accordance with the explanation of the interrogative statement "the divine form" (*aiśvaraṃ rūpam*), which occurs in the verse meaning "he did not fulfill the requested object," it is appropriate that the meaning be precisely "the Vaiṣṇava form characterized by knowledge, sovereignty, and so forth. Furthermore, it should be understood that the Vaiṣṇava nature of the Universal Form (*viśvarūpa*) is established because Lord Kṛṣṇa, when about to show the form—saying "Behold my forms, O Pārtha" (Gītā 11.5) and "But you are not able to see Me" (Gītā 11.8)—demonstrates its belonging to Himself and its non-difference from Himself.

By this [explanation], having interpreted the term *aiśvaram* as *śaivam* and thereby demonstrated that the chapter on the form of Viṣṇu (*viśvarūpādhyāya*) is devoted to Śiva, certain non-dualists who follow the school of Śaṅkarācārya—such as those in the *Rāmāyaṇa-bhārata-sāra-saṃgraha* and other works—have presented the view that "the entire scripture indicated by this is devoted to Śiva, and Śiva alone is the supreme reality. This presentation is rooted in dogmatism and does not conform to the intended meaning of their own teacher.

The Śaiva claim that Śiva alone is the supreme reality (*paraṃ tattvam*) has been fully resolved by the *Śaṅkarabhāṣya*. Regarding the fact that the *Mahābhārata* and other texts have Vāsudeva as their ultimate purport, the reason stated in the opening sections (*upakrama*) should be considered here as well. Thus, the purport of all the scriptures is that the reality which is the cause of the universe is the supreme principle known as Nārāyaṇa. A detailed exposition is found in the *Paratattvaprakāśikā* composed by the venerable Vijayīndrayatīndra:
"All individual selves are naturally the servants of the Supreme Self;
realizing 'I too am your servant,' I bow down."

This and more may be seen in the *Rahasyatrayasāra*, in the section on the supreme reality of the Supreme Deity (*paradevatā-pāramārthya-adhikāra*), composed by the venerable Vedāntadeśika, who established the supremacy of Vāsudeva through such citations from the words of Śiva.
Furthermore, by the Lord Vyāsa:
"I bow to You, Nārāyaṇa, the primordial Person, the immutable cause of all causes."
From the lotus-bud of whose navel Brahmā emerged, from whom this world [arose].

In the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* and other texts, beginning with [Bhāg. 10.40.1], Nārāyaṇa’s status as the cause of all and his nature as the supreme reality are elaborated upon through his being the cause of the four-faced Brahmā, who is skilled in the creation of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*). Now, if it is argued that Śiva possesses the causality of the universe because he is non-different from the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), we reply: is this so in the state of liberation (*mukti*) or in the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāritva*)?

The first [alternative] is not tenable; for since that [liberated soul] has the nature of being devoid of attributes (*nirdharmaka*) by virtue of its identity with the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), the activity of creating the world is impossible for it. Consequently, the statement "excluding the activity of creating the world" (*jagadvyāpāravarjam*)—which prohibits the activities of creation and so forth that do not even apply to anything other than the Supreme Reality—would be redundant. By this, it appears that the author of the Sūtras intends that even in liberation, there remains a difference between the liberated soul and the Supreme Self.

Nor should it be said that the Sūtra is merely intended to state the nature [of the cause], for by the use of the word "excluding" (*varjam*), the existence of another distinct operation is obtained, making such an interpretation impossible. In the second case, however, since non-difference itself would be absent at that time, it would be impossible to speak in this manner. Furthermore, this is not tenable because no Tīrthakaras whatsoever accept Śiva and others as the cause. Moreover, the author of the Brahma-mīmāṃsā himself refuted the status of Paśupati Rudra as the cause of the world by means of the Sūtra, "On account of the lack of consistency in the case of the Lord" (2.2.37), through the process of rejecting the doctrine of Paśupati.

It should not be understood that he merely denies [Rudra’s] status as an efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇatva*), while implying that he possesses both types of causality; for it is more appropriate to understand the meaning as being that the kind of causality attributed to Brahman by the sūtra "From which the origin, etc., of this [world]" (1.1.2) does not belong to Rudra, as there is no evidence for such an interpretation. Even great poets, who seek the destruction of their sins through the glorification of the Lord's qualities, convey this very meaning of the scripture. For instance:
"To Nārāyaṇa, whose eyes are as long as lotus petals..."

Salutation to the Supreme Person, whose navel-cavity is the birthplace that ordains the various activities of the mobile and immobile beings, and by whom the majesty of Mahābali has been reduced to a mere name. (Candrāloka 1.16)
At the conclusion of the great aeon, the Self-born Creator—the architect of the city of the three worlds, whose sole abode is the path of the navel—arises moment by moment.
Regarding him, [the question arises]: what is his substratum, of what nature is he, and in what manner is he established?
"entered his belly to see him; salutations to that treasure-house of the universe. (Anargharāghava 2).

Now, if it is asked, "In that case, what is the status of those scriptural passages that indicate Rudra as the cause?", it is replied: In those instances, the word *rudra* refers to Vāsudeva who dwells within him (as its inner controller); thus, even those passages have as their sole purport that Nārāyaṇa is the cause. By this, it should be understood that the claim made by Nāgeśa and others in works such as the *Mañjūṣā*—that the Brahman of Sound (*śabdabrahman*) is the cause of the world—is contrary to the established doctrine of the knowers of Brahman and was not intended by Pāṇini and other authorities.
"But Vāsudeva, the Supreme Person, is the one propounded by the Śrutis and other authorities"—
this is the conclusion established by such authoritative sources as the commentary of Śaṅkara.
Regarding the investigation into the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*):

In the *Smṛti* that follows the Śruti text "And therefore, in brief" (*ataśca saṃkṣepam am*), which summarizes the essential meaning of all the scriptures, it should have been stated that "At the time of creation, he undergoes transformation (*pariṇāma*); at the end of creation, he returns to his original state," or something similar. However, by stating instead, "And at the time of creation, he creates everything," it must be understood that the intended meaning of the Śruti and Smṛti is that the Lord Nārāyaṇa is the efficient cause of the universe—just as a potter is the efficient cause of a jar—and not the two-fold material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*).

And thus, the view explained by Śrī Vyāsa and others—that in passages such as *yato vā* (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1), the ablative case in *yataḥ* signifies only the efficient cause (*nimitta*)—is the correct opinion, because that very [view] was formulated by him in his summary verse (*sagrahaśloka*). This same opinion is also favored by Pāṇini and Patañjali, since in the Mahābhāṣya there is no denial of Brahman’s status as the efficient cause, nor is its status as the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) explicitly stated.

Now, one might object: "In the rule *janikartuḥ prakṛtiḥ* (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.30), Pāṇini employs the term *prakṛti*; therefore, since it is impossible to describe Brahma’s intention based on the mere usage of the term 'material cause' (*upādāna*), and because such an interpretation is not contradicted by the fact that [the term] is compatible with its being the 'best' [cause], it can be argued that he used that term to include both types of causes. By this, those who claim that the term was used for the sake of including grammarians [are also addressed]. [Note: The provided text contains a repetitive and likely corrupted phrase: *evamkalpanasyottamatvāvirogamātreṇaivaṃkalpanasyottamatvāvirodhitvāt*. This has been interpreted as: "because such a conceptualization is not contradicted by the mere fact that it is compatible with its being the best."]

As for those grammarians who assert that Brahman is the material cause (*upādānatva*) [of the world], they do not follow Pāṇini’s intention at all. Rather, Pāṇini’s intention is as follows: in certain passages concerning creation, such as "from which indeed these beings are born" (*Taittirīya Upaniṣad* 3.1), "from the Self, space was produced" (*Taittirīya Upaniṣad* 2.3), "all these beings, verily, arise from space alone" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 1.9.1), and "therefore, from this Brahman, name, form, and food are born" (*Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad* 1.1.9), [the word] "from which" (*yataḥ*)...

Even though such passages are heard with the word denoting the cause in the ablative case, these alone are not the creation-texts found in the Śrutis; rather— "He desired: 'May I be many, may I procreate. He performed austerity. Having performed austerity, he created all this, whatever there is—thinking: 'May I be many, may I procreate. He performed austerity. Having performed austerity, he created all this, whatever there is" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6). "He reflected: 'When I have departed from this body, shall I be departed? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.35).

"Established in what shall I be established? He created *prāṇa* (the vital breath); from *prāṇa*, he created faith (*śraddhā*). "The Self (*ātman*), indeed, was this alone in the beginning; there was nothing else whatsoever blinking. He thought: 'Let me now create the worlds. He created these worlds. "It thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate. It emitted heat (*tejas*). That heat thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate. It emitted water (*āpas*). Those waters thought: 'May we be many, may we procreate.'"

"They created food" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.4); "This deity thought: 'Come, let me enter these three deities with this living self and differentiate name and form'" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.3.2); "He who ordains Brahman in the beginning, and who indeed bestows the Vedas upon him."

"They indeed take refuge in that God, who is self-luminous and awakened, saying: 'I seek refuge in Him' (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.18); 'He is the maker of all, the knower of all, whose source is the Self' (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.16). He, the Lord Nārāyaṇa, first created the waters; then the Blessed One himself created the Brāhmaṇa from the water (Mahābhārata, Sabhā Parvan 43.3).
O Kaunteya, at the end of a Kalpa, all beings enter my own Prakṛti; at the beginning of a new Kalpa, I send them forth again" (Bhagavad Gītā 9.7).
"Taking hold of my own nature, I project forth this entire multitude of beings again and again, by the power of nature. (Gītā 9.8)

"By Me the fourfold order of society was created according to the division of qualities and actions" (Gītā 4.13). Numerous such passages concerning creation are found, composed of words in the nominative and instrumental cases denoting the cause. The purport of all these statements regarding creation is that the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva alone is the cause. Whether He is the efficient cause (*nimitta*) or the material cause (*upādāna*), the specific nature of the subject must be determined by understanding the essential character of the reality itself.

If an entity were to undergo transformation (*pariṇāma*) as its own self, then it would be an inherent cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*); however, if it does not transform, then it is merely an instrumental cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*), such as a staff for a jar. But no one accepts that Vāsudeva undergoes transformation either as a non-conscious entity or as another conscious entity, because such a transformation is incompatible with his supreme nature. Therefore, Vāsudeva is merely the instrumental cause of the world.

As for the ablative case in the scriptural passage beginning with "from which" (*yato vā*), it denotes the instrumental cause alone—just as in expressions such as "the jar is produced from a staff" or "joy arises from a son"—and thus the word *prakṛti* in the Sūtra refers to the cause.

The author of the *Vṛtti*, however, knowing this very intention of the Teachers, explains that in the sūtra "the source (*prakṛti*) of the agent of birth" (Pāṇini 1.4.30), the word *prakṛti* refers to the cause (*hetu*). Thus, the meaning of the sūtra is: "the source (*prakṛti*), i.e., the cause (*hetu*), of that which is being born (*janikartuḥ*), is the *apādāna*. Haradatta also states in his *Mañjarī* under the words "others, however," etc., that because the word *prakṛti* denotes the cause in general, the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) follows the word "son" in examples such as "joy arises from the son" (*putrāt pramodo jāyate*).
For it is clear to everyone that the son is not the material cause (*upādāna*) of joy, but rather its instrumental cause (*nimitta*).

Now, an objection is raised: in the *Manoramā*, during the occasion of commenting on the rule *jānakartuḥ*, it was stated that the view of the *Bhāṣya* and Kaiyaṭa is that the word *prakṛti* refers merely to the "original material" (*upādāna*). There, taking up the cue-word (*pratīka*) "the *Bhāṣya* and Kaiyaṭa," it was said, "this alone is the correct explanation," and so forth; thus, the established usage of the word *prakṛti* in that very sense follows from both the *Bhāṣya* and Kaiyaṭa, as well as from the *Bhāṣya* that rejects [the rule].

Furthermore—according to the view of the author of the *Vṛtti*, the connection of the governing term *kāraka* (which denotes a cause in general) with the word ending in the locative of selection (*nirdhāraṇa-saptamī*) is impossible; for just as one cannot say "among causes, the material cause" (*upādānakāraṇam*), so too it is not possible to say "among causes, the cause. If it is argued that the explanation "the source (*prakṛti*) is the cause" (*hetu*) is undermined by the faults of contradicting common worldly usage, contradicting the *Bhāṣya*, and the impossibility of syntactic connection, we reply: [it refers to] the primary [cause].

According to Amara’s lexicon (*Nāmaliṅgānuśāsana*): "The word *prakṛti* is feminine; it denotes nature, the eight constituent elements, the components of a kingdom, and the female organ"; and according to the Medinīkośa: "'*Prakṛti* [is used] for the equilibrium of the *guṇas*, for ministers and other [officials], and for inherent nature (*svabhāva*); [it is also used] for the female organ, the male organ, and the group of subjects (*paura-varga*)'; and in such passages as Gītā 7.20, "By his own *prakṛti* he is impelled," it refers to inherent nature (*svabhāva*); and in the *Campūrāmāyaṇa* (Ayodhyākāṇḍa 8.2), "The skillful king, with palms joined, petitioned the *prakṛtis*," it refers to the ministers and other components of the kingdom; and [in the phrase] "That *prakṛti* is not independent... [it refers to the primordial matter].

Because we observe usage in such expressions as "the suffix alone should not be employed" (*prayoktavyā nāpi kevalaḥ pratyayaḥ*), where words containing the term *pratyaya* (suffix) function as designators of the suffix itself, the first reason—"because it is well-known in that very [context]"—is inconclusive. Consequently, since the word *prakṛti* (base) possesses multiple meanings, its restriction [to a single sense] is untenable.

Now, one might object: "In that sūtra, between the two possible interpretations—whether the word *prakṛti* refers to cause in general or to a specific cause—the phrase 'by way of common usage' (*prasiddheḥ*) excludes its status as referring to cause in general, while the restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*) establishes that it refers specifically to a specific cause. To this we reply: It is stated in the commentary (*vṛtti*) on the sūtra "The [term] for that is used in the sense of *prakṛti*" (Pāṇini 5.4.24), which says: "Because of its co-occurrence with the word *vikṛti*, the word *prakṛti* here refers to the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*). Thus, by the explicit statement of the commentary, it is established that the word *prakṛti* denotes the material cause.

Furthermore, according to the *Śekhara* commentary on that very sūtra, which states, "The terms 'prakṛti' (material cause) and 'vikṛti' (modification) refer respectively to the material cause and its effect through their mutual co-occurrence," it is understood that the word *prakṛti* denotes a specific type of cause only when it occurs in co-occurrence with another word. In the present case, however, since such co-occurrence is absent, it is impossible to speak in that manner.

"In the case of rejection," the second reason as well does not establish the point for the opponents, because the meaning intended by them is obtained from that very commentary (*bhāṣya*). To explain: regarding the rule *janikartuḥ*, it is indeed said—"This rule could also have been stated [separately]: 'A scorpion is born from cow dung; durva grass is born from cow-hair and sheep-hair. [The question is: 'They depart from those [materials]; if they depart, why do they not depart completely? [The answer is: 'Because of continuity (*santatatvāt*')."

Alternatively, it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "Others and yet others appear. Relying on worldly convention, this is said: for in the world, when a product emerges from a cause—as in the phrase "whatever is born from whatever"—Kaiyaṭa shows the example, "like the fruit produced by a tree," and states that according to the Vaiśeṣika and Sāṃkhya doctrines, the product does not emerge from its material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*).

In this regard, one finds no evidence whatsoever in the works of Bhartṛhari and Kaiyaṭa to suggest that the word *prakṛti* in the sūtra refers to a material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*). If it is argued that examples such as "a scorpion is born from cow dung" and "dūrvā grass is born from cow dung and soma" serve as proof, we say no; for by this [interpretation], examples such as "joy is born from a son" would also be included as illustrations. Furthermore, there is the maxim: "An example is not to be taken as a definitive rule."

For this very reason, they say that the illustrative examples (*udāharaṇa*) found here and there in the *Bhāṣya* are not intended to be exhaustive enumerations, but rather are merely for the purpose of providing illustrations. If it is objected, "In that case, why were those very examples not provided by the author of the *Bhāṣya*?", we reply: no, because it is improper to subject independent teachers (*svatantra-ācāryas*) to such an interrogation.

In this example, because the specific factor to be understood exists as a cause, and because joy is not observed in the son—who is the cause—but is clearly perceived in the father and others, the departure of the perceiver (*boddhuḥ*) from that [son] is clearly apprehended. However, since the blades of *dūrvā* grass are continuous, even though separation exists, the exit from the cause is not clearly perceived. Therefore, by the word "certainly" (*dhruvam*), in order to dispel the possible doubt as to whether the status of the ablative (*apādānatā*) might belong to the cow’s hair and so forth, [the author uses] "from the cow's hair" (*go-romabhyaḥ*).

This is an example, among others. Now, if it is argued that the example "gomayāt" and so forth is therefore redundant, we say no; for it is understood from an examination of the *Bhāṣya*—such as the passage beginning "khadvendromālendra"—that the demonstration of exactly two examples at a time is established as the style of the author of the *Bhāṣya*.

By this, the following objection is refuted: "In the case of the statement 'a scorpion is born from cow dung,' whatever portion of the cow dung constitutes the material cause (*upādāna*) of the scorpion's body, that portion, having undergone transformation into the form of the effect, has departed from the great mass of cow dung which was its original cause; since such departure (*apakrama*) is clearly perceived there, that example is useless."

Just as a portion of cow dung, having transformed into the body of a scorpion within a heap of cow dung, departs from that state, so it is not the case that the essence of *dūrvā* grass—which is the effect of cow dung—departs from it; this is shown by the example provided to illustrate the negative instance (*vyatireka-dṛṣṭānta*). For this very reason, the departure [of the essence] is explained specifically in relation to the *dūrvā* grass in the passage beginning with, "They depart from those [elements], but they do not depart entirely."

There is a way out here: even so, it is not perceived as clearly separate, like the body of a scorpion, because there exists a connection with its cause; for when there is a connection with a cause, that cause is indeed non-interruption (*aviccheda*). The meaning is that, just as when a long-bodied serpent is perceived within a hole emerging from a lotus stalk, non-interruption is the cause.

If it is argued that the justification for the departure [of the suffixes] in the rule *tāstebhyaḥ* applies equally to both [masculine and neuter], we say no; for if that were the case, the masculine gender indication in the rule *tyadāditaḥ śeṣe puṃnapuṃsakato liṅgavat* would have to be modified. Consequently, it is not easy to determine from the Bhāṣya and Kaiyaṭa on this point that the word *prakṛti* in the sūtra refers to the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*).

Furthermore, by the statement "it is not approved by the Bhāṣya which is intent on refutation," it is implied that this is not the view of the author of the Sūtras. Thus, according to the opinion of the Sūtrakāra, the suffix *kāra* alone [denotes] the material cause (*prakṛti*); consequently, all instances such as "joy arises from a son," "a scorpion arises from cow dung," and "a pot arises from a stick" are merely examples for the purpose of the Sūtra.

Nor should it be argued that there is no inconsistency in rejecting [the rule] when there is a difference in result—on the grounds that in the case of *prāpti* (attainment), the word *prakṛti* refers to a cause in general, whereas in the case of *pratyākhyāna* (rejection), it refers specifically to a material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*), since a difference in result is evident from the application and non-application of the ablative (*pañcamī*) in the example "joy arises from a son" (*putrāt pramodo jāyate*). For such a rejection is possible even when there is a difference in result, as seen in rules such as "not in a *bahuvrīhi*" (*na bahuvrīhau*) and "not after *kva*, etc. (*na kvādeḥ*).

Since it is understood from the words of the author—that is, from the direction of what was stated—that the word *prakṛti* in the Bhāṣya refers to the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*), even according to the view of the Bhāṣya, the word *prakṛti* refers only to the general property of being a cause; thus, there is no difference in the result.

If it is argued that in the expression "joy arises from the son" (*putrāt pramodo jāyate*), the ablative case after the word *putra* is used in the sense of a cause (*hetu*) due to the application of the rule *vibhāṣā guṇe'striyām* (Pāṇini 2.3.25)—where the term *vibhāṣā* is separated as a distinct *yogavibhāga*—this is not so; for such a *yogavibhāga* is not seen in the Bhāṣya. Furthermore, even in cases such as *yato vā* ("from which"), one who maintains that the ablative denotes a causal factor (*nimitta-kāraṇatā*) could likewise claim that the ablative is used here in the sense of a cause via *yogavibhāga*. However, the specific grammatical operations triggered by case endings denoting *kārakas* must be sought in both instances [of the *putra* example and the *yato vā* example].

The Bhāṣya has been composed to inform one who considers that there is no separation (*viśleṣa*) at the stage of the transformative form (*pariṇāmikārāma*) that such a separation does indeed exist. Consequently, it is difficult to maintain—on the basis of the Bhāṣya on the *pratyākhyāna* (rejection)—the notion that the word "base" (*prakṛti*) refers to a secondary form of material cause (*upādānākāra*), because the Bhāṣya remains consistent even without that assumption. For that alone which cannot be otherwise accounted for is the warrant for such an assumption.

Furthermore, the third reason stated with the words "And what [more]? (*kiṃ ca*) and so forth is also not tenable; for, in the *Kāśikāvṛtti*, among the thirty-two sūtras read under the section on *kārakas* (*kārakādhikāra*), there is nowhere to be found a reading of the word "kāraka" ending in the locative case (*saptamyanta*), nor is there any mention of the phrase "the locative of selection" (*nirdhāraṇasaptamī*). On the contrary, in the sūtra concerning "kāraka," there is the statement: "The term 'kāraka' is introduced as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) whose scope is the technical designations (*saṃjñā*) such as *apādāna* and the rest. And in the section prescribing the designations such as *drava* and so forth, in every individual sūtra, [it says]: "That which... (*yat*)... [and so on].

In such statements that demonstrate the meaning of various rules—such as "that *kāraka* is designated as the *apādāna*," "that *kāraka* is designated as the *saṃpradāna*," "that *kāraka* is designated as the *karman*," and "that *kāraka* is designated as the *kartṛ*"—the qualifying word "kāraka" is found in the nominative case (*prathamānta*). By this, it is determined that the intention [of the author] is that the word "kāraka" ending in the locative case (*saptamyanta*) must be transformed into the nominative case to fit the rule, for the locative is used in the rule [to indicate the sense of the nominative].
Therefore, what Ratna has stated is not correct.

But surely, in his commentary on that [sūtra], the *Padamañjarī*, Haradatta refuted the reading with a nominative ending and determined the intention of the root text (*mūla*) to be the use of the locative of selection (*nirdhāraṇa-saptamī*) with a singular number referring to the general category, stating: "In the section on qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇādhikāra*), the meaning is obtained as 'among the kārakas, that which is fixed (*dhruva*) when there is separation'"; relying on that, the author of the *Ratna* [states] regarding the *Vṛtti*: "According to the *Vṛtti*, it is a selection..."

If it is argued that [the rule] beginning with "of that which ends in the seventh case" has already been stated, it is replied: the word *kāraka* is of two kinds—conventional (*rūḍha*) and etymological (*yaugika*). Of these, the second is derived from the analysis "that which performs (*karoti*) an action," ending in the suffix *ṇvul*, meaning "an independent agent (*svatantra-kartṛ*) in an action. Since fixed points (*dhruva*) and so forth lack independence with respect to the primary action, the term "kāraka" (in its conventional sense) is applied to them as "causes" (*nimitta*). Thus, there is no contradiction.

Furthermore, the word *kāraka* here is a synonym for "cause" (*nimitta*) and denotes a qualifier. If it is objected that, in such cases as "he asks the boy's father the way," the designation of *karman* (object) would apply because the boy possesses the status of being a cause as defined by the father, we reply: no. Through the question and answer—"For what purpose? [The purpose] of the action"—it is intended that only the cause of the action is meant. Moreover, based on the underlying principle, the action to be considered must be one inherent in the actual usage.

In the example *prakr̥ṣyate māṇavakasya* ("the boy is dragged away"), the boy does not possess the status of an object (*karman*) because he is not determined by the action of asking (*pṛcchi-kriyā*). In the rule beginning with *dhruvam*, the word "action" (*kriyā*) is obtained through the force of the qualifier "kāraka"; that [action] is general, whereas in that context, specific actions such as "separation" (*apāya*) are particular instances. Since the non-difference between the general and the particular is well-established, the author of the Vṛtti states: "That which is fixed (*dhruva*) in separation—that kāraka is designated as the *apādāna*," and so forth. This is precisely on the basis of this principle.

The *Mañjarī* intends that the meaning [of the rule] is: "that which is the cause for the departure (*apāya*) in an action is the *apādāna*"; thus, the *Mañjarī* proceeded for the purpose of considering the justification for the reading ending in the nominative (*prathamānta*) as accepted by the author of the *Vṛtti*, and not for the purpose of imagining an intention of the *Vṛtti*-author regarding a reading ending in the locative of separation (*nirdhāraṇasaptamī*).

For this very reason, [the author] has introduced the root text "And the word *kāraka*" with the following commentary: "Thinking, 'What is the use of this obsession with providing remedies for faults? Let there simply be the inclusion of the term *nimitta* (cause),' he says... By this, it is suggested that if the reading were in the ablative case (*nirdāraṇasaptamī*), a grammatical fault would arise; therefore, one must strive to avoid it, and thus the recourse to the nominative case reading (*prathamāntapāṭha*) is preferable. [This refers to the rules: "The cause of fear for those words whose meaning is fear" (Pāṇini 1.4.25), and "The source of the agent of birth" (Pāṇini 1.4.30).

In the two sūtras [1.4.20], because the word *hetu* (cause) and the word *kāraṇa* (instrumental cause)—which is a synonym for *prakṛti* (material cause)—are distinct in their specific meanings as "the cause of fear" (*bhayahetu*) and "the cause of production" (*utpattikāraṇa*), and because the referent of the recurring first-case kāraka-word is general in the sense of being "the cause of an action," there is no inconsistency. This is because grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is possible—as in the case of "The pot is a substance" (*dravyaṃ ghaṭaḥ*)—and the meaning is ultimately determined to be "the cause of the action of fearing" and "the cause of the action of producing. Thus, there is no logical flaw whatsoever.

Nor can it be argued that the employment of terms such as "cause" (*hetu*) and so forth is thus rendered useless; for they serve their purpose by indicating the alternative view that the designation "kāraka" (agent/cause) is a rule of technical nomenclature (*saṃjñā-vidhi*). Even under the alternative view where the term "kāraka" is governed by a locative case expressing selection (*nirdhāraṇa-saptamī*), its meaning remains general in the sense of "being a producer of an action" (*kriyā-janakatva*), whereas "being a cause of birth" (*janana-hetutva*) is a specific instance. Just as there is the conventional usage "the jar among substances" (*dravyeṣu ghaṭaḥ*), there is likewise no contradiction in the conventional usage "the cause of fear among causes of action" (*kriyā-kāraṇeṣu bhaya-hetuḥ*) or "the cause of birth among causes."

Otherwise, there would be the fault of the impossibility of syntactic connection (*anvayāsaṃbhava*). For this very reason, Kaiyaṭa and Nāgeśa, stating that "in the view that [the locative] expresses selection (*nirdhāraṇa*), since selection lacks a substratum, the meaning [of the rule] is obtained through the locative of selection as mentioned immediately above," considered only the fault of the impossibility of the designation (*vidheyanupapatti*) to be the issue, and did not mention the fault of the impossibility of syntactic connection. Their position is that the impossibility of syntactic connection is easily resolved by the existence of both the general and the particular in the manner described.

Furthermore—since it is understood from a close examination of the *sūtra* and the *bhāṣya* that the authors of the *sūtra* and the *bhāṣya* do not intend for the locative case in "among the *kārakas*" (*kārakeṣu*) to be a locative of specification (*nirdhāraṇa-saptamī*), as they might otherwise have said "in the case of *kārakas*" (*kārakeṣv iti brūyāt*); therefore, the statement in the *Padamañjarī*, "the locative 'among the *kārakas*' (*kārakeṣu*) is a locative of specification, and the singular number refers to the class in general," appears to be a mere restatement of an argument by some opponent who is ignorant of the intention of the authors of the *sūtra* and the *bhāṣya*.

Furthermore, regarding the term "kāraka," there are only two possible interpretations based on the Bhāṣya: first, that it is an etymological (anvartha) designation meaning "that which performs an action" (*karoti kriyām*), and second, that it refers to the action itself, derived from the analysis "that which effects the designations of agent, object, and so forth" (*kartṛ-karmādi-vyapadeśaṃ karoti*). A third position—that the locative case here denotes selection (*nirdhāraṇa-saptamī*)—is not tenable; rather, it is merely a speculative invention of some. It is precisely these scholars, such as Dīkṣita and others, who, relying on the two positions established by the Bhāṣya, apply the rules beginning with *dhruvam* in two distinct ways.

In this context, since the word *kāraka* refers to "action" (*kriyā*), in examples such as *kārakād datta-śrutayor āśiṣi*, it should be understood that the word *kāraka* refers to technical designations (such as *apādāna*) prescribed under the governing rule for *kārakas*. Thus, to point out a fault in a position that is not supported by the *Bhāṣya*, was not even mentioned by the author of the treatise (*granthakṛt*), and was merely imagined by someone on their own authority, is entirely improper.

As for the objection that if the word *prakṛti* (material cause) were taken to mean cause in general, and if the word *kāraka* (agent/cause)—which is a synonym for *nimitta* (efficient cause)—were to follow [in the definition], then because both would have the same meaning, there would be no verbal cognition [of difference], just as in cases such as "the pot is a jar" (*ghaṭaḥ kalaśaḥ*) or "the pot is a pot" (*ghaṭo ghaṭaḥ*), we reply: that is not so. For the relationship of generality and particularity between the two has been established immediately below. Furthermore, the claim that "difference appears as a qualifier (*prakāra*) in the cognition of the word" is unsatisfactory. Nor should it be argued that the appearance of the word in verbal cognition has been established in works such as the *Kaustubha*, for there is no more solid evidence for that.

By relying on the fact that the word *kāraka*—through its etymological derivation (*nirukta-vyutpatti*)—is intent upon action (*kriyā*), and by accepting it as a locative of domain (*viṣaya-saptamī*), [it follows that] being a producer (*janakatva*) is the state of being a domain. Since action is general and birth (*janman*) is particular, there is no scent of inconsistency in the sense that "the source (*apādāna*) is the cause of the action in the form of birth. Thus, even if the word *prakṛti* refers merely to a causal factor (*kāraṇa-mātra*), there is no sublation (*bādhaka*).

Even on the view that *kāraka* is a technical designation (*saṃjñā*), there is no fault, because the relationship [of the ablative] with the generative cause is one of "coloration" (*uparañjakatayā*) toward the capacity to produce an action (*kriyājanakatva*), which is obtained through the force of the etymological definition (*anvarthasaṃjñā*) of the suffix *-ṇa*. And thus—examples such as "the jar is born from a lump of clay," "the jar is born from a staff," and "joy is born from a son"—are all illustrations of this [rule], and therefore all desired results are established. In this regard, Nāgeśa and others, who attempt to justify the ablative in cases like "joy from a son" or "a jar from a staff" by superimposing the status of a material cause (*upādānatva*) onto what is not a material cause, or the status of a quality (*guṇatva*) onto what is not a quality, are indeed unrestrained.

Alternatively—regarding the word "yataḥ" in both the Śruti and the Sūtra, the suffix -tasi is used in the sense of the instrumental case. Thus, the construction of the Śruti is: "from which Brahman these beings are born. The construction of the Sūtra is: "that from which the birth and so forth of this world proceed is Brahman. Here, the instrumental case in "yena" denotes cause (*hetu*), as in the expression "by means of a staff, a jar is produced. For this very reason, the Blessed One said: "By Me, the presiding lord of Māyā, Nature gives birth to the moving and the unmoving;
by this cause, O son of Kuntī, the world revolves" (Gītā 9.10).

Thus, in the Gītā, by stating that Prakṛti, impelled by the side-glance of Hari—the presiding lord and sovereign of all—creates the worlds of moving and non-moving beings, it is established that the Lord is merely the efficient cause (nimittakāraṇa) as the impeller.

The meaning of the verse is as follows: O Kaunteya! Nature (prakṛti), also known as the Pradhāna, being impelled by Me—the Supreme Lord who is the witness—gives birth to the world of moving and non-moving beings. For this reason—that is, by virtue of that witnessing glance corresponding to the specific karma of each living being—the world revolves again and again; it is born and transforms into the form of various diverse objects.

The meaning is as follows: Just as in the world a minister or similar official, being subordinate to a king, acts upon a certain task once he understands the Lord’s intention merely through a glance or a gesture—thinking, "He is directing me toward this work"—so too this primordial nature (*prakṛti*), being dependent on the Blessed One, creates the universe consisting of the moving and the non-moving, knowing the intention of the Lord Hari merely through His glance.

Nor should it be asked how such knowledge can belong to the insentient *pradhāna*; for that statement was made with the intention of referring to the presiding deity (*abhimāninī devatā*) of that [nature].

Gadādhara also, in his *Vyutpattivāda*, while discussing the fifth case-role (*pañcamī-kāraka*), states regarding examples such as "a jar is born from a lump of clay" (*mṛtpiṇḍāt ghaṭo jāyate*): "The source (*apādāna*) of the agent of birth [is expressed by the fifth case]. In this context, being the material cause (*prakṛtitva*) does not mean being the substrate of transformation (*vikāritva*), because even in the absence of a relationship between material cause and modification—as seen in cases such as "Bharata was born from Kaikeyī," "he arose from that," or "born from the wind"—the fifth case is observed. Therefore, being the material cause is simply the state of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*); indeed, usages such as "a jar is born from a stick" (*daṇḍād ghaṭo jāyate*) are accepted.

By such reasoning, intending that in the sūtra "the source [prakṛti] of the agent of birth," the word *prakṛti* refers to the instrument (*karaṇa*), he states that Brahman cannot possibly be the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*) of insentient things such as substance; thus, the use of the ablative case in passages such as "from which [arise] substance, quality, and action" is justified only if the word *prakṛti* in its present context signifies merely a cause (*kāraṇamātra*).

This is what must be understood: those who assert that Brahman is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world are only three or four; among them, some are grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇas*), while others are the authors of the Sūtras and the Bhāṣya. For them, the Word-Brahman (*śabda-brahman*) is the manifesting material cause (*vivarta-upādāna*) of the world, but not its transformative material cause (*pariṇāmi-upādāna*), because Brahman is changeless (*nirvikāra*). "Brahman is without beginning or end, the essence of sound, the imperishable syllable;
from which proceeds the process of the world, as it manifests in the form of objects."

Thus they say, based on the statement of Harisvāmin: "The intention of the venerable [author] is that this entire world is superimposed upon the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*). In this view, regarding the scriptural passage "from which indeed" (*yato vā*), it is more appropriate to take *yataḥ* as the suffix *tasi* applied to a locative case form, meaning "in which," rather than as a suffix applied to an ablative case form. Nor should it be argued that the ablative case is asserted because of the verbal root *jan* (to be born).

By the rule *tatra jātaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.25), which prescribes suffixes such as *aṇ* after a word in the locative case (*saptamīsamartha*) in the sense of "born there"; by the rule *saptamyāṃ janer ḍaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.98), which prescribes the suffix *ḍa* for the root *jan* when an upapada ending in the locative is present; and by the use of the analytical sentence *mandurāyāṃ jātaḥ* ("born in the stable"), it is appropriate for the locative case to be used in conjunction with the verbal root *jan*. Furthermore, according to the Grammarian (*vaiyākaraṇa*), who maintains that the locus of superimposition (*adhiṣṭhāna*) exists in the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*), the status of being a locus (*adhiṣṭhānatva*) is indeed present therein.

For it is necessary to rely on the fact that [the word] ends in the locative case (*saptamyanta*) for the sake of comprehension, and because it is more logical to employ a word ending in the case-ending that conveys the intended meaning. Otherwise, one would have to resort to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and other such devices. Although in this view there is a duality as to whether the "vastness" (*brahmatva*) belongs to the *parā* speech or to the *madhyamā* speech, nevertheless, according to the *Mañjūṣā*, it must be determined that this reality belongs to the *parā* speech alone.

Others, however, maintain that Brahman, which is distinct from *śabda* (the Word), is the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) of the world; all else remains as in the previous view. Here too, the employment of the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is of questionable purpose; it appears more appropriate to employ the locative case (*saptamī*). In these two views, Brahman’s status as the material cause of the world is due to its being the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of *māyā* or *avidyā*, which are the material causes of the world.

Others, however, assert that Brahman is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world either by virtue of having *prakṛti*—which is of the nature of transformation—as its body, or by virtue of being the controller of *prakṛti*. In this regard, they maintain that the world has Brahman as its material cause because the world is produced from *pradhāna*, which is [Brahman’s] own body, or because the world is produced from *pradhāna* which is dependent upon Him.
