They explain that the word "from which" (*yataḥ*) found in the Śruti and the Sūtra refers to *pradhāna* presided over by Brahman; thus, it is *pradhāna* itself that transforms into the form of the world through the proximity of the Puruṣa (the Person).

Others, however, say that primordial matter (pradhāna), impelled by God, transforms itself into the form of the world; therefore, they claim that very matter is the material cause. Still others believe that atoms are the cause of the world, evolving into the forms of dyads and so forth.

However, those who maintain that Brahman is the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) of the world do not all accept the transformation (*pariṇāma*) of Brahman; therefore, it must be examined what the purpose of asserting Brahman’s status as the material cause is in their view. By this, the claim made in the first chapter of the *Mañjūṣā*—that because nothing exists apart from Brahman, the world is false according to the Sūtra "its non-difference [from Him]" (*tadananyatvam*), and thus even Vyāsa’s intent was that the world is false—is refuted.

This is because the cognition of non-difference from the cause is possible only with respect to a transformative cause (*pariṇāmikāraṇa*), whereas Brahman is non-transformative. Furthermore, by one who accepts Vāsudeva’s superiority over all—including Śrī Vyāsa, Pāṇini, and Patañjali—it is understood that the world’s being the material cause of Brahman is not accepted; thus, the world’s non-difference from Brahman is also not admitted.

As for the purport of the sūtra "non-difference from that" (*tadananyatvam*), we shall explain later that it is a statement of non-difference based on such factors as dependence upon that [Brahman], though some has already been explained previously.
And thus—the world’s having Brahman as its material cause is merely figurative.
The creation-texts declare that Hari is the efficient cause of the world;
therefore, on account of the difference between these two [causes], non-difference cannot be established at all.
Now, as for what was said—that Vāsudeva is the efficient cause of the world and not the material cause, and therefore he is distinct from everything—that is not correct; for it has been stated:

"An eternal portion of My very self becomes the individual soul in the world of living beings and draws toward itself the senses, with the mind as the sixth, which abide in material nature" (Gītā 15.7–8).

This is because it would contradict the statement that the individual soul (*jīva*) is a part (*aṃśa*) of Him, since we observe only non-difference between a part and the whole. For if there were difference between the two, the status of being a "part" would be untenable. To this it is replied: A part is indeed of two kinds—differentiated and non-differentiated. Among these, the differentiated part is similar to its own whole; and that is the individual soul (*jīva*). The non-differentiated part, however, consists of the Inner Controller (*antaryāmī*) and the forms of incarnations such as Rāma and Kṛṣṇa. Consequently, [the scriptural statement] "He is indeed a part of Me" means he is similar to a part of Me, but not identical with My essential nature (*svarūpa*); the rest is clear.

And this similarity consists in being a part (*aṃśa*) of oneself, but not in being identical with my own nature; the rest is clear. Furthermore, "similarity" means by virtue of being dependent on oneself (*svāyattatvena*); just as one's own part is dependent on oneself, so too is the individual soul (*jīva*) dependent on oneself—this is the sense. Alternatively, it means that he who is a part of me is subordinate to me and not independent; for whatever is dependent on something else is designated by the term of that thing, as in the expression "the king is the kingdom"—this is the sense. These very points constitute the summary of the essence of all scriptures, as stated in the fifteenth chapter of the *Gītā*: "But the Supreme Person is another, declared to be the Supreme Self (*paramātman*)."
"The Imperishable Lord, having entered the three worlds, sustains them" (Gītā 15.18).

Thus, the declaration of Vāsudeva’s superiority over the entire phenomenal world—denoted by the terms *kṣara* (the perishable) and *akṣara* (the imperishable)—is consistent. If there were no difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord, then how could His aforementioned status as the supreme of all be logically established? Therefore, the statement regarding [the soul] being a "part" (*aṃśa*) does not establish a real difference. By this, the assertion of certain [advocates] that the difference described in the Gītā through its opening and concluding sections is not real, but merely conditional (*aupādhika*), is refuted.

This is because the distinction is stated in the fifteenth chapter, "The Compendium of the Essence of the Meaning of All Śāstras. Nor should it be argued that this distinction is also merely adventitious (*aupādhika*), for in the "Compendium of the Essence of the Meaning of the Śāstras," there is no possibility of such a conceptualization since it establishes only the reality of the meaning.

Others, however, maintain that while the word *jīva* refers to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) who has that [individual] as His body, there is the conventional usage of the *jīva* being a "part" (*aṃśa*) of the Supreme Self because it is a single component of the qualified whole (*viśiṣṭaikadeśatvena*). Nevertheless, they assert that due to the difference in essential nature (*svarūpabheda*), the *jīva* is indeed distinct from the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*). According to the view of the *Mañjūṣā*, since there is no sentient being other than God and since God is partless, it would be impossible to describe a connection with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*); consequently, the status of the *jīva* as a "part" mentioned in the scriptures would be untenable.

Here, by the qualification "eternal" (*sanātana*), the intention of the great sage Śrī Vyāsa is understood to be that the reality of the individual soul (*jīva*) is beginningless. Since Pāṇini did not prohibit the beginninglessness of souls, that too is certainly accepted by him as well. Consequently, the definition of the connection with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) as the cause for the conventional usage of "being a soul"—which is not agreed upon by either of those two—is [the point at issue].

The following point must be noted here: no one can establish that the individual soul (*jīva*) is a primary part (*mukhya-aṃśa*) of the Lord (*Īśvara*). One who maintains that there is no sentient being other than the Lord and that the Lord is partless is unable to postulate a "part" for the Lord through a connection with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), and thereby define its status as a soul or its nature as a part of the Lord. Thus, rather than relying on such illogical and unfounded conceptualizations, it is better to postulate that the soul—which is distinct from the Lord by its very nature—is a part of Him due to its dependence upon Him and so forth. The statement that the soul is a part does not prove the non-difference of the self.
Therefore, it does not obstruct the supreme excellence of Śrī Vāsudeva.

**The Removal of Apparent Contradictions with the Words of the Gītā:** Now, an objection may be raised: the status of Vāsudeva as the all-pervading Lord is dependent upon difference (*bheda*), yet that very difference is prohibited in the *Gītā*. For instance, in the passages: "That yogin, having become Brahman, attains the liberation of Brahman" (Gītā 5.24); "He attains the stainless state, free from passion and become Brahman" (Gītā 6.37); and "Having become Brahman, serene in soul, he neither grieves nor desires" (Gītā 18.54)—in these instances we find the term "become Brahman" (*brahmabhūta*). Furthermore, in the passage: "Having cast off these qualities, he becomes fit for becoming Brahman" (Gītā 18.53), the same term is used. [This would imply a distinction between the individual soul and Brahman, which contradicts the doctrine of non-duality.]

Regarding the phrases "for the sake of becoming a *brahma*" (*brahmabhūyāya*) and "He who departs goes to My state; there is no doubt in this" (Gītā 8.5), as well as "My devotee, having realized this, attains My state" (Gītā 14.19)—where the Blessed One uses the term "My state" (*madbhāvam*)—it means that he has attained the state of being a *brahma*. For the sake of becoming a *brahma* (*brahmabhūyāya*) means for the sake of attaining My own nature (*matsvarūpa*). Thus, in these two instances, "one who has attained the state of *brahma*" (*brahmabhūtaḥ*), "for the attainment of the state of *brahma*" (*brahmabhūyāya*), and "for remaining therein" (*tatra sthityai*) are the intended meanings.

"Madbhāvam" means "into my being"; "madbhāvāya" means "for the sake of my existence," that is, for the sake of existence within me. "Madbhāvam" means "my being"; "madbhāvāya" means "for the sake of my existence," that is, for the sake of existence within me. The statement "he attains my being" refers to the attainment of liberation:
"Having transcended these three qualities which arise from the body, the embodied soul, freed from the sufferings of birth, death, and old age, attains immortality. (Gītā 14.20)
This has been explained by the Blessed One himself in the following verse; therefore, it is improper to assume an intended meaning regarding a lack of difference in their essential nature.

"Abiding in Brahman" means having the firm conviction that "Brahman alone is everything. "Attained to Brahman" and "for the sake of becoming Brahman" (which, according to Śaṅkarabhāṣya, means for the sake of liberation)—this refers to abiding in one's own essential nature characterized by uncontracted knowledge and so forth. "For the sake of equality with Brahman" means for the sake of being free from saṃsāra. This is precisely the meaning of the term *madbhāva* (my state of being). However, in one place [the Rāmānujabhāṣya] states: "'Freedom from the suffering of birth and so forth. Regarding the phrase 'become Brahman,' [it means] one whose mind is established everywhere in Brahman."

It has been explained in the *Pūrva-bhāga* [of the Bhāṣya] that these names are for the purpose of becoming an object of love, for the purpose of fixing the mind upon Him, and for the state consisting of freedom from suffering and unsurpassed bliss, which is "having Me as one's sole mind. Therefore, there is no intention in these words to imply a difference in their referents. And thus, there is no contradiction with the statements of the *Gītā* regarding Vāsudeva’s being the omniscient supreme reality.

It should be understood that single-minded devotion (*tanmanaskatva*) is the primary limb of the worship of the Blessed One, as this is taught again and again through such passages as "Be intent on me, my devotee" (*Gītā* 9.34; 18.65) and "Meditating on me with undivided minds" (*Gītā* 9.22). Therefore, these statements from the *Gītā* do not have the meaning you have asserted, because they intend to convey the supreme omniscience of Vāsudeva, the Teacher of the *Gītā*, and of Pāṇini.

If it is argued that although there is a distinction between the transmigrating soul and others due to its possession of different attributes, non-distinction is appropriate for liberated souls because they are pure— being devoid of all merit and demerit— and thus lack opposing attributes, it is replied:
I shall declare again the supreme knowledge, the best among all forms of knowledge,
knowing which all the sages have attained the highest perfection from this state.
Having taken refuge in this knowledge, they have attained my own nature;
even in the world of the moving, they are not born again, and at the time of dissolution, they do not suffer. (Gītā 14.2)

Thus, with these two verses, having first praised the unborn [nature] by means of what will be stated later in "My womb is the great Brahma" (Gītā 14.3) and so forth, and having declared its fruit along with an illustration, the Lord then describes the very similarity (*sādharmya*) of those liberated ones with the Blessed One, in order to dispel the delusion that they are identical with the Supreme Self. This similarity consists in equality; and that is to be understood as being free from the miseries of birth, death, and so forth, as possessing qualities such as freedom from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*) distinct from being the creator of the world, and as being the enjoyer of eternal bliss.

Furthermore, in the *Brahma-mīmāṃsā*, the author of the Sūtras states that for the liberated, there is no agency in the creation of the world, according to the Sūtra: "Excluding the activity of the world" (*bra.sū.* 4.4.1); there is only the experience of eternal bliss, according to the Sūtra: "In mere enjoyment" (*bhogamātre*); and there is the attainment of the Blessed Lord, according to the Sūtra: "That which is to be approached by the liberated" (*muktopasṛpye*) (*bra.sū.* 1.3.2). Regarding this point, [the scripture says]: "When the seer perceives the golden-hued one, the maker, the Lord, the Person, the source of Brahman;
then the knower, having shaken off both merit and demerit, stainless, attains supreme equality" (*mu.* 5.3).

Thus, there is also the support of scripture (*śruti*). "The seer" (*paśyaḥ*) means the observer (the worshipper); "stainless" (*nirañjanaḥ*) means pure; "equality" (*sāmyam*) means equality with the Supreme Self who is the object of worship. The remainder is clear. Consequently—the truth established by *śruti*, *sūtra*, and *smṛti* is that even in liberation (*mukti*), there is indeed difference.
From such statements in the *Gītā* as "having become Brahman," etc., oneness (*aikya*) appears to be perceived.
Thus, this objection was refuted by the strength of the words of the *Gītā* and the *śruti*.
"Fix your mind on Me, be devoted to Me, sacrifice to Me, and bow down to Me;
thus you shall come to Me alone—this I promise you as the truth, for you are dear to Me" (Gītā 18.65).
Thus, through meditation, there is the attainment of the Blessed Lord.

In the *Śaṅkarabhāṣya*, the word *tattvam* is analyzed as follows: an alternative interpretation is shown wherein *saḥ* (He) refers to the Self (*ātman*) characterized by the qualities taught in the passage beginning with "Being alone" (*sadeva*), and *tattvam* means the real entity (*vāstavam vastu*).

However, some argue that since Śvetaketu was a single incarnation of the Lord—like Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and others—the statement of non-difference can be explained in that way; thus, they claim that this [text] does not establish the identity of all individual souls (*jīvas*) with the Supreme Self.

Furthermore, since the illustrative sentences such as those concerning the birds and the thread were heard nine times in that context with the intent of establishing difference, it is appropriate to apply the illustrative principle to the subject sentence, "That thou art," as having the same intent of establishing difference; thus, one should reflect that the notion of the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) is not to be entertained. That the illustrative sentences have the intent of establishing difference has been demonstrated elsewhere.

In the commentary of Raṅgarāmānuja, however, the meaning of "tat tvam asi" is as follows: the word *tvam* (you) refers to the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*) because its primary sense is untenable; the word *tat* (that) refers to the Inner Controller through its secondary application (*lakṣaṇā*) to the Self denoted by the term "Being" (*sat*).

If it is objected that—since the word *tvam* (you) must everywhere logically refer to the person being addressed, and since Śvetaketu is the one being addressed in this context—it is improper to assume it refers to the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*) without referring back to him—the following is the response: This is possible, just as when Devadatta is addressed with the intention of referring to his son, one says, "O Devadatta! You have done this. However, there is this distinction: in the example, because the primary meaning of the word *Devadatta* is untenable, there is a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word *Devadatta* toward his son; whereas in the case of the word *tvam*, there is a metaphorical indication toward the Inner Controller. Thus has this scripture been explained.

By this, the statement in the *Mañjūṣā*—namely, "the superimposed identity with Brahman belongs even to the pure, non-differentiated meaning of sentences such as 'That thou art'" (*Mūla* 4.25)—is refuted. For that [statement] teaches the oneness of the two forms of the Blessed Lord alone; since that oneness is real, it is improper to describe it as superimposed. Furthermore, even if the reference were to Śvetaketu who is being addressed, only his dependence upon or similarity to Him would be understood in Śvetaketu, so that identity itself is not even applicable.

Furthermore, since the teacher Pāṇini—who intended [to teach] that Vāsudeva is the supreme of all—did not acknowledge the identity of the Lord with the individual souls (jīvas) exemplified by Śvetaketu;

(2) and because [the scripture states]: "The fifteen parts have reached their foundation, and all the gods have returned to their respective deities; the actions and the self consisting of consciousness become one in the supreme, imperishable [Brahman]" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.7); and as it is said: "Just as rivers flowing toward the ocean vanish there, having abandoned name and form... (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 3.2).

"Thus, O wise one, liberated from name and form, he attains the divine Person, higher than the high. (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.8) "He who truly knows that supreme Brahman becomes Brahman itself; in his lineage, no one ignorant of Brahman remains. (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.9)

Thus, because the *Atharvaśiras* concludes by establishing both the oneness (*ekībhāva*) with Brahman and the becoming Brahman (*brahmabhāva*) for the knower of Brahman, there is indeed identity between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman in liberation. The oneness and the state of being Brahman established here are nothing other than the very nature of Brahman (*brahmatva*). Since it is impossible for one who is not Brahman to become Brahman, this scripture, which would otherwise teach an impossibility, would be non-authoritative (*apramāṇa*).

By this [it is shown that] even prior to liberation, the soul's vastness exists, though it is unmanifest due to defects; when those defects are removed through the knowledge of reality, it becomes manifest. Thus, identity exists by its own nature, and therefore difference and the conventional usage based upon it are merely adventitious (*aupādhika*). Consequently, the difference described in the *Gītā* is unreal, whereas the non-difference stated in "Vāsudeva is everything" is real.

Regarding this, they say: since many scriptural passages such as "Two birds... and "When he sees... are found to be intent upon duality, the non-duality described in the *Gītā* is untenable. Furthermore: "Those whose purpose is well-ascertained through the knowledge of Vedānta, who are ascetics engaged in renunciation, and whose being is purified..."

Regarding the preceding mantra, "They all, at the time of the final end, are completely liberated from the supreme immortality in the worlds of Brahman" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 6.20), it is heard in scripture that those qualified persons—having acquired mastery over the Vedas and all the scriptures following them through diligent study of the Śāstra of Brahma-mīmāṃsā, and having surrendered all their actions to the Lord—go to Satyaloka; dwelling there for a long time, they receive instruction from its ruler, the Four-faced One (Brahmā), and by specifically realizing the true nature of the Lord, they become liberated at the conclusion of that life-span.

By this seventh mantra, that very process is shown: "The Person consists of sixteen parts; upon the cessation of fifteen parts, he becomes liberated. In this context, the "parts" (*kalā*) are the sixteen entities—beginning with *prāṇa*—which are the cause for the individual soul (*jīva*) to maintain the body. And they are as follows: "He created *prāṇa*; from *prāṇa*, faith, space, air, light, water, earth, the senses, mind, food; from food, vigor, austerity, sacred formulas, action, worlds, and in those worlds, name" (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 6.2).

The six questions mentioned [in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad] are to be understood as follows: therein, *prāṇa* is inhalation and exhalation; *śraddhā* is the intellect of faith (*āstikyabuddhi*); *anna* is edible matter; *vīrya* is the substance that causes the production of the body; *tapas* is the vow that is the means for attaining knowledge; *mantras* are the *ṛg*-verses and so forth; *karman* is action in the form of merit and demerit; *loka* is the physical sphere (*golaka*), the locus of the senses; *nāma* is [names] such as Devadatta; *pratiṣṭhāḥ* are the sustainers of the body; *kalāḥ* are the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, as well as the deities presiding over them; and *karmāṇi* are meritorious deeds, as well as the deity presiding over them.

All the gods—everyone other than those who identify with the constituent parts (*kalā*)—reside within the living beings (*jīva*), who are like reflections. Then, the self consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya ātmā*), which is the individual soul (*jīva*), and all the gods (both those identifying with the *kalās* and others), become one in the imperishable, unchanging, supreme Self (*paramātman*). Just as in expressions such as "in this task all the ministers and others become one," the meaning is that they become of one mind; so too, in the state of the supreme Self, they become of one mind and do not disagree.

This is the meaning: (the supreme Self is the overseer, and we are all His servants—thus they become firm-minded); or else, it means that being single-minded, they perform the action ordained by the supreme Self; or else, it means that they come to abide in one place together with the supreme Self. Only in this sense is the suffix *cv* appropriate.

For the suffix *cvī* is prescribed in the sense of "becoming what one was not" (*abhūtatadbhāva*) by the rule: "The suffix *cvī* occurs after a word denoting an agent when used with the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, or *as*, in the sense of *saṃpad* (attainment)" (Pāṇini 5.4.50). In this context, the expression "becoming what one was not" (*abhūtatadbhāva*) is a statement by Kātyāyana. Its meaning is as follows: when it is intended to express the arising of a thing that previously did not possess a certain attribute, in that very attribute.

Consequently, the meaning of the sūtra is that the suffix *cvī* occurs in its own sense after a word denoting an object that is about to arise as a possessor of an attribute qualified by its own prior absence, through the relation of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

The proponents of duality (*bhedavādin*), who follow Pāṇini, may argue that because single-mindedness and other such qualities were previously absent, once ignorance is removed by knowledge and liberation is attained through the grace of Vāsudeva, those qualities come into being; thus, the suffix *cv-* occurs in the word *eka* to denote an object characterized by the property of having single-mindedness and so forth which was previously non-existent. However, this cannot be said by those who maintain non-duality (*ekatvavādin*) and consider themselves followers of Pāṇini.

In their view, since both unity (*ekatva*) and greatness (*bṛhattva*) are eternally existent (*sat*), it is impossible to establish the aforementioned grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between that [quality] and its absence. Nor should it be argued that even if unity and so forth are eternal, the suffix *cvī* can be easily explained by taking into account the prior non-existence of their manifestation; for the meaning of the rule [Pāṇini 5.4.50] is that *cvī* occurs after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) when one intends to express the production of a thing in a form characterized by a particular attribute, and thus that attribute is presented through that very form.

For this very reason, there is no usage of the form *ekīkaroti* in the sense of *śuklīkaroti* (he makes white). In the present context, since the word *eka* lacks the capacity to convey manifestation (*abhivyakti*) as such, it is impossible to apply the suffix *cvi*. Nor should one argue that—just as it is stated in the *Mañjūṣā* and *Uddyota* that the *cvi* in *brahmībhavati* is Vedic (*chāndasa*)—here too the *cvi* is Vedic and has its own meaning (*svārthika*). This is because, since the formation is established by the aforementioned rule itself, it is improper to assume it is Vedic or anything else.

Regarding the statement *brahmībhavati*, the *Śekhara*—citing the rule *kṛbhvasti* from the *Kaumudī*—states: "In this case, the agency of becoming (*bhavanakartratva*) must be understood as belonging to the very non-Brahmin who is the base (*prakṛti*), through its identity with the modification (*vikāra*). However, in the *Mañjūṣā* and other works, it is said that the suffix * cvi* occurs in its own sense (*svārthe*). One should reflect upon which of these is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

Nor should it be argued that the *Śekhara* is devoted solely to describing the intention of the *Kaumudī*, whereas the *Mañjūṣā* reveals its own established doctrine; for in the *Śekhara*, after beginning with "In reality, but others [say]... and so forth, it does not state, "The suffix *cv-* is [used] because of its being Vedic," as is stated elsewhere. Thus, there is no evidence for such an assumption.

If it is argued that [the suffix *cvi*] is postulated for the sake of achieving non-contradiction, then—due to the absence of a decisive criterion (*vinigamanāviraha*)—one could say that the very argument regarding the suffix *ṇa*, *ji*, and so forth, is intended merely to describe the intention of another (i.e., the opponent). Furthermore, the suffix *cvi* occurs only when there is the attainment of a superimposed state upon something that is not actually such; for this very reason, the *Śekhara* states: "The suffix *cvi* does not occur when greatness, which is not primary, arises as primary through the grace of God and so forth. According to this principle, one must also admit here that identity is superimposed. And since, in that [opponent's] view, what is superimposed is false (*mithyā*), real identity would not be established.

Furthermore, even if the suffix *cvipratyaya* is accepted in its reflexive sense (*svārthe*), since this would only yield the meaning "Brahman possesses Brahman-hood," the desired conclusion—that the individual soul attains the state of Brahman—would remain unestablished.

In the eighth mantra, because it is stated that "one attains the divine Person" (*puruṣam upaiti divyam*), the interpretation of the phrase "they become one" (*ekībhavanti*) as referring to identity of essential nature (*svarūpa-aikya*) is weak. Furthermore, in the ninth mantra, by the statement "he becomes Brahman itself" (*brahmaiva bhavati*), it is likewise taught that there is only the attainment of Brahman; nor should it be said that its meaning is the state of the individual soul (*jīva*) becoming Brahman, for in that very context, the Śaṅkara-bhāṣya explains that the word "becomes" (*bhavati*) has the sense of "attaining" (*prāpnoti*).

And thus—having first explained that the word *puruṣa* in the preceding mantra refers to Brahman, the meaning of that very preceding mantra is further elucidated by the ninth mantra; therefore, even the "becoming immortal" mentioned in the final sentence of the ninth mantra is a secondary confirmation (*anukīla*) of this same point. Its meaning is that "one becomes liberated. For this very reason, it is said in the *Gītā*: "Having come to Me, the high-souled ones, having attained supreme perfection, do not undergo rebirth, which is transient and an abode of suffering."
"From the world of Brahmā down to the mortal realm, O Arjuna, those who attain perfection return again;

but for one who has attained Me, O son of Kuntī, there is no rebirth" (8.15–16). By stating "you shall come to Me alone" (Gītā 9.34; 15.65), the attainment of the Lord is declared as the supreme fruit for the yogins devoted to the Lord, and not identity with Him. His intention is that attainment is not identity.

(3) Now, one might object: since the *Vājasaneyaka* states, "Being Brahman, he merges into Brahman" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 4.4.6), the fact that merging into Brahman is described as occurring within Brahman itself implies that the state of being Brahman exists even prior to liberation; thus, there is no difference [between the pre-liberation and post-liberation states]. To this, they reply: the meaning of the scripture is that the word "Brahman" refers to the individual soul (*jīva*), so that "being Brahman"—meaning while still delimited by the state of being a soul (that is, without yet having abandoned the condition of being a soul)—he "merges into," or reaches, Brahman, the Supreme Self. Thus is the sense of the Śruti.

Even in liberation, the individual soul (*jīva*) is not independent; rather, by virtue of being the property of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), it exists entirely dependent upon Him. This alone is the intended meaning of the non-abandonment of the state of being a soul in liberation. Nor should it be doubted that the word "Brahman" does not denote the individual soul. For in the commentary on the *Jijñāsā* section, in the explanation of Śaṅkara’s Bhāṣya—"For this very reason, one should not suspect that the word 'Brahman' has a different referent such as a genus (*jāti*) and so forth"—Ānandagiri states in his *Nyāyanirṇaya*: "By the word 'and so forth' (*ādi*), the inclusion of the individual soul (*jīva*), the lotus-seated one (*kamalāsana*), and the collection of sounds (*śabdarāśi*) is intended. Thus, there is no dispute regarding its denotation of the individual soul.

(4) If it is argued that non-difference is logical because the identity of Brahman and the world is stated by the Śruti text, "All this, indeed, is Brahman," we say no; for it has been established that the Śruti does not intend non-difference as its primary purport.

(5) Nor can it be said that the statement, "I am Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10), expresses the identity of the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman; for that passage—beginning with "In the beginning, this was indeed Brahman; it knew only itself"—does not have the identity of the soul and Brahman as its intended meaning, since it is a declaration of "I am Brahman."

The meaning of the scriptural passage is as follows: "In the beginning, before the world, Brahman alone existed; that Brahman knew itself, [thinking] 'I am Brahman'; from that cause of such knowledge, it became all, it became full"—this is the state of things prior to creation. How can this sentence, which signifies that the knowledge "I am Brahman" arose in Brahman, serve as a proof for the non-difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (Īśvara)?

Now, one might object: "By the subsequent passage beginning with 'Whosoever among the gods...', it is stated that whosoever among the gods and others is the qualified aspirant knows that Brahman; and Vāmadeva also, seeing this very Brahman, [said] 'This is indeed so even today. Since it is declared—by way of restating the knowledge of the meditator—that 'He who knows this, 'I am Brahman,' becomes all this,' the identity of the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) is established. If this is argued, we say: no.

In this regard, the statement "I am Brahman" (*ahaṃ brahmāsmi*) is not a restatement of the knowledge derived from meditation; rather, it is a restatement of a portion of such passages as "That [Self] made itself... (*tad ātmānam*). By this, the sentence "Brahman indeed... (*brahma vā*) and others contained within that context are indicated. This is because the meaning understood from it is precisely this: "He who now knows that very Brahman which was described in the preceding passage, 'Brahman indeed was this in the beginning,' and which is well-known as being eternally perfect and so forth, like one possessed of such knowledge."

Consequently, this [passage] is not capable of establishing the identity of the self; for even though it is a restatement of the knowledge of the worshipper, the description of the meaning "I am similar to Brahman" is possible even when there is no actual identity, and thus its purport does not lie in identity. In this context—in such expressions as "he knew" (avet) or "he became" (abhavat)—the past tense is not intended to be significant, because the Self's knowledge of its own nature is perfect and its existence is eternal.

(6) Now, one might object: In the fourth [chapter] of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, within the Upakosala-vidyā (ChāU 4.10–15), three fires—the Gārhapatya, Anvāhāryapacana, and Āhavanīya—are taught to Upakosala. Therein, we hear the instruction regarding the identity between the Self and the Person residing in the sun, the moon, and lightning, expressed as: "The Person who is in the sun... the Person who is in the moon... the Person who is in lightning—He am I, He indeed am I. Therefore, if it is argued that the oneness of the Self is established by scripture (*śrauta*), we say: no.

In all three statements, such as "I am that," the meaning is either "I am dependent on Him" or "I am similar to Him. If identity with the Self were intended here, then in all three instructional passages, one should have simply said, "The person who is in the sun," rather than mentioning the different locations such as the moon; thus, the mention of the distinction between the locations of the moon and so forth would be redundant.

Nor should it be said that the mention of the difference in stations is for the purpose of making known that the Person residing in the sun and so forth is one and the same; for such a knowledge is not relevant here. Nor should it be argued that even in the view of the dualists, the statement regarding the difference in stations such as the moon is redundant, since the difference [of the Self] from those dependent on the sun and so forth is established simply by stating its dependence on the Self.

The statement of non-difference between those [presiding deities] is for the purpose of teaching that there is no difference in essence among all inner controllers (*antaryāmin*), while acknowledging the multiplicity of their respective substrates (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and those they govern. However, one who maintains absolute unity (*aikyavādin*) cannot speak in this manner, because he must propound only that which is accepted by the doctrine of unity as being pure unity itself. Furthermore, it must be asked of the proponent of unity: do you accept the identity of the Sun and the Person within it, or not?

If he says "I accept [this]," then the designation ought to be "the sun is the person" (*ādityaḥ puruṣa*), and not with a sense of difference as in "the person in the sun" (*āditye puruṣa*). If he says "no," then it must be stated that the proponents of difference can easily say that for others as well, there is no identity with the person.

In the *Taittirīya*, however, after briefly introducing the attainment of the supreme Brahman by those who know Brahman in the passage, "The knower of Brahman reaches the Supreme" (*Taittirīya Upaniṣad* 2.1), and having shown there a correspondence with the wording of the mantra, "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite," the text proceeds—starting from "From that very Self, space was produced" (*Taittirīya Upaniṣad* 2.1.7)—to describe the characteristics of the aforementioned Brahman as the creator of the world and so forth, through the Brahman-texts, as well as the gradations within bliss.

Having examined the second chapter, and having established—through the dialogue between father and son in the Bhṛguvalli—the very definition of Brahman as the cause of the world as stated in the second chapter, and having shown the method of meditation, the Veda-Person clarifies the meaning of the fruit-statement found in the mantra "He attains all" (*so 'śnute sarvān*) by means of the passage beginning with "having departed from this world" (*asmāl lokāt pretya*, Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.10.5); thus, through both summary and detailed exposition, he declares the very distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*para*).

In this regard, the following is heard in scripture: "Having departed from this world, having reached this self consisting of food, then the self consisting of vital breath, then the self consisting of mind, then the self consisting of consciousness, then the self consisting of bliss—he moves about through these worlds, eating what he desires and assuming whatever form he desires, singing this Sāman. (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.10), and so forth.

Having prescribed the worship of the Blessed One both with reference to the self (*adhyātma*) and with reference to the deities (*adhideva*) through such passages as, "He who is here in the person and he who is yonder in the sun, he is one; he who knows thus [attains] satisfaction" and "in rain," etc. (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.10.2), the statement "he is one" (*sa ekaḥ*)—which follows the two sentences beginning with "and he who" (*yaśca*) in order to remove any suspicion of duality regarding the Brahman indicated as the object of worship—refers to the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*) of all humans, characterized by the term "person" (*puruṣa*).

By establishing the oneness (non-difference) of the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of all the gods, as exemplified by Āditya, he makes known the absence of difference among all the forms of the Lord who is the inner controller. He states the fruit of the aforementioned meditation and of the knowledge of that absence of difference regarding the form of the inner controller in the passage beginning with "He who knows thus" (*sa evaṃ vid*).

The meaning is this: the qualified seeker who, having thus worshipped the Lord in the manner described, realizes his non-difference from the Inner Ruler (antaryāmin)—that knower, having departed from this world, that is, having gone upward from this body, [attains] that which is denoted by the respective terms such as "consisting of food" (annamaya) and so forth, insofar as it resides within those respective sheaths (kośas).

Having approached—that is, having attained—the Self, which is the Supreme Self (meaning, having become liberated), he is "one who eats desires," that is, one who possesses the enjoyment of desired objects; here the word *anna* refers to objects in general, while the word *kāma* refers to what is desired. The suffix *-in* is added to the *karmadhāraya* compound [to form] *kāmānnī*. He is "one whose form is desire" (*kāmarūpī*); here the word *kāma* refers to what is desired, and the suffix *-in* is added to the *karmadhāraya* compound [to form] *kāmarūpī*, meaning "one who possesses a desired form. Here too, as before, the suffix *-in* is used. Wandering through—traversing—these worlds, such as the earth and others.

This [Sāman] to be described—namely, the specific Sāman beginning with "Hā huva," or rather, this Brahman as Sāman propounded in the scriptures—one should sit singing, performing the chant, and praising it; one should sit wherever there is delight. He shows the Sāman: "Hā huva. This is an indicator of a particular joy born from the attainment of supreme bliss; therefore, there is no need for deliberation regarding its specific meaning. "I am food" means: "I am the sustainer of my own dependents."

"I am an eater of food, one whose nature is the enjoyment of sense-objects," as stated in such passages as "eating, playing, and rejoicing" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.12.3). "I am the maker of *śloka*s," meaning I manifest the glory of Hari everywhere; the sense is that through Hari’s grace everywhere, such good fortune has come to me. He says, "I am the first-born," referring to this entire state of the liberated Four-faced One (Brahmā): "I am the first-born of the *ṛta*," which is the Lord Hari, who is of the nature of knowledge or Truth.

To the question "Why is it called 'first'?", he says: "In the beginning He existed" (Muṇḍaka 1.1.1); "He who first creates Brahmā and who indeed sends forth the Vedas to him; that God, the light of self-knowledge, I seek as my refuge, desiring liberation" (Śvetāśvatara 6.18); "Hiraṇyagarbha arose in the beginning; once born, He was the sole Lord of all that exists."

"He supported this earth and this heaven; to which god shall we offer worship with oblation? (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 8.7.3). From such passages, it is heard that the Four-faced One (Brahmā) was the first to be born. Furthermore, he is the "navel" (*nābhi*), meaning the support, of the "immortals" (*amṛta*), that is, the class of liberated beings; for the word *nābhi* is well-known in its sense of "support," as in the phrase "like spokes in the nave of a wheel. [And as stated in the Brahma Sūtra: "The effect [is dissolved] in the Word, because the movement [of the soul] is thus established" (4.3.10): "When the dissolution of the world arrives, they all, together with Brahman..."

From such passages as, "At the end of the Supreme, those whose self is the Supreme enter the supreme state," it is understood that because the four-faced Brahmā (the *kāryabrahman*) is mentioned therein, and because his entry into the supreme state along with [the liberated soul] is declared, he serves as the locus for the liberated; furthermore, because it is stated that at the end of the Supreme one enters the supreme state together with him, it is known that he is the one who leads [the soul] to the Supreme Brahman (*parabrahman*).

Regarding the passage, "He leads them to Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.15), the meaning is as follows: "He" refers to the non-human person (*puruṣa*); "them" refers to the liberated souls; and "to Brahman" means he leads or causes them to attain both the effected Brahman (*kāryabrahma*) and the supreme Brahman (*parabrahma*). In this context, the distinction is that the human person is Vāyu, and the [other] is the four-faced one (Brahmā). Vāyu leads them to the effected Brahman, while the four-faced one leads them to the supreme Brahman. Furthermore, the scriptural text, "This is the bridge to immortality" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.5), declares that Hari is the refuge of all liberated souls.

Having thus revealed his own glory attained through the study of the Śārṅga [Purāṇa] and the practice of recitation, he says "He who" (*yaḥ*), meaning that another teacher as well will attain whatever happiness is appropriate for them. He who is the qualified person (*adhikārī*) gives—that is, instructs—these authorities (*māḥ*), namely the scriptures (*śāstrāṇi*) which establish the preeminence of Viṣṇu, to others who are worthy. That qualified person, *it eva* (from this very fact), experiences exactly such happiness as is suitable for himself.

(But it is not the state of being the first-born). "He gives"—this is an elliptical expression that includes hearing and other activities appropriate to oneself. "Mā mām... avāḥ" (Do not let him... burn me); because of Vedic usage, there is a transposition of persons, resulting in the middle voice (*madhyama-puruṣa*). Since in the list of roots beginning with "ava in the sense of protection," the reading "dīpty-avāpti-āliṅgana" (shining, obtaining, embracing) exists, the root has the sense of "attaining.
And he who shall study this righteous dialogue of ours—by him I shall have been worshipped through the sacrifice of knowledge; such is my conviction.
Even that man who, possessing faith and free from malice, should merely hear this,
he too shall be liberated and attain the auspicious worlds of those who have performed meritorious deeds.

Thus it is understood, for the Blessed One has stated that the attainment of auspicious worlds is the fruit for both the teacher and the listener. In this verse, the word "sa" (he) refers to the teacher, while the particle "api" (also) includes the listener. "I am the food"—I am the sustainer of all; "food" here means the food of Hari. In this context, "being food" means "that which is being eaten. "I eat"—I consume the one who eats, namely, the enjoyer of the fruits of karma. By the command of Hari, I withdraw everything. The underlying sense is that since all beings are dependent on the Lord, performing the tasks ordained by Him is their inherent duty (*dharma*).

"I have surpassed the entire world and all that moves; I have become superior through my qualities," meaning "I am the best by virtue of my attributes. If one asks, "In that case, are you independent? he says: "Suvarṇajyotiḥ" (He whose light is the Golden One). He is one whose light—the Supreme Self—is the impeller. This refers to the phrase "this [world]. I am impelled by the Supreme Self, which is flawless supreme bliss; that is to say, I am dependent upon Him. "Ya evam" (he who is thus...).

He who is Viriñca—who knows thus, "I am dependent [on Hari], and by the grace of Hari I have become one possessed of the fortune previously described"—the connection with the preceding phrase is: "he remains singing the Sāman.

By describing that experience of the Four-faced One (Brahmā) as the primary qualified recipient, the Veda-Puruṣa teaches through this illustration that all liberated souls, according to their respective fitness, are entitled to experience bliss in liberation.

In this context, because the attainment of Brahman, its praise, the chanting of the *sāman*, and so forth are described, the purport of the Śruti is that there is indeed difference [between the soul and Brahman] even in liberation. The state of being "possessed of Brahman" (*brahmavattva*), which is the fruit of the meditation on the nature of Brahman as taught in the sentence, "One should meditate upon it as 'Brahman'; he becomes possessed of Brahman'" (*Taittirīya Upaniṣad* 3.10), is likewise merely the possession of the qualities of Brahman, and not identity with It. This is precisely how this passage has been explained by the learned masters, beginning with Saṅkarācārya.

Now, if it is argued that even this scriptural distinction between liberation (*mukti*) is merely conceptual (*kālpnika*), we say no. This is because, in the state of liberation, there is no persistence of *māyā*, nor is there any other basis for its conceptualization; thus, there is no evidence for its reality in that state. Furthermore, as for the claim that there is a distinction between primary and secondary liberation in liberation, and that the scriptural texts regarding the "fruit" (*phala-śruti*) refer only to secondary liberation—such views may be advanced by the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇas*) according to their own whims, but there is no binding authority for them here.

By such passages as, "These true desires are covered by untruth" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.3.1), it is established that the true desires and other attributes, which are veiled in saṃsāra by ignorance and the like, become manifest upon liberation when ignorance is removed; therefore, in liberation, desires and so forth possess only reality and not the nature of *māyā*.

Now, if it be argued that—since in this very Upaniṣad it is stated that Brahman alone undergoes manifoldness in the passage, "He desired: 'May I be many, may I procreate'" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6), and since it is stated that He alone entered everywhere in the passage, "He entered into that very [creation]" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6), and because there is no self other than Him, non-difference alone is logical—it is replied: the Lord Himself enters everywhere as the controller in His manifold forms; this is the meaning of those passages, for in the Vājasaneyi [Saṃhitā], the state of being the inner ruler of the individual souls (*jīvāntaryāmitva*) is taught by virtue of His being the controller of the souls.

Furthermore, because the Antaryāmī Brāhmaṇa states that there is no difference between the forms of the Blessed Lord, and because there is a lack of evidence for the existence of a self distinct from the Blessed Lord—this being the intended meaning—the non-establishment of the identity between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*) has been explained at length elsewhere.

(8) Now, an objection: In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, in the fourth [chapter], fourth [section], and the sixth [chapter], fifth [section], after negating duality through such passages as "Where there is, as it were, duality" and "Then one smells another, one sees another" (Bṛ. 4.4.6, 6.5.15), and having taught the absence of any entity other than the Self by means of the statement indicating that in liberation nothing remains but the Self alone—"But where the Self has become all this, then by what and whom should one smell, by what and whom should one see?"—it is further stated regarding the liberated ones: "After departing, there is no consciousness."

If it is argued that the absence of knowledge has been established, and since that [absence] is necessarily caused by the absence of objects, it is therefore known that in liberation there is only the oneness of the Self (*ātmaikatva*), we reply: by that cited scriptural statement, neither the absence of difference in liberation nor the mere persistence of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) is understood as the absence of knowledge. If by that [statement] the absence of knowledge were being propounded, then the absence of the Self itself would have been indicated, because the Self is of the very nature of knowledge (*jñāna*).

Furthermore, if one were to understand that the fruit of self-knowledge (*ātmajñāna*) is indeed the destruction of the self (*ātmanāśa*), no one would exert themselves in hearing or other means for its attainment. And in the absence of such engagement, the injunctions regarding it would become useless, rendering the entire Śāstra purposeless. However, the meaning of the phrase "there is knowledge" (*saṃjñānam asti*) is as follows: the word *saṃjñā* is derived with the suffix *aṅ* in the sense of the object (*karman*) according to Pāṇini Sūtra 3.3.106 (*ātaścopasarge*), and thus it denotes the object of knowledge (*jñānaviṣaya*).

The meaning is that a person who has passed away and remains liberated no longer possesses the consciousness of those who are not liberated; that is to say, one who is not liberated does not perceive the liberated soul.

The meaning of the passage "where, as it were, there is duality" (*yatra hi dvaitamiva*) is as follows: the term *dvaita* means "dual" (*dvīta*), that is, characterized by two modes or characterized by duality (which is to say, possessed of difference). From that, in the sense of "the state of being that," the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to Pāṇini’s rule *hāyanāntayuvādibhyo’ṇ* (5.1.13); because it belongs to the *yuvan*-class, the form *dvaita* results, signifying "difference. Thus, when—i.e., at which time—there is duality, that is, difference, then one smells the other, sees [the other], and so forth.

And thus, it is stated that smelling, seeing, and so forth, are pervaded by duality. Here, the mention of "smelling" and the rest is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for "eating," "sporting," "enjoying," and so on, as mentioned in such passages as *Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 8.12.3: "Eating, sporting, enjoying. The word "for" (*hi*) indicates that this is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Now, one might ask: "If the pervasion is already established, what remains to be proven? To this he says: "Or where [there is] the Self... He states an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) if knowledge were not admitted in liberation: "By this, the person knows."

The literal meaning, however, is as follows: when and where the Self alone existed, then by what could one smell whom, or see whom? For [the scripture] says, "He plays, sports, and rejoices," and so forth; thus, he both smells and sees. Consequently, if liberation were the state where only the Self remains, then the scriptural passages indicating such things as "eating" (*jakṣaṇa*) would become invalid. By this, it is logical that the phrase "there is no consciousness" (*saṃjñā nāsti*) means simply that it is not an object of cognition.

Just as a green gram seed thrown into a heap of green gram cannot be distinguished and grasped as "this green gram was thrown by me" due to the homogeneity of the collection, so too, one who has been liberated and enters the assembly of the liberated is not specifically recognized by the liberated ones as "this one is liberated," because he is devoid of the ordinary name and form. This is the intended meaning.

Furthermore, in the sixth section [of the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad*], after prescribing the expulsion from the country of one who knows Brahman and so forth as being "other than the Self" (*anyatrātmanaḥ*)—as in the passage, "The Brahmin is excluded, he who knows Brahman as other than the Self" (6.4.6)—the final sentence of that same section teaches the non-difference of all things, including Brahman, from the Self: "All this is what this Self is. By this, the identity of the Self is established; and because of that very identity, it is stated that there is no existence of the Self elsewhere.

And thus, it must be stated that the act of expulsion prescribed for one who knows [the deity] to be situated elsewhere results specifically for one who possesses the knowledge of such a distinction. This is because the sentence "That which this Self..."—which is engaged in order to dispel the doubt raised by the prohibition of [the deity's] residence elsewhere, namely, "Are Brahmā and the others without a support?"—does not convey non-difference; for its meaning is: "All this previously mentioned [deities] like Brahmā, wherever they abide, [abide in] this Self, the Supreme Self, who is the support of all.
Thus, [the deities] like Brahmā are not without support, but rather exist depending upon the Supreme Self.
The gods have taken refuge in Rudra; Rudra has taken refuge in Brahmā;
Brahmā has eternally taken refuge in me; but I have not taken refuge in anyone.

This is because of the words of the Blessed One, as well as the statements in the *Gītā*: "All beings dwell in Me" (9.4) and "All this is strung upon Me, like clusters of jewels on a thread" (7.7). Furthermore, the word *yad* is either a locative form with its case-ending elided according to Pāṇini’s rule *supāṃ suluk* (7.1.39), or it is an indeclinable. Nor should it be argued that the statement "Whatever else one knows apart from Brahman" (*yo 'nyatra brahma veda*)—which prescribes a fault for knowing [Brahman] elsewhere—already establishes that abiding in the Self is the correct position, rendering the sentence "Whatever this... (*yadayam*) redundant.

By that very [reasoning], since even Brahmā and the others are shown to be without support through dependent origination, the self-supporting nature [of a creator] cannot be established. Furthermore, this "Self" taught as the object of injunctions such as the hearing [of the scriptures] in passages like "The Self, indeed, is to be seen" is none other than the Supreme Self (paramātman).

(9) Now, one might argue that the mantra found in the *Īśāvāsya Upaniṣad*—“When for the knower all beings have become the Self alone, what delusion, what sorrow can there be for him who perceives oneness?”—is proof for the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*), since it describes the fruit of such knowledge as the absence of delusion and sorrow. To this, they reply: this mantra, beginning with “in which” (*yasmin*) and ending with “there” (*tatra*), [refers to the state of liberation].

The sixth mantra, beginning with "He who [sees] all beings," reiterates the Lord's state of being the support of all and His state of being the inner ruler (antaryāmin) of all; for one who perceives the oneness of that which exists in the form of the inner ruler, the absence of delusion and grief is a further result. The reiteration, moreover, serves the purpose of conjunction (*samuccaya*). The intended meaning is that the aforementioned result belongs both to the knower of the Lord as the support of all and the inner ruler of all, and to the knower of His oneness.

The word-for-word construction (*akṣarayojanā*) is as follows: "In whom (*yasmin*), Hari, all beings (*sarvabhūtāni*) abide (*tiṣṭhanti*); in those beings (*tatra bhūteṣu*), the Self alone (*ātmaiva*), which is indeed Hari, has come into being (*abhūt*)—that is, it exists; the past tense is not intended [to be significant here]. The rest is easy to understand. However, if one attempts to construe this with the intent of establishing the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*), the use of the locative case becomes untenable; this is explained at length elsewhere. To say more: "He is the bridge to immortality" (*Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad* 2.2.5), "Singing this Sāman, he sits" (*Taittirīya Upaniṣad* 3.10.4), "The supreme goal of the liberated," and "Because of the designation of Him as that which is to be approached by the liberated" (*Brahmasūtra* 1.3.2).

1.3.2) Because of such designations as the Supreme Self’s being the liberated support, His being the object of their praise, and His being served by them, there is indeed a difference between the liberated soul and the Supreme Self even in the state of liberation. For this very reason, the Śruti passage, "The others live upon a mere fraction of this very bliss" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.3.32), states that the liberated ones experience an enjoyment similar to a single portion of the Lord's bliss.

Because it is stated that the bliss of the Blessed One is His very nature in the passage, "Ānanda knew Brahman" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.4.3), and because it is established by universal experience that the bliss of one cannot be attained by another—since it is difficult for anyone else to experience the bliss of another—it follows that other beings, namely liberated souls (*muktajīvas*), subsist upon and experience only a "fragment of bliss," meaning a bliss similar to that [of the Lord]. This is so because verbal roots have multiple meanings; the root *jīv* (to live) is used here in the sense of "experiencing."

Regarding the mantra from the *Īśāvāsya Upaniṣad*, "I am that very Person," since that which exists in Pūṣan and others also exists in Prāṇa, the meaning is "I am he"—meaning I am dependent upon him or similar to him—and thus there is no intention to convey non-difference; enough of this prolixity.

Because the Vedas and other scriptures are declared to be infinite in the Śruti and Smṛti texts—such as "The Vedas are indeed endless" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 1.3.6) and "The scripture is infinite; much remains to be known"—it is impossible for a person to master all the scriptures within a human lifespan. Therefore, the Lord Gītācārya, in the fifteenth chapter of the Gītā within the *Sarvasāstrārthasaṃgraha*, instructs Arjuna that the very essence of all scriptures is the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*). Consequently, that alone is the meaning of all scriptures, which should be grasped by the wise. For in that regard, the Lord said: [The verse follows: *“I know the beings of the past and the present, and those of the future, O Arjuna; but no one knows Me.””* Thus, the wise should discern that this distinction alone is the purport of all sacred teachings. In that context, the Lord further declares: [The verse follows: *“The world is deluded by the pairs of opposites arising from desire and aversion; therefore, O Kaunteya, none are free from them except those who take refuge in Me.”* Hence, the wise should understand that the essential meaning of all scriptures is precisely this distinction.
There are these two persons in the world: the perishable and the imperishable.
The perishable consists of all beings, while the one who is unchanging is called the imperishable.
But the Supreme Person is another, declared as the Supreme Self (Paramātman),
the imperishable Lord who, pervading the three worlds, sustains them.
Since I transcend the perishable and am superior even to the imperishable,
therefore I am celebrated in this world and in the Veda as Puruṣottama, the Supreme Person.
He who, being thus undeluded, knows me as the Supreme Person—
he, O Bhārata, knowing all, worships me with his whole being.
Thus has this most secret scripture been spoken by me, O sinless one;
by understanding this, O Bhārata, one becomes wise and capable of performing his duty.

(Gītā 15.13–20). The meaning of these verses is as follows: there are three categories, namely "the Perishable" (*kṣara*), "the Imperishable" (*akṣara*), and "the Lord" (*īśvara*). Among these, by the term "the Perishable," one should understand the general category of conscious and unconscious entities characterized by the property of perishing, because it is stated right here [in verse 16]: "The Perishable is all beings. By the term "the Imperishable," one should understand the eternal entity devoid of the property of perishing, because it is called "the Unchanging" (*kūṭastha*). According to the *Paspāśāhnika* of the *Mahābhāṣya*, which states "by the unchanging and immovable ones," the word *kūṭastha* is accepted as having the meaning of "eternal."

Such is the nature of Lakṣmī; however, the perishable nature of the conscious being (cetana) is mediated through the body and other effects of *prakṛti*. This state of the person (*puruṣa*) pertains to both [Lakṣmī and the individual soul]. Consequently—[distinguished] from the two classes of Lakṣmī and her other conscious and unconscious entities—the Person who is distinct is the Supreme (*uttama*). If one asks who that is, he says: "the Supreme Self" (*paramātman*). The meaning is: he who is described as such in the scriptures.

He states its uncommon attribute: "He who" refers to that Supreme Self, the Lord who is the master of all, the imperishable one, and the performer of the sustaining and nourishing of the three worlds, as has been declared. He clearly explains the ground for applying the term *Puruṣottama* with the words "because."

One who, being undeluded—that is, free from confusion—knows Me, the Supreme Person, in the manner described above, is all-knowing; he knows the meaning of all scriptures, because it is stated in every scripture exactly thus. With his whole being—in all the aforementioned ways such as recognizing My nature as the Supreme Person—he worships Me (meaning, he regards Me as the one to be worshipped). This is the most secret scripture, the scripture that teaches the duties that must necessarily be performed, or the dharma prescribed by the scriptures.

This scripture has been taught; having understood—that is, known—it, the wise one, who possesses discernment regarding what ought to be done, and for that very reason is "one who has accomplished his task" (kṛtakṛtyaḥ)—meaning he would have performed his duty by both hearing this true scripture and practicing its meaning—such is the connection [of the words]. The rest is clear. The Supreme Self, denoted by the term Puruṣottama, who is distinct from the entire multitude of the moving and unmoving world, is the subject expounded by the scripture; the sense is that for one who knows Him and is blessed, birth becomes fruitful.

The term *sarvabhāvena* is a *karmadhāraya* compound; the word *bhāva* denotes the modes (such as being the Supreme Person, etc. previously mentioned. For this very reason, the prior description of the Lord’s supremacy over all and so forth is purposeful. If one who desires liberation does not worship Him in this manner, that description would be useless in the scripture, because the purpose of describing the qualities is to result in knowledge and meditation.

Alternatively, the meaning may be: "with my entire being," that is, by way of being the father and so forth, as stated in *Gītā* 9.17, "I am the father of this world"; or, it may mean "with complete conviction" (*saṃpūrṇapramṇā*), which is to say, with supreme devotion (*paramabhaktyā*). As for the interpretation of those who follow Nāgeśa—who explain the compound *sarvabhāvena* as a genitive *ṣaṣṭhī*-tatpuruṣa, meaning "the state of all," and thus the sense of the sentence "he worships in every form" (*sarvarūpeṇa bhajati*)—that explanation is not to be respected.

If that were the case, then only the "all-formedness" (*sarvarūpatva*) would need to be established first, rather than the "supremacy of the Person" (*puruṣottamatva*) and so forth. And thus, it is the intention of the Teacher of the Gītā that the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) is the meaning of all the scriptures. It has been previously demonstrated that this very same intention belongs to Pāṇini as well.
In the Rāmānuja school, the terms "the Perishable" (*kṣara*) and "the Imperishable" (*akṣara*) are explained as referring to the groups of the liberated and the unliberated.

In the Śaṅkara school, however, the term "the Perishable" refers to the collection of transformations (*vikāra*), while the term "the Imperishable" refers to the seed of the origin of the Person denoted by the term "the Perishable."

In this manner, other scriptural and traditional statements as well, which appear to be non-dualistic, should be interpreted as being dualistic; and indeed they have been so interpreted by the proponents of Brahman (Brahmavādins) elsewhere through the presentation of many proofs, establishing them as having the intent of duality between Brahman and the individual soul (jīva). Furthermore, in every Vedānta text and in every specific teaching, the descriptions of creation and so forth, as well as the descriptions of the relationship between the object of worship and the worshipper between Brahman and the jīva, demonstrate the superiority of Vāsudeva and have the intended meaning of the distinction between Brahman and the jīva—this has been elaborated at length by those very same authors.

By this [it is shown that] what was stated by Mañjūṣā—namely, "In every Vedānta, the description of creation and so forth is for the purpose of establishing the unity of the Self"—is refuted; as well as what was stated therein: "The sentence 'That thou art' (*tat tvam asi*) and others possess a non-differentiated meaning (*akhaṇḍārtha*), [denoting] even the pure Brahman through a superimposed identity. Furthermore, on the occasion of Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the Bhāṣya—which is intent upon explaining the meaning of the Ṛgvedic verse "Four are the horns" (*catvāri śṛṅgā*, ṚV 3.8.10)—it was said: "The word has manifested its own non-difference"; and on the occasion of determining the purport of the Śruti passage "Like flour" (*saktum iva*), it was said: "[The verbs] have the same verbal suffix" (*samānakhyātayaḥ*).

Because the apprehension of difference has ceased, [the doctrine] is contradicted by all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and is not accepted by Vyāsa, Pāṇini, and Patañjali; for it has been stated that the description of creation and so forth serves to establish the excellence that constitutes the basis for Hari being the object of worship.

For this very reason, the Blessed Vyāsa, in the aphorism "From which [proceeds] the origin and so forth of this" (*Brahma-sūtra* 1.1.2), having stated that the creatorship of creation and so forth is the defining characteristic of Brahman—the object of inquiry—indicated thereby its superiority and, consequently, its distinction from the sentient and insentient world. This very distinction thus indicated, he clarifies in almost every section (*adhikaraṇa*) through such [reasons] as "Because of the designation of difference" (*bhedavyapadeśāt*), which demonstrate that [Brahman] possesses qualities not found in the individual soul (*jīva*).

"Grammar should be studied so that we may attain equality with the Great God"—since the commentators have explicitly described the intention of the Vedic verse "four [cows]" (*catvāri*) as being precisely this attainment of equality with the Blessed One for students; and since the commentators did not explain *sakhāyaḥ* and *sakhayāni* as "those who have abandoned the contemplation of the Veda" or as "attainments of union" (*sāyujyāni*), Kaiyaṭa’s and others’ explanations to that effect should be considered doubtful.

Even in the sense of *sāyujya* (union), there is no attainment of identity with the Self, even for those of extremely subtle vision; for the meaning of the term *sāyujya* is simply a specific kind of conjunction that is incapable of being perceived as a distinction [between two entities]. And thus, Kaiyaṭa’s statement that "everything is one" and Nāgeśa’s statement that "there is an abandonment of the notion of difference through the Self" are to be reconsidered. This is because the intended meaning is not obtained according to the literal phrasing of those [statements], and because it is not stated in the Bhāṣya. As for the literal meaning of the Bhāṣya: here, the locative case (*atra*) is either a locative of the object (*viṣaya-saptamī*) or it has the sense of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhy-artha*).

In this context, *brahmaṇam* means "in Brahman" or "as Brahman"; *sakhāyaḥ* means "friends. He states the fruit of friendship with Brahman: "friendships" (*sakhyāni*). The word *sakhyam* ends in the suffix *ya*, according to Pāṇini 5.1.126 (*sakhyuryaḥ*), denoting either the state (*bhāva*) or the action (*karman*). The phrase "of the Vāsudevakas" is to be supplied as the remainder. It means that they obtain friendships—that is, they become friends—with the devotees of Vāsudeva. Here he explains the word [from the verse] with the words "he who is this... (*ya eṣa*).

It is "difficult" (*durga*) because it is accessible only through dwelling in the teacher’s house, the study of the scriptures, and so forth; it is a "path" (*mārga*) that must be sought, according to the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) "That is to be sought," and the word *mārga* is derived from the root *mārg* (of the *cur*-class) with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of the object. It is "accessible by one alone" (*ekagamya*), meaning accessible primarily [through the teacher]; it is "within the scope of speech" (*vāgviṣaya*), meaning established by the scriptures (*śruti*). He states the qualification [for inquiry] by means of a question and answer, beginning with "Who? and so forth. He asks for the reason why they possess this qualification: "Why? He states that very reason: "Because they are auspicious" (*bhadrāḥ*).

In the speech—the organ of speech—of these grammarians, there resides (nihitā) auspiciousness (bhadrā), which consists of the eternal perfection characterized by liberation; that is, the excellence consisting of the capacity to expound the meaning of the Vedas preceded by the analytical distinction of roots, suffixes, and so forth, which is itself the means for the knowledge of Vāsudeva’s supremacy, the instrument for attaining liberation. Alternatively, that excellence which consists in the knowledge that the supremacy of Vāsudeva is the means to liberation is established in their speech—that is, in the Vedas and other scriptures—and that excellence belongs to them.

The intended meaning is as follows: regarding that knowledge of Vāsudeva as the essence of all things—which is declared at the beginning of the Vedas to be the means for attaining liberation—that knowledge belongs exclusively to the grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*), who possess the expertise in expounding the scriptures that produces such knowledge. For they alone are capable of accomplishing the acquisition of knowledge arising from the Vedas and other scriptures, as well as the task of expounding those scriptures; since they have studied the science of words (*śabda-śāstra*) which is the instrument for that [knowledge], it is toward them alone that the grace of the Lord and of His devotees (*bhāgavata*) is directed. It is for these [grammarians]...

This is because they possess the primary qualification for the study and teaching of the true scriptures. As for the plural number in the word *sakhyanī* (of the Sāṅkhyas), it is due to the difference among those who propound them. It has already been established previously that Pāṇini does not accept the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
Wherever the scriptures appear to be mutually contradictory, their meaning should be investigated in accordance with what is perceived [in other parts of the texts].

According to this statement, the apparent contradiction found in sentences such as "Tat tvam asi" (That thou art), which seem to conflict with scriptural texts on difference like "Two birds... (*dvā suparṇā*), must be resolved by determining that their true purport lies in difference alone—by interpreting them as referring to similarity and so forth. "Dṛṣṭam" means direct perception. The literal meaning is that scriptural texts such as "Tat tvam asi" are to be interpreted in a way that does not contradict perception and scripture favorable to perception, thereby removing the perceived contradictions.

However, those scriptures that are consistent with direct perception and are intent upon [the reality of] difference—such as "Two birds, united together... and so forth—should be understood [as authoritative]. This alone is the correct interpretation of the Vedic statements; furthermore, this is the consensus even of the teacher Pāṇini, who intended to convey that Vāsudeva is the supreme among all. Thus say other followers of Pāṇini.

Regarding the three aphorisms beginning with "Because there is no distinction in the production of pleasure, pain, and cognition, [the self] is one" (Vai. 3.2.12), and continuing with "Due to their distribution, they are many" (20) and "And because of the authority of the scriptures" (21), Kaṇāda raised the objection that the self is one and established the plurality of selves as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*). On this point, the authors of the *Upaskāra* commentary and its sub-commentary maintain that by the first [aphorism] the objection of unity is raised, and by the two subsequent ones the conclusion of plurality is established.

The commentator Candrakānta, however, explains the three aphorisms [of Kaṇāda] by asserting that non-duality alone is the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), while plurality is merely adventitious (*aupādhika*). However, since Kaṇāda is categorized as a proponent of difference (*bhedavādin*) in the *Śaṅkara-bhāṣya* and other works, Candrakānta’s interpretation contradicts the original source. Therefore, statements such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) do not have non-duality as their primary purport; consequently, there is no contradiction with difference, which is the view agreed upon by Vyāsa and Pāṇini.

**The Refutation of the Indivisibility of Word and Meaning** Now, [the opponent may argue]: "The word and its meaning, as well as the sentence and its meaning, are indeed indivisible (*akhaṇḍa*). Only the indivisible sentence is the conveyor of the indivisible meaning. As stated in the *Mañjūṣā* during the investigation of linguistic power (*śakti*): "For one of pure mind, both [word and meaning] are conveyors of that which has the indivisible as its object; thus, when the cognition of Brahman arises regarding all conveyors of knowledge, by that very same analogy, the Grammarians maintain the cognition of Brahman regarding all word-meanings," as in the verse beginning with "Like flour" (*saktum iva*). [Response: This is not so. For it is observed that words such as "cow" (*go*) and "horse" (*aśva*), which denote different objects, do not produce a single, unified cognition. Furthermore, since the meanings of words are established through convention (*saṃketa*), they must be divisible. Moreover, if the meaning were indivisible, there would be no distinction between the meaning of a sentence and the meaning of its constituent parts. Consequently, the relationship between word and meaning would be impossible, and the very foundation of grammar would collapse. Therefore, the claim that words and their meanings are indivisible is refuted.

If it is argued that—since this has been stated in the *Paspaśā* section of the *Udyota* commentary on the *Bhāṣya* during the investigation of the meaning of the Śruti—it is established that because Brahman is indivisible and because the cognition of Brahman arises everywhere, everything is indeed Brahman and there is no reality whatsoever apart from Brahman; therefore, it is appropriate to interpret sentences such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) as being intended to convey non-difference (*abheda*)—to this they reply: This is not correct, because the author of the Sūtras and the author of the Bhāṣya have not explained the relevant Śruti passage in that manner.

Because that matter is useless as it lacks connection with the subject matter to be propounded by the present treatise; because the indivisibility of the object (*viṣaya-akhaṇḍatva*) has not been established as a formal conclusion (*siddhānta*) in the Veda, in Pāṇini’s system (*tantra*), or in the *Brahma-mīmāṃsā*; and because grammarians do not possess the notion of "Brahman-hood" (*brahmatva-buddhi*) everywhere, its definition is irrelevant to the present context.

By this, the following [position] should be considered: that the object of the cognition produced by a means of knowledge is indeed an indivisible entity (*akhaṇḍārtha*), because the apprehension of the word’s denotative power (*śakti*) occurs with respect to that which is indicated by its attributes (*dharmopalakṣita*), aided by prohibitive statements such as "not here, no diversity" (*neha nānā*); thus, there is a cognition of precisely that indivisible entity indicated by those attributes. This has been stated in the *Śaktivāda* (Mañjūṣā 4.25), and likewise in the *Vṛttivāda*: "Therefore, according to the Vedāntic view, in sentences such as 'That thou art' (*tat tvam asi*), there is only the cognition of an indivisible entity in the function [of the sentence]" (p. 33). Furthermore, the statement in the *Samarthasiddhi-uddyota*, "Therefore, in the Vedāntic system, in sentences such as 'That thou art', there is only the cognition of an indivisible entity in the function," should be reflected upon.

Since it will be stated later that the sentence "neha nānā" (here is no diversity) does not negate the existence of categories of objects in general other than Brahman, and since this has been established as the settled conclusion (*siddhānta*) elsewhere by the proponents of Brahman (*brahmavādins*), the indivisibility (*akhaṇḍatva*) of Brahman is not proven on the basis of that [sentence] alone. Furthermore, because a mental cognition of the second kind [i.e., non-relational] does not arise in everyone at all times, and because such a cognition resides only in specific individuals—such that a cognition of that nature is not produced in everyone from statements like "tat tvam asi" (that thou art)—[the claim fails]. This is also the case for the venerable Vyāsa and Pāṇini...

Furthermore, Patañjali’s formulation regarding the scope of the subject matter is untenable.
