To explain: first, the example "as in the case of the Vedāntins" is inappropriate, because in their view it is difficult to maintain that the word and its denoted object are non-distinct (*akhaṇḍatva*), since in their system there is no reality other than Brahman that could be considered illusory (*māyika*).

Moreover, by the term "Vedāntin," the Blessed Bādarāyaṇa alone is primarily intended, and not other commentators or sub-commentators, as they lack universal consensus; for only a person universally acknowledged can serve as a valid example.
When his purpose had been thus made known by them, the Blessed One, the Supreme Person and Great Yogi, descended through Parāśara upon Satyavatī.
The Blessed Lord Hari himself retrieved the lost Vedas;
he divided them into four parts and further subdivided them into twenty-four.
In a hundred ways, in one way, and likewise in a thousand ways,
as well as in twelve ways, Kṛṣṇa manifests for the sake of making his true nature known.

"By the authoritative citations cited by the learned scholars, such as: 'He composed the Brahma-sūtras, whose status as sūtras is manifest,' and by the words of the Blessed One, 'I alone am the author of the Vedānta and the knower of the Vedas' (Gītā 15.15), it is established by all that Vyāsa alone is the author of the Vedānta. One should not suspect that the Gītā speaks the truth of Vāsudeva and not of Vyāsa; for both are indeed incarnations of the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa himself.

Someone might disagree [with this] on the grounds that Kṛṣṇa is not distinct from Nārāyaṇa, citing the statement by Śrī Śaṅkarācārya at the beginning of his *Gītā-bhāṣya*: "The Lord Viṣṇu, known as Nārāyaṇa, the primordial creator, was indeed born as Kṛṣṇa through a portion of himself from Vasudeva and Devakī for the sake of protecting Bhauma Brahmā and the status of Brahmanhood"; and because other teachers have likewise stated this elsewhere. However, regarding Vāsudeva, based on the previously cited authorities such as "requested by them" (*tair vijñāpita*), who else could be [the one meant]?

Furthermore, because his status as an incarnation of Nārāyaṇa is understood from such authoritative sources as, "From Puṇḍarīkākṣa was born Bhava, the author of the Mahābhārata," and so forth; for this very reason, the learned follower of the Śāṅkara school stated:
"Śaṅkara is Śiva himself, and in Vyāsa there is Hari, Nārāyaṇa.
When a dispute arises between the two, what shall we do? We are but their servants."

Thus, both the commentary on the portion of the verse beginning with "composed by the great sage" (*mahāmuni-kṛta*) in the *Śrīdhari* commentary on the *Śrīmad Bhāgavatam*, and the statement "by the sage Vyāsa, who is an incarnation of Nārāyaṇa," corroborate that Vyāsa is an incarnation of Nārāyaṇa.

And how could that Vyāsa, in the *Gītā*, elsewhere, and in the *Brahma-mīmāṃsā*, accept the Lord Nārāyaṇa’s possession of numerous qualities such as being the creator of the universe? If that [theistic] reality were his intended view, then the demonstration of the derivation [of the word *brahman*] in the sūtra, "If it be said that [it does not denote Brahman] because of words denoting modification, no; because of abundance" (*Brahma-sūtra* 1.1.13), and so forth—whereby the communication of an object possessing the attributes signified by those respective words—is rendered inconsistent.
Furthermore:
"Whatever names are renowned as secondary designations of the Great Soul..."
I shall declare those verses, sung by the seers, for the sake of prosperity.

Thus, in the *Mahābhārata*, there is a declaration of intent to recount the names of the Blessed One, distinguished by the qualities perceived through the power of the etymological explanations (*nirukti*) shown by the great seers; and in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*: "O Maitreya, the word 'Bhagavat' is applied to the supreme Brahman, which is pure and known as the Great Sovereignty (*mahāvibhūti*), the cause of all causes."

O Sage, the syllable *bha* is endowed with two meanings: it signifies "one who sustains" (*saṃbharta*) and likewise "one who supports" (*bhartṛ*). Similarly, the meaning of the syllable *ga* is "one who leads," "one who causes to go," and "one who creates" (*netā*, *gamayitā*, *straṣṭā*).
Sovereignty, vigor, fame, splendor,
as well as knowledge and discernment— of these six, the term "bhaga" is used.
Beings dwell there within that Self of beings, the Self of all; and He, the imperishable, dwells likewise as the meaning of the syllable *va* within all beings without exception.
In this very way, O Maitreya, the great sound "Bhagavān" belongs to Vāsudeva, who has become the Supreme Brahman; it does not apply to anyone else.
In this context, the expression of the object of worship is endowed with technical definitions;
this word is not used figuratively, whereas elsewhere it is used figuratively.

Thus, having provided an etymological derivation (*nirukti*) for the word *bhagavat*, the assertion that the Blessed Lord—who is understood through that [etymology] as being characterized by attributes such as creatorship—is the denotation of the word *bhagavat* would not be consistent. Consequently, since the integrity of the word and its meaning (*śabdārthākhaṇḍatva*) is not accepted by that venerable Vyāsa, it is improper to cite "the Vedāntins" as an example.

And in the Śruti: "This very Self is in the heart; this is its designation: 'He who is in the heart. Therefore, day after day, one who knows thus goes to the heavenly world" (Chāndogya 8.3.3). "The name of this very Brahman is 'Satya' (Truth)" (Chāndogya 8.3.4). "Now, there are indeed three syllables: *sīt*, *yaṃ*, and *iti*. That which is *sat* is immortal; that which is *ti* is mortal; and by *yaṃ*, he holds both together. Because he holds both together with it, therefore, day after day, one who knows thus [goes to the heavenly world]."

In the Dahara-vidyā, following the explanation of the etymological meanings of the two names of the Lord residing in the space within the heart-lotus—namely *hṛd* and *satya*—and the subsequent description of the fruit for the knower of the Lord as qualified by those [names], and furthermore, after stating that the name *hṛdaya* consists of three syllables in the passage "This very *hṛdaya* has three syllables" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 7.3.1), the *Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā* describes the fruit of meditating upon those three syllables; therefore, the demonstration that words and so forth are indivisible is contrary to the Śruti.

The great sage Pāṇini also does not accept the indivisibility (*akhaṇḍatva*) of words and their meanings, nor of sentences and their meanings, because he teaches specific meanings through his rules (*kārya*). For instance: "The [suffix *ghañ*] is used after the root *antar* when joined with the sense of 'outside' or 'clothing'; after *mṛṣ* in the sense of 'endurance'; and after *prakāśana*, *stheya*, and *ākya*; after *parāji* in the sense of 'not enduring'; after *dhvāṅkṣa* in the sense of 'reproach'; the third case ending is used in the sense of 'completion'; [the suffix *nañ* is used] after those things whose opposition is eternal; after *ava* in the sense of 'necessity'; [the suffix *lyuṭ*] after a verb in the sense of 'characteristic' or 'cause'; and the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is used in the sense of 'cause' and 'that which possesses the cause'."

The suffixes *kuṇḍa* and *goṇa* are added after the word *jānapada*; the suffixes *tumun* and *ṇvul* are added after a verbal root when another action is intended as the purpose of that action; the suffix *yaṅ* is added to a monosyllabic root beginning with a consonant when there is a frequent repetition of the action; the suffix *yat* is added after *rājan* and *śvaśura*; the suffix *kaumārā* is used in the sense of "being from childhood" or "not having been so before"; the suffix *deya* is used in the sense of a debt; the suffix *caraṭ* is used in the sense of "having existed previously"; the suffix *pathaḥ* is used in the sense of "skilled therein"; the suffix *rūpa* is used in the sense of praise; the suffixes *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *asti* are used in the sense of becoming; the suffixes *kṣayya* and *jayya* are used in the sense of possibility; the suffix *saṃparibhyāṃ karotau* is used in the sense of ornamenting; the suffix *nivāce* is used in the sense of protection from wind; the suffix *putre* is optionally used; and the suffix *na* is not applied after the root *añc* in the sense of worship.

The intention behind [the inclusion of] these rules—*tujoḥ stāṅṅāśiṣyanyatarasyām*, *añceḥ pūjāyām*, *varṣasyābhaviṣyati*, *bhiyo hetubhaye ṣuk*, *aśanāyodanyadhanāyā bubhukṣāpipāsāgardheṣu*, *nityavīpsayoḥ*, *rājanvān saurājye*, *praṣṭho'gragāmini*, and *vāhanamāhitāt*—is so that, when these words are employed, the listener may have the specific meanings [indicated by them] presented to their mind, thereby triggering the grammatical operations such as the designation of *sarvanāman* (pronominal) and other operations related to the subsequent member of the compound.

He establishes this. The wise, who are experts in the true nature of words and meanings and who understand the intention of the Teacher, having discerned the specific meaning in each instance of word-usage, inform others at the time of teaching and other such occasions; thus they bring joy both to themselves and to others.

Kātyāyana also restricts the production of suffixes to specific meanings through statements such as "and [the suffix does not apply] when [the meaning] is not present due to the sense" (*arthāccā'sannihite*). In the rule *upadeśe 'janunāsika it* (Pāṇini 1.3.2), the word *upadeśa*—ending in the suffix *ghañ* denoting the instrument—is intended to convey a specific meaning; therefore, Kātyāyana’s statement *upadeśane 'c* need not be commenced. Furthermore, because the technical name *sarvanāman* is based on its literal meaning (*anvartha*), the statement *saṃjñopasarjanībhūtāḥ* need not be commenced. Thus he says:

Through the application of the rule *kartṛkarmavyapadeśāt*, the term *kriyā* (action) is obtained; furthermore, because the designation *upapada* is a "great technical term" (*mahāsaṃjñā*), the author of the Bhāṣya states that since rules such as *karmaṇyaṇ* (Pāṇini 3.2.1) can also be considered *padavidhi*s (rules dependent on word-forms), the requirement of semantic competency (*samarthavacana*) need not be stated in the context of *upapadavidhi*s. From this, it is understood that the indivisibility (*akhaṇḍatva*) of both words and sentences is accepted, and that the presentation of an indivisible meaning arises either from a word or from a sentence—this being a view consistent with the three Mīmāṃsā Sūtras.

If it is asserted that a word brings about the presentation of an indivisible meaning alone, and that there is no subsequent connection with specific meanings serving as the limiting conditions (*upādhi*) for grammatical operations (*kārya*), then the instruction of grammatical operations based on specific meaning-limiting conditions, the assignment of technical names (*saṃjñā*) according to their literal sense (*anvartha*), and the explanation of those names as being etymologically significant would all be rendered meaningless. Furthermore, it would imply that the Teacher composed the grammar without knowing the inherent power of the nature of words, thereby attributing ignorance to the Teacher.

Furthermore, those who, at the beginning of their treatises, follow the grammar of Pāṇini while asserting specific meanings would be censurable for "asserting a meaning that is non-verbal. Moreover, just as sentences such as "That thou art" (tat tvam asi) produce the cognition of a non-differentiated, partless Brahman, [if one were to claim that words like] "the king's man" (rājapuruṣa) likewise produce the cognition of a mere individual person unconditioned by either difference or relation, there would be no comprehension of the intended meaning, resulting in the collapse of all worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*).

One might argue: "For those who say that all this is illusory (*māyika*), there is no inconsistency for us. This should not be said, because in such a doctrine, there is an absence of the words of the Three Sages (the *Munitraya*). Nāgeśa has established the fact that words possess parts in the *Samarthasūtra-udyota* with the passage beginning with "some say" (*kecit*) and ending with "they say" (*prāhuḥ*). Whether this is his own view or that of another is a separate matter of inquiry. Scholars state therein that the indivisibility (*akhaṇḍatva*) of both word and meaning is not accepted by the Vedas and other authorities, because words are observed to have constituent parts (*yoga*).

For Pāṇini, who effects grammatical operations by means of various limiting adjuncts (upādhi) and who likewise employs etymologically meaningful names (anvarthasaṃjñā), the indivisibility (akhaṇḍatā) of those two [the name and the operation] is not accepted.
By explaining his name Patañjali in accordance with its etymological meaning through [the practice of] yoga itself,
he demonstrates that the attainment of the meaning of the Vārttika does not require [the text to be] indivisible.
The Examination of Difference:

Now, although difference is impossible to define—since the cognition of difference, such as "a jar is different from a cloth," must be preceded by the cognition of the locus and the counter-correlate grasped as distinct; and in that case, if that very difference is the same [as the relation], there is self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*); if it is another difference, then that too must be known in relation to two things already grasped as distinct, and if that is the same as the first difference, there is mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*); if it is a third, separate difference, there is the consequence of a circle (*cakraka*); and if one accepts a succession of differences, there is infinite regress (*anavasthā*)—nevertheless...

Because the final division cannot be established, there is a failure to establish [the division] all the way down to its root; thus, the root itself perishes. For this very reason, Kaiyaṭa and others employ the term "non-existent universal" (*asatsāmānya*) for difference. Its non-existence is according to the manner described above, and its universality is due to its being a purely positive concomitant (*kevalānvayin*). Nevertheless, since worldly transaction proceeds only through a difference that is charming only so long as it is not investigated—that is, one that is illusory (*māyika*)—there is no impairment of its status as conventionally real (*vyāvahārika*), just as the object such as a jar possesses the status of being denotable by the word "jar."

Otherwise—there would be mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) such that "this is a jar because it is the locus of jar-ness" and "this is jar-ness because it resides in the jar. This is because it is precisely the indefinable (*anirvacanīya*), which is charming only so long as it is not investigated, that serves as the basis for linguistic usage regarding all objects. For this very reason, Śrī Harṣa has said: "When you and I dance along, relying on the consensus of all the world and its scriptures, what recourse can there be for you in arguments concerning the cognition of reality and linguistic usage?"
The resort to the doctrine of ineffability is the path for those two;
for as there is no birth of the existent, so too there is no birth of the non-existent.
Thus,
it is precisely the state of being produced that establishes the indefinability of that which is produced.
There is another inference concerning the unreality of difference, and yet another concerning the illusion of difference.
Logic that relies on the reality of difference is quickly refuted by contradiction with the Vedas,
as well as by the scriptural passages concerning the knowledge of the One— such as "In this, there is no plurality"— found at the conclusion of the Upanishads.

If it is argued: "Enough of this," as stated by the author Śrī Harṣa in his work *Khaṇḍanakhaṇḍakhādya*—which is the very essence of the doctrine of the indefinable (*anirvacanīya*)—since he has established in his *Mañjūṣā* on the theory of negation (*nañ-vāda*) that the general category of categories, and even within that, the nature of difference itself, is indefinable (illusory, false), and therefore, because the category of difference does not exist at all, it is improper to interpret the Vedas and other scriptures as being intent upon difference; thus, non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman remains unestablished.

Regarding this, they say: It is true that Nāgeśa has spoken thus; nevertheless, wise men who take refuge in valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and are adept at investigating the reality of categories do not heed his statement. For instance, Śrī Harṣa and Nāgeśa—by saying "while we dance, relying on the consensus of all the world and its scriptures," and so forth—by way of restatement, establish the indefinability (*anirvacanīyatva*) of the entire manifest universe, which is established by all means of knowledge and perceived as existing.

Furthermore, from their own texts it is understood that the intention of those two [teachers] is that the entire world, other than Brahman, is non-existent (*asat*). Consequently, by their very words, the indefinability (*anirvacanīyatā*) of the two treatises composed by them first becomes established; for since the indefinability of all things—established therein—and the two treatises themselves are included within the category of "all objects," once the indefinability of the indefinability of all things is proven, [the treatises themselves are also established as indefinable].
The reality of the difference between all things is thereby established; thus, the opponent’s desired conclusion is not proven, while our own intended position is established.

Furthermore, the proponent who asserts that "the category of difference itself does not exist" must be asked: do you say that difference does not exist because all things—such as jars, cloths, and so forth—are one (due to the absence of intrinsic difference), or do you say it does not exist because you do not perceive the difference between objects?

In the first instance—in the *Sūtra* "Due to the diversity of word-meanings" (*vaicitryeṇa padārthānām*) and in the *Sarūpasūtra* "Because of the connection of word-meanings with diverse powers" (*padārthānāṃ vicitraśaktiyogāt*), according to Kaiyaṭa, and from the usage of other learned authorities such as "Because word-meanings possess diverse powers" (*padārthānāṃ vicitraśaktitvāt*)—and from the *Mahābhāṣya* on the *Sūtra* "Haya-vara-ṭ," it is understood that this is inherent; for every individual object, there exists a specific property denoted by terms such as "nature" (*svabhāva*), "own-nature" (*ātmasvabhāva*), or "power" (*śakti*), which consists in its resting solely in that particular object and excludes everything else distinct from it.

Thus, since it is established that difference exists inherently in each individual object based on such cognition, the notion of unity regarding all things is proven to be an error. It is not the second [alternative]: for you, who are engaged in proving that everything established by all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as real is actually indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*), the presence or absence of cognition—and the existence or non-existence of an object—do not serve as determining factors for you or for those who accept your authority; therefore, your own lack of such cognition is irrelevant to the argument.

It is clearly known to those who have studied your works that you and he, having resorted to a different form of dress and concealed their true nature, proceeded at will for the sake of proving the non-existence of all things. However, there is this much distinction between you and your friend: you maintain that the single entity called Brahman is the only reality, while all others are indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*). Thus it is argued.

If people were to rely upon your doctrine, then they would be devoid of the discernment of various objects established by worldly convention— such as "this is a Brahmin" and "this is not a Brahmin," "this is a mother," "this is a beloved wife," "this is a woman with children," "this is a wife," "this is milk," "this is wine," "this is an outcaste," "this is gold" and "this is not gold," "this is approachable" and "this is not approachable," "this is edible" and "this is not edible"—
and consequently, through the non-performance of what is prescribed and the practice of what is censured, [they would fall].
"Through the impairment of the senses, a man meets with downfall" (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.219).

In light of such statements from the *Arthavāda* passages, as well as Vedic injunctions such as "Speak the truth, practice righteousness, do not drink liquor," those who lack the conviction in their authority and whose hearts are devoid of discrimination between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, might commit improper acts such as the killing of a Brahmin and thereby incur great calamity.

Consequently, since there would be no object for the scriptures devoted to the injunctions and prohibitions of the Śruti and Smṛti, as well as for the various corresponding rules on expiation (*prāyaścitta*), they would lack authority by virtue of conveying non-existent objects—just like the statement "there is a rabbit's horn. (Furthermore, because one would not practice them out of the conviction that they lack authority, there would also be a lack of authority consisting in non-performance. If it is argued, "But for us, who maintain that everything is indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*), all of this is precisely what we desire," [the reply is: No.

In the view of those who speak thus, because the generality of categories other than the *sphoṭa* and Brahman is false, even the scriptural authority of the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsa, and so forth would be indefinable (due to being illusory, i.e., unreal). Furthermore, since there is a lack of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) to establish either the *sphoṭa* or Brahman, it would follow that the very nature of the *sphoṭa* and of Brahman (or Īśvara) remains unestablished.

Furthermore, [the view that] the Brahman known as *sphoṭa* itself undergoes transformation (*vivarta*) into the form of the world would contradict such statements from one's own school as: "Relying on the burden of the sole, self-established reality of consciousness (*cidātman*)," (Māṇḍūkya-kārikā 2.31). Nor should it be argued that because it is called "self-established" (*svataḥsiddha*), there is no dependence on means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its establishment; for when questioned as to what this "self-establishment" actually consists of, it cannot be defined by one who maintains that everything is ultimately indefinable (*anirvacanīya*).

If its reality is declared to be unestablished, then there would be a fallacy of contradicting one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*) due to the collapse of the doctrine that everything is indeterminable (*sarvānirvacanīyatā*), as well as self-contradiction (*svavyāhati*). Furthermore, because the very nature of Brahman would remain unestablished, there would be no distinction from the view of the Nihilists (*śūnyavādin*). It should not be argued that there is a great distinction because we accept the existence superimposed upon the world while they do not accept either of those two.

When you deny existence (*sattva*) [of Brahman], it is effectively stated that "it does not exist. Since, in your view, the general category of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is non-existent, and there is thus an absence of any means of knowledge to establish the existence of Brahman, it follows that Brahman itself is said to be non-existent. Therefore, the distinction [between your position and the denial of Brahman] is difficult to justify. One who, having denied existence as established by valid cognition, speaks of a superimposed (*āropita*) existence, is particularly worthy of praise; for superimposition is indeed a resort for those with no other way out.

If it is argued, "We indeed accept that even through a false statement, the existence of God is understood by means of valid cognition such as scripture," it is replied: for they say that the non-existence of non-existent things like a rabbit’s horn is established by their lack of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*).

If one were to accept the non-existence of the Vedas and other scriptures on the grounds that they possess the nature of a Brahmin’s body—which [the opponent] holds to be unreal—then there would follow the fallacy of over-narrowness (*avyāpti*), since the definition of non-existence does not apply to the Vedas and such, which are not non-existent. Furthermore, even for one who asserts that falsity consists in being the mode of an error, it is impossible to speak of the non-existence of those [scriptures], because non-existence must be defined in the manner already stated, which would lead to the very same fallacy mentioned above.

Furthermore, if it is admitted that even by means of a false cognition (*mithyā-buddhi*) the reality (*satyatā*) of Brahman is understood, then, due to the lack of distinction, it would be possible to assert the reality of all objects as well by that same means. Moreover, since there is no evidence establishing the falsity of the very means of knowledge that cognizes the falsity of everything, and because the statement "not here, not manifold" (*neha nānā*) exists as something distinct from the *sphoṭa* and other such entities, the non-duality (*advitīyatva*) of the *sphoṭa* and so forth remains unestablished.

Nor should it be argued that the scriptural statement "nahe nānā" (there is no difference), while teaching the falsity of other things, also teaches its own truth; for [the rule] "pūrvatrāsiddham" (Pāṇini Sūtra 8.2.1) [applies].

8.2.1) According to the reasoning of Kaiyaṭa, if the rule *pūrvatrā'siddham* were to establish its own invalidity (*asiddhatva*), then, because all [other] rules would be established (*siddha*), this very sūtra would be impossible and thus useless. Similarly, if the statement "all" (in the verse *sarvam...*) were to indicate its own falsity while teaching the substitution of *ā* for *ai*, it would follow that the other [rules] are not established as false; consequently, the sentence "neha nānā" ("here there is no diversity") would result in being meaningless.

If it is argued that there is indeed a conventional distinction (*vyāvahārika-bheda*) everywhere, this must be addressed: Is "conventionality" (*vyāvahārikatva*) the same as being superimposed (*āropitatva*), or is it another property dependent upon human activity? It cannot be either; for, as established by the previously cited *Mahābhāṣya* and other texts stating "this is established by its own nature," the existence of the Veda is proven to be inherently natural (*svābhāvika*) everywhere. Consequently, both superimposition and dependence on human activity are absent in that case.

If it is asked, "How is difference established by that statement in the Bhāṣya?", it is said in that Bhāṣya: "Among those who exert equal effort and study equally, some are endowed with results while others are not... In that case, what can be done by us? It is simply inherent (svābhāvika)," so it was stated.

It is established by the experience of everyone in the world that even when the effort and the study are identical and conducive to the same result, one person obtains the fruit while another does not; in that regard, no one is seen to be able to act as either a facilitator (*sādhaka*) or an obstacle (*pratibandhaka*) regarding attainment or non-attainment. Rather, what is the cause? This is the meaning of that commentary (*bhāṣya*). That very distinction, which differentiates [an entity] from other individuals, is designated by the word "difference" (*bheda*); thus, the mutual difference between categories (*padārtha*) is established.

Nor should it be argued that its existence is merely conventional (*vyāvahārikatva*) because difference is established through worldly convention; for if this convention were the cause of the very difference that serves as the basis for such diverse conventions, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*): the establishment of difference depends on the existence of convention, and the establishment of convention depends on the existence of difference. If another convention were posited as the cause of the prior difference, then by assuming an infinite series of such conventional differences, an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would result. Therefore, it is established that difference is indeed the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of things themselves.

Having this very point in mind, the learned have stated: "All word-meanings, indeed, are distinct and possess distinct properties" (Anubhūtiprakāśa 2.2.670). All word-meanings possess distinct properties—that is, they inherently possess properties that serve as their own mutual differentiators; for this very reason, they are distinct, meaning they possess difference relative to one another. Thus say even the commentators on the Advaita-paribhāṣā.

And thus, there is no room for defects such as self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*). Furthermore, since difference must be accepted for the sake of conceiving it as merely conventional (*vyāvahārika*), the effort to refute it is futile. Moreover, if "difference" were not some kind of category (*padārtha*) at all, then the activity of all philosophical schools (*tīrthakara*) in establishing their own positions and refuting those of others would be impossible.

Furthermore, there would be no cognition among those persons to be enlightened regarding their victory or defeat based on the knowledge of the relative strength or weakness caused by the faultlessness or faulty nature of their own and others' positions; nor would there be engagement or non-engagement therein, since faultlessness and so forth are dependent upon difference (*bheda*).

Moreover, if distinct categories of objects were not admitted, the persistence and exertion involved in establishing one's own position and refuting that of others would be fruitless. This "non-difference" has been refuted at great length in various treatises by many teachers.

Furthermore, the venerable Bādarāyaṇa, while establishing as his final conclusion (*siddhānta*) in the *Ānandamaya* and other sections that qualities such as consisting of bliss (*ānandamayatva*) belong to Brahman—the object of inquiry—addresses the objection that because the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman are non-different, the soul too must possess qualities such as consisting of bliss. He does so by citing the scriptural declarations of difference: "Because of the declaration of difference" (1.3.5); "And because of the declaration of difference, [the Self] is other [than the body]" (1.1.21); "For both [types of texts] regard the body as distinct from Him" (1.2.20); "And because of the declaration of distinction and difference, [the Self] is neither of the two [the elements and the vital breath]" (1.2.22); and "Because of the declaration of difference."

By such statements as "(1.3.5) because of the difference between deep sleep and departure" (1.3.42), which show that the two possess distinct attributes, he intends to establish that there exists some entity called "difference" (bheda) that is distinct from the substrate (dhātu).

Furthermore, by stating in various places—such as *tulyāsyaprayatnaṃ sarvarṇam* (Pāṇini 1.1.9), *sthānivadādeśaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.56), *pañcamī vibhakte* (Pāṇini 2.3.42), "But [the difference] is due to the intervention of place and time, because of the simultaneous distinctness of their locations" (*pra.2.ā.*), "It is established by the inclusion of the form, or through the similarity of form" (*pra.2.ā.*), and "This is inherent"—that Pāṇini, Kātyāyana, and Patañjali acknowledge the essential nature of difference (*bhedasvarūpa*). This is what is understood from them.

Therefore, the negation of the essential nature of difference contradicts the words of the three sages. In that regard, it is quite clear that the two factors—similarity (*sādṛśya*) and extension (*atideśa*)—are based upon difference. The explanation of the term "distinguished" (*vibhakta*) is that distinction (*vibhāga*) is difference (*bheda*). Regarding "being otherwise" (*ānyabhāvya*)—that is, difference—the position of the universal (*jāti*) and similarity (*sādṛśya*) were adopted as a pair to avoid the impossibility of grasping the word-potency (*śakti*) in all individual instances due to their infinity and their distinctness. *Ākṛti* is the universal (*jāti*), while similarity (*sādṛśya*) is the commonality of form (*rūpasāmānya*).

The details should be understood from the Bhāṣya and other works. Furthermore, how can one who asserts that the very nature of difference does not exist at all be capable of imagining such things as its being illusory (*māyika*)? For that [illusoriness] is itself of the nature of difference. The statement "this is illusory" is merely a conventional expression. Now, an objection may be raised: according to the maxim *nañivayuktamanyasadṛśādhikaraṇe tathārthagateḥ* ("when joined with *nañ* or *iva*, there is a comprehension of something else similar to the locus"), the use of the word "other" (*anya*) implies similarity even in the case of non-difference. Otherwise, since similarity is possible only within difference, the mention of "difference" would already be implied by the phrase "locus of similarity," and the inclusion of the word "other" in the maxim would be redundant.

Furthermore, if it is argued that the statement in the *Nañarthavāda* section of the *Mañjūṣā*—namely, "The commentary on the sūtra 'and in the sense of non-agent' indicates that similarity exists even where there is non-difference"—shows that the mention of similarity does not imply difference, we say: no. By the statement "similarity exists even in non-difference," it is understood that similarity is everywhere rooted in difference. Wherever authorities speak of similarity despite the identity of the individual entities, it should be understood that such a statement is made only by some figurative means.

And by "conjunction" (*saṃghayana*), it is meant that through the repetition of a single entity, multiplicity is produced; thus, similarity is established because the common property resides in multiple instances. Consequently, since similarity is based on cognition, the fact that similarity indicates difference remains unimpaired. Nor should it be argued that, in this case, the mention of "another" (*anya*) is redundant.

Having heard the statement of some that "similarity may be possible even in the absence of difference," people might be led astray; therefore, in order to prevent such confusion and to demonstrate that similarity is established only when there is indeed difference, this [distinction] is necessary. If similarity were easily established even in the absence of difference, then the following passage in the *Mañjūṣā* regarding the meaning of the particle *iva*—namely, "only a property residing in multiple things can be a common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*), because even a single thing becomes manifold through repetition therein"—would be rendered purposeless.

However, [the rule] beginning with *akartari ca kārake* is not appropriate, because it is not indicated therein by the Bhāṣya; for in that context, the Bhāṣya does not even undertake this investigation. By this demonstration that the non-existence of all things (their being illusory) is difficult to maintain—it is clearly stated that through this [rule], there is only the appearance of everything, such as its status as a creator, and not any real entity whatsoever; due to the force of beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*), that is merely the object of an error. Even the Śruti passages beginning with *yato vā* merely restate this...

By the passage, "Even such scriptural texts as 'Brahman is truth, knowledge, and bliss' teach that pure Brahman is non-dual and pure, through the renunciation of attributes, in conjunction with other scriptures such as 'There is no diversity here'" (1.pa.30.31), [the author] establishes the indeterminability of the world in the first chapter, presents the determination of the unreality of the phenomenal world (*prapañca-asattva*) formulated by the author of the *Mañjūṣā*, and cites the relevant text from the *Mañjūṣā*.

Regarding the discussion on the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*): the elaboration by Pāyuguṇḍi Vaidyanātha concerning the unreality of the world (*prapañcāsatyatva*) is rooted in dogmatism and is merely imagined by his own childishness. If the state of being the denotation of a word were to necessitate that something remain unexamined, then—since it would follow that everything taught would necessarily be unreal—all things would have to be spoken of as such, leading to the undesirable consequence of the total cessation of all worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), because linguistic usage would no longer be functional.

The refutation beginning with "by being the locus of potness" (*ghaṭatvāśrayatvena*) and so forth should be addressed only against the *hetukas*—those who establish categories of existence by means of logical reasons alone—and not against those who rely on the authority of scripture (*śruti*) and other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), for the latter do not employ mere logical reasons to establish categories of existence; furthermore, there is no fault in the cognition and linguistic usage [of terms] such as "pot" and the like.

Regarding the claim that Kaiyaṭa is also in agreement here with the non-existence of difference—as seen in his usage of the phrase "by the word *asat-sāmānya* (non-existent universal)" and so forth—that is questionable, because that Kaiyaṭa does not intend a meaning identical to this [present] one. To explain: his own text states, "When the negative particle (*nañ*), which functions as a non-existent universal (*asat-sāmānya*), is qualified by terms such as 'Brāhmaṇa,' its meaning is a Kṣatriya or the like who is non-existent as a Brāhmaṇa, or otherwise non-existent. Thus, his position differs.

In this regard, since the non-existence of the unreal entity [of difference] has been explained by that very [author] in the statement "he does not exist as a Brahmin," it is understood that the non-existence of the difference is not due to its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*), but rather because it conveys the non-existence of its own counter-correlate-determinant (*svapratiyogitāvacchedaka*), such as Brahminhood, in its own substratum (*svānuyogin*), such as a Kṣatriya. Here, "its own" (*svam*) refers to the difference (*bheda*).

Furthermore, if difference (*bheda*) were non-existent by its very nature (*svarūpataḥ*), its status as a *kevalānvayin* (an absolute universal) would be untenable; for being a *kevalānvayin* consists in not being the counter-positive (*apratiyogitva*) of an absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*), whereas non-existence consists in being the very nature of that counter-positive, and thus the two are mutually contradictory. Therefore, let the wise discern how Kaiyaṭa could possibly be favorable to this [view].

Since all authorities—including the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsa, and Purāṇas—teach that Brahman possesses attributes (saguṇa), no delusion regarding any attribute of Brahman can arise. Because there is no delusion concerning the attribute of Brahman being the cause of the world, passages such as "From which [the world arises]" (*yato vā*) do not merely restate an object that is the focus of a delusion regarding its being a "circumstantial definition" (taṭasthalakṣaṇa). Furthermore, the Śruti passage "Not here, manifoldness" (*neha nānāsti kiñcana*) establishes the absence of difference in the form of separate existence between Brahman and its attributes.

Furthermore, because [the passage] does not convey the non-existence of any entity other than Brahman—due to its being devoid of internal difference—and because it does not convey the absence of attributes in Brahman, and because the scriptural passages beginning with "from which" (*yato vā*) have not been explained by the two authors of the Sūtras, Śrī Vyāsa and Pāṇini, as having the meaning intended by the author of the Mañjūṣā, all of this is baseless; therefore, the interpretation of the cited scriptures shown [by us] is correct.

Thus, since objects such as pots and cloths, as well as their difference (*bheda*), are established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), there is no evidence for their being illusory (*māyika*). Therefore, the claim that "transactional usage proceeds through an illusory difference that is charming only so long as it is not investigated," and that "only an object charming only so long as it is not investigated serves as the cause for transactional usage," is merely superficially attractive and deludes ordinary people; enough of this elaboration. There is no proof whatsoever for the illusoriness of objects.
As for the proof regarding the existence of difference as an object, the Sūtra and the Bhāṣya have already been shown.
Therefore, the position of difference is the one accepted by the author of the Sūtras and others;
consequently, interpreting the Śrutis as having difference as their primary purport is superior.

Regarding the refutation of the claim that Gautama [the author of the *Nyāyasūtra*] agrees with the position that the world is unreal (*asat*), there is the following passage from the third chapter of the *Mañjūṣā*: "Gautama also says: 'This conceit regarding the means and objects of knowledge is like a delusion concerning the objects of a dream' (*Nyāyasūtra* 4.2.21); 'Or it is like an illusion, a city of the Gandharvas, or a mirage' (*Vyāsasūtra* 4.2.32); 'There is no proof because of the absence of a reason' (*Nyāyasūtra* 4.2.33)," and so forth, ending with the phrase "detailed elsewhere. This section of the text demonstrates Gautama’s agreement with the unreality of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*).

Regarding this, Vācaspati states: "The Vijñānavādin objects. From this introduction, it follows that the first two sūtras present the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), while the third is the sūtra of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). Just as the conceit (or cognition) in a dream is without an external object, so too the conceit regarding the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) in the waking state is likewise without an external object. The sense is that, like the things in a dream and so forth, even objects such as jars and cloths during the waking state are merely illusory (*māyika*). This being the position reached, he states the established conclusion with the word "hetu" (the reason).

Because the reason in the form of non-perception exists at the time of waking and so forth, even though dreams and the like are non-existent; yet, since there is perception of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth during the waking state, the reason in the form of non-perception is absent. Thus, there is "non-establishment" (*asiddhi*), meaning the non-establishment of non-existence. The point is that non-perception and perception are the reasons for non-existence and existence respectively, and in this context, these correspond to being sublated and not being sublated by cognition.

Having provisionally accepted the non-existence of dreams as stated by [the opponent], the meaning of the *siddhānta-sūtra* has been described; however, in reality, there is no proof [of non-existence] because the reason—non-perception—is absent. That is to say, the non-existence of the object perceived during the waking state is unproven, because even a dream is perceived, and thus the reason consisting of "non-perception" is absent; consequently, there is no proof—that is, no proof of non-existence—due to the absence of the reason, which results in the absence of an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Thus, the inference that establishes the existence of waking objects remains unproven. And so it is.

Since it is understood from the *Nyāyabhāṣya* and other sources that Gautama’s view is that objects do not lack existence in dreams, illusions, and the waking state, it must be concluded that the doctrine of indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatāvāda*) is not accepted by Gautama. Thus, while this is the literal meaning, the *Bhāṣya*, *Vārttika*, and other texts explain as the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that "in the waking state, for those things perceived in close proximity—which remain unsublated throughout empirical usage—being perceived in close proximity is not a reason for their unreality (or illusory nature)."

And thus—the fact that the doctrine of indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatā*) is in accordance with the Sūtras has already been largely established. Therefore, it is improper to assume that Gautama’s intention lay in [proving] indeterminability. This is because we do not find in his Bhāṣya or other works such a statement as "of those things belonging to a class that remains unsublated so long as worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) continues," nor any other sentence of similar meaning. To claim that "it was explained in the Bhāṣya and elsewhere" after interpreting the Sūtra by supplying a sentence not seen therein indicates a deep-seated hostility toward the learned.

"Let these people be deluded by the apprehension of contradictory objects. And in the *Vārttika* it is said: "Those who claim that all cognitions are false must be questioned regarding the primary [cognition]; for we do not perceive anything that is without a primary [basis]. By this, it is stated that if one accepts the validity of any given cognition on the grounds of its having a real object, otherwise the falsity of the cognition under consideration cannot be established.

Furthermore, by the two subsequent sūtras—"And like memory and volition, the conceit regarding dream-objects [is real]" (3.2.34) and "The destruction of false perceptions occurs through the knowledge of reality, just as the conceit regarding dream-objects perishes upon waking" (3.2.35)—Gautama has stated that the objects in memory, volition, dreams, and delusions are indeed real; therein, he speaks only of the destruction of false perception and the conceit of the dream, but not of the non-existence of the object itself. The meaning of these sūtras should be understood from the Bhāṣya and other sources.

For this very reason, in the fifth chapter (*stabaka*) of the *Kusumāñjali*, at the conclusion of the work, after refuting the view that dream-cognition is a form of memory, [Udayana] states the truth of dreams with the words: "Therefore, this must be accepted as a direct experience (*anubhava*); and there is indeed some degree of reality even to dream-experience, because it corresponds [with subsequent facts]," and so forth.

As for what was stated—namely, that the claim of the indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatva*) [of the world] being based on scripture is untenable because "there is no proof of its being rooted in scripture" due to the absence of a reason—this too must be considered. For the indeterminability of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is not established by the absence of scriptural testimony; rather, it is established by the presence of such testimony. Furthermore, it is understood that this doctrine lacks a scriptural basis, since the Blessed Great Sage Vyāsa, in the second chapter (*Samayapāda*) of the *Yogasūtra*, rejected the view of those who deny external objects through five sūtras beginning with "Not non-existence, because of perception" (*nābhāva upalabdheḥ*, 2.2.27).

If this doctrine were based on the Vedas (*śrauta*), then how could that great sage, who set out to determine the meaning of the scriptures, reject that Vedic sense? Furthermore, it is clear that the view of someone who does not accept the authority of the Vedas has been refuted there in the *Samayapāda*. It has been stated that the Kāṭhaka passage "neha nānā" (4.11) and the Vājasaneyaka passage do not intend to establish the indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatā*) of the world, because the two authors of the Sūtras did not explain them in that manner.
Furthermore, even by the strict rules of grammar (*akṣaramaryādayā*), such a meaning cannot be obtained. To explain:

if *nānā* is taken in the sense of "different" and *iha* in the sense of "in the Supreme Self," then the sentence-meaning would have to be expressed as "in this Brahman, there is no distinct entity whatsoever. This being the case, it would follow that the world has no existence as something separate, but not that the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) does not exist at all. Consequently, the implication is that the world is dependent upon Brahman. And this was stated by the Blessed Lord: "All this is strung upon Me, like clusters of gems on a thread" (Gītā 7.7).

By this, the claim that "the non-existence of the world is established precisely because of its negation upon what has been apprehended" is refuted; for the stated meaning is not obtained through negation. This is because such a restrictive rule [of non-existence] is established by other systems, and the ancient grammatical masters, headed by Pāṇini, do not accept such a doctrine. Furthermore, according to Nāgeśa’s statement that "falsity is the state of being a mode of error," negation does not establish the world as a mode of error.

Since the Śrutis beginning with "neha" (not here) have not been commented upon by Pāṇini and Patañjali, it is as if there were no royal decree stating that the meaning of the Śruti must be exactly as intended by Nāgeśa; therefore, the Śruti can be interpreted in other ways as well. For instance: in the Śruti, the word *nānā* has "being" (*bhāva*) as its primary sense and refers to difference (*bheda*), because Kaiyaṭa states in the commentary on the rule *vinañbhyāṃ nānāñau na saha* (Pāṇini 5.2.27), "In common usage, the word *nānā* denotes a state of being separate. Thus, there is no disagreement regarding its reference to difference.

"By the mind alone this is to be attained"—this is the preceding statement in the *Kaṭhaka*. This is to be understood: by the ninth mantra, "From which it rises," the fact that the Supreme Self, denoted by the term *prāṇa*, is the support of all deities is declared; and by the tenth mantra, "That which is here," which makes known Hari—the very support of all deities—as the support of all things and the controller of all in both this world and the next, [it is shown that] the form of the Lord existing in both worlds is indeed non-different, yet for those who perceive difference therein...

"It is a great calamity" has been made known. This eleventh mantra—explicitly stating that the non-dual nature of Brahman is to be known and that there is not even an atom's worth of difference within that Brahman—reaffirms the aforementioned undesirable result for one who perceives duality, while verbally articulating what was already indicated by the preceding mantra. This non-dual nature of Brahman mentioned in the previous mantra is here referred to by the pronoun "this."

This—this non-different nature of Brahman—is to be attained—that is, contemplated—with a pure mind; [it is to be sought] here and in the hereafter within Brahman, wherein there is not even a trace of manifoldness or difference. The intended meaning is that there is no distinction among the forms of the Blessed Lord. He states the result for one who perceives such difference: "From death... and so forth.

He who is the qualified seeker, here—in this context where the nature of the Supreme Self exists as both [the manifest and the unmanifest]—sees as if there were multiplicity; that is, he perceives as if there were duality. He falls into "death upon death"—the meaning is that he reaches a state even more wretched than death itself, which bestows further death. In the Vājasaneyi [Upaniṣad], however, it is recited: "It is to be perceived by the mind alone; it is not here" (6.4.19), and so forth.

In this context—the word *brahma* is carried over from the preceding sentence, "They have perceived that supreme, ancient Brahman," and it must be transformed into the nominative case. That Brahman, which was described as having five gates, is to be "beheld" (contemplated) here—within this Brahman that is to be seen—by the mind alone, after one has practiced the scriptures preceded by the teacher's instruction; that is, it is to be contemplated by a consciousness purified by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) consisting of knowledge that there is not even a trace of difference within the nature of Brahman. The remainder is clear.

And thus, it should be understood that the statement "not here, manifoldness" (neha nānā) indicates the absence of difference between Brahman and its form, but it does not, by way of teaching the non-existence of anything other than Brahman, teach the non-existence of the world.

Alternatively, since the words *vinā* and *nānā* are derived in the sense of "not together" (*na saha*) by the rule *vinañbhyāṃ nānāñau nasaha*, the word *nānā* is a synonym for *vinā*. Furthermore, the meaning of "not together" is the absence of concomitance (*sāhityabhāva*). This is because it is stated in the *Uddyota* on the rule *tasya bhāvaḥ*: "In such expressions as 'nānātva' (diversity), 'sahatva' (togetherness), and 'yaugapadyam' (simultaneity), the word *nānā* occurs in the sense of that which is not co-existent (*asahabhūta*), while the word *saha* occurs in the sense of that which is co-existent (*sahabhūta*); therefore, the suffix [is applied] in the sense of non-co-existence. Thus, it refers to the state of being non-co-existent.

The word *iha* here does not refer to Brahman, but rather to the phenomenal world (*prapañca*). Because of the preceding statement, "This is to be attained by the mind alone," the word *idam* is supplied as an ellipsis. And because it is joined with the word *nānā* (various/diverse), it takes the accusative ending according to the rule *pṛthagvinānānābhistṛtīyānyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 2.3.32). Thus, the meaning of the Kāṭhaka passage is: "In this phenomenal world (*iha-prapañce*), no object whatsoever (*kiṃcana vastu*) exists as something diverse—that is, separate from the Supreme Self; rather, it is indeed inseparable from Brahman."

In the Vājasaneyi [Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa], however, from the statement "They perceived the ancient, foremost Brahma-city" (13), the word *brahma* is supplied; and because it is joined with various words, it takes the accusative case. The connection is as in the Kāṭhaka passage. Here, in this interpretation, the inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*) is verbal; whereas in the previous interpretation, it is logical—the existence of all things as being inseparably connected to the Lord, established by the Lord’s own words: "There is no being, moving or unmoving, that can exist without Me" (Bhagavad Gītā 10.39).

In the subsequent sentence, "From death," the word *iha* likewise refers only to the phenomenal world (*prapañca*). The meaning is: "In this world (*iha*), he who sees as if there were multiplicity (*nāneva*)—that is, as if there were a separation from the Lord. The sense is that for one who perceives the absence of inseparability from the Lord within the phenomenal world, a great calamity ensues. For this very reason, the words *iha* and *nānā* are meaningful in the Śruti; otherwise, since the fact that nothing exists apart from Brahman would already be established by the mere statement, "There is not even this much" (*nedam asti kiṃcana*), or "There is nothing at all" (*atha vā—nāsti kiṃcana*), what purpose would those two words serve?

On this point, a certain partisan of Nāgojibhaṭṭa says: since the word *nānā* is derived from the negative particle *nañ* with the suffix *naṅ* by the rule "vinañbhyām," and since the commentary on that rule establishes that this suffix is *svārthika* (denoting its own meaning), its referent is "difference" (*bheda*). In that case, since the relation [of difference] is obtained through the force of the co-occurring word, only the aspect of difference is directly denotable; thus, it is not a synonym for the word *vinā*. Therefore, the interpretation of "neha nānā" as "not without" (*vinābhūtaṃ na*) is incorrect.

Regarding the phrase "it is appropriate": other grammarians (vaiyākaraṇas) who do not follow Nāgeśa argue that, based on the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the relevant *sūtra*—"The suffixes *nañ* and *anān* occur after the words *vinā* and *nañ*, which express non-accompaniment, in their own sense"—the author of the *sūtra* and the *bhāṣya* agree that the words *vinā* and *anān* are synonyms in the sense of non-accompaniment. Consequently, they maintain that the interpretation of the scriptural passage "not here is diversity" (*neha nānā*) as "not separated" (*vinābhūtam na*) is both logical and in accord with the views of Pāṇini and Patañjali.

In passages such as "There is no God other than Viṣṇu who bestows liberation," one can say that the word *na*, though unestablished in the sense of difference (*bheda*), functions as if it had multiple meanings. By stating, "The portion consisting of difference alone is what is intended by the power [of the word], because the Bhāṣya says it is used in its own sense (*svārthika*)," it is implied that the suffix *añ* is applied to the negative particle *na* when it has the meaning of difference. This, however, is to be considered.

In the Sūtra, one should simply say "na" (not) rather than employing the word "saha" (with); and in the Bhāṣya, instead of explaining it by way of its distinct meaning [as "different"], it says "from those expressing non-coexistence," thereby clarifying that meaning. This is because the negative particle "nañ" has multiple meanings, and in this context, since there is no co-occurrence, the sense obtained is that the suffix "añ" does not apply after a word containing "nañ. Thus, the intended meaning is secured.

By this commentary, through the acquisition of the restrictive rule (*niyama*) "from those whose meanings are expressed by the base or the suffix as included in the sūtra," that commentary fails to establish the production of a suffix from a *nañ* whose meaning is a distinction (*bheda*) not included in the sūtra. In the section on primary derivatives (*svārthika*), in certain cases—such as the scope of sūtras like "in the sense of compassion" (*anukampāyām*)—the meaning such as "compassion" included in the sūtra becomes understood from the base as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*); however, in other cases, it is understood from the base independently (as the qualificand), as in the case of the present sūtra.

Furthermore, the demonstration—found in that very same work under the section beginning with "agra" (*agra*)—that even in the state of liberation (*apavarga*), there is an absence of any real entity distinct from consciousness according to the Nyāya school, is also weak. This is because in the Nyāya system, since individual souls (*jīva*) are manifold, and because both liberated souls and Brahman exist in the state of liberation, and because they are real, it is impossible to maintain the absence of those [entities] at that time.

This is in accordance with the statement by Udayanācārya in the *Nyāyamañjarī* (Āhnika 9): "Real difference and generality [exist]; the selves are indeed diverse; the knowledge of the self is the means to liberation; and in liberation, the liberated ones abide in their own essential nature."

By the sūtra *tadabhāvaścāpavarge* (Gau. Nyā. 4.2.45), which means that because liberated beings lack a body and sense organs, there is an absence of the production of cognition due to the absence of contact between the senses and external objects, it is not established that there is a mere absence of knowledge in the liberated state; for this does not prove the non-existence of categories distinct from the mind (*citta*). This very sūtra has been explained in this same manner in the Bhāṣya and other works.

The meaning of the words of the Sūtra, however, is that there is no such contingency; "since" is the ellipsis to be supplied, and from the context, "of the liberated ones" is understood. Regarding liberation—namely, mokṣa—for the liberated ones, since there is the absence of that [body], i.e., the absence of the body and sense organs which are the causes of knowledge, therefore there is no contingency—that is, no contingency of the production of bondage.

Furthermore, having thoroughly examined mature classical Nyāya treatises such as the Bhāṣya, Vārttika, and Tātparyaṭīkā, [we find that] in the *Nyāyamañjarī* composed by the eminent scholar Bhaṭṭa Jayanta—a work intended to clarify the purport of the *Nyāyasūtra*—the false doctrines such as Vijñānavāda are refuted in the fifth, seventh, eighth, and ninth chapters (*āhnika*). Since the existence of external objects distinct from consciousness and so forth has been established there with valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it follows that "the doctrine of indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatāvāda*) is not accepted by Gautama."

Furthermore, this [position] contradicts such scriptural passages as "He enjoys all" (*Taittirīya Upaniṣad* 2), as well as the *Brahmasūtra* (4.4.1), which begins with "having attained. Consequently, it is impossible to determine from either the works of Gautama or any other texts that objects are non-existent during the waking state and so forth.

If it be argued that the mantra, "Than whom there is nothing higher, than whom nothing smaller or greater exists; standing alone like a tree in the sky, by which Puruṣa all this is pervaded" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1; Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.9), establishes by the negation of all things both higher and lower than the Full Puruṣa that Brahman alone is the one real entity and everything else is unreal—then let the meaning of the mantra be considered.

This is the meaning of the mantra: because there is nothing higher—nothing superior—to the Full Person (*pūrṇa-puruṣa*), nor anything lower—nothing inferior; that is, such a thing exists. In response to the doubt as to what the dimensions of this existing entity might be—whether it is smaller or greater—it is said: "than whom there is nothing smaller," and so forth. Because there is nothing smaller and nothing greater—"smaller than the small, greater than the great" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6.1; Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.20)—it is so stated. The use of the masculine form *kaścit* ("anyone") instead of the neuter *kiñcit* is a Vedic archaism.

Thus, there are four sentences in the first half [of the mantra]. Nor should it be argued that even in the second sentence, because of the ellipsis (*anuṣaṅga*) of the negative particle (*nañ*), the purport of the mantra is simply "neither the supreme nor the non-supreme reality exists. This is because, according to the maxim stated in the *Mahābhāṣya* on the rule *paṅaḥ katvā ca* (Pāṇini 1.2.10)—namely, "those rules which are prescribed in the middle [of two others] are obligatory"—it cannot be said that the negative particle is not to be supplied to the second sentence, as it is situated between two negatives.

If, however, there were a continuous connection [of the negation], then because the prohibition would be obtained by the mere continuation of this [negation] even in what follows, the employment of two negative particles (*nañ*) would be redundant. Furthermore, if the absence of all entities other than Brahman were understood from this sentence, then since no possibility for the suspicion of minuteness (*aṇīyastva*) and so forth could arise due to the non-existence of any such entity, there would be the undesirable consequence that the subsequent prohibitive sentences beginning with "than which nothing is minuter" (*yasmānnāṇīya*) would not be uttered; moreover, there would be the undesirable consequence of contradicting the mantra "smaller than the small" (*aṇoraṇīyān*), which indicates the existence of another entity distinct from the *puruṣa*.

By this, the claim that "yasmāt paramaparaṃ ca na" constitutes a single sentence is refuted, because the aforementioned logical inconsistency remains unavoidable. If it is argued that, since the word *rudra* occurs in the preceding mantras, this mantra must refer to Śiva, he replies: one should not think so here. One might say that the word *rudra* refers to Śiva based on the etymological derivation: "Because he causes (*drāvayate*) disease (*rujam*), therefore [he is] Rudra, O Janārdana. However, this is not the case here.

Because in the latter half of the verse, "They perceive Hiraṇyagarbha being born," there is heard a mark (*liṅga*) indicating that the one propounded by this mantra is the son of Viriñca; because such [a status] is impossible in the case of Rudra, whereas it is possible only in the case of Vāsudeva; because this is therefore an exclusive mark of Viṣṇu; and because, by the force of that [mark], the maxim "the conventional sense prevails over the etymological" does not apply; and because the Śruti has scope in reference to Vāsudeva. In heaven—that is, in his own abode, Vaikuṇṭha—he stands alone, devoid of equals or superiors, motionless like a tree.

And thus, the sense is that [the Lord] does not engage in the creation of the world and so forth like a potter or similar craftsman; rather, he creates by mere will. Regarding the reading *yena* found in some versions, the construction is: "by which person this [world] remains full. This should be understood: if the first quarter-verse (*pāda*) conveys the non-existence of all things—both supreme and non-supreme—then the statement beginning with "by which this... would be purposeless, because it is impossible to speak of pervasion and the like in the absence of any pervaded entity.

By this [explanation], there is a superimposed identity with the partless, pure Brahman, and the apprehension thereof occurs when the negating statement "not here, not manifold" (*neha nānā*) is reflected upon. Even such scriptural passages as "Truth, Knowledge, Infinite" (*satyaṃ jñānamanantam*) teach the pure, non-dual Brahman by abandoning all attributes for one of purified mind, in conjunction with the realization of "not here, not manifold," as stated in the Mañjūṣā and other works: "The reasoning that takes the reality of difference as its object is one thing, while the reasoning that takes the illusion of difference as its object is another;
the reasoning that takes the reality of difference as its object is destroyed because it contradicts the Veda."

The statement of Śrī Harṣa, "Because of the scriptural teaching that there is a single cognition, there is neither 'this' nor 'that'," and so forth, is also refuted. This is because the scriptural passage concerning the single cognition can be explained through similarity, and because it has already been stated that the scriptural passages such as "there is no diversity here" do not intend to establish that Brahman is devoid of attributes (*nirdharmaka*) or that the world is unreal. Furthermore, according to Nāgeśa’s established doctrine, the Vaiśeṣikas and others are speakers who deny the true nature of reality; thus, one could say that Gautama [the author of the Nyāya-sūtras] asserts indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatva*) by denying the existence that resides in the real object.

By the commentary ending with the words, "In the sūtra *tasya bhāvaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.1.119), the teachers teach that suffixes expressing the sense of 'being' (*bhāva*) are prescribed only when there is indeed a distinction between the meaning of the base and the meaning of the suffix; furthermore, the definition 'substance (*dravya*) is a collection of qualities' is etymologically precise," it is demonstrated that there is indeed a distinction between the two. Since its non-existence (*asattva*) was not mentioned therein, the intention of the three sages is that it is indeed existent (*san*).

Therefore, the claim made by others that difference (*bheda*) is non-existent should not be accepted by followers of Pāṇini, as it is not stated in the *Bhāṣya* and other such works. As for the statement, "The non-existence of difference is also clear from that *Bhāṣya* and elsewhere," this is merely a figurative expression regarding the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*). This is because it proceeds in accordance with Kaiyaṭa’s commentary, which states, "Setting aside the investigation into real difference and non-difference, one relies upon the difference well-known in the world," and Uddyota, which explains that the intended meaning is simply that "real difference does not exist at all. Consequently, since those two [interpretations] lack any foundation in the original texts, they are to be considered doubtful.

Furthermore, when one's own five fingers are being observed, they are perceived in a distinctly divided form; since this difference is established by the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of everyone, who could possibly deny it? And whose tongue would be moved to say that it does not exist, given that no grounds for sublation (*bādhā*) or other such reasons are seen? Therefore, this Nāgeśa, relying on the Vijñānavāda position—which contradicts the Vedas and was refuted by the venerable author of the Sūtras in such aphorisms as "There is no non-existence, because [the world] is perceived" (Brahma Sūtra 2.2.28)—[has spoken thus] regarding the Śruti and other scriptures.
And it appears that he manifests hostility toward the words of the great seers (*maharṣi*). Here is the summary:
"The path of those two [the Buddhists and Jains] consists in resorting to the doctrine of the inexpressible (*anirvaktavyatā*);
their reasoning is devoted to partial truths, as it contradicts the Veda."
Those who speak thus, being proponents of the reality of the distinction between entities,
should be answered in such a way that one's own self becomes serene.
The scriptural text, "There is one consciousness,
not a plurality here," does not truly teach the non-existence of attributes within the Self.
The Vedas do not state the non-existence of entities, but rather declare their very reality; such is the definitive conclusion of those who possess knowledge.
Therefore, resorting to the doctrine of indeterminability (anirvacanīyatva) provides us with no way forward;
rather, the entirety of the Vedic word is the faultless path.
For one who negates the reality of things established by the Vedas,
they consider service at the feet of the Vijñānavādins to be the only refuge.
Therefore, the view that "all is real" is the logical one accepted by the wise; for the great seer Vyāsa, the author of the Sūtras, did not undertake the investigation of non-existence.
The doctrine of the Vijñānavādins has been rejected by the authors of the commentaries, is not approved even by Pāṇini, and is contrary to the Śruti and Smṛti.
Relying upon this, the friend of the wise Śrīharṣa dances with joy;
therefore, the person who says "the logic that adheres to the reality of difference is exhausted" is one who speaks thus.
"Just as one who perceives the non-existence of Brahman must say 'it is non-existent,' so too have the followers of Gautama and likewise the proponents of Brahman declared."

Objection from a bystander: Here some object as follows—having made the declaration at the beginning of the *Mañjūṣā*, "This *Vaiyākaraṇasiddhāntamañjūṣā* is being composed," [the author] proceeds to establish the falsity of the world and the oneness of the Self; furthermore, in order to demonstrate the authoritative status of that [teaching], he cites the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, and *Purāṇas*, as well as the statements of other founders of systems (*tīrthakaras*), as authorities. Therefore, we conclude that everything stated therein is approved by the great sages such as Pāṇini and is authoritative.

Nor should one suspect a contradiction here with other Tantras that are intent upon the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), or those intent upon the reality of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*). This is because the author will establish in the second chapter that all such works are auxiliary to the spiritual scriptures (*adhyātma-śāstra*) which teach the oneness of the Self; for a contradiction between a primary work and its auxiliaries is nowhere observed, and the authors of the scriptures themselves accept the non-contradiction between them.

Nor should it be argued that there is no restriction such that only Pāṇini and others must be intended by the word "grammarian" occurring in the statement of the proposition; rather, let some other person, such as Indra, be intended by that term as the grammarian.

By these very Bhaṭṭācāryas, in the *Śekhara*, it was established that the fourteen sūtras beginning with "aiuṇ" constitute *śruti* (revealed scripture). This was done by referring to Sanaka and others who were engaged in ascetic practice and had been instructed by Maheśvara for the sake of attaining the knowledge of Brahman; for, according to the authority of both Śruti and Smṛti—expressed in the words, "It is to be heard from the Vedic texts and reflected upon through reasoning"—the fact that Brahman is to be heard is declared by *śruti* itself. Consequently, because they are rooted in that [instruction], Pāṇini’s work is established as being rooted in *śruti*.

By stating that the statement from the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*, "the Veda of Vedas" (*vedānāṃ vedaḥ*; Chā. 7), which means "I have also studied grammar," refers precisely to this subject, and by noting that it is supported by scripture; and by noting that the author of the *Bhāṣya*, Patañjali, has honored this work by stating, "In the present day, it is clear in the *Bhāṣya* that Pāṇini’s grammar alone is the indicator of correctness"—thereby establishing its unsurpassed authority, [the author proceeds] with the scripture, preceded by a discrimination between correct and corrupt words.

Since it has been established that those who desire spiritual prosperity (*abhyudaya*) through the use of correct words must study the grammar of Pāṇini alone, the extraction of its definitive doctrines would necessarily be required by all. Consequently, as the exposition of those doctrines is thus justified, and given the examples from the *Mahābhāṣya* found here and there, the term "grammarian" (*vaiyākaraṇa*) occurring in the opening statement must be intended to refer specifically to teachers such as Pāṇini and his successors.
It is with this entire point in mind that it was stated in the *Kalā*: "Of the grammarians—Pāṇini and the rest.
This is the response of the neutral observer (*taṭastha*).

Here they proceed: first, by means of another’s mouth, wishing to establish his own intended doctrine of non-duality (*advaita*), [the author] defines the nature of the *sphoṭa* according to the path shown by Bhartṛhari in the *Vākyapadīya*: "Brahman, which is without beginning or end, is the imperishable essence of speech;
it manifests in the form of objects, from which the process of the world proceeds."

Having determined that it is difficult to establish—without first proving its non-duality—the two components of the definition of *sphoṭa* stated in the opening verse, namely, its being the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*) of the manifestation (*vivarta*) of the world consisting of name and form (*nāmarūpa*), and its being the "all-pervading" (*brahma*), and further having ascertained that this proof of non-duality is impossible without establishing the illusory nature (*māyikatva*) of the world, he exerted great effort in that work which he esteemed as a scripture titled *Arthasāra*, which establishes the doctrine of the oneness of the Self; thus, he possessed very firm latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) regarding it.

The oneness of the Self alone is taught throughout all the scriptures; knowing this otherwise, one might think that other systems focused on duality are merely auxiliary to the spiritual treatises that establish non-duality (*advaita*), and that even the Sāṃkhya, Vaiśeṣika, Gautama, and others have their ultimate intent (*tātparya*) in non-duality itself. Therefore, there is no contradiction between those systems and non-duality. However, Śrī Śaṅkarācārya and others, not understanding my intended secret meaning, perceive duality in the Sāṃkhya texts and so forth.

Thinking that such was their intended purpose (*tātparya*), [the author] set out to refute them. Likewise, in order to demonstrate that the activity of others as well is directed toward the refutation of the theory of *sphoṭa*, he first provided a definition of the nature of *sphoṭa* as it has been rejected by them. Then, in order to produce a false impression among the ignorant that his own favored doctrine of the oneness of the Self (*ātmaikatva*) and so forth is also the intention of Pāṇini, he made the formal declaration "The Established Doctrine of the Grammarians" (*vaiyākaraṇasiddhānta*) and composed the work titled *Mañjūṣā*, which has the theory of *sphoṭa*—another name for non-duality (*advaita*)—as its underlying purport.

In that regard, following the determination of the three functions known as *śakti*, *lakṣaṇā*, and *vyañjanā* in the first chapter, [the author] addresses the objection beginning with "Now, what is this word that is the locus of *śakti*? and ending with "if it is argued that even a genus (*jāti*) is impossible. By means of this passage, he demonstrates that—whether one holds the view that phonemes (*varṇa*) are produced or that they are manifested—the phonemes and their manifestations alike possess the qualities of arising and perishing; consequently, it is difficult to define a "word" (*pada*) as a collection of phonemes characterized by a specific sequence, or a "sentence" (*vākya*) as a collection of such words.

Having raised the objection that the cognition of meaning is untenable due to the absence of the cognition of expressive words—which themselves depend on [the cognition of] phonemes and so forth—the author, intending to resolve this by asserting that "there exists a certain word called *sphoṭa* which possesses meaning, and from the cognition of it arises the understanding of the object," first defines the nature of the *sphoṭa*. Having defined it with an extremely concise passage beginning with "In this regard, it is said," which describes the process of dissolution and creation as stated in other systems (*tantrāntara*), he explains that during dissolution, all things belonging to the body of the entire world become merged into the conscious Lord (*īśvara*).

From the Lord, who is Māyā, even in the absence of His own desire to create, there occurs an appearance together with Puruṣa due to the power of the karma of living beings; and that [Māyā] undergoes transformation into the form of the Supreme Lord’s will to create. From Him, there arises a reality known as the *bindu*, which consists of the three qualities (*guṇas*) such as *sattva* and is of the nature of *śakti*. In that [reality], there are three aspects: the conscious (*cit*), the unconscious (*acit*), and that which is a mixture of both.
