Among these, the unconscious aspect, consisting of the impressions (*saṃskāras*) of both word and meaning, is called *avidyā*.

The *nāda* is a mixture of consciousness (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*); the *bindu* is the conscious portion. From that conscious portion in the form of the *bindu*, there arises the *nādamātra* (the mere sound), which is devoid of specific phonemes, dominated by knowledge, endowed with a particular state suitable for creation, mixed with sentience, and known by the alternative name *śabdabrahman*; it becomes the material cause of the universe. This [sound] arises from the movement of the wind produced in the region of the *mūlādhāra*—which is situated below the navel and shaped like a wheel—due to the force of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) residing in the cavity resulting from the conjunction of the effort born of the desire of a person wishing to express a known object; from that [place], and thence...

As that vital breath (marut) proceeds sequentially through the regions of the navel, heart, and throat, it assumes the names *parā*, *paśyantī*, *madhyamā*, and *vaikharī* as it is manifested in those respective locations. Although that *nāda* designated as *parā* persists throughout all these states, the *nāda* reached at the stage of *madhyamā*—which is manifested by the *nāda* of *vaikharī*—bears the designation *sphoṭa*.

But it [the phoneme]—being "the locus of space," according to the *Mahābhāṣya* on the sūtra "*aiuṇ*," resides in external space and also in the locus of space within the hearts of all living beings; and because it is the object of the cognition "this is that very letter *ga*, this is that very word, this is that very sentence," and because it is known as residing in those respective locations, it is eternal, one, and all-pervasive (*vibhu*).

It appears as if possessing multiplicity only by conforming to the sequence of the phoneme-refinements (*saṃskāra*) inherent in the manifesting sounds (*dhvani*); thus, colored by properties such as "g-ness" which reside in the manifesting sounds well-known in the world, it produces the cognition of meaning only when manifested by the final phoneme among the series of sounds.
Brahman, which is without beginning or end, is the imperishable essence of sound;
from it proceeds the evolution of the world through the manifestation of objects.
From Prakṛti, who is primarily characterized by the power of action (kriyā-śakti) and whose form is the Bindu, arose Parā Śabdabrahman, the cause of both sound and its meaning.

From such statements by Bhartṛhari, it follows that the supreme Word alone manifests (*vivartate*) in the form of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) consisting of name and form. Since the single *sphoṭa* is the material cause (*upādāna*) of both all words and their meanings, it possesses a dual nature; consequently, its two effects—the word and the meaning—also possess a dual nature. Furthermore, because it is perceived internally by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which is refined by the audible speech (*vaikharī*) grasped by the ear, it is the object of the conventional usage "internal *sphoṭa*" (*āntarasphoṭa*).

By this, there is no room for the doubt as to how there can be perception of the sphoṭa residing within the heart of each respective living being, since it is perceived by the sense of hearing. Thus, he determined the nature of the individual sphoṭa (vyaktisphoṭa) to be that the word which conveys the meaning is purely mental (buddhyātmaka), and not some external, gross entity perceptible by all ears.

Desiring to explain its true nature according to the supreme established doctrine that the *sphoṭa* as a genus (*jātisphoṭa*) is the ultimate refinement [of the theory], [the author states]: "A genus (*jāti*) is a property existing both in the word and in the meaning which produces the cognition of a recurring form; and that [property] residing in the word is the signifier (*vācaka*), while that residing in the meaning is the signified (*vācya*)."

In this regard—having established that the genus (*jāti*), which consists of the nature of the properties residing in the word, is one, eternal, and all-pervasive, along with its causes; and having shown that although this [genus] appears as manifold due to being colored by various forms such as *g-ness* and *r-ness* residing in the manifesting articulations (*dhvani*) according to the sequence of phoneme utterances, it does not follow that there would be the simultaneous presentation of multiple meanings, nor the lack of distinction between the words *saraḥ* and *rasaḥ*, because it presents word-meanings such as "pot" as delimited by that single genus.

This is because of the absence of the manifesting totality (*abhivyañjana-sāmagrī*) consisting of the coloring (*dharmarūṣaṇa*) by those respective properties that bring about the presence of those respective meanings. As stated in the words of Hari: "The genus (*jāti*) manifested by many individuals is known as *sphoṭa*. After explaining its nature in detail with such passages, [it is concluded that] this *sphoṭa* is internal and denotes the meaning; and the denoted meaning, too, is mental (*bauddha*), being permeated by the existence of the intellect (*buddhisattāsamāviṣṭa*). Otherwise, since the existence of a jar would already be understood from the very statement "there is no hare’s horn, there is a jar," the statement "the jar exists" would be redundant.

Furthermore, there is no fault in employing the expression "it exists. However, if one accepts a Buddhist category of entity (*padārtha*), then since that which exists in the mind possesses external existence, the employment of the expressions "it exists" or "it does not exist" is appropriate for the purpose of making known its absence [externally].

Therefore, all objects are merely mental constructs (*buddha*), and external existence is a mere consensus (*saṃvāda-mātra*). In the section establishing that the existence of objects generally consists in their being mental constructs, [the author] states that in error there is "only the superimposition of the form of cognition upon the object," and so forth; having declared the non-existence of the silver and other things appearing in error, he proceeds with the passage beginning "The phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is exactly like this" and ending "Enough of this digression," to demonstrate the oneness of the Self—that which is Brahman alone—and that the entire universe apart from That is illusory (*māyika*).

In the first chapter, [the author] established that Brahman is the illusory material cause (*vivartopādānakāraṇa*) of the world, that its true nature is being the substratum of error, and that the world's illusory character consists in its being a mode of error; furthermore, in each of the other three chapters, he described the oneness of the Self and so forth. In that context, during the discussion on the nature of *māyā*, he specifically refuted the commentary of Śrī Śaṅkara and particularly demolished the notion of ignorance (*avidyā*) as a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*) established in his school's doctrine. The relevance of that [refutation] here is to be considered. Let us now return to our subject matter.

In this regard, concerning the statement "Brahman is Truth," no one other than the Cārvākas and their ilk disagrees. However, people cannot tolerate the assertion that the commonality of all things (*vastusāmānya*) is illusory (*māyika*). This has been explained in detail by the various teachers who engaged in the investigation of the higher and lower principles (*parāpara-tattva*) within their respective treatises.

Now, one might object: "Granted that this may not be the view of other teachers, we say that it is indeed accepted by Pāṇini and others, because Nāgeśa establishes this in the *Mañjūṣā* with the formal proposition beginning 'For the Grammarian' (*vaiyākaraṇe*) and so forth. To this they reply: We know that the teacher Pāṇini did not compose this treatise for the purpose of establishing the doctrine of the oneness of the Self (*ātmaikatva-siddhānta*), since he began with the section on technical terminology (*saṃjñā-kāṇḍa*) which is useful for the science of word-formation (*śabda-saṃskāra*). The venerable author of the *Bhāṣya* as well—

With the words "Now begins the instruction on words" (*atha śabdānuśāsanam*) and "Of which words? (*keṣāṃ śabdānām*), [Patañjali] stated that the subject matter (*viṣaya*) of this treatise is words and its purpose (*prayojana*) is the knowledge thereof. By this, Nāgeśa—speaking in his *Śekhara* commentaries that the Teacher (Patañjali) commenced the treatise having kept in mind the formal proposition (*pratijñā*) "Now, therefore, we shall explain words"—also maintains that words alone are the subject matter of this treatise.

If this were so, some might think that the venerable Pāṇini considers Vāsudeva to be the supreme among all, and thus how could another person object? To show that such pride should not exist—since the teachers do not have such an intention because there is no supporting reason, whereas others can demonstrate that their intention lies precisely in the distinction between the Selfs, as seen from the evidence—the subsequent section [of the text] is introduced for the purpose of making this known.

Regarding the oneness of the self (*ātmaikatva*) and other doctrines established in works such as the *Mañjūṣā*, the Upaniṣadic scholars maintain that the words of Pāṇini and others serve as proof for these points; however, this is merely a powerful statement [of their own] regarding the absence of his actual consent. As for the claim that the very same commentary (*bhāṣya*) which Nāgeśa and others cite as authoritative for their own specific arguments establishes the doctrine of the oneness of the self—that is nothing more than a mere wishful thought. This is because there is no royal edict or similar authority to the effect that the meaning of that commentary is precisely what Nāgeśa and others have stated.

Because it is possible to interpret [the Mahābhāṣya] otherwise by conforming to the Śrutis and other authorities, both ancient and modern scholars of subtle intellect—those devoted to the sacred teachings who are experts in grammar—having reinterpreted the Mahābhāṣya (which was cited as an authority in the *Śekhara* and other works to justify their own preferred methodology), refute the conclusions set forth in the *Śekhara* and similar texts; this is indeed well known.

This being the case, how could those proficient in the science of the Self (*adhyātmavidyā*) consider as valid the interpretation of the words of Patañjali—the crest-jewel of the most orthodox believers—composed by Nāgeśa and others, which contradicts such authorities as the Vedas?

Furthermore, regarding the *sarūpa-* sūtra (1.2.64) and the *striyām* sūtra (4.1.3), there is the Bhāṣya determining the nature of gender (*liṅga*), which states: "Therefore, it is not possible for grammarians to rely upon worldly gender; some philosophical conclusion (*svakṛtānta*) must necessarily be adopted. What is that conclusion? Contraction (*saṃstyāna*) and procreation (*prasava*) are gender."

Regarding this, Kaiyaṭa states in his commentary on the *Sarūpasūtra*: "In that context, one who adheres to the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādī*) resorts to the appropriate position—namely, 'the worldly' (*laukika*). Furthermore, in the *Uddyota*, the meaning of the word *kṛtānta* found in the *Bhāṣya* is given as "established doctrine" (*siddhānta*). However, in the commentary on the *Striyām* sūtra, Kaiyaṭa, taking the term *svakṛtānta*, explained it as "one's own established doctrine" (*svasiddhānta*). Kaiyaṭa further notes: "He says 'one's own established doctrine' (*svakṛtānta*) by relying upon the Sāṃkhya school of thought."

Having introduced Kaiyaṭa with the words, "He says—'svakṛtānta'—relying on the Sāṃkhya doctrine," Nāgeśa concludes: "By this, he indicates that grammar follows the Sāṃkhya scriptures. In that very same sūtra, Nāgeśa himself explains Kaiyaṭa’s gloss, "the established doctrine of the Sāṃkhyas," as meaning "of the teacher Patañjali, who is a follower of the Theistic Sāṃkhya (Seśvara-sāṃkhya).
From this, it is determined that both the author of the Bhāṣya and the author of the *Pradīpa* consider the teacher Pāṇini to be a follower of the Theistic Sāṃkhya doctrine.

Sāṃkhya is indeed twofold: that which is without a Lord (nirīśvara) and that which is with a Lord (seśvara). It is clear to the learned that in both cases, the distinction between the Puruṣas and the non-illusory nature of the world are propounded. Thus, it can easily be stated that Pāṇini also intended only this distinction. To facilitate easy understanding, something is briefly described here, summarizing how both types of Sāṃkhya are proponents of dualism (bhedavādins).

Regarding the first [view]: there are two principles (*tattva*), namely *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, and the *puruṣas* are many, because of the specific determination of the causes of birth, death, and so forth, and because their activities do not occur simultaneously. As stated in the *Sāṃkhyakārikā*: "The multiplicity of *puruṣas* is established, and also from the diversity of the three *guṇas*" (Kārikā 18). *Prakṛti* transforms into the form of objects to be enjoyed for the sake of the experience of the *puruṣas*, whereas the *puruṣas* themselves are manifold. Having explained this very verse in this manner, Gauḍapādācārya and others established the plurality of *puruṣas* according to the Sāṃkhya doctrine.

In the second [system]: there are three principles—primordial matter (prakṛti), the individual self (puruṣa), and the Lord (īśvara). Although primordial matter is insentient, when impelled by the Lord, it transforms into the form of objects suitable for the enjoyment of the living being denoted by the term puruṣa, and thereby accomplishes both the experience and liberation of that puruṣa.

And thus—from the *Yoga-sūtras* composed by the great sage Patañjali, the teacher of the Sāṃkhya with God (Seśvara-sāṃkhya)—it is determined that: Nature (*prakṛti*) is the means for experience and so forth; the person (*puruṣa*) is the experiencer; God (*īśvara*) is the impeller; and liberation for the person results from devotion to God (*īśvara-praṇidhāna*). For it is stated therein: "The [guṇas] have the natures of illumination, activity, and stability... [and so on].

For it is said in the seven aphorisms [of the Yoga-sūtras]: "The object of perception (*dṛśya*) consists of the elements and the senses, whose nature is illumination, activity, and inertia, and which exist for the sake of experience and liberation" (2.18); "By devotion to the Lord (*īśvarapraṇidhāna*)" (1.23); "The Lord (*īśvara*) is a distinct *puruṣa* untouched by afflictions, actions, their fruitions, or latent impressions" (1.24); "In Him, the seed of omniscience is unsurpassed" (1.25); "He is the teacher even of the ancients, being unconditioned by time" (1.26); "His designator is the syllable *praṇava*" (1.27); and "Its repetition and meditation upon its meaning" (1.28).

Having established the three principles (*tattva-traya*), [the author]—through a group of six sūtras beginning with "From devotion to the Lord" (*īśvarapraṇidhānāt*)—demonstrates that the worship of the Blessed One, its definition, His omniscience, His status as the Guru of Brahmā and others, His being signified by the *praṇava* (Om), the repetition (*japa*) of the *praṇava* which denotes Him, and the meditation on the Lord who is denoted by it, constitute the limbs for attaining the perfection of yoga, which is the means to liberation in the form of isolation (*kaivalya*). By means of the relationship between the object of worship and the worshipper, he establishes the difference between the Person (*puruṣa*) and the Lord; [and further demonstrates that] "even though it has perished for one who has attained his goal, it is not destroyed... [Yoga Sūtra 4.32].

Since the plurality of *puruṣas* is established by the sūtra, "Because that [pleasure and pain] is common to others" (Yoga Sūtra 2.22), and because of the statement in the *Udyota* on the sūtra "In the feminine" (Pāṇini 4.1.3)— which asserts that "even though *prakṛti* is insentient, she is impelled by God, with the assistance of various unseen forces (*adṛṣṭa*) and so forth, to accomplish the purpose of the *puruṣa*, characterized as experience and liberation"— and since the Sāṃkhya system does not state that the world is illusory (*mithyā*), it is understood that, according to the Sāṃkhya view, the world possesses reality and there exists a plurality of selves (*ātman*).

Our conclusion is that, according to the view of the author of the *Sūtras*, Pāṇini—namely, that both the world and the individual selves are real and distinct, while God is their regulator and their object of worship, and is therefore the highest—it is not tenable to postulate the oneness of the self and so forth. I have set forth these two [arguments], along with the doubt and its resolution, for the easy understanding of those seekers who stand at a neutral position.
[This concludes] the refutation of the existence of mental constructs (*bauddha-sattā*).

Indeed, in the *Mañjūṣā*, while establishing the existence of word-meanings (*padārtha*) as being mental (*bauddha*), [the author] cites as authoritative evidence the examples from the Bhāṣya on four sūtras—*upadeśe 'janunāsika it* (P. 1.3.2), *hetumati ca* (P. 3.1.26), *paṅkti-viṃśati-* (P. 5.1.59), and *tad asyāsty asmin* (P. 5.2.94)—and mentions the illustrations of water in a mirage and so forth found in the treatise. Furthermore, because of the statement "of the phenomenal world" (*prapañcasya*), the mental existence (*bauddhī sattā*) of both existent and non-existent word-meanings is intended by the Bhāṣya.

If it is argued that, therefore, it is logical for this world to be non-existent just like a rabbit's horn and so forth—which are entered into the existence of the intellect—then that is true. However, one who speaks thus must first consider the following, O long-lived one: if we were to assert the non-existence of objects merely on the basis of their being in the intellect and by means of the example of the rabbit's horn, then, according to your own line of reasoning, since Brahman and the *sphoṭa* are likewise objects of cognition produced by words and are equally entered into the existence of the intellect, [they too would be non-existent].

How shall we resolve the objection of others that, by the analogy of a rabbit’s horn, even those two [Brahman and *sphoṭa*] would be like a flower in the sky? Or how could our own established position—that "the reality of Brahman and *sphoṭa* exists, while everything else is unreal"—be tenable? Furthermore, if linguistic usage were based on the actual existence of an object, then the cause therein would simply be the mental existence (*buddhi-sattā*) of that object; thus, the teaching of the Teachers would not be required, as linguistic usage could easily proceed even by taking external existence as its basis.

[Objection: But surely external existence (*bahiḥsattā*) is not the object of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), since by the word "jar" existence itself is understood; in that case, affirmation would be redundant and negation would be impossible for what is already known, so that the affirmations and negations "the jar exists" and "the jar does not exist" would be untenable. If, however, one accepts mental existence (*bauddhasattā*), then the affirmations and negations "the mental jar exists externally" and "it does not exist externally" would be consistent—[if you say this, we reply: no.

Just as when the word "jar" is uttered, there is no manifestation of "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) or "knowability" (*prameyatva*), which reside in the jar but are distinct from "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*), so too there is no manifestation of "existence" (*sattā*), which likewise resides in it; for since existence is not [directly] known [from the word], the aforementioned fault does not apply. Furthermore, it is not tenable to claim that "existence" is also denoted by the word, because one does not experience a cognition of a jar qualified by existence merely upon hearing the word "jar."

Furthermore—although it is a rule that existence (*sattā*) is a cause with respect to linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), even when there is a mental apprehension (*saṃskāra*) of a rabbit's horn and the like within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), the proof for this is simply the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) concerning that object; thus, as Nāgeśa has stated, it is possible to say, "A rabbit's horn does not exist. Moreover, for one who does not possess primary external existence for things such as a rabbit's horn, the acceptance of a conceptual existence (*bauddhasattā*) is appropriate; but for one who possesses primary external existence for things such as a jar, why should that [conceptual existence] be accepted?

The primacy of existence (*sattā*) has been clearly stated in the *Uddyota* on the *matup*-sūtra. However, some maintain that existence alone is not the object of linguistic usage; rather, they argue that even things such as "the horn of a hare" are seen to be the objects of linguistic usage.

Granted that you may have the wish that this commentary establishes the existence [of objects] as mere mental constructs (*buddhi-sattā*), nevertheless, this commentary does not negate the primary external existence (*mukhyā bāhya-sattā*) of entities such as jars and cloths, nor is it capable of displacing their inherent property of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*). Therefore, one who asserts that the world is non-existent by virtue of being a mere mental construct—thereby equating it to a hare’s horn—is merely honored within his own circle. All the passages from the commentary cited here refer exclusively to external existence.

In this regard, the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra "upadeśe 'j" states: "One standing here instructs Devadatta, who is in Pāṭaliputra, as being 'one with armlets, earrings, and rounded arms. For the statement "standing in Pāṭaliputra" and so forth refers specifically to Devadatta and others as qualified by their external existence. The intention of the *Bhāṣya* is that the intellect possesses the capacity to take as its object things separated by space and time; thus, even an entity situated in another location becomes an object of the intellect.

The phrase "and [the word] *hetumati*" from the Sūtra, as well as the commentary (*bhāṣya*) stating "of existing objects of cognition," signifies that [the word *hetumat*] refers only to objects characterized by existence delimited by prior time; thus, its scope consists solely of objects qualified by multiple instances of existence. For this very reason, [Patañjali] employed the term "of existing" (*sataḥ*) earlier; otherwise, he would have used the expression "existing objects of cognition" (*buddhiviṣayān sataḥ*).

The statement from the *Mahābhāṣya* on the sūtra "paṅktiviṃśati-"—namely, "Terms such as 'twenty' and so forth will apply to a collection; 'saṃgha', 'samūha', and 'samudāya' are not different in meaning"—does not establish the existence of objects as mental constructs (*buddhisattā*). Rather, it serves only to indicate the distinction between the part and the whole, or the quality and the possessor of the quality. Furthermore, the commentary on that same sūtra—which states, "When the quality is primary, one says 'the cloth is white'; when the possessor of the quality is primary, one says 'the white cloth'"—neither establishes the existence of objects as mental constructs nor does it negate their external existence (*bahiḥsattā*).

For this very reason, Vararuci, while prescribing the elision (*luk*) in the rule *guṇavacanabhyo luk* [Pāṇini 5.2.94], raised the objection: "If it is argued that [the usage] is established because there is no distinction [between quality and qualified], we reply that a distinction is observed. He then established the final position (*siddhānta*) by stating that since a quality exists without deviating from the possessor of the quality, the usage *paṭaḥ śuklaḥ* ("the cloth is white") is established precisely through non-difference; therefore, the commencement of the rule for elision would be useless. However, because one observes the distinct usage *ghaṭasya śuklaḥ* ("the whiteness of the jar"), he concluded that a distinction between the two must indeed be acknowledged, and thus the rule must be commenced.

In this regard, even the author of the Bhāṣya, considering that [the desired result] is established precisely because there is no distinction [between the quality and the qualified], does not reject the statement regarding elision (*lugvacana*). By this, they understand that the distinction between the quality (*guṇa*) and the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*) is agreed upon by both [parties]. However, we who are like [ordinary people] have no authority over the initiation or rejection of such statements; for even the most subtle object is accessible to the perception (*pratyakṣa*) of yogins, and thus it cannot be said that it does not exist simply because it is not within the range of our own perception. Through the tradition of instruction and the observation of its effects, it exists—just as in the case of bile (*pitta*), which, though burning, is not perceived as a distinct modification during the onset of a fever.

"It exists"—thus it is stated in the Vedānta that "the three states of being are subtle, for a subtle state is to be known through the signless. This was declared in the rule *vartamāne laṭ*. Its meaning is as follows: just as the threads within a cloth, though burning along with the fire, are not perceived in their true nature, so too each individual moment—whether it be a modification (*vikṛti*) occurring when there is a conjunction (i.e., the presence of a collection of causal factors) or a specific action existing in a moment—is not seen because of its extreme subtlety. He says "it exists" to show that one should not claim that moments and such do not exist merely because they are beyond the scope of our perception.

"Tribhāvāḥ" refers to those yogins whose cognition (*bhāva*) extends across the three times (*triṣu kāleṣu*); they possess knowledge regarding objects existing in the gross, subtle, and three-fold durations of time. They "perceive" (*vedayante*)—that is, they know—that "transformation" (*vikṛti*), which is characterized by action and consists of subtle moments and so forth. [The causative suffix] *ṇic* is used here for the sake of the root meaning itself. Through inference based on the impossibility of explaining effects otherwise, and through the tradition of instruction, even subtle matters are accessible and must be known by us.

Thus, it should be understood that the venerable author of the Bhāṣya instructs that when one seeks to establish that yogic perception is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding an object that is beyond the sensory perception of persons such as ourselves, the claim that such an object does not exist—made by someone who, while asserting that yogic perception is a valid means of knowledge regarding such an object, simultaneously denies its existence—is not to be respected by those who rely on valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇika*). In this regard, the *Mañjūṣā*’s statement—"In such a case, for us there is a cognition called conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)"—is to be considered.

Since the perception of a yogi is a valid cognition (*pramāṇajñāna*) because its object is ultimately real, whereas the cognition called conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is devoid of a real entity and arises at a time when [the object] is not being perceived, it has been determined by the author of the *Yogasūtrabhāṣya* and others that conceptual construction does not function as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, in a context where a valid cognition is functioning, it is impossible to admit a conceptual construction that contradicts it.

The Bhāṣya passage beginning with "In the injunction of a quality, such as 'Let twenty cows be brought,' there is the status of being the object of the injunction for the substance possessing that quality," means that they exist through a state of concomitance characterized by mutual exclusion (parasparaparihāra), and not through non-difference (*abheda*). Furthermore, the Bhāṣya on that same sūtra, "Because of non-separation" (*avyatirekāt*), also has the sense of being invariably concomitant (*avyabhicaritatva*).

And thus, it appears that the purport of the *Bhāṣya* is that the difference between part and whole, as well as between quality and qualified, is extremely subtle in its essential nature (*svarūpataḥ*). For this very reason, in the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra *tasya pūraṇe ḍaṭ* (Pāṇini 5.2.48), it is stated: "Because of their distinctness (*anyatvāt*), both [theories] are justified; the illustration of the tree and its branches [shows this]. By this, the author of the *Bhāṣya* asserts that a compound formation (*vṛtti*) is justified through the distinction between part and whole—just as in the case of *vārkṣī*—and likewise through the distinction between the meanings of the base and the suffix in forms such as *pañcama*.

In the sense of "a part of a tree," the suffix *añ* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.3.140 (*anudāttādeśca*) to form the word *vṛkṣya*. Even here, we find no evidence in the Bhāṣya for the existence of conceptual reality (*bauddhasattā*) or for the unreality of difference (*bhedasyāvāstavatva*).

The *bhāṣya* on the *matup*-sūtra, however, which states "an entity does not deviate from existence," means that [the word] does not deviate from the existence of a thing that performs causal efficiency (*arthakriyākārin*); thus, it refers exclusively to things characterized by external existence (*bāhyasattā*), because only that which is externally existent possesses causal efficiency. Therefore, there is no deviation, since such efficiency is absent in cases like the horn of a hare. As for the *pradīpodyota* commentary on these four sūtras, it is merely intended to delight the minds of the ignorant.

By this [statement], the following views are shown to be contrary to the Bhāṣya: Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the *Paṅkti* sūtra, which states, "And words, based on objects established by the intellect, produce in the intellect itself a form of the object; thus, even though there is no real difference [between the word and the external object], they cause that [difference] to be understood"; as well as Uddyota’s remark, "Words denote only objects imagined by the intellect, not the absence of external objects, nor do they state the absence of words' capacity to denote external objects"; and likewise the passage from the Mañjūṣā with the same meaning.

Because the commentary does not state the non-existence of external objects nor the absence of words denoting external objects, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the collapse of linguistic usage such as "bring the jar. Furthermore, even *brahman* and *sphoṭa*, which are established solely by the scriptures, would then be reduced to the status of a hare's horn. Therefore, an object merely imagined by human intellect should not obstruct the objective existence of things as cognized through valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). It is only by accepting mental existence that the justification for linguistic usage is maintained.

Furthermore, if one accepts that linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) is possible even for non-existent things by admitting their conceptual existence (*bauddhasattā*), then the recourse to the principle of *vyapadeśivadbhāva* (treating a thing as if it were what it is designated) and the rule *ādyantavadekasmin* would be redundant; for since the states of being "first" and "last," as well as the status of being a stem-suffix (*dhātu*) or a member (*avayava*) obtainable through *vyapadeśivadbhāva*, are all encompassed within conceptual existence, operations conditioned by "being first" and so forth would be easily accomplished.

Furthermore, if one accepts the existence of all things as being common to everything, then since non-existent objects would themselves be non-existent, it would be impossible to establish the distinction that a word is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) when it has an existent object, and invalid (*aprāmāṇya*) when it has a non-existent object. Moreover, in such a case, resorting to the mental modification (*vṛtti*) called conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) would also be untenable.

If it is argued that there is no such fault because the existence of a mental construct (bauddhasattā) merely serves as the basis for the conventional usage "the horn of a hare does not exist," then we reply: in that case, it would also be impossible for the water of a mirage and the like to serve as an illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta) of a mental construct; since the unreality of the world cannot be established by means of such an example, you should understand that the reality of the world is thereby proven. Furthermore, the Commentator never asserted anywhere that external existence does not belong to objects such as jars; therefore, the mention of the water of a mirage as an example should be considered with caution.

Nor is there non-existence [of the world], because subverting cognitions such as "this is not a jar" do not arise in the same way as [the cognition] "this is not silver. Furthermore, since it is stated that objects are impermanent in the words, "They are impermanent, coming and going" (Gītā 2.14), and because the learned have declared, "discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities," the path supported by valid means of knowledge is that the world is impermanent. Now, one might object: "The wise agent, having performed all actions within the intellect, extends his policy..."
Having perceived through the word those objects denoted that are affected by suffering, one should establish their sequence within the intellect.

If it is argued that—since the *Mañjūṣā* states in its first chapter that in the commentary on the sūtra "The closest proximity [of sounds] is *saṃhitā*" (Pāṇini 1.4.109), it is the mental object (*bauddhārtha*) alone that is the object of cognition, and thus it is logical that the mental nature of objects and the fact that only that [mental object] is the object of cognition are both approved by the Bhāṣya—[we reply]: here they say that since neither of these two points is explicitly stated in that Bhāṣya, neither is approved by the Bhāṣya.

For in that [text], only the fact that objects are the objects of cognition is stated; by that much, neither is your desired point established, nor is there any loss for our opponents. In that context, because the organ of speech lacks the capacity to utter two phonemes simultaneously, and because the subsequent phoneme arises only after the preceding phoneme has perished, there is no possibility of temporal sequence (*paurvāparya*) between what is already destroyed and what is currently present. Consequently, due to the absence of proximity (*saṃnikarṣa*), the Sūtra is untenable; thus [the author] says, "Indeed, there is no temporal sequence among phonemes," and so forth.

When the opponent has raised the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) that phonemes (*varṇa*) are non-eternal, [the author] provides the resolution with the words beginning "in the intellect" (*buddhau*), stating that there is no fault in the position that sounds (*śabda*) are eternal. The Commentator states the meaning of the verse: "The sequence of sounds exists only as an object of the intellect. This is the explanation of the meaning of the first quarter-verse. The phrase "having done so, the treatise is set forth" is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.

To the question "What are those words?", he says: "And here, that very man who acts with foresight (*prekṣāpūrvakārī*) perceives: 'In this context, this word ought to be employed. This commentary is intended to explain the meaning of the second and third quarters [of the verse]. The meaning of the two terms *dhīraḥ* ("wise") and *tanvannītiḥ* ("practicing policy") is "one who acts with foresight. Its further sense is "a learned person (*paṇḍita*) whose intellect has the nature of pervading all objects of knowledge. The word *bhavati* ("is") is to be construed with the word *kartā* ("the agent") found in the verse.

The agent—that is, the one who employs [the means]—is the subject; this is the meaning. The phrase "he sees" is an explanation of the meaning of the third quarter [of the verse]. The literal meaning is clear. By this, the literal sense is indicated as follows: having seen—that is, having ascertained—"I shall make known the meanings to be taught by means of words," that is, by these specific words; or alternatively, the literal sense is indicated as: having ascertained the meanings to be expressed by words, thinking "this is the meaning expressed by this word. By this, the interpretation "meanings accompanied by words" is rejected.

The statement, "He perceives that this word should be employed for this meaning," is an explanation of the intended meaning (*tātparya*). The sense is that, according to the maxim "the composition of words follows from having understood the meaning," the wise person determines: "This word denotes the meaning to be communicated; this word should be employed here for this meaning. He establishes that the sequence [of words] is an object of cognition by stating: "In this word, first this phoneme, then this, then this"; the ellipsis is to be supplied as "there is a sequence."

The connection with the verse is: "one should place this [word] before or after [that word] in the mind. The word *kartā* (the agent) is to be supplied here as the subject. The optative suffix (*liṅ*) is used in the sense of possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*). The underlying meaning is as follows: since words are eternal and yet must be employed as characterized by a specific sequence, they are objects of the intellect; thus, the sequence residing within them necessarily becomes an object of the speaker's intellect as well. Consequently, the priority and posteriority (*paurvāparya*) are also objects of that intellect. Having determined that this very priority and posteriority is the cause for the application of the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*), the teachers set the treatise into motion.

If it is objected: "Is it not the case that the *sphoṭa* alone is the eternal word (*śabda*), and that the sequence of phonemes (*varṇa*) does not belong to it because it is partless—as has been stated? How then can it be said [that there is a sequence]? We reply: No. For, according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that the scripture is the instructor of words by way of the analogy of the "line-drawn cow" (*rekhāgavaya*), it is necessary to superimpose the properties of the manifestor (*vyañjaka*) upon the manifested (*vyaṅgya*) *sphoṭa*—just as one avoids the contingency of the word "pot" (*ghaṭa*) presenting the cloth (*paṭa*)—because of the presence of sequence in the manifestor which stands in the place of the line. This is because you yourself have stated that even in that case, there is the presence of the sequence of phonemes.

Since both the suggested (vyaṅgya) and the suggestor (vyañjaka) possess the sequence of phonemes (varṇakrama), by this it is stated that objects of cognition are merely objects of the intellect; however, those of subtle intellect who are free from envy should understand that there is no "mental existence" (bauddhasattā) distinct from that [intellectual object].

Furthermore, in the *Stānivatsūtra*, the author of the Bhāṣya does not explicitly state that word-meanings are mental (*bauddha*). For in that context, regarding the instruction "The mango trees are to the east of the village," the cognition of "mangoness" (*āmratva*)—which applies to the general class of trees existing in the region east of the village—is also applicable to the *nyagrodha* trees located there. That cognition is set aside by a specific instruction: "Those which have milky sap, aerial roots, and broad leaves are *nyagrodhas*."

Therefore, it has been stated by Puru that what is taught does not bring about the transformation of a banyan tree into a mango tree; by this commentary (*bhāṣya*) as well, it is established that the meaning of a word becomes an object of the intellect (*buddhiviṣaya*), but not that it resides within the intellect (*buddhistha*). In the *bhāṣya*, the phrase "being withdrawn" (*apakṛṣyamāṇa*) means "being removed" (*nivartyamāna*), and not "withdrawn from its place in the mind. It is stated in the *Uddyota* that there is a superimposition (*āropa*) upon the real object of the cessation and arising occurring within the intellect, but not that the intellect possesses the substrate of removal or addition belonging to the object.
Now, it might be argued: "If the Buddhist doctrine is not accepted, [one must rely on such texts as] 'He uttered "Bhūḥ," he created the earth' (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 2.2.4.2), and:
'But in the beginning, the Lord fashioned separately for all beings their names, their actions, and their distinct conditions from the words of the Veda alone' (Manusmṛti 9.21)."

Thus, the creation of the earth and other elements as described in the Śruti and Smṛti—based on words such as "bhūḥ" (earth) and so forth—would be untenable if it were preceded by knowledge of their meanings; for prior to creation, the absence of an external earth would prevent the emergence of both the apprehension of the word-potencies and the cognition of the objects (the earth and others) intended to be created.

It is true that one could argue: "If external objects are accepted, then Hiraṇyagarbha possesses the apprehension of the powers (*śakti*) of words such as 'earth' with respect to those objects existing within his own intellect, and he also possesses the cognition having them as its object; thus, because the knowledge of the objects to be created exists, the creation described in the Śruti and other texts is logically consistent. However, according to the purport of the Śruti and Smṛti, [Hiraṇyagarbha] created the earth and so forth after cognizing them through words such as 'earth' as they existed in a previous *kalpa*. Therefore, even if there were no external objects prior to the creation, there is no inconsistency in the description of creation.

This is because Śrī Śaṅkarācārya and others have stated in the commentary on the sūtra "samānanāma-" that even though the great dissolution (mahāpralaya) destroys all worldly transactions, it is possible for Hiraṇyagarbha and others to reconnect with the transactions of a previous kalpa through the grace of the Supreme Lord; and also because of the explanation of Manu’s statement: "Whatever [Vedas] he had at the beginning of the previous kalpa, he created them again at the start of creation by perceiving them from the very words of the Vedas. Thus, [the continuity of knowledge is established] through the apprehension of the powers of objects existing in another kalpa and through the resulting cognition.

Since the creation described in the Śrutis and other sources is logically consistent, this cannot serve as proof that the meaning [of words] is mental (*bauddha*). Patañjali nowhere in his Bhāṣya explains these Śrutis and other texts in the manner asserted by Nāgeśa. It appears that Nāgeśa stated this either because he had not consulted Śaṅkara’s commentary on the two sūtras, *Śabda iti cet na* (Brahmasūtra 1.3.28) and *Samānanāmārṣeyam* (Brahmasūtra 1.3.30), or because he considered the meaning stated therein to be inconsistent.
Only the wise are capable of responding to the various alternative methods demonstrated in the Mañjūṣā; therefore, I do not engage with them here, for fear of prolixity.

Some, however, maintain that the mental modification known as conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), which has non-existent things such as a rabbit’s horn as its object, does not depend upon the objective thing being the referent of a word; for only that which possesses a relation to space and time is a referent of a word, and since a rabbit’s horn lacks that, it is not a real entity. This is clearly stated in the section on the indeterminability of ignorance (*avidyā*) in the *Advaitasiddhi* and its commentary, where it is said: "Non-existence is the state of being indefinable (*nirupākhya*), because being indefinable consists in not being the referent of a word."

It has been stated [in the *Vyākhyā-candrikā*]: "Because of the absence of a relation with space and time, that which is a mere void (*tuccha*) cannot be the object of a word's function (*padavṛtti*). However, the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) produced by words such as 'hare's horn' does not depend upon a word's function, because that status belongs only to verbal cognition and its opposite [error]. This is their intended meaning: that through the power of the word itself, cognition arises even without depending on the apprehension of the word's denotative power (*śaktigraha*) in the case of words like 'hare's horn'; this is the purport of the sūtra "śabdajñāna" (verbal cognition).

And thus, since for those who do not accept [external objects] the [notion of] existence can be maintained even in the absence of Buddhist existence, their postulation of it is entirely in vain. Wise men would not tolerate the claim made in the *Advaitasiddhi* and other works that this statement was made because they failed to properly consider the meaning of the cited *Mahābhāṣya*; nor should it be said that its intended meaning is merely the absence of connection with a location distinct from the intellect, for there is no reason for such a restriction, and following the literal path of the text is preferable to such a construction.

Nor should it be argued that if one accepts that there is no verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) here without knowledge of the linguistic function (*vṛtti*), then the rule regarding being a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) would not apply—since the cause for a verbal cognition produced by a particular word is the knowledge of the function as defined by that word. This is because the intention is that there is no fault, since one posits that the object of cognition is distinct from cognitions such as those arising from resonance (*anuraṇana*). Nor should it be argued that even so, the status of being a nominal stem would not be established in the absence of a linguistic function.

In the case of imitation (*anukaraṇa*), because it possesses meaningfulness through its capacity to convey the object of imitation by means of the relation called similarity (*sādṛśya*), it possesses the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Furthermore, because it conveys an unreal object by means of the relation of being the object of a mental modification (*vikalpa*) known as a function (*vṛtti*) that arises subsequent to the cognition of the word, its meaningfulness—and thus its status as a nominal stem—is established. Moreover, one may also say that all this is merely the view of Kaiyaṭa and not his own, since he has first explained the very point stated in the *Kaiyaṭa* on the *matup*-sūtra with the words "In this way, even an unreal object [can be denoted]," and then concluded with "Even existence (*sattā*) is denotable by a word; such is its nature."

Nor should it be said that this is also accepted by Nāgeśa because of his commentary in the *Kalā*, where he explains: "and [it is] not the intention of one who accepts that the word-meaning is a mental construct (*buddhistha-padārtha*). For we understand that his commentary is intended to conform to the literal wording of the text, namely, "the state of that" (*tadbhāva*). If this were his own desired view, then he would have stated simply: "existence (*sattā*) too is denotable by words."

The entire *Mañjūṣā* treatise, which is devoted to establishing the ideality (*bauddhatva*) of all word-meanings, serves as a corroboration of what was stated by Kaiyaṭa. Or, even if it were the case that this is also the view of Nāgeśa according to the direction indicated by Kalā, even so, nothing is lost for those who maintain the truth of the phenomenal world as established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

It should be understood that [the claims] that objects possess the nature of being mental forms—as stated in the *Pradīpa* following the phrase "established by the intellect" (*buddhivyavasthāpita*), etc.—and that they possess a body consisting of mere appearance—as stated in the *Mañjūṣā* as "a false object whose body is mere appearance"—are not tenable; for neither the author of the Sūtras nor the author of the Bhāṣya has stated that an object possesses the nature of being a mental form or the like. Furthermore, if this were accepted, it would result in the undesirable consequence of falling into the position of the Vijñānavādins.

This doctrine, however, has been refuted by Vyāsa in the second quarter of the second chapter of the *Brahma-mīmāṃsā*. Let the learned recognize that this doctrine was not accepted even by Pāṇini and Patañjali.

Nowhere does the author of the *Bhāṣya* state that the categories of existence have a mental (cognitive) reality; rather, he states that they do not have external existence. Therefore, objects such as jars and the like are real.
Therefore, the grammarians ought not to say that the jar and so forth are non-existent;
however, Kaiyaṭa, Bhaṭṭoji, Nāgeśa, and other grammarians have said so.
Relying on the opinions of others, this is not the view of the author of the Bhāṣya;
for, having reflected upon the Bhāṣya itself, the wise declare it thus.
The refutation of the claim that all tantras are auxiliary to non-duality (*advaita*):

Now, it was stated in the *Mañjūṣā*: "The intention is that [this work] is an auxiliary to the spiritual sciences (*adhyātma-śāstra*) by means of establishing the self as distinct from the gross and subtle bodies; furthermore, it was stated in that very same place that this is also for the purpose of determining the truth (*tattva-nirṇaya*) during debates with teachers and others."

If it is argued: "By this, it is indicated that all other systems besides the non-dualistic (advaita) scriptures which establish the internal [reality] are of such a nature"—since this was stated during the occasion of defining the present tense in the *Ākhyātārthavāda*—it follows that non-duality alone is ultimate (*pāramārthika*), while the plurality of selves and so forth taught in other systems such as Sāṃkhya are not ultimate; therefore, since the difference taught in Sāṃkhya is merely illusory (*māyika*), it is likewise logical for its followers, the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*), to hold that same view. To this we say: no.

For those who take refuge in the Vedas and the means of knowledge that follow them, it is said: "Know the Self as the rider in the chariot, and the body as the chariot itself" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.3.3). Likewise: "Then this Self, having struck down this body and caused ignorance to depart, having ascended to another state... and similarly: "...they fashion another form, newer and more beautiful" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.3); "It is not slain when the body is slain" (Gītā 2.20; Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.18); and likewise: "The embodied one, casting off worn-out bodies, enters into others that are new."

Since the distinction between the self and the body is established by the scriptures themselves—such as the Gītā (2.22): "The bodies of the eternal embodied one are said to have an end," and the Brahma Sūtra (3.1.1): "Upon entering another [body], it departs enveloped [by subtle elements], as determined by the questions and their explanations"—there is no need for the systems of Sāṃkhya and others to effect that discrimination. Consequently, there is no necessity for postulating those systems as auxiliary (*aṅga*) to this [Vedāntic inquiry].

Furthermore, regarding the conceptualization of the relationship between parts and the whole, it has been constructed by someone staying in some corner of the earth with eyes closed, aided solely by their own mental impressions, according to the maxim of a cat drinking milk.

If the relationship of "the marked and the marker" (*aṅkāṅkibhāva*) described by Mañjīṣa were real, then Gautama and others would also have composed their respective scriptures with the prior intention that they bear the mark of the non-dual scripture which teaches the nature of the Self; and if that were the case, such a status of theirs would certainly have been known even to Śaṅkarācārya and his successors. However, since they did not possess such knowledge regarding those [scriptures], [Śaṅkara] stated: "Because of seeing, it is not that which is not based on the Word" (*Brahma-sūtra* 1.1.5), and "On account of the designation of the object of seeing, he [is Brahman]" (1.3.13).

If it is argued that there is the fault of rendering other Smṛtis irrelevant (*smṛty-anavakāśa-doṣa-prasaṅga*), we say no, because that would lead to the same fault regarding other Smṛtis [such as those of Manu]. (2.1.1) "And because the formation [of the world] is impossible, [the world] is not [established] by inference. (2.2.1) "By this, Yoga is refuted. (2.1.3) "If it be said that for some [there is a doctrine] based on inference, we say no, because [the scripture] shows that the body is grasped as being presented in the form of a chariot, and so forth. (1.4.1) Such is the commentary composed by Śaṅkarācārya, which aims at refuting the systems of Sāṃkhya, Yoga, and others; likewise, the sūtra "And it is merely a reflection" (2.3.40).

In the view of those who maintain the plurality of selves, such as the Sāṃkhyas and others, since there is no distinction in the proximity of all selves [to the mind], and because the conjunction of the mind with one self is not differentiated [from its conjunction with others], it would follow that when one self experiences pleasure or pain, all selves would likewise experience pleasure and pain; this is the statement of the fault. Likewise, [the sūtra] states: "Because [the self] is not perceived by another" (Brahmasūtra 3.2.17).

The commentary composed by Śaṅkarācārya on the three sūtras beginning with *2.3.41*, which aims to demonstrate the inconsistency of the doctrine of the plurality of selves; likewise, the many sūtras whose purport—according to the method of Śaṅkarācārya’s Bhāṣya—is to refute those who maintain that Pradhāna is the cause [of the world]; the respective Śaṅkara-Bhāṣyas on those sūtras; and furthermore, [the sūtra] *etena yogaḥ pratyuktaḥ* (Brahma-sūtra 2.1.3).

2.1.3) Thus, in the sūtra dedicated to the rejection of the *Yogaśāstra*, [it is stated]: "The Sāṃkhya-Yoga doctrine—that the knowledge of the distinction between the self [and the material world] is the means to liberation—is contrary to the established tenet of the Vedāntins, which holds that the realization of the oneness of the Self is the means to liberation."

There is no means for attaining the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) other than the knowledge of the Self according to the Vedas as intended by their purport (*tātparya*), because of the Śruti text "Him alone" (*tameva*); for the commentary of Śaṅkara states that the Sāṃkhyas and Yogins who maintain duality are not seers of the unity of the Self. Likewise, regarding that same sūtra, the statement "But that cause is attained through Sāṃkhya and Yoga" (*sāṃkhyayogābhipannaṃ*, Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.8) does not refer to the systems of Yoga that have been rejected, but rather refers to those centered on Vedic knowledge and meditation; this is because it is stated that those two lack the status of being based on the Śruti. Furthermore, in that very sūtra: "All... [the text continues].

Regarding the passage from Śaṅkara’s commentary on that very sūtra which describes the intention of the Sūtrakāra—namely, "The Vaiśeṣika and other systems must be refuted because they are intent upon the plurality of selves and thus contradict the established doctrine of those who know Brahman; therefore, they are to be disregarded"—and likewise, in response to the objection that "even those [systems] assist in the knowledge of reality through reasoning and logical proof," the reply states, "Let them indeed assist; however, that knowledge of reality arises only from the Vedānta texts. This [passage] concerns the status of those intent upon reasoning as a means to the knowledge of reality.

The *Śaṅkarabhāṣya* contains passages intended to disparage scriptures other than the Vedānta-śāstra, such as: "They are to be disregarded [as mere] mental constructs," and likewise in the *Maitreyī-brāhmaṇa* of the Vājasaneyi (4.15): "Oh, what skill in inference has been displayed by those bull-like logicians who lack even horns! Furthermore, in the *Śaṅkarabhāṣya* on the *Bhṛguvallī* of the Taittirīya (10.4), having raised the objection regarding the contradiction of the doctrine of the unity of the Self with the Sāṃkhya and others—stating "contradiction with Kapila, Kaṇāda, and so forth"—[it says]: "Of them..."

If Sāṃkhya and the other systems were limbs (*aṅga*) of Advaita, then the statement that they are ignorant—on the grounds that they lack the authority of Mūsa (the Veda) and contradict the Vedas—would be a manifestation of ignorance regarding the intentions of their respective authors; for if they were limbs, one would have said simply that there is no contradiction with them because they are limbs, and that alone is what ought to have been stated.

Furthermore, since all scriptures are subordinate to the Advaita scripture according to the method stated here, the desired conclusion is established by the very statement that even the systems of Kaṇāda and others—which are intent upon the perceived duality—are auxiliary to the spiritual science (*adhyātma-śāstra*) during the occasion of defining the illusory nature (*māyikatva*) of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) in the first chapter; thus, there is no contradiction with them. [The author proceeds] by noting that Kaṇāda and others, for the sake of the capacity of the students to be instructed, conceal the illusory nature and the like of the phenomenal world—which is known to be illusory and vast—and [teach it] as being vast.

The statement that [the view] beginning with "creation from known atoms and so forth" is a denial of their illusory nature (*māyikatva*) is futile. Nor should it be argued that such a statement proves their illusory nature, because the reality of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) cannot be established without denying that very nature. For if the illusory nature of the phenomenal world were established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then this statement would have been a proof for it.

By stating, "This world is unreal and without foundation" (Gītā 15.4), one negates the illusory nature of the universe; since this [negation] would render the world invalid as a source of knowledge, the charge of "speaking otherwise" against them would ultimately result in a groundless accusation.

Furthermore, if Kaṇāda and others possessed the knowledge that the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is illusory (*māyika*), then they ought to have taught us this very scripture of ours as an auxiliary to the non-dualistic (*advaita*) scripture that establishes the inner self (*adhyātma*), declaring: "All this is indeed the very nature of the Self"—thus teaching the reality (*vāstavārtha*). Only by speaking in such a manner would they be trustworthy authorities (*āpta*) and worthy of the title of teacher (*ācārya*). For only those who speak according to reality are trustworthy authorities and teachers, as it is said in the system of Gautama: "A trustworthy authority (*āpta*) is one who speaks the truth."

And because it is stated in the *Mañjūṣā*: "An *āpta* (reliable person) is one who possesses a complete certainty regarding the reality of things through direct experience, and who does not speak otherwise due to the influence of passion and so forth" (Pramāṇasamuccaya 1.1.4); and "The state of being an *āpta* consists in the absence of any effort conducive to either the obstruction of one's own desired [result] or the production of an undesired result regarding a particular action, provided that there is freedom from defects such as error" (95.15).

Because those who speak while denying the true nature of reality lack truthful speech and are, instead, speakers of falsehood, they are determined to possess only such efforts as are conducive to their own desired ends and so forth; thus, being non-authoritative (*anāpta*), their words would be untrustworthy. For one who gathers the meaning of the scriptures and establishes them in practice, and who practices them himself—that person is called an *ācārya*.

Because of this traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*), those who, by instructing others in the meaning of the scriptures as they have experienced it according to reality, establish them in right conduct (*sadācāra*), are indeed worthy of the title "Teacher" (*ācārya*). How, then, could those who teach matters contrary to what has been experienced be entitled to the status of a Teacher?

Furthermore, one must ask him who asserts that Kaṇāda and others—possessing the cognition of selfhood everywhere—denied that very cognition and taught their disciples that atoms are the cause: "Were you thus deluded in a dream, or did Kaṇāda and the others come to you and speak thus? For your own experience is one thing, and the matter they taught is another."

The first alternative cannot be maintained here; for according to your own view, just as a dream-pot is non-existent because it is subsequently sublated by the cognition of a real pot, this [non-dualism] would likewise be non-existent. The second alternative is even less tenable, since it is impossible for Kaṇāda and others—who now exist as nothing more than their fame—to come into your presence today. Furthermore, what was stated in the first chapter [of the *Brahmasiddhi*] should be considered. Consequently, the systems of Sāṃkhya, Yoga, and Kaṇāda do not constitute limbs of the Advaita system.
Any claim to the contrary is rooted in a stubborn desire to force all other systems into conformity with one’s own preferred Advaita.

Therefore, they possess absolute independence. Regarding them, even the plurality of the self (*ātman*) and other such tenets established as their doctrine are ultimately real (*pāramārthika*) and not merely illusory (*māyika*), because no statement suggesting such a [merely illusory] status is found in the Sāṃkhya and other systems. Furthermore, it has already been explained previously that Pāṇini is an adherent of the doctrine of difference (*bhedavādī*).

By this, even Nāgeśa—who in his *Uddyota* on the rule *striyām* states that "he indicates that the grammarian follows the *Sāṃkhya* treatise"—has admitted that Pāṇini is a proponent of difference (*bhedavāditā*), because it is logically established that since the Sāṃkhyas are proponents of non-difference, a grammarian who follows them must likewise be such.

The Sāṃkhyas' doctrine of difference (bheda), however, is determined from the Śaṅkara-bhāṣya cited previously—"For the one named Kapila does not accept the vision of the Self as one, because he admits a plurality of selves"—and from the Śaṅkara-bhāṣya on the Smṛti-adhikaraṇa, as well as from the texts of the Sāṃkhya school and others.

Indeed, having introduced the aphorism “*tattvādhyavasāyaḥ*,” and having provided the transition “this treatise [is begun] because [otherwise] it would be useless,” and having presented the commentary on that aphorism from the words “*tasyām avasāyāyām*” up to “*tadāśayaḥ*,” it is established that this treatise—which has the purpose of refuting the Buddhist position—is a limb (*aṅga*) of the inner science (*adhyātma*). This is because it is demonstrated in the *Mañjūṣā* by the passage beginning with “*anena*” and concluding with “*sarvatantrāṇām evaṃvidhatvam sūcitam*,” that all systems of thought are thus subordinate to non-duality (*advaita*).

If it is argued that [the Nyāya system] is in agreement with the *Gautamadaśasūtrabhāṣya*, they reply here: The venerable Gautama, the author of the Sūtras, having stated in the first sūtra that "the knowledge of the truth regarding the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth leads to the cessation of suffering," further maintained that among those, the knowledge of the self (*ātman*) is primary, and that this requires the purification of the self (*ātmasaṃskāra*). The means for that are the restraints (*yama*), observances (*niyama*), and so forth, which are to be understood from the Yoga-śāstra. This is established by the sūtra: "The purification of the self occurs through restraint and observance, and through yoga by means of the methods prescribed in the science of the inner self" (4.2.46).

He also states another means of proof (*sādhana*). In that context, "for that purpose" means for the sake of liberation; "from Yoga" means from the Yoga-śāstra; the rest is clear—this is the meaning of the first sūtra. "Knowledge" refers to the science of the Self (*ātmavidyā*); "by those who know it" means by those expert in the science of the Self; the rest is clear—this is the meaning of the second sūtra. [Objection: But if the primary goal is the knowledge of the reality of the Self, how is this the meaning of the introductory sūtra?

Now, one might object: "If the knowledge of the reality of the Self is thus established through the very discourse of debate (*vāda*), what is the purpose of wrangling (*jalpa*) and cavil (*vitaṇḍā*)? To this objection, it has been stated in the Sūtra: "Wrangling and cavil exist for the sake of protecting the determination of truth, just as one uses a covering of thorny branches to protect the growth of seeds" (NS 4.2.50).

And this is explained in the Bhāṣya: "Some, out of attachment to their own position, overstep the rules of logic (*nyāya*); regarding that—[the phrase] 'for those who have not produced the knowledge of reality (*tattva*) and whose defects have not been abandoned, while they are striving for that purpose'—it is explained as follows. *Nyāya* refers to the rule of correct inquiry; *tadartham* means for the sake of the knowledge of reality; *etat* refers to the two-fold [debate], namely *jalpa* and *vitaṇḍā*. The rest is easy to understand.

The intended meaning is as follows: whether in a formal debate (*vāda*)—that is, in an assembly for the investigation of truth—or in the context of other systems (*matāntara*), the preservation of one's own position by refuting the fallacious arguments (*kutarka*) employed by those who hold them is the fruit of *jalpa* and *vitaṇḍā*. Let the wise reflect upon how the following implication is obtained from this Sūtra and Bhāṣya: "That [the system] of Gautama is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to Advaita; indeed, all systems possess such a nature (i.e., being auxiliaries to Advaita)."

Nor should it be said that the intention [of the author] is that this [system of Advaita] is a limb (*aṅga*) of Advaita because those who know the Advaita scriptures resort to *jalpa* and *vitaṇḍā* for the sake of defending their own tenets; for since even those who know all systems (*sarvatantra-jña*) resort to *jalpa* and *vitaṇḍā* to protect their respective tenets, the status of being a limb of all systems (*sarvatantrāṅgatva*) would be established, and thus Nāgeśa’s desire would remain unfulfilled. For his desire was this: that the Advaita scripture alone is primary, while everything else is secondary by virtue of being its limb.

How could it be logical to conceive of a distinguished scripture as being a subsidiary (*aṅga*) to all other systems (*tantras*) merely by way of partial assistance? Furthermore, how can lack of primacy (*aprādhānya*) be established by mere assistance alone? For in the world, wise people do not consider a person who assists others to be secondary. If subsidiarity were established by mere partial assistance, then one could say that even the Advaita scripture assists others in part; thus, it too would become a subsidiary to another, and its intended preeminence would fail to be established.

Furthermore, the introduction to the sūtra "tattvādhyavasya" (having ascertained reality)—namely, the objection, "In that case, this treatise is rendered useless by that [work]"—as well as the statement regarding the purpose of the treatise, "This treatise has the refutation of that [opinion] as its aim," would be improper. Likewise, the statement regarding the purpose of the treatise for the sūtra "tattvādhyavasāya" (ascertainment of reality) would also be improper. (Note: The repetition of the final phrase in the source text appears to be a scribal error.)

This is because the aphorism "the determination of reality" (*tattvādhyavasāya*) does not function to define the purpose of the treatise; because it has not been so explained by the author of the *Bhāṣya* and others; and, on the contrary, because in the *Bhāṣya* on the first aphorism it was explained specifically as having the purpose of *jalpa* and *vitaṇḍā*, stating: "Debate (*vāda*) culminates in that [determination] and has the knowledge of reality as its fruit; *jalpa* and *vitaṇḍā* exist for the sake of protecting that; *jalpa* and *vitaṇḍā* are its specific forms, existing for the sake of defending the determination of reality."

Furthermore, it is not well said that in the sūtra "for that purpose" (*tadartham*), the term *yoga* is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the Vedāntas as well; for in the four-part system (*catur-lakṣaṇī*) composed by Vyāsa—which is universally accepted as Vedānta—one observes descriptions of the nature of restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*). Although it is established from the *Mañjūṣā* that Nāgeśa’s intended work on Advaita Vedānta is the one titled *Paramārthasāra*, even there we do not see any description of the nature of restraints, observances, and so forth. Therefore, the statement regarding this indication is fruitless.

If it is argued that since self-knowledge arises from the Vedāntas alone, that too must be studied, and that the mention of "understanding" (*bodhana*) is merely an incidental result (*upalakṣaṇa*), we reply: the author of the Sūtras himself stated in the sūtra *jñānagrahaṇa-* that the study of the science of the Self (*ātmavidyā*) is also a means for the ascertainment of reality (*tattvādhyavasāya*), just like the restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*). In that context, the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*) means the science of the Self. Thus, there is no purpose in saying that it is merely an incidental result.

This is the established position of the Naiyāyikas: because of the statement in the *Bhāṣya*, "Ānvīkṣikī alone is the science of the self (*ātmavidyā*)," and because, taking "the science of the self" as the subject for commentary, it is explained that "Ānvīkṣikī is indeed the science of the self. Furthermore, because Vātsyāyana, in his commentary on the opening sūtra "The means of valid cognition, the objects of valid cognition... etc., stated "here, in this science of the self (*adhyātmavidyā*), the knowledge of the self is the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*)," and because the author of the sūtras, in the remainder of the first sūtra—"From the knowledge of reality, the attainment of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*)"—declared that his own system has both the knowledge of the reality of the self and the liberation achieved thereby as its two fruits.

The study, retention, and constant reflection upon that very [scripture] must be performed; through these and other stated ancillaries (*aṅga*), there arises the ascertainment of the Self (*ātma-adhyavasāya*), and by means of that, liberation (*apavarga*). Thus, the system of Gautama is primarily the means for achieving liberation and cannot be an ancillary to anything else. This is likewise the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of all systems; therefore, it is not the case that all [systems] have non-duality as their ancillary.

By this, the subsequent passage from the *Mañjūṣā*—which states, "Only the Upaniṣads are the primary science of the self (*adhyātmavidyā*) and the primary knowledge of reality; that which is taught in the Upaniṣads is indeed the primary [knowledge], while everything else is merely its means"—is also to be reconsidered.

This is because, while the existence of God and His authorship of the world are well-known from such scriptural passages as "Being alone, my dear, was this in the beginning" (Chāndogya 6.2.1) and "From which indeed... (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1), the Naiyāyikas abandon these and take refuge in inference alone; thus, it is understood that for them, the status of *ānvīkṣikī* as the science of the self (*adhyātmavidyā*) is determined only within their own system and not in the Upaniṣads. Furthermore, one can infer that they lack the conviction that the knowledge arising therefrom is a means to liberation. This is also supported by the statement of the learned: "The Upaniṣadic philosophy has been abandoned by them."

And it is stated in the *Śāṅkara Gītābhāṣya*: "The Upaniṣadic philosophy has been abandoned by the Vaiśeṣikas, as well as by the Sāṃkhyas, the Ārhats, and the Buddhists. Furthermore, in the *Sūtra-bhāṣya*, in the section on the Whole (*Samudāyādhikaraṇa*, 2.2.4), it is said that the established doctrine of the Vaiśeṣikas is not to be relied upon because of its connection with fallacious reasoning, its contradiction of the Vedas, and its lack of acceptance by the learned; and since that [Vaiśeṣika] is a partial nihilist (*ardhavaināśika*), the established doctrine of the total nihilists (*sarvavaināśika*) is all the more not to be relied upon due to their commonality as nihilists.

In this context, the term *vaiśeṣika* is also an elliptical designation for Gautama [the Naiyāyika], because both schools share the same intention regarding this subject. For this very reason, Sureśvarācārya, having introduced the section on "The Great and the Long" (*mahaddīrghādhikaraṇa*, 2.2.2), which refutes the views of the Vaiśeṣikas and Naiyāyikas, interprets it as being aimed at the refutation of both systems.
Furthermore:
"It is the lamp of all sciences and the means to all actions."
It is proclaimed in the section on knowledge that it is the support of all phenomena.

Thus, by the presentation of this authority, it is stated in the *Nyāyabhāṣya* of Gautama that [the science of logic] is beneficial to all branches of knowledge (*sarvavidyopakārakatva*). By citing the authority—"Inquiry (*ānvīkṣikī*), the three Vedas (*trayī*), commerce (*vārtā*), and the science of government (*daṇḍanīti*) as the fourth"—the commentators have established that the science of inquiry (*ānvīkṣikī*) is beneficial to all branches of knowledge, including the three Vedas, by subsuming all such sciences within the three Vedas. Therefore, since its status as being beneficial merely to the science of the self (*adhyātmavidyā*) is not proven, the phrase "its means" (*tadupāya*) must be considered; for its intended meaning is "the means to that [science of the self] alone."

Furthermore, since it is *ānvīkṣikī* alone that is the subject matter under discussion regarding the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the general statement "something else" (*anyat*) is to be questioned; for nothing other than *ānvīkṣikī* is heard of in the context of the means of valid cognition, nor is it mentioned in the *Nyāyabhāṣya* and other such works.

If it be objected: "In the *Nyāyamañjarī*, at the occasion of defining the nature of liberation (*mokṣa*), it is stated that liberation—consisting in abiding in one's true nature—is established through the meditation on the Self according to the method taught in the Vedānta, namely, 'The Self, indeed, is to be seen' (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad*); since this establishes that the system of Nyāya is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to Vedānta, how can it be justified as an independent [system]? [The reply is: True. Such a statement was made in order to distance the system from the charge of non-Vedic character (*avaidikatva*) that might arise from the remark in Śaṅkara’s commentary: "The Vaiśeṣikas have abandoned the Upaniṣadic philosophy. It was said in that manner for the purpose of removing that perceived defect.

Let it be granted that the *Upāsanākāṇḍa* is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the *Upaniṣads*; nevertheless, this does not establish its status as an auxiliary to the Advaita scriptures, because the *Upaniṣads* do not have non-duality as their primary purport. Furthermore, Jayanta himself maintains the view that "all scriptures are exclusively devoted to duality" (*dvaitapara*); thus, the dispute concerns precisely its status as an auxiliary to Advaita. Moreover, the intention of the authors of those respective systems is that all those systems in which a specific fruit is heard of have liberation (*mokṣa*) as their fruit through their own independence.
For this very reason, it should be understood that the efforts of Śaṅkarācārya and others toward refuting those respective systems become fruitful.

Furthermore, the *Nāgeśāmatadvaita-śāstra* establishes that Brahman is the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*), teaches the absence of plurality in the self (*ātman*), and the non-existence of external objects; whereas systems such as the *Gautamīya* teach that God is the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*) and that there is a distinction between selves and that external objects do exist. Thus, regarding the primary object of knowledge, there is a great mutual disagreement between them.

"Thou art That," "The knower of Brahman becomes Brahman itself"—since such scriptural statements aimed at non-duality culminate in identity, the followers of that [view], such as the author of the *Muktāvalī* and others, hold this to be the case. Consequently, what discerning person would consider two utterly contradictory systems of scripture to stand in a relationship of primary and subordinate (aṅga-aṅgin), or what Naiyāyika would justify such a thing? Therefore, the claim that the system of Gautama and others is subordinate to the Advaita scripture is already established by its own commentary (*bhāṣya*) and should simply be disregarded.
In brief, if one were to say, "We consider all tantras to have non-duality as their constituent limb," then that wise person would be one whose intellect is praiseworthy.
However, there exists a contradiction with the Advaita system as intended by Nāgeśa;
therefore, these [tantras] do not have that [Advaita] as their constituent limb, especially in light of the Gautamīya and other tantras.
Refutation of the claim that the Bhāṣya supports the oneness of the self:

If it is argued that the oneness of the self is determined by the fact that the venerable Patañjali—speaking of the twofold nature of the self through the distinction of limiting adjuncts such as the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) in the Bhāṣya on the two sūtras, “*ṇeraṇau yatkarma ṇau cetsa kartā’nādhyāne*” (Pāṇini 1.4.52) and “*karmavat karmaṇā tulyakriyaḥ*” (Pāṇini 3.1.87)—which state, “How can there be two selves? There is the inner self and the bodily self”—must be accepted; we say no, because those two sūtra-commentaries were not composed for the purpose of establishing the oneness of the self.
