To explain: in that regard, in the first case, there is the objection that the *ātmanepada* ending should occur because the self (*ātman*), which is the object (*karman*) in the non-causative state in the phrase "the self kills itself" (*hanty ātmānam*), becomes the agent (*kartṛ*) in the causative state in the phrase "the self causes itself to be killed" (*ghātayaty ātmā*). To this objection, the rule "a prohibition must be stated regarding the self when it is the object" (*ātmanaḥ karmatve pratiṣedho vaktavyaḥ*) was formulated. Its meaning is that even though the self is the object in the non-causative (*aṇau*) and the agent in the causative (*ṇau*), the *ātmanepada* ending does not occur by virtue of this [general rule].

This is not a statement of negation intended to mean that [the agenthood] should be established in the first stage because there is an absence of agenthood in the second stage of the object; rather, with this in mind, he says: "Or rather, not so, because of the agenthood of the causative (*ṇyanta*) [root]. To explain its meaning, he says: "In this case, the object of the non-causative (*a-ṇyanta*) is one thing, while the agent of the causative is another. How so? 'There are two selves,' and so forth. The meaning of the *Bhāṣya* is clear. The underlying idea is as follows: the inner self is the Lord (*īśvara*), the inner controller (*antaryāmin*); the bodily self is the individual soul (*jīva*).

According to the system of Patañjali, there are two conscious entities, as is obtained from the *Yogasūtra*: "Īśvara is a Puruṣa. This is the function of the inner self (*antarātman*) with respect to the Puruṣa (the individual soul): to impel it toward its respective appropriate activities in accordance with its various merits and demerits. Consequently, the Puruṣa experiences pleasure and pain according to its own karma; when the living being (*jīva*) performs a meritorious act, then the inner self remains awake to bestow the fruit corresponding to that act. That itself constitutes its happiness.

When the individual soul (*jīva*) performs an evil deed, then the inner self (*antarātmā*) feels aversion toward it; that itself is its suffering. As for the explanation that "the inner self is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), whereas the bodily self (*śarīrātmā*) is the body alone—according to the *Kosā*, 'self' [is defined as] effort, fortitude, intellect, nature, and the physical form"—this is inconsistent with the commentary stating "it experiences pleasure and pain," because both the body and the internal organ are insentient (*jaḍa*) and thus incapable of being the experiencer (*bhoktṛ*).

Furthermore, in the Bhāṣya, while it should have said "the body" (*śarīra*), the word "self" (*ātman*) is redundant; for even in the Sāṃkhya system, it is accepted that the *puruṣa* alone is the enjoyer, as stated: "The *puruṣa* exists because there must be an experiencer, and because of the activity for the sake of isolation" (Sāṃkhyakārikā 17). Moreover: "Nature (*prakṛti*) is said to be the cause in the agency of effects and instruments;
the *puruṣa* is said to be the cause in the experience of pleasures and pains" (Gītā 13.20).

Thus, because the *Gītā* establishes that the person alone is the enjoyer; and because Pāṇini, by prescribing the suffix *kyaṅ* after words such as "pleasure" (*sukha*) in the rule *sukhādibhyaḥ kartṛvedanāyām* (Pāṇini 3.1.18)—which refers to the experience (*anubhava*) whose object is pleasure and so forth residing in its own locus—demonstrates that both the pleasure and the experience reside in the self (*ātman*). This is clearly stated in the *Mañjarī*: "The experience of a word is experience. The meaning of *sukhayate* is that [the agent] himself experiences the pleasure inherent in himself.

By this [it is shown that] the excellence of the limbs and their deficiency belong to the embodied self (*śarīrātman*), because the experience of pleasure and pain is established through perception; furthermore, since that experience is a property of consciousness, it is impossible for the body to possess it. As for the expression "he kills himself," the meaning is that the person destroys himself by practicing unrighteousness; as for "he causes himself to be killed," the meaning is that the Inner Self, which is the Lord (*īśvara*), causes the person—the individual self—to be killed, leading him away solely on account of his own evil karma.

The meaning of the commentary on the sūtra "karmavat karmaṇā" is likewise exactly this; therefore, it does not intend to establish the absolute identity [of the self]. Consider this: how could it be understood from this commentary that there is no difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the supreme self (paramātman), merely by assuming that the commentary's intent is to show that the difference in the single self is adventitious (aupādhika)?

Furthermore, even that discussion regarding the unity of the conscious Self—which appears in the *Vṛttipariccheda* of the *Mañjarī*, where it is stated in the commentary on the *Sadvitīyasūtra* that "all things possess consciousness by the force of the scriptural declaration, 'Listen, O stones! and that "God is established by the Śruti and other means as the cause of the world and as the Inner Controller (antaryāmin), and thus the unity of the conscious [Self] alone is accepted in the Vedānta due to parsimony (*lāghava*)"—is merely a demonstration of ignorance that obscures the true purport of the Bhāṣya and Vārtika on that very sūtra.

It can be asserted that the knowledge of all things as being endowed with consciousness—based on the universal cause, namely God, through relations such as being the unmanifested material cause—is possessed not only by Nāgeśa, but also by the great seers Kātyāyana and Patañjali; for they too were those who had ascertained the meaning of the Vedānta scriptures, were possessors of vast knowledge, had directly realized the higher and lower [realities], and were incarnate beings.

In this regard, what Vararuci stated—that [the suffix *san*] occurs "with respect to insentient things"—indicates that "the conventional usage of 'possessing consciousness' applies to everything by virtue of the consciousness of God (*īśvara*). By this, it must be understood that even according to the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*), there is no such usage for everything in that manner [i.e., as inherently sentient]. And thus, the conventional usage of "possessing consciousness" applies only when a conscious being distinct from God exists; since there is no conscious being other than God in the case of riverbanks and the like, the desiderative suffix (*san*) does not apply due to the absence of desire (*icchā*). Therefore, his statement [of the rule] for the sake of the suffix *sa-* (which denotes the agent) is purposeful.

And thus, the identity of consciousness [with the earth] is not accepted by him. For Bhāskara, however, there exists a certain conscious deity named "Appropriation" (abhimāninī devatā) who is distinct from Īśvara; taking that [deity] as the basis, he maintains that the banks and so forth possess consciousness. This is the intended meaning [of the Sūtra]: "In the case of desire, [the earth is] existent by means of the Sūtra itself."

This, however, must be understood: this *Bhāṣya* proceeded by relying upon the opinion of those who know Brahman, whereas the *Vārtika*, because the established doctrine of those who know Brahman was not fully understood by everyone, did not rely upon it. Regarding the doubt that their view—that such scriptural passages as "The waters spoke," "The clay spoke," and "The waters reflected" are not authoritative, because it is impossible for insentient things like water to be agents of speech and so forth, since in the world speech and the like are never observed in insentient objects such as jars and cloth—it should not be thought thus.

In every instance, there exists some presiding deity; taking her as his referent, the Vedic Person (Vedapuruṣa) conducts himself in this manner. In the Śruti, the meaning of terms such as "the waters" (āpaḥ) is that they are the deities presiding over them. And this very point has been established by the venerable Vyāsa in the aphorism: "But the designation refers to the presiding deities, because of the distinction and the inclusion" (Brahmasūtra 2.1.5).

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: in passages such as "the clay spoke," there is the conventional usage of speech and other actions attributed to the presiding deities (abhimānin-devatā) of the clay and so forth; for the existence of presiding deities in all such cases is established by means of mantras, explanatory passages (arthavādas), histories, and other sources. If everything were conscious solely due to the consciousness of the Lord (Īśvara), this [usage] would not be tenable. Thus, the doctrine that there is no presiding deity whatsoever other than the Lord—a position asserting the Lord alone as the sole conscious principle—is contrary to the established conclusion of the knowers of Brahman.

Furthermore, in both the Sūtra and the Bhāṣya, since there is no explicit statement that [the elements] possess consciousness by virtue of the consciousness of the Lord (īśvara-cetanā), the meaning of the Sūtra and Bhāṣya is simply that they possess consciousness because of the presiding deity (abhimānidevatā). This is because there is no reason to abandon the established conclusion (siddhānta) of those who know Brahman.

Regarding the rule *dāmahāyanāntācca* (Pāṇini 4.1.27), it should be understood that the departure or exit [of a calf] is metaphorically attributed to the rope (*dāma*), which is insentient; for such figurative usage toward insentient objects is observed, as in the examples: "his bonds have slipped" and "his bonds slip away. This is done in accordance with worldly usage, namely, that [the calf] "goes. To indicate that uncontradicted worldly usage is also adopted in the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*) without contradiction, the justification there is provided solely in accordance with worldly usage.

In that context, the word *cetana-vat* (possessing consciousness) occurring in the statement of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) in the Bhāṣya refers to a living being delimited by a body produced by karma. However, it has been established previously that Nāgeśa is a partisan of the Vijñānavāda school who speaks in contradiction to the Siddhānta established by the knowers of Brahman; therefore, his statement is not to be trusted.

Furthermore, the description of the purport of this [Mahābhāṣya] as being the identity of consciousness contradicts the Paspaśāhnika-bhāṣya, which describes the purport of the mantra "catvāri śṛṅgā," for in that passage, similarity itself is stated to be the fruit [of the study of grammar]. Specifically, it says: "Grammar should be studied so that we may attain equality with the Great God."

Under the governing rule "And in the case of a dual compound of deities" (Pāṇini 6.3.26), Pāṇini, by formulating the three sūtras "dyau- for diva-", "divasa- before pṛthivī-", and "uṣāsoṣasaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.3.29, 30, 31), intends to convey that there exists a deity presiding over the heavenly world and so forth.

Nor should it be said that there is no recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the term "devatādvandva" in the three sūtras [of Pāṇini 6.2.141–143], for the *Kaumudī* states "devatādvandva" in all three sūtras; furthermore, regarding the example *dyāvākṣāmā* in the first sūtra, the Vedabhāṣya explains that by the rule "devatādvandve ca" (Pā. Sū. 6.2.141), the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) applies to both the preceding and following members, and since this [rule] was not formulated prior to "devatādvandve ca," its recurrence therein is established.

The exclusion of *pṛthivī* in the rule "Not when the following member begins with an unaccented vowel, except in the case of *pṛthivī*, *rudra*, *pūṣan*, and *manti*" (Pāṇini 6.2.142), as well as the example "dyāvāpṛthivī janayan," serve as proof for this stated meaning. For if [the word] were not the presiding deity (*abhimānidevatā*), then the rule "In a Dvandva of deities" (Pāṇini 6.2.141) would not apply to provide the original accent for both the preceding and following members; consequently, since the prohibition would not take effect, the mention of *pṛthivī* in the exclusion rule would be redundant. Furthermore, in the cited example, the substitution of *dyāvā* would not occur.

If the intention is that there is a duality of deities due to the consciousness of Īśvara, then one should simply say "Īśvara-dvandva. Furthermore, the term "generating" (janayan) should be understood as being in reference to the object being conceived. By this, the objection that such a statement is improper because generation is impossible due to [Īśvara's] immutability is refuted.

Furthermore, in the sixth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, within the section concerning the description of creation in the dialogue between the father and son, there is the designation of fire and the other elements as having agency preceded by reflection: "It [the Self] thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate. It emitted heat. That heat thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate. It emitted water. Those waters thought: 'May we be many, may we procreate. They emitted food" (Chā. 6.2). And: "Come, let me enter these three deities with this living self..."

Thus, there is their treatment as deities; and by such passages as, "He who dwells in the earth," and "He who dwells in the self" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.3), the fact that the earth and other elements are under the control of the Blessed Lord is stated. Furthermore, by such passages as, "Whom the earth does not know," the fact that they are unaware of the true nature of the Lord as the Inner Ruler (Antaryāmin) is stated. This teaches that the deities presiding over those [elements]—which are denoted by the word *tejas* and so forth—are distinct from the Lord, and it also implies a plurality of conscious beings. It is well known to all the world that for insentient things like fire (*tejas*) and the rest, activities such as "seeing" are impossible.

"Nārāyaṇa governs the deities presiding over earth and so forth"—this is the Śaṅkara commentary on the Vājasaneyi [Upaniṣad]. Even words denoting deities such as Āditya, which refer to objects like light, designate that conscious self of the deity endowed with sovereignty and other attributes, because they are treated as such in the mantras, arthavādas, and so forth. Furthermore, conscious presiding agents are accepted even in the case of clay and other materials; this is supported by the mantra "The clay spoke" and by the Śaṅkara commentary on the sūtra *bhāvaṃ tu* (1.3.33) regarding this very point.

If it is argued that—in passages such as "one kills oneself by oneself" (*ātmānam ātmanā hanti*)—the *karma-saṃjñā* (object designation) is set aside by the subsequent *kartṛ-saṃjñā* (agent designation), and this is resolved in the Bhāṣya by resorting to a distinction between the self qualified by the ego (*ahaṃkāra*) and so forth; and that from the *Manoramā* commentary on the rule *sādhakatamaṃ karaṇam* (Pāṇini 1.4.42), as well as from the corresponding section in the *Mañjūṣā* concerning the meaning of *su*-suffixes, it is understood that the identity of the self with the agent (*ātmaikatva*) is the view accepted in the Bhāṣya—then we reply: [this applies] to a single self, such as Devadatta, in relation to a single...

The intention of the Bhāṣya is that the simultaneous application of the designations "agent" (*kartṛ*) and "object" (*karman*) to a single action is easily established [as impossible]. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Ratnavyākhyāna* by Bhairava: "When there is an authoritative usage, this conceptualization is for the sake of grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*), but one cannot use words as one pleases based on such a conceptualization. Consequently, this Bhāṣya does not establish the identity of the individual self (*jīvātman*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*), nor does it refute the distinction between the individual and the supreme selves established by the scriptures.
Furthermore, a Bhāṣya with this specific sequence [of words] should be sought.

Furthermore, the exclusion of living beings (*prāṇin*) in rules such as *Pāṇini Sūtra* 2.3.17 (*manyakarmaṇyanādare vibhāṣāprāṇiṣu*), 8.3.72 (*anuviparyābhibhyaḥ syandateraprāṇiṣu*), and the Vārttika *aprāṇijāteścārajāvādīnām*, as well as the mention of "non-sentient" (*acitta*) in rules such as *Pāṇini Sūtra* 4.1.47 (*acittahastidhenoṣṭhak*) and 5.1.89 (*cittavati ntyam*), [indicate] the existence of individual souls (*jīvas*) who possess bodies commenced by karma other than that of the Lord (*īśvara*) and the respective presiding deities (*abhimānidevatā*).

And it teaches the plurality of individual souls (*jīva*). For if everything were conscious by virtue of being presided over by the Lord (*Īśvara*) or by a presiding deity (*abhimāninī devatā*), then since all would possess life and a mind, there would be no one to exclude; thus, the purpose of exclusions (*paryudāsa*) and the like would clearly be rendered useless. It is for this very reason that the statement in the *Mahābhāṣya* on the sūtra "In its place, the most similar" (Pāṇini 1.1.50)—which describes clods of earth and the like, as well as phonemes, as being insentient—is consistent. It should be understood that the plurality of selves is the consensus of the three sages (the *Munitraya*).

The scriptural text "Two birds" (Ā.U. and the Sūtra "And on account of staying and eating" (Brahma-Sūtra 1.3.7), which state that the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) coexist within a single body, are evidence for the plurality of conscious entities. Nor should it be argued that this was stated there by taking into account a difference based on limiting adjuncts (aupādhika-bheda); for no reason is seen in the Śruti or the Sūtra to show that they intend such a difference based on adjuncts. This is because such an interpretation would be a resort only when no other way out exists, and furthermore, it is difficult to maintain a connection with limiting adjuncts for the pure Brahman.

Furthermore, having described the view that everything possesses consciousness because the Lord is conscious, the description of the purport of the Bhāṣya as asserting the oneness of the Self is contrary to all means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), is not the doctrine of Bādarāyaṇa, and is not the system of Pāṇini; this is the truth. This has been explained at length with supporting evidence that the identity of Brahman and the individual soul (*jīva*) cannot be established based on the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *ṇeraṇau karma-vat*.
"Were it not for the Lord, however, everything would lack consciousness";
thus do the wise determine by means of such authorities as the Vedas.

Regarding the demonstration that creation is preceded by volition (*īkṣā*): as was stated at the beginning of the discussion on *sphoṭa*, "Even in the absence of the Lord's desire to create (*sisṛkṣā*), the powers of the Blessed One manifest within the field of Māyā," that too is not tenable. For it has been cited from the *Chāndogya*: "He thought, 'May I be possessed of a self'" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka* 3.2.1); "He desired, 'May a second self be born to me'" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka* 3.2.4); "From that [heat] which was intensely heated, Brahman was produced; from that, food was born" (*Ārṣeya* 1.8); and "He reflected: 'Upon the departure of what shall I depart? Upon the stability of what shall I be established? (*Chāndogya* 6.11.1).

"I shall establish [myself]"; he emitted the vital breath (*prāṇa*). To him, that [breath] said: "Prajāpati, desiring offspring, indeed performed austerities (*tapas*); having performed austerities, he brought forth a pair" (*Ṣaḍviṃśa Brāhmaṇa* 1.4), and because in such passages the creation is heard to be preceded by *īkṣā* (contemplation).

As for the statement that "even in the absence of a desire to create, there are creations of *māyā*," this must be considered; for in the Śruti, the Lord's creation is heard to be preceded by vision (*dṛṣṭi*).
Refutation of the consensus of Caraka and others:

Regarding that which was stated here in the fourth chapter of the *Mañjūṣā*, in the exposition of secondary derivative (*taddhita*) formations, where—on the premise of the non-existence of a plurality of selves—the words of Patañjali and Caraka were cited: "The embodied self is omnipresent; therefore its pervasiveness [is established], because it is great and omnipresent, and because it is eternally connected with the mind which follows the body's actions; one should know it as residing even in a single womb, though it reaches all wombs"—even that does not prove his [position].

Therein, the first statement establishes the all-pervasiveness of the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*), the cause of the universe, according to the direction of such Śruti texts as: "Nārāyaṇa stands pervading all that is within and without" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 4). The second, however, means that the individual soul (*jīva*) does not reside in only one body; rather, it becomes connected with various bodies by means of the mind, which follows the karma that initiates those numerous bodies:
"One should uplift oneself by means of the self; one should not let the self sink down.
For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self" (Gītā 6.5).
The mind alone is the instrument for both the bondage and liberation of human beings;
one should uplift the soul by means of the mind, and one should not cause the soul to perish.

The purport of this statement is that, due to the exhaustion of karma, the individual soul (*jīva*) is born in various wombs; therefore, since the non-difference between the individual soul and the Supreme (*parameśvara*) is not established by this either, his desired conclusion is not proven. The construction is: "One should know that even while situated in a single womb, [the soul] pervades all wombs by the power of karma. In this context, the purport of the statement lies precisely in this meaning, as evidenced by the natural sense of the phrase "following the karma of the body," and not in the oneness of the self (*ātmaikatva*), because the Lord (*īśvara*) lacks the karma that initiates a body.

Since Patañjali, in the *Yoga-sūtra* (2.22), established through such statements as "the [subtle body] perishes once its purpose is fulfilled" that there is a plurality of selves (*ātman*) and a distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*), it is appropriate for this statement of Patañjali’s also to describe reality in a manner that does not contradict that [established doctrine].

Nor should it be argued that it is improper to explain the meaning of Yoga in accordance with Caraka; for Yoga directly teaches the means for attaining liberation (*mokṣa*) and is thus primary (*mukhya*), whereas Caraka is concerned primarily with the means for achieving worldly pleasure (*aihika-sukha*) and is therefore secondary (*amukhya*). It is illogical to interpret a secondary work in accordance with a primary one. Furthermore, as stated above, Caraka has no intention (*tātparya*) regarding the oneness of the Self (*ātma-ekatva*), whereas the commentators beginning with Śrī Śaṅkarācārya have determined in their *Sūtra-bhāṣya* that Yoga does not intend to teach the oneness of the Self.

Furthermore, even though Patañjali states in the *Paramārthasāra*—in the fourth chapter on the investigation of mental fluctuations (*vṛtti*), concerning the unity of the Self—as an illustration of the authority for that unity: "Just as the one sun shines in all reservoirs of water, so the Supreme Self, abiding in all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), shines"—this too can be interpreted from the perspective of the Inner Ruler (*antaryāmin*). Moreover, the [interpretation] regarding the plurality of selves contradicts the Yoga Sūtra, "He has accomplished his purpose" (*kṛtārthaḥ*). The meaning of that sūtra will be explained immediately hereafter.
Furthermore: "Two birds, inseparable companions, cling to the same tree; one of them eats the sweet fruit, while the other looks on without eating" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.1).
"There are these two persons in the world: the perishable and the imperishable.
The perishable consists of all beings, while the one who stands at the peak is called the imperishable" (Bhagavad Gītā 15.8).

The doctrine of the oneness of the Self, as stated above, contradicts thousands of Śruti and Smṛti texts. The meaning of this Śruti passage is as follows: "Two" means two distinct entities characterized by duality; "suparṇau" means having the form of *suparṇas*—*suparṇa* being Garuḍa; "sayujā" means joined together; "sakhāyau" means they are friends through the relationship of benefactor and beneficiary—the individual soul (*jīva*) being the beneficiary and Hari being the benefactor; "samānaṃ vṛkṣam" means the single tree known as the body; "pariṣasvajāte" means they have embraced it—they both abide therein.

"Pippalam" means the fruit produced from the *aśvattha* tree known as the body—that is to say, the fruit of karma. "The other" is the individual soul (*jīva*); "the other" is the Lord (*īśa*). "Not eating" means not consuming; the sense is that the Lord does not partake in the fruit of karma. "From all sides" (*abhi*) means everywhere; "he shines" (*cākaśīti*) means he manifests. The rest is easy to understand. Śaṅkarācārya, however, explains: "Two birds" (*suparṇau*) means those with beautiful flight, or they are called "birds" because they are similar to birds in general. "Friends" (*sakhāyau*) means having a common renown, or having a common cause for manifestation.

The sage Raṅgarāmānuja, however, explains: "That which is joined (*yuj*) is *yuk*, meaning a quality; [the two] have qualities such as being free from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*), thus they are of equal qualities (*samānaguṇau*). *Saśāyau* means companions (*sahacarau*). The rest is the same. This scriptural passage has been explained by all as being intended to establish difference (*bheda*). As for the meaning of the *Gītā*, it has already been stated previously.

Nor should it be argued that the *Śruti*, the *Gītā*, and other such texts should be disregarded because they contradict the *Paramārthasāra*; for it is improper to disregard the *Śruti* and other scriptures on the basis of a human-authored work. Indeed, for the followers of the Veda, it is an ornament to disregard any human-authored statement whose meaning contradicts the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*. All of this has been stated in accordance with the view that both the *Caraka* and the *Paramārthasāra* were composed by Patañjali.

In reality, however, neither of those two texts was composed by the great sage Patañjali, the author of the Mahābhāṣya; therefore, it is improper to cite the words of Caraka’s *Paramārthasāra* while referring to him by the name "Patañjali," as in the expression "Patañjali in the Caraka."

This is because, in the introductions to their commentaries on Caraka, such as Cakrapāṇidatta and others, they state that the medical treatise named *Caraka* was composed by the ṛṣi Caraka—as seen in the phrase "refined by the great commentary of Patañjali" (*pātañjalamahābhāṣyacatakapratisaṃskṛtaiḥ*)—and because in medical texts there is no mention anywhere by anyone of its being composed by Patañjali or refined by him, nor is there any usage among the assemblies of experts in Āyurveda regarding its authorship by Patañjali.

Since the author of the *Bhāvaprakāśa*, the sovereign physician and master of Āyurveda who delineates the lineage of teachers, does not include Patañjali therein; and since Rāmabhadra’s *Patañjalicarita* states—"The sūtras [were composed] in the Yogaśāstra and the Vārttikas in the Vaidyakaśāstra, from him"—thereby asserting that a certain work titled *Vārttika* on medicine was indeed authored by Patañjali:
"I bow with palms joined in reverence to that foremost of sages, Patañjali, who removed the impurity of the mind through Yoga, that of speech through the Word, and that of the body through Vaidyaka."

Thus, because the name of a work is not mentioned in this verse, some scholars maintain that Patañjali composed a medical treatise other than the *Caraka-saṃhitā*. However, since the *Paramārthasāra* is included among the works attributed to the "Lord of Serpents" (Ahipati) by Cakrapāṇidatta and others, as well as by King Bhoja, the ruler of Dhārānagara—and given its absence from the list of works attributed to Patañjali in the *Patañjali-carita* and in traditional verses such as "yogena"—investigators conclude that it was not composed by either Ahipati or Patañjali.

If it is argued that "Caraka" and "Śeṣanāga" are merely alternative names for Patañjali himself, and therefore we conclude that both of those two works were composed by Patañjali, it is replied: if this were so, then since the *Paramārthasāra*—composed by Rāmakṛṣṇa—is even more ancient than the *Mahābhāṣya* by the great sage Patañjali and other works such as those by Śrī Śaṅkarācārya, it too would be regarded as highly authoritative due to its status as a work of the Sage (ārṣa) and thus attributed to Patañjali.

They might restate [the passages] as supporting their own desired non-dualism (advaita). However, since no such citations are seen in the works of Śaṅkara, Gaṅgādhara, and others, they maintain that Śeṣanāga was some recent scholar who preceded Nāgeśa Bhaṭṭa, and not another name for Patañjali; nor do they consider the *Caraka-saṃhitā* and the *Sāra* to be his compositions.

It might be argued that in the *Gītā*, the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva states, "All these [persons] are indeed noble, but the man of knowledge is alone my own," (7.18). Since he teaches the nature of the Self with the restrictive particle *eva* in the phrase "the Self alone" (*ātmaiva*), it is logical that identity with the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is what is sanctioned by the scripture. To this we reply: because the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*), who is the qualified seeker, with Brahman contradicts the *Śruti*; because it contradicts the introduction and conclusion of the *Gītā*; and because it contradicts the *Brahma-mīmāṃsā*. The *Gītā*...

It is more appropriate that [the word *iva*] has the sense of determining similarity (*sādṛśyāvadhāraṇa*). Alternatively, according to the statement of the learned authorities that "particles have multiple meanings," and because Śrī Śaṅkarācārya, while explaining the meaning of the mantra "tato bhūya iva te" (Iśa Upaniṣad 9.12), explained the phrase "bhūya iva" as "bhūya eva," one understands that the words *iva* and *eva* are synonymous; thus, the word *eva* here carries the sense of *iva*. Therefore, the purport of the Gītā does not lie in identity. This has been explained in greater detail during the analysis of the meaning of the verse beginning with "Vāsudeva."
"The Lord of Serpents composed a treatise named *Paramārthasāra*";
thus no one says this in the assemblies of learned physicians who are well-versed in the Vedas.
Therefore, those who are wise and follow the path of the Vedas and the Smṛtis do not respect a determination of the meaning of the scriptures made according to that [erroneous view].
Regarding the refutation of the diversity of Brahman based on ignorance (*avidyā*):

even that which was stated in the *Mañjūṣā*, in the section analyzing the meaning of verbal suffixes (*sub-artha*) within the discussion on agency (*kartṛtva*), namely—"Or rather, since Brahman alone, by the power of ignorance, possesses the nature of both apparent diversity and the absence thereof, the conventional usage of its birth and destruction in those forms should be understood as charming only so long as it is not investigated"—this presentation of Brahman’s apparent diversity and so forth is merely based on the superficially appealing statement of a certain individual; it is nowhere found in the scriptures.

Because the Lord’s subjection to ignorance and the resulting multiplicity based upon it have not been stated [by you], this [work] is contrary to the scriptures; being a mere fabrication of your own imagination, it is as untrustworthy as the words of a madman. By this, [it is refuted that] in the first chapter of the *Mañjūṣā* it was said: "Since Brahman itself, qualified by those respective forms such as 'A' and so on, is not stated to be the jar and so forth, and because if it were so, the consequence of its being subject to modification would follow."

If it is argued that the conventional usage of "thatness" (tattva) occurs by virtue of being qualified by various things such as pots and so forth, and not by virtue of being identical in nature to them—if this is the case, then what has been accomplished by one who set out to prove the non-existence of the phenomenal world apart from Brahman? Nothing at all. Such figurative usage is indeed accepted by everyone; thus, those who assert the reality of the world apart from Brahman and the difference between the two have already won. Furthermore, the multiplicity of the Lord’s forms—such as Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and others—is repeatedly taught in the scriptures as being truly real.
Therefore, one should never consider it to be merely figurative, as there is no evidence for such a conclusion.

This is what must be understood here: Nāgeśa states that the statements of the authors of the Vedabhāṣya and others are not to be trusted, saying: "The Vedabhāṣya is to be disregarded because it contradicts the Mahābhāṣya; furthermore, the blind faith of the Neo-Mīmāṃsakas—who claim that the Veda is always of a single, fixed sequence and has never been composed by anyone—is unacceptable because no such archaic statement to that effect is found, and because it contradicts the words of the author of the Mahābhāṣya and others. Thus, he asserts that their testimony is unreliable.

Likewise, even among the followers of Pāṇini, there is Kaiyaṭa’s statement in his commentary on the *san* sūtra: "by means of the vision of the non-duality of the Self (*ātmādvaitadarśana*"); Mañjūṣā’s statement: "the diversity attributed to Brahman is figurative (*upacarita*) due to the power of ignorance (*avidyā*"); and Vaidyanātha’s statement in the *Īpāyiguṇḍa*, at the occasion of explaining the sentences from the *Advaitamañjūṣā*: "he states the final established doctrine (*paramasiddhānta*)," and so forth; as well as similar statements by Dīkṣita and other grammarians, and by Bādarāyaṇa: "everything is endowed with consciousness by the conscious Lord (*īśvara*), and the diversity of the Lord is due to the power of ignorance."

The authors of the *Sūtrakṛta*, many of the teachers who composed commentaries (*bhāṣya*) on their sūtras, and Patañjali—since they did not establish such a conclusion regarding passages like "Listen, O stones" (*śṛṇota grāvāṇaḥ*), and since no such statement by Pāṇini is found—may well respond to Nāgeśa that [his view] is unacceptable.
Now, in the *Vṛttipariccheda*: "By whom one perceives the single, immutable being in all beings..."
Know that knowledge which perceives the undivided within the divided to be sāttvika.
But know that knowledge to be royal which, through its distinctness, perceives the various manifestations as separate within all beings.
But that which is attached to one single effect as if it were the whole, which is without cause, devoid of reality, and trivial—that is declared to be tāmasa. (Gītā 18.20–22)

Regarding these words from the *Gītā*, Nāgeśa Bhaṭṭācārya states: "If it is argued that the meaning of the first statement is that 'knowledge concerning the non-duality of the Self is *sāttvika*,' and that because this very [knowledge] is subsequently established as non-dual, the text is explained as being intent upon the oneness of the Self, and thus its apparent plurality must be declared to be merely figurative (*upacarita*), then we reply: if the primary statement has non-difference as its intended purport (*tātparya*), then the use of a grammatical construction involving different loci (*vyadhikaraṇa-nirdeśa*) in the phrase 'in all beings' (*sarvabhūteṣu*) would be inconsistent; for [the text says]: 'by whom all beings are seen as one...'"

One perceives with undecaying knowledge. The meaning is that by means of that knowledge, one perceives the undivided—devoid of difference—one Being, the immutable Supreme Self (paramātman). Through this construction, it is shown that among the diverse individual souls (jīvas) who are designated as "beings," the Reality existing within them as the Inner Controller (antaryāmī) is indeed one; and that [one] is Brahman, known by the name Vāsudeva. By this, the intended purport is that while there is a distinction between the individual souls, the Lord who is their Inner Controller is one alone; there is no distinction among the forms of the Inner Controller, yet there is a distinction of the Inner Controller from the individual souls.

The Lord’s role as the inner ruler (*antaryāmitva*) has been stated in the two passages: "And I am seated in the heart of all" (Gītā 15.15) and "The Lord, O Arjuna, dwells in the heart-region of all beings" (Gītā 18.61). Consider this: how could a meaning fabricated at will—by closing one's eyes and disregarding the sense obtainable from the natural force of the words therein—ever be acceptable to the hearts of those who know the truth?

But as for the second [type of knowledge]: that knowledge which does not perceive the Blessed Lord as He exists in all beings as a unity; or rather, that which perceives Him within all beings in His form as the Inner Ruler (antaryāmin) as if He were distinct—that is to say, it perceives the form of the Inner Ruler as being variously different; or, it knows—perceives—all entities and objects as manifold and diverse—that knowledge is of the nature of *rajas*. This is the meaning.

The meaning is as follows: although knowledge concerning other sentient beings than Viṣṇu may be *sāttvika*, knowledge of the difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), as well as knowledge of the difference among the forms of the Inner Controller (*antaryāmī*), is indeed *rājasa*. As for the third type, however, the notion of Viṣṇu-ness in the individual soul and the notion of the entire world [being the self] are *tāmasa*.

Others, however, state the purport of the three verses as follows: "The knowledge that there exists a universal genus (*ātmatva-jāti*) within the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and so forth, is *sāttvika*. That knowledge which perceives even the non-difference of the Self among Brahmins and others as being differentiated by their respective distinct forms is *rājasa*. And the knowledge attached to the propitiation of spirits, ghosts, and the like, which yields very meager results, is *tāmasa*. Therefore, these [verses] cannot serve as proofs for the oneness of the Self.
Consequently, the statement of Nāgeśa—that "the manifoldness of the one Brahman is accepted due to the influence of ignorance"—is considered untenable.
"Since Brahman attains a state of multiplicity through the power of ignorance"—
this is what neither Pāṇini nor even the King of Serpents (Śeṣa) has ever said.
The refutation of the view that [the world] has the nature of mere appearance:

As for the statement cited from the *Paramārthasāra*, beginning with "the inner controller of consciousness," and the claim that "the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) has as its object mere appearance and is rooted in the latent impressions of delusion denoted by the terms 'māyā,' 'vāsanā,' and 'avidyā'" (Maṅgalācaraṇa 1)—this too must be examined. For such a work is not reckoned among authoritative texts by those who accept valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*), and it has already been established that there is no certainty regarding its authorship by Patañjali; furthermore, Vyāsa, Pāṇini, and Patañjali themselves have not stated this.

In some places in the scriptures, Māyā is stated to be the cause of the world; however, the knowers of Brahman have previously declared that it is *pratibhūti* (manifestation) and the will of the Lord (*īśvarecchā*). As was cited earlier from the Chāndogya Śruti and other sources:
"My womb is the great Brahman; in it I place the germ. From that, O Bhārata, the birth of all beings takes place" (Gītā 14.3).
The great elements, ego-consciousness, intellect, and the unmanifest;
the ten senses and the one [mind], and the five objects of the senses. (Gītā 13.5) Desiring to produce various kinds of beings, he meditated upon his own body.
In the beginning, he created the waters alone; into them he cast his seed.
Then that golden egg came into being, possessing a radiance equal to a thousand suns;
within it was born Brahmā himself, the grandfather of all the worlds. (Manu Smṛti 1.8–9)

Thus [it is said]: because of the teaching of those attributes in the Sūtra, "On account of the teaching of his attributes within," and because in the Smṛtis cited in the commentary on the Sūtra, "Name and form," the creation of the world is described as consisting solely of categories distinct from Māyā—which is synonymous with *vāsanā* (latent impressions). Furthermore, by the Sūtra-maker himself, in the Sūtra "Name and form," it is stated that only the triply-transformed fire and the other elements are the cause of the world. Moreover, if the world were merely a body of appearance, there would follow the consequence that it lacks causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), just like a shell-silver or similar illusory objects.
Even in the *Paramārthasāra*, it was not asserted that the manifold world of pots, cloths, and so forth is merely an object of appearance.

Nor should it be said that its being such [as the absolute] is intended by him through the citation of the example of silver in mother-of-pearl; for the purpose of showing that example is to demonstrate its perishability (*naśvaratva*). Even the statement in the *Sāra* that "it is an illusion" has as its purport precisely this perishability. For this very reason, the statement in the *Sāra* that "this world was made by [the Lord]"—which describes the universe as the object of an act of creation—is consistent; for an entity whose nature is mere appearance cannot be the object of an act of creation, as is not observed in the case of silver in mother-of-pearl and the like.

However, perishability is observed in a jar, which is the object of the activity of a potter and others. The very example [cited] here is untenable; this is explained in detail elsewhere. In that context, the meaning of "from primordial matter" (*prakṛteḥ*) is "taking as its cause a substance for the world other than mere mental impressions" (*saṃskāra*). The meaning of "made" (*kṛtam*) is "the object of an act of creation. The meaning of "by his own majesty" (*svavibhūtyā*) is either "through the possession of his own sovereignty" or "by his own power."

By this, it is stated that the cause of the world is indeed a reality distinct from the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), and that the world is not merely an object of appearance. For it is established by the witness of all the world that the object of an error is not the object of volitional action (*kṛti*); this is because no creator of such things as mother-of-pearl-silver is ever observed. As for Nāgoji’s commentary on that [passage], it does not conform to the literal words found there; for the word *māyā* employed in the *Sāra* refers either to *prakṛti* as mentioned in the opening verse, or to the will of the Lord (*īśvarecchā*) and so forth.

By providing a counter-argument—stating that when one seeks the locus of ignorance (*avidyā*) consisting of error and its latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), the Supreme Self alone is the locus, just as it is for an *avidyā* distinct from it—and by demonstrating that this indicates the view of the authors of the Sūtras and the Bhāṣya that ignorance is indeed nothing other than error and its latent impressions, [the opponent] reveals their own ignorance of the intention of Śaṅkara’s Sūtra-Bhāṣya and other works, which seek to establish ignorance as a beginningless positive entity (*anādibhāvarūpāvidyā*).

However, it is difficult to reconcile Nāgeśa’s statement with the assertions of Miśra and others. Nor should it be argued that there is no contradiction because of Mañjūṣā’s statement, "In this [work], the section on the Deity (*devatādhikaraṇa*)," etc.; for there is no reason to restrict [the scope] in such a manner, and because elsewhere Miśra and others do not establish *māyā* according to the method stated by Nāgeśa. Furthermore, if the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) has the nature of a mere appearance (*pratibhāsa*), then it would be of the nature of cognition and momentary; consequently, since abandoning and acquiring [objects] would be impossible, all worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) would be destroyed.

The doctrine of consciousness-only (*vijñānavāda*) and the doctrine of momentariness (*kṣaṇikavāda*) were refuted by the Blessed One [Kṛṣṇa] and by Vyāsa through these two [sūtras]: "Not non-existence, because of perception" (*nābhāva upalabdheḥ*, Brahma-sūtra 2.2.28) and "And because of momentariness" (*kṣaṇikatvācca*, Brahma-sūtra 2.2.31). For this very reason, the learned do not approve of these two doctrines.
And in the *Bhāgavata*:
"There she beheld the entire universe, the moving and the stationary, the quarters, and peace."
The terrestrial globe, together with its mountains, continents, oceans, wind, fire, moon, and stars.
The wheel of light, water, space, heaven, and the atmosphere;
the sense organs derived from the primary elements (vaikārika), the mind, the subtle elements (mātrās), and the three qualities (guṇas).
Seeing this wondrous variety— the distinctions of seed, time, nature, karma, latent impressions, and gender—
within the mouth of his son as it was opened wide at his breast, he felt doubt along with the cowherds regarding the Self.

Thus, because it is stated in the tenth [canto] that the entire manifold universe of moving and non-moving beings exists within the belly of the Blessed One, they say that the world is not illusory (*māyika*). Nor should it be argued that such knowledge is merely an error, on the grounds that Yaśodā’s doubt in the subsequent verse—“Is this a small thing, or is it the Māyā of the God? Or rather, alas, is it a delusion of my own intellect? (40)—indicates that it is indeed a misconception.
Furthermore, whatever innate spiritual power (*ātma-yoga*) this child of mine possesses;
furthermore, [I know] that which is not within the range of discursive thought (*vitarka-gocara*) exactly as it is. (41)
I bow to that state which is difficult to discern— that upon which mind, intellect, and action directly depend, by which they are sustained, and from which they arise. (42)

Thus, by this half-verse, it is shown that this is not an error; rather, [the father] determined: "This possession of sovereignty is innate to my son. This sovereignty is not common to mere mortals, but could only belong to the Blessed Lord (Bhagavān) himself, who is the support of the most diverse world that transcends the reach of speech and mind. Therefore, by the power of my good fortune, the Blessed Lord himself has become my son. Having thus resolved, he bowed to him with the thought that he was the Blessed Lord. Since it is stated thus, it is impossible for that knowledge to be an error. As for the literal meaning of the words of the verse, it should be understood from the commentaries on the *Bhāgavata*.
Long ago, at the end of the kalpa, having drawn your own transformed body within yourself, you alone, the primordial Person, lay upon that water on the couch of the lord of serpents,
while the perfected ones contemplated the state of the supreme self within their hearts.
He is that very same one who now moves before our eyes and sustains us as his servants.

This is because Vyāsa has stated in another context that the entire universe exists within the belly of the Blessed Lord, as in *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 4.7.42. Furthermore, regarding the name "Śrīgarbha" in the *Sahasranāma*, Śaṅkara’s commentary states: "The god is the source of manifestation (*udbhava*), the agitator (*kṣobhaṇa*), and the Supreme Lord; he is Śrīgarbha. The etymological explanation of this name is: "He whose belly contains the world-form of *śrī*, which is [His] sovereign power (*vibhūti*). Other commentators have not explained it thus; however, a certain crest-jewel among poets [has done so]. By this name, the quality of containing all the worlds within His belly is attributed to the Blessed Lord.
Furthermore, because of the explanation of the verse "The three worlds dwell within Viṣṇu" as meaning that the three worlds exist within the belly of Viṣṇu, the world is not illusory (*māyika*).
On the occasion of describing the qualities of the Lord, Bhaṭṭa Murāri—the sovereign among learned poets—states:
"When the great aeon (*mahākalpa*) ceases, O sole abode on the path of [His] navel..."

Salutations to that Abode of the Universe, the architect of the three worlds, who at every moment becomes the self-born creator; salutations to him who entered his own belly to observe: "What is the substratum? Of what nature is it? And wherein is its arrangement? (2)

Thus he says. This is its meaning: "Viramati" means when the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*) has ended; "mahākalpe" means when another Brahma-cycle has arrived; "sṛṣṭikāle sati" means when the time of creation is present; "paraḥśilpī" refers to the Supreme Artificer, the original creator—the rest is clear.

Since Brahmā, as the first artificer, could not in any way comprehend the relationship between container and contained or the arrangement of the constituent parts of things, the statement that he entered the belly of the Lord in order to understand them indicates the scripturally established truth that every object endowed with all attributes exists within the Lord's belly in a subtle form.

Since objects that have illusion as their material cause and whose domain consists merely of appearances cannot possibly endure for a long duration, it would be inconsistent to speak of their entering the Lord’s belly in order to perceive them, as such a residence therein would be impossible. Therefore, it is understood that both points asserted by Nāgeśa are incorrect.

If it is asked, "How can the words of a poet, which consist of imaginative speculation (*utprekṣā*), serve to determine the meaning of a scripture?"—it is replied: This poet did not merely speculate upon this matter according to his own fancy; rather, he spoke by relying on the authority of the words of the Sages (*ārṣa-vacana*). What, then, is that [scriptural authority]? "The Grandfather (Brahmā) entered once more into the belly of the Lord of Śrī (Viṣṇu), the Lotus-born one, dwelling within those very worlds while still in the womb."

Thus says the *Laiṅga Purāṇa*. The meaning of the statement is that the entire universe exists within the belly of the Blessed Lord in a subtle form. The word *anvāsyan* means "perceiving. By this, Nāgeśa’s claim that Hiraṇyagarbha creates after knowing the Bauddhas who are distressed by their state (*padārta*) is to be considered.

But how is the explanation of Śaṅkarācārya and others—that [the Lord] creates without recollecting those established in previous kalpas—justified? It is said: because there is evidence for both views, the intended meaning is that He creates after seeing those residing within His belly and having correctly ascertained the nature of things, without recollecting those established in previous kalpas. Now, [it may be objected]: in the *Devatādhikaraṇa* (Brahma Sūtra 4.1.3), it is stated: "Knowledge alone is the supreme Brahman; knowledge is held to lead to bondage.
This entire universe consists of knowledge; nothing exists beyond knowledge."

If it is argued that the entire universe has Brahman as its essence, which is of the nature of knowledge—this being established by the statement in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*, "O Maitreya, know that both knowledge and ignorance are indeed knowledge"—we reply: In that regard, while it is appropriate to describe Brahman as "knowledge" based on the Vedic scripture, "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge," His status as a "binder" is also certainly accepted, given the statement, "He is the binder by the bond of worldly existence, and the liberator from the bond of worldly existence."

In this regard, the distinction is as follows: for those who perform prescribed action with desire, Hari—who is of the nature of knowledge—acts as a binder because He causes them to experience worldly pleasures by bestowing the fruits of their respective desires. However, for those who perform prescribed action without desire, with the understanding that it is a duty to worship the Lord, He acts as a liberator by granting them liberation.

This entire universe—consisting of all that exists—is of the nature of knowledge (*jñānātmaka*), meaning it has Brahman as its essence; that is to say, it has Brahman as its creator through acts such as grasping, and is thus owned by Him and governed by Him. There exists nothing else superior or higher than Brahman, who is of the nature of knowledge. Furthermore, both *vidyā* (knowledge) and *avidyā* (ignorance)—that is, wisdom and lack of wisdom—are themselves dependent upon knowledge alone. Because they are subordinate to it, they are designated in grammatical apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), just as one speaks of "the king's kingdom."

In this context, "knowledge" (*jñāna*) refers to the knowledge of Hari’s state as the Supreme Person (*puruṣottama*), while "ignorance" (*ajñāna*) is that which is inseparable from it, produced by the delusion of dualities and so forth. This has been explained in the *Gītā* at the beginning of the seventh chapter with the words, "whose knowledge has been carried away by various desires" (7.20), and so on; thus, according to the intended meaning of these statements, the aforementioned objection finds no ground.

By this [statement], having introduced the following words—“Brahman itself without limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) is knowledge (*vidyā*), and that same Brahman with limiting adjuncts is ignorance (*avidyā*)”—the claim that “the world is Brahman qualified by limiting adjuncts” because everything has Brahman as its self is untenable, since that stated meaning cannot be obtained through the literal force of the words. For this very reason, this sentence was introduced in the *Kalā* [section] with the words: “He states his own intention—‘without limiting adjuncts,’ etc. By this, it is understood that there is another meaning to the statement.

The connection of a pure entity with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) is difficult to establish, because that [pure entity] is devoid of attributes; likewise, its being accessible to yogis in meditative absorption (*samādhi*) is likewise impossible. Therefore, the very distinction between the "unconditioned" (*nirupādhi*) and the "conditioned" (*sopādhi*) is improper.

By means of the sūtra *saṃjñāmūrti*, the author of the sūtras declares that water and the other elements, once tripartitely differentiated (*trivṛtkṛta*), are the cause of the world—this is the meaning of the Śruti.
This is acceptable to Pāṇini, the foremost of Vedic scholars, and it is desired by him;
therefore, since this is uncontradicted, it must indeed be the intention of Patañjali as well.

Therefore, Nāgeśa’s statement that "the nature of manifestation consists in being produced by mental impressions (*saṃskāra*)" is not accepted by the three sages [Patañjali, Vyāsa, and Vācaspati]. This concludes the refutation of the view that Yoga Sūtra 4.17 (*akṛta-anuṣṭhāna...*) concerns the illusory nature of difference.

In this regard, [the author] states that even the *Yogasūtra* is consistent with his own doctrine of the oneness of the Self (*ātmaikatva*) within the Mañjūṣā; for, at the occasion of defining the all-pervasiveness (*vibhutva*) of the internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*), he raises the objection that "since unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*), latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and so forth would be common to all, there would follow the simultaneous experience of pleasure and pain by everyone. He then clarifies this point with the sūtra: "Because everything is illusory (*māyika*), there is no fault, as [the mind] is like a lotus leaf in water; though destroyed for one who has attained their goal, it is not destroyed because it is common to others" (*Yogasūtra* 2.22). Thus he explains.

Having established [the context] with the words, "How is it possible that one [soul] is both unperished and perished? and so forth, [the opponent] asserts that the plurality of souls is illusory (*māyika*). That is baseless. For instance: in the sūtra cited, no word is heard that indicates the meaning of being *avidyaka* (unreal/illusory); furthermore, since no such word is heard in the preceding or subsequent sūtras, neither the carrying over (*anuvṛtti*) nor the exclusion (*apakarṣa*) of such a term is possible; and because this section of the sūtras constitutes the "Means" (*sādhana*) chapter, there is no determination therein that any means of realization is illusory.

Nāgeśa’s statement—that [the opponent's view] is untenable because the meaning is not obtained in that manner according to the literal phrasing (*sūtrākṣara*) and context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Sūtra, and because it is taught by the Sūtra itself—and that in Patañjali’s system there is an absence of *māyikatva* (illusoriness) for any entity whatsoever—is incorrect.

Nor should it be argued that, since it is impossible for a single object to be both destroyed and not destroyed for different persons, one must resort to the assumption of *māyikatva* for one or the other due to lack of any other alternative; for, given the plurality of souls as the intended meaning of the Sūtra, the states of being destroyed and not destroyed are logically consistent through the distinction between different qualified practitioners (*adhikārin*). This very point has been explained in exactly this way by Maṇḍana Miśra and others.

Furthermore, the claim that "the Puruṣa is not one, as is the case with Pradhāna," because the plurality of Puruṣas is established for the sake of accounting for the systematic order of saṃsāra—such as birth, death, the experience of pleasure and pain, and liberation—and because the oneness of Prakṛti and the plurality of Puruṣas are directly taught by Śruti itself; and the assertion that "the meaning of the Śruti passage 'One unborn female' is precisely what is restated by this Sūtra"—this contradicts the intended meaning of the *Yoga-sūtras* and the intended meaning of the Śruti, which is that the plurality of individual souls (*jīva*) is indeed real. This is contrary to the meaning of the *Miśra-grantha*.

Therefore, this is the meaning of the aphorism: when there is doubt as to whether the Puruṣa is one, like Prakṛti, or manifold, he states the established conclusion—“kṛtārtham” (once its purpose is accomplished). “Tat” refers to Pradhāna.

With respect to one whose purpose has been fulfilled—that is, with respect to the *puruṣa* for whom the experience consisting of the consciousness of objects, senses, pleasure, pain, and so forth, has ceased to be an object of cognition—it is "destroyed," meaning its activity has ceased (even though it does not undergo transformation through the objects and so forth that serve as the basis for that *puruṣa*'s enjoyment). Yet, it is "not destroyed" in the sense that it remains active (transforming through objects and so forth). With respect to whom? With respect to those whose purpose is not yet fulfilled. Why? Because it is common to others—that is, because it is common to all *puruṣas* other than the *puruṣa* whose purpose has been fulfilled.

The intention is as follows: although *pradhāna* is common to all, it does not serve the purpose of one who is detached from objects when it transforms into the form of those very objects; however, for the non-discriminating person (the person possessed of passion), it becomes capable of serving their purpose by transforming into the form of an object of enjoyment. Thus, even though *pradhāna* is a single entity, its destruction or non-destruction is logically established according to the distinction between the detached and the passionate person; this proves the plurality of *puruṣas*.

It is a universal worldly consensus that Sāṃkhya and Yoga are proponents of dualism. Furthermore, in the *Ṣaṣṭitantra*, the teacher Pañcaśikha states regarding the Sāṃkhya school's view that the world is not illusory (*māyika*):
"The supreme form of the *guṇas* does not come within the range of vision;
that which has entered the range of vision is utterly void, like an illusion."

This has been explained by the following [verse]. Its meaning is as follows: the multitude of things (the world), which is the effect of the *pradhāna* consisting of the three *guṇas*, is like *māyā*—that is, like an object created by *māyā*. Just as an object produced by a magician perishes immediately, so too does the effect of *pradhāna* perish quickly. Thus, in the view of the Sāṃkhyas, the world is not illusory (*māyika*), but rather real and capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākārī*); therefore, according to their system, even the difference inherent within the world is indeed real.

Furthermore, as Miśra has stated: "In that Sūtra, the scriptural declarations of oneness cannot be contradicted by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because they can somehow be explained even figuratively through the absence of division in space and time. Thus, the compatibility of both unity and plurality is established by distinguishing between the conventional and the ultimate levels of reality.

By the use of the word "devotion" (*bhaktyā*), the unity [of the two] is secondary (*gauṇa*) and not primary (*mukhya*); furthermore, by the phrase "in some way" (*kathaṃcit*), since the distinction of space and time is eternal, the absence of such a distinction is itself impossible, and thus the notion of such a conceptualization is strained—this is the intention of the Miśras. In the *Bhikṣu-grantha*, according to the sequential correspondence, the identity is conventional (*vyāvahārika*), like that between a face and the moon, whereas from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), there is difference, like that between a jar and a cloth—this is the intention of the Bhikṣu.

For this very reason, when explaining the intention of the author of the Sūtras—who, in the aphorism defining Īśvara (*Yoga Sūtra* 1.24), "Īśvara is a distinct Puruṣa untouched by afflictions, actions, their fruitions, or latent impressions," asserts that Īśvara is entirely distinct from all others—Vijñānabhikṣu has skillfully demonstrated that the ultimate aim of both Sāṃkhya and Yoga lies precisely in the plurality of selves (*ātmanānātva*).

This is the summary here: it is well known that Patañjali was one among the Sāṃkhya teachers; therefore, just as in the Sāṃkhya system, in this system as well, the world and the plurality of selves are indeed real. Consequently, it is logical to describe this sūtra as having the intention of establishing real difference. Among the commentators, such as the author of the Bhāṣya and others, not a single one stated that the difference indicated by this sūtra is merely illusory (māyika).

"Indeed, those Sāṃkhyas and Yogas are dualists," so said the venerable Śaṅkarācārya; no scholar explains this sūtra as referring to a difference that is merely illusory (māyika). Therefore, learned people do not respect Nāgeśa’s interpretation. Nor should it be argued that the meaning of Śaṅkara’s commentary, "Indeed, they are dualists," is "adherents of the conventional dualism" (vyāvahārika-dvaitavādinaḥ); for if that were the case, it would be illogical for him to proceed with the refutation of their views.

This [commentator] also, following the path of the *Miśra* school in his commentary on the *Yogavṛtti*, has explained this Sūtra. Thus, the statement that the Sūtra indicates a *māyika* (illusory) distinction in the *Mañjūṣā* is contrary to the many commentaries on the *Yogasūtra*; moreover, it suggests that Śrī Śaṅkarācārya and others were ignorant of the intent of the Yoga Tantras. The explanation that the *māyika* distinction is stated by the Sūtra "akṛtārtha...
is the one agreed upon by the many commentators on the *Yogasūtra*.
Nor is it accepted by Patañjali, the author of the Yoga Sūtras;
indeed, in the Sāṃkhya-Yoga system, there is no category whatsoever that is illusory (māyika).
Regarding the meaning of the verse beginning with *janmādy asya*:

one should not raise the objection that in the first verse of the *Bhāgavata*, "From whom the birth etc. of this [world proceed] through [His] connection" (*janmādy asya yato 'nvayāt*), it is stated by the Blessed Lord Vāyu that the creation performed by the Lord—or that which is created by Him—is unreal (*mṛṣā*). This is because the intention here is that Bādarāyaṇa intends to show that the effect of the three qualities (*triguṇa*) is unreal when considered in relation to the Supreme Brahman.

The literal meaning is as follows: because the locative case is heard in the word *yatra* (wherein), which refers to the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*), the genitive in *mṛtāḥ* (dead) is used to express the relationship of the locus of the object (*vaiṣayikādhāra*). Just as there is an exchange (an error) regarding light and so forth in things such as a mass of hair, so too—in whatever form of the Blessed One, even in the incarnations (*avatāra*) such as Rāma and Kṛṣṇa—the "threefold creation" (*trisarga*), which is the connection with (or the effect of) the three qualities (*guṇa*), is false (*mṛṣā*); it does not exist. [As stated in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad: "He is alone and devoid of qualities," and "All... [etc.]

This is because of the statement, "devoid of qualities" (Gītā 13.14). Alternatively, there is a word-division as *amṛṣā iti*. *Vinimaya* means effect (*kārya*). The locative case in *yatra* is used with the intention of expressing the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) of the related entities, from which the suffix *tral* is derived. The three words refer to *prakṛti*, which consists of the three qualities (*guṇatraya*). The meaning is as follows: whatever is the effect of light and so forth is *amṛṣā*—that is, true (*satya*), because it is capable of purposeful action (*arthakriyākāritva*). Likewise, whatever is the effect of *prakṛti* consisting of the three qualities, such as the Great Principle (*mahat*) and so on, in relation to that [Brahman], is *amṛṣā*—true; it is not false (*mithyā*).

If one were to say that [the author] intends here to maintain that only what is created by Brahmā is illusory (*mithyā*), then the statement "devoid of deception" (*nirastakuhaka*) would be inconsistent, as it asserts the absence of *māyā*. For that [statement] would be appropriate only if [Brahmā] were the creator of a real world; otherwise, like a magician, his nature would be merely deceptive (*māyika*). Thus, the inconsistency is quite clear. Furthermore, according to the Sāṃkhya school, even that which is created by a magician is not false (*mithyā*).

Furthermore, it should not be forgotten that it was previously established—and will be further demonstrated—that the doctrine of the unreality of the world contradicts the words of the Blessed One, "This is unreal and without foundation"; the details, however, should be sought elsewhere.

By this, it should be understood that both of the following positions are inconsistent: first, that which Nāgeśa asserted in two places in the first chapter, having cited the *Kūrma Purāṇa* passage—"O Brahmin, earth and so forth reside within the mind and never exist externally; they are experienced by everyone even in slight errors, intoxication, and the like"—namely, that the entire world resides only within the mind and does not exist outside; and second, that which Vaidyanātha stated regarding the *Kalā*, namely, that by the expression "never" (*kadācana*), the entire phenomenal world is non-existent externally.

For instance—the intended meaning of the statement is as follows: an object experienced during a dream (*svapna*) is not perceived upon waking; when there arises the inquiry as to where that [object] was located, it is understood that the very object experienced while awake exists within the mind in the form of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), and is experienced through the awakening conditions (*udbodhaka-sāmagrī*) such as the dream-form, but not as something existing externally while awake, because a dream is not experienced by others. This is the purport of the words, and not that external objects do not exist at all.

The interpretation, however, is as follows: O Brahmin, that very earth and so forth, which exists in the form of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) within the mind, is not experienced in dreams and the like; for it lacks the capacity to be experienced by everyone when it has entered into states such as dreaming. The distinction is this: that which is capable of being experienced by all is external, whereas that which is capable of being experienced only by the dreaming person exists within the mind in the form of a latent impression. Thus, the meaning [of the verse] is not that external objects do not exist at all; therefore, there is no intention to deny the reality of external things in the verses beginning with "birth" and "the earth, O Brahmin. This has been stated in brief; the details are found elsewhere.

The refutation of the view that Īśvara possesses the nature of all deities: In the *Mañcūṣā*, within the investigation of the meaning of secondary suffixes (*taddhita*), [the author] establishes the existence of a deity distinct from sound according to the system of Jaimini—by means of the passage "And because even Jaimini accepts this" following the sūtra "Not so, because there is no other deity," which states that in cases such as "the oblation for Indra" (*aindraṃ haviḥ*) or "the mantra for Indra" (*aindro mantraḥ*), the deity is the meaning of the secondary suffix, and that "deity is not something over and above the word" (as established in the section on animals), and that "animals are not authorized in ritual acts. Furthermore, he establishes that "the status of being a deity... [is as follows].

Having defined *devatātva* (the nature of a deity) as "being the intended object (*uddeśyatva*)—that is, being the substratum of a fruit other than heaven produced by the renunciation of an oblation (*havis*) accompanied by a mantra—and being the object of praise by a mantra," [the author] states, for the sake of establishing his own doctrine of the oneness of the Self: "And the status of being the intended object belongs to the consciousness of the Lord (*īśvara-caitanya*) as delimited by both the word and the body mentioned in the mantra; and that very [consciousness] is what is denoted by the words 'Indra' and so forth mentioned in the mantra, based on the wording of such mantras as 'Indra is Mitra'."

By the phrase "There is no sublation" (*na bādha*), Nāgeśa supports the view that the deityhood belongs precisely to the consciousness of the Lord (*īśvara-caitanya*) as qualified by the specific forms (*vigraha*) made known by those respective words—forms which are established through the force of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) stating, "Indra is thousand-eyed, the breaker of the cow-stall, the wielder of the thunderbolt"—and which possess the powers of consuming the oblation, sovereignty, and bestowing the fruit of satisfaction.

Regarding this, they say: "The statement that 'it is because Jaimini accepts [the existence of a deity]' is not tenable; for in the ninth book, in the section on the Deity (*devatādhikaraṇa*), the *Bhāṭṭadīpikā* states: 'The definitive conclusion of Jaimini’s view is that the deity is indeed the word itself, in accordance with the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), regardless of whether its referent is conscious or unconscious. It has no physical form whatsoever; therefore, it does not bestow the fruit [of the ritual]. Rather, it is the *apūrva* alone that bestows the fruit produced by the action. Even for me who speak thus, my speech is defiled only by the remembrance of Hari.'"

Upon examining Khaṇḍadeva’s *Jaiminimataniṣkarṣa*, titled *Śaraṇam*, as well as the expiation for the faults arising merely from repeating what was taught therein, one understands that the existence of a deity distinct from sound (the Veda) is not the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of Jaimini. Although there is no difference between these two authors in their status as eminent scholars, because Khaṇḍadeva’s summary is proven by the [authoritative] tradition of instruction, Khaṇḍadeva’s statement alone is more powerful; therefore, it is that which should be respected.

The statement of Pārthasārathi Miśra and others in the *Tiryañc-Adhikaraṇa* (6.1)—namely, "Because there is no possibility of the gods making a renunciation intended for themselves, and because they lack a physical body, they lack the capacity [for ritual action], and thus they have no entitlement"—as well as the corresponding speech of Kumārila, serve as evidence for the existence of such a tradition of instruction.

Furthermore, one must consider how, by the words "not because of the absence of other deities" (*na devatāntarābhāvāt*), an additional deity can be obtained according to the literal sense of the text while simultaneously teaching that the gods have no entitlement to ritual action.

Furthermore, the very expression "by means of a sūtra" by Nāgeśa, the author of the *Mañjūṣā*, reveals his extraordinary mastery of the *Pūrvatantras*. This statement is not seen anywhere in the reading of Jaimini’s sūtras, nor was it commented upon by Śabarasvāmin, the author of the *Bhāṣya*, who explains each sūtra individually, nor by Kuma[ra]bhaṭṭa, the author of the *Vṛtti*.

In the *Devatādhikaraṇa* of the *Uttaramīmāṃsā*, Śaṅkarācārya, while citing this passage to support the objection that gods do not possess the qualification [for Vedic study], did not state that it is a *sūtra*. Traditionalists maintain that this is a passage from the *Śābarabhāṣya*. Followers of Jaimini’s school argue that the assignment of a *sūtra* number to this passage in the commentary on Śaṅkara’s *Bhāṣya*, as well as the description of it as "the meaning of the very first *sūtra*," are based on a lack of careful attention.

Furthermore, in the *Devatādhikaraṇa* of Śaṅkara’s *Bhāṣya* on the *Brahma-sūtras* (1.3.8), after refuting the view of Jaimini—who maintains that deities lack a physical form (*vigraha*) and so forth—the author establishes the possession of a form as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*). Therefore, Khaṇḍadeva’s assertion that Jaimini’s own position is precisely that "there is no deity distinct from the word" is indeed correct. If Jaimini had also accepted that a deity exists as something distinct from the word, then one could have argued that the possession of a form is established through the force of *arthavāda* passages and the like.

Consequently, even the refutation of the systems of Śaṅkara and Jaimini would be based solely on a failure to understand their true intentions. The great poet Śrī Harṣa, describing the relevant and irrelevant meanings through *śleṣa* (double entendre), states that Jaimini maintains that the gods possess physical bodies (*vigraha*): "The state of being the sage Jaimini arose for him as he assumed the form of the universe; unable to endure the physical forms of the gods who enjoy the sacrifices, he reduced my thunderbolt to futility."

By this [verse, Naiṣadhīyacarita 5.39], the meaning is that [he is so called] because of his fashioning of universal forms—that is, by assuming numerous incarnations such as the Fish, the Tortoise, and others—and because of his composing sūtras of manifold purpose. The meaning "because of his direct perception of all categories of existence" is also suggested. The remainder is clear.

The Blessed One, Bādarāyaṇa, the author of the Sūtras, established in the aphorism "The fruit [arises] from Him, because that is logical" (Brahma-sūtra 3.2.38) that the Lord is the bestower of the fruit, whereas dharma bestows the fruit by means of the *apūrva*. Subsequently, having introduced the view of Jaimini with the aphorism "Jaimini [holds] dharma [to be the cause], for that very reason" (Brahma-sūtra 3.2.40), he concluded the final position (*siddhānta*) that—since dharma and the *apūrva* are insentient and thus incapable of being givers—the view that the Lord alone, as the supervisor of all, is the bestower of the fruit according to the aforementioned reasoning is the correct one.

Furthermore, if Jaimini were to accept a deity distinct from the word [itself], then it would be appropriate to refute his view with the sūtra, "But Bādarāyaṇa [holds that] the Person [is the cause], because of the mention of the motive" (Brahmasūtra 3.2.42), on the grounds that the very same [deity], when propitiated through its essential core, ought to be the bestower of results.

Furthermore, in Jaimini’s system, many sections such as "But the injunction is the commencement" (2.1.5), which are intended to establish the existence of an *apūrva*—a potency capable of producing results like heaven that manifest at a later time—would become unnecessary to undertake, since the production of results could occur simply through the grace of a deity possessing a physical form.

And that which has been stated by him: "The Lord's consciousness alone is the deity as the intended recipient, denoted by the words 'Indra' and so forth mentioned in the mantra, who consumes the substance being offered—as in: 'He is Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, Agni; and he is the heavenly, fair-winged Garuḍa.'"

"The seers speak of the One Being in many ways; they call him Agni, Yama, Mātariśvan" (Ṛgveda 1.164.46). Regarding this, it is said: "They say, 'Sacrifice to that one,' 'Sacrifice to that one,' [referring] to each individual deity; yet this is merely its manifestation, for he alone is all the gods" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.6). Since his status as the self of all deities is established by such passages, even a deity distinct from the [mere] word is indeed the Lord (Īśvara).

On this point, the following must be said: the statement that "there exists a deity distinct from sound, and she also possesses a physical form" is indeed elegant; moreover, this should be accepted with nodding heads and with praise by all orthodox believers (*āstika*) other than the Mīmāṃsakas. For the venerable author of the Brahma-sūtras, in the sūtra "Bādarāyaṇa [holds that there is eligibility] even for those above [the gods], because of the possibility" (1.3.23) and so forth, has established that they possess the qualification (*adhikāra*) for the worship of the Lord.

If there were no existence of the gods as entities distinct from words, and no corporeal form, then the commencement of that section [of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtras] would be purposeless, since it would be impossible to engage in ritual activity toward them.
