However, in his view, the lordship attributed to them, their consumption of oblations in the form of Indra and others, their existence as something over and above the word, and their bestowal of fruits are all untenable. [The phrase "indrādirūpeṇa havirbhojanam, śabdātiriktatvaṃ phaladatvaṃ cāyuktam" is repeated in the source text.]

The argument that "it was not stated by Jaimini" and "because it was accepted even by Jaimini," as well as the reasoning regarding his being the Lord (Īśvara), are inconsistent; for in the Mīmāṃsaka school, there is no such thing as God. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Śaktivāda* section of the *Bhūṣaṇasāra*: "For the Mīmāṃsakas, there is no convention (saṃketa) [of God] as the power (śakti); because they lack a God, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the non-existence of the presentation of meaning and so forth, due to the absence of the apprehension of that convention."

Regarding the sūtra *kasye* (Pāṇini 4.2.9), Kaiyaṭa states: "The deity is the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) of the sacrifice, and the object of praise through the mantra; such is the meaning of the word 'deity'. This is because it is impossible for there to be a single source of light regarding the existence of gods and others distinct from Īśvara, or regarding Hari’s superiority over them, in passages such as: "Agni is indeed the lowest of the gods, Viṣṇu the highest; between them lie all other deities" (AiB 1.1); "He who dwells in cognition," "He who dwells in the self," and "The Lord of all beings" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad). Thus, he asserts that the term *devatā* refers to the deity as the recipient of the sacrifice.

Since the diversity of volitions has already been established by numerous proofs cited previously, it should be considered that there is only one Lord who is denoted by such titles as Indra and so forth, and who constitutes the respective deityhoods through those various forms.

In passages such as, "Now, those living beings here [in this world]—even so do all these creatures go day after day to that world of Brahman, yet they do not find it, for they are held back by untruth" (Chāndogya 8.3.2), there is the hearing of plural forms such as "living beings. Furthermore, in the sixth section of the eighth chapter, there is the hearing of Indra’s residence for one hundred and one years in the state of studenthood (*brahmacarya*) under Prajāpati in order to receive the knowledge of Brahman. This shows that the status of being the Lord of Beings (*bhagavat*) is not applicable to anyone other than the Blessed Lord Lakṣmīpati.

At the occasion of its exposition, the Blessed Vyāsa has provided a determination of the nature of *varvat* (the supreme reality); and in the *Bhāgavata*, Śrīdhara’s commentary on that passage serves as the authority for the absence of identity between the conscious self (*cetana*) [and the material qualities].
Now, it may be argued:
"Sattva, rajas, and tamas are the qualities of *prakṛti*—by these..."
The Supreme Person alone,
endowed with these [qualities], assumes here the designations of Hari, Viriñci, and Kara for the sake of the maintenance and other functions [of the world];
therein, indeed, the auspicious goals of men who possess the quality of *sattva* shall be realized.

Regarding the statement in the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* (1.2.24), "Thus, for Hari alone, there is a difference of names due to the difference in his functions such as protection," one should not say that the identity of Barhi, Viriñci, and Hara is what Vyāsa intended; for by this, non-difference is not being asserted. Rather, it means: "Viṣṇu, situated in various places, awakens their respective powers."
The one and only Mahāviṣṇu accomplishes everything directly and easily.

Because of such statements, it is understood that Hari, residing within even Viriñca and others, performs creation and other functions; since he is situated in each of those places, they possess the status of being denotable by the terms "Viriñca" and so forth, just as those situated on a bed are denoted by the word "bed. Thus, there is no fault. Nor should it be argued that because of the statement in Bhāgavata 1.2.27, "The peaceful ones, free from envy, partake of the portions of Nārāyaṇa," these beings are identical to him; for the meaning is that they are similar to the portions of Nārāyaṇa, not that they are of his very nature. Therefore, there is no fault.

Scriptures such as the Śrutis and Smṛtis of this kind are to be explained in this manner. It should be understood that, since the doctrine of the oneness of the Self has been refuted in the *Śāstradīpikā* (1.1.1), this [interpretation] is not tenable according to the system of the Mīmāṃsakas.

As for the Śruti passage beginning with "Indra, Mitra," etc., Mādhavācārya has explained in his *Vedabhāṣya* that it praises either Agni or Āditya through their connection with qualities perceived by the force of etymology (*yoga*) of the words "Indra" and so forth; thus, it refers to one of these deities, such as Agni, and not to Īśvara in the manner asserted by Nāgeśa.

Furthermore, in the view of one who asserts the identity of consciousness, since there is no consciousness other than God, and because it is impossible to speak of a connection with adventitious attributes due to God’s pure nature, even a difference based on limiting adjuncts (upādhi) cannot be asserted.

One must consider that, due to the absence of an agent of action, the sacrifice itself would necessarily be non-existent; consequently, because there would be no enjoyer of the fruit produced by it (and thus no enjoyer of fruits such as heaven), the entire Veda and other scriptures would become invalid, being merely the ravings of a madman or the talk of a child. Thus, the identity with the conscious principle (Brahman) asserted by him would be entirely without proof. Nor can it be argued that everything is rendered consistent through the connection with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), for it has already been stated that such a connection is impossible with respect to the pure reality.

If it is argued that the author of the *Mañjūṣā* spoke in accordance with the introduction to the *Ṛgvedabhāṣya*, stating: "From that Supreme Lord, from the sacrifice—the one worthy of worship (*yajñāt-yajanīyāt*), the one to whom everything is offered (*sarvahutaḥ*) by all"—we say no. For in his commentary on the *Puruṣasūkta*, Mādhavācārya explained this portion of the mantra as follows: "From that sacrifice" refers to the previously mentioned mental sacrifice; "from the one to whom everything is offered" means that the Person, who is the self of all, is the one in whom [the universe] is offered during the sacrifice, and thus he is "the one to whom everything is offered" (*sarvahuta*). Thus he interpreted this part of the verse.

Bhaṭṭabhāskara also [rejects this], because he explains that the term *sarvahut* refers to that in which the Supreme Person (*puruṣa*), the self of all, is offered as a sacrificial animal (*paśu*) from that mental [sacrifice]—interpreting it with the suffix *kvip* in the sense of a locus—and because he explains the passage beginning with "Indra" as referring to Agni and the other deities; thus, there is no certainty regarding the authority of the meaning stated in the introduction (*upoddhāta*). Furthermore, it has been stated previously that there is no evidence for the Lord having the form of Indra and the others.

Regarding this, the claim that "there is no contradiction because the *Bhāṣya* and the *Upodghāta* state that Īśvara is the self of all" should be considered [with caution], for that meaning is not established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). As for the term *sarvahuta*, its sense is that "the whole (*sarvaḥ*)—meaning either full (*pūrṇaḥ*) or pervasive (*vyāptaḥ*)—is offered (*hūyate*). The authority for the word *sarva* having these two meanings was stated during the commentary on the verse concerning Vāsudeva. Alternatively, it may mean "offered by all" (*sarvaiḥ hūyate*), with the suffix *kvip* in the passive sense, thus meaning "that which is being offered by all. Indeed, in Vaiṣṇava sacrifices, there is the fact of being offered by all.

Furthermore, what is called *havana* (offering) is "pleasing" (*prīṇana*), as stated in the *Kaumudī*: "It is also [defined] as pleasing," according to the *Bhāṣya*. This is an activity conducive to a desire inherent in the Supreme Deity and others, which is denoted by such terms as "pleasure" (*prīti*) or "satisfaction" (*prasāda*) regarding their respective objects. That desire takes such forms as: "This person is my devotee," "May he obtain this desired fruit," or "May he attain me. Such an activity consists of praise, or the dedication of performed Vedic (*śrauta*) and Smārta rites to the Lord.
In that regard: [One should dedicate to] Viṣṇu, who is without beginning or end, the Great Lord of all worlds...
"By constantly praising the Overseer of the World, one shall transcend all suffering" (*Sahasranāma* 6).
Thus, it is remembered that praise is a means to the fruit by way of generating joy;
[the Lord] is imitated through body, speech, mind, senses, intellect, or even the self, according to one's own nature.
"Whatever one does entirely, one should dedicate that to Nārāyaṇa.

(Bhāgavata 11.11.37) "Whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer in sacrifice, whatever you give away, and whatever austerity you practice, O son of Kuntī—perform all that as an offering unto Me. (Gītā 9.27)

Thus, because of the traditional teaching on the dedication of all performed and prescribed action, you will be liberated from the bonds of action consisting of good and evil fruits; with your self united through the yoga of renunciation, being freed, you shall come to Me. (Gītā 9.28)

This is because the Lord has stated that the fruit belongs to the one who offers (*arpaṇa*). Now, an objection is raised: the commentary on the *Pāṇini Sūtra* 4.2.25, "And *sarva* [is called *prajāpati*]," which states "of what? (*kasyet*), is an authority for the fact that everything has Brahman as its self. Regarding this, Kaiyaṭa explained: "The sense is that there is no difference between cause and effect. The contextual meaning of the *Bhāṣya* is that since Brahman, which is the cause, is the self of all, the word *kaḥ*—which denotes *prajāpati* in the form of all things—will receive the designation of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*).

If it is argued that we understand from this commentary (*bhāṣya*) that the identity of all things with Brahman is accepted by him [the author], it is replied: "This *bhāṣya* and the subsequent *bhāṣya* constitute a pair; these two are merely the bold assertions (*prauḍhokti-mātra*) of two partial proponents (*ekadeśinau*)," as stated in the *Uddyota* and the *Śekhara*. Therefore, they are not accepted as the final established doctrine (*siddhānta*).

Furthermore, taking up the *Bhāṣya* passage, "And Prajāpati is everything," the *Uddyota* explains: "For this very reason it is said in the *Gītā*: 'You nourish all equally; therefore you are everything. Thus, the intention of the *Bhāṣya* is described as being that in Brahmā’s being everything, the cause is not his being the self of all (*sarvātmakatva*), but rather his pervading all (*sarvavyāpana*). Since it is thus established that the *Bhāṣya* itself accepts a distinction between Brahmā and Brahman, this *Bhāṣya* is not an authority for the view that Brahmā is the self of all.

The meaning of the passage beginning with "tadyadyadidam" (3.4.6) is as follows: that injunction for the worship of each individual deity—such as "Sacrifice to this one, sacrifice to that one"—is itself His emission (*visṛṣṭi*, i.e., His command), for it is indeed the injunction for worship being performed with reference to the Blessed Lord. They state the reason for this: "He is. All the gods are indeed dependent upon Him, being subject to His control; they are denoted by the word *brahma*.

For this is well-known from such scriptural passages as, "He who dwells on the earth" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.7.3). Regarding the presentation of the censure of other views held by the ignorant, Śaṅkara’s commentary states: "This creation is not a division of gods. One must seek the evidence for this statement being intended as a censure.

In this regard, Śaṅkarācārya has explained that by the twenty-one terms beginning with "earth" and ending with "semen"—namely: earth, water, fire, intermediate space, wind, heaven, sun, directions, moon, stars, ether, darkness, light, all beings, vital breath, speech, eye, ear, mind, skin, consciousness (the Self), and semen—the respective presiding deities are to be understood as they appear in the twenty-one sections [of the *Taittirīya Āraṇyaka*].

By the very scriptural passages such as, "He whom the earth does not know, who controls the earth from within," which reveal the knowledge of the Inner Ruler (Antaryāmin), it is clearly understood that the words "earth" and so forth refer to the deities presiding over them; otherwise, since the lack of knowledge on the part of the earth and other elements is self-evident due to their insentience, such a statement would be redundant. Furthermore, the grammatical coordination expressed in the phrase, "He alone is all the gods," is to be understood according to the principle of dependence, as in the expression "the king's kingdom."

If it be argued that the sacrifice performed by those who are subject to His command constitutes the worship of the Blessed Lord, it is replied: all teachers who maintain the authority of the Vedas declare with one voice—on the strength of the cited scriptural texts—that the Blessed Lord governs everyone; therefore, there is no one here to oppose this. The status of the Governor as the Supreme Overseer of all is self-evident, for without Him, the governance of all would be impossible. Furthermore, "worship" (yajana) is defined as an activity that generates delight.

Because all the gods regard [the sacrificer] as their own, even their worship is like a self-sacrifice; thus, it brings pleasure to the Self, and consequently, the Self becomes gratified with those who perform that sacrifice. This is established by universal experience in the world, where kings and others become pleased toward the one who honors their own people.

"And from that, he obtains his desires, which are indeed ordained by Me" (Gītā 7.22). Thus, the Teacher of the Gītā maintains that even when one worships another deity, He alone is the bestower of the fruit. Regarding the Sūtra, "The view of Brahman [is to be applied] because of its excellence" (Brahma-sūtra 4.1.5), an objection is raised: since the meditation on Āditya is enjoined in passages such as, "He who, knowing this thus, meditates upon Āditya as Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.19.4), that [meditation on Āditya] should not be performed because it does not yield the fruit; rather, only the meditation on Brahman should be performed because it yields the fruit. To this, [the author replies]: it is precisely the meditation on Āditya [that is intended].

In that regard as well, Brahman alone will grant the fruit, because He is the presiding lord of all, according to the statement: "The fruit [comes] from Him, for that is logical" (*phalamata upapatteḥ*). Thus, Śaṅkarācārya maintains that the Blessed Lord, being personally pleased by one's own meditation, bestows the fruit. Alternatively, the meaning of the scripture is that the term "the station of Indra and so forth" refers to the Supreme Self as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of those deities such as Indra who are denoted by those respective titles; thus it speaks of the inner controller, the Supreme Self.

By performing all actions directed toward the Inner Controller (antaryāmin), Indra and the other deities also become pleased through the worship of their own respective supervisor, just as in the world ministers and others become well-disposed by honoring the king’s messengers.
"Knowing Me as the enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities, the Great Lord of all worlds, and the Friend of all beings, one attains peace" (Gītā 5.29).
"I alone am the enjoyer and also the Lord of all sacrifices;
but they do not recognize Me in truth, and therefore they fall" (Gītā 9.24).
Thus the Blessed Lord declares that Hari is the enjoyer of all sacrifices. And this [enjoyment] should be understood as occurring through sacrifice performed by Himself and by His own devotees.

In this regard, the narrative from the Sabhā Parva of the Mahābhārata should be recalled: at Yudhiṣṭhira’s Rājasūya sacrifice, all the kings, great sages, and others were delighted by Kṛṣṇa—the Great Lord of all happiness—receiving the first honor; they praised Sahadeva as he performed the worship, and the gods, being pleased, showered down flowers.

One should not think that there is no difference from Nāgeśa’s view on the grounds that, by accepting the eating [of the oblation] in all sacrifices based on authorities such as "the enjoyer" (*bhoktāram*), one is simply adopting the position of the Supreme Lord himself. For Nāgeśa maintains that there is only a single conscious entity, the Lord, who assumes the forms of Indra and others due to limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), and that it is in those forms that he eats in the sacrifices; thus, in his view, the factual reality is that deities such as Indra do not exist separately.

In the view of those who maintain the doctrine of difference (*bhedavādins*), however, there is a great distinction based on the authority of such scriptural passages as: "Agni is indeed the lowest of the gods, Viṣṇu the highest; between them lie all other deities. According to this, the gods who consume the oblations (*havirbhujas*) exist in reality as many; among them, Viṣṇu is the supreme, and being the inner controller (*antaryāmī*) of all, he consumes the oblation. Thus, the actual state of affairs is that in all sacrifices, both the gods and their inner controller, Viṣṇu, partake of the food. Therefore—

"Those who sacrifice to the gods go to the gods; those devoted to the ancestors go to the ancestors; those who worship the spirits go to the spirits; and even those who sacrifice to me go to me. This statement regarding the attainment of various states by the worshippers of those respective objects is consistent [only if those states are real]. If the status of Indra and others were merely adventitious (*aupādhika*), then upon the cessation of that adventitious condition, Indra and the others would also cease to exist; consequently, since the object to be attained would not exist, the statement regarding its attainment would be inconsistent.

Furthermore, the statement "because even Jaimini accepts an additional deity" is contradictory to his own words. To explain: in the section defining the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*), having related the ancient legend from the *Mārkaṇḍeya-purāṇa* and other sources—where it is said that Jaimini, being doubtful regarding certain matters mentioned in the *Mahābhārata*, once approached Mārkaṇḍeya and asked, "O Blessed One, sever my doubt," to which [Mārkaṇḍeya] replied, "He is not within my reach; there dwell four birds on the Vindhya mountains, and I shall ask them"—[the author proceeds as follows].

His intention is this: even though he is a disciple of Vyāsa, this person has an impure mind and does not consider what was spoken by Vyāsa to be correct; he believes that the Lord is not the bestower of fruits, but rather that the individual agent alone is the bestower of fruits. Furthermore, he does not find it reasonable that animals, birds, and other such beings possess the qualification for knowledge as stated by Vyāsa. Therefore, by becoming a disciple of these [animals], once their qualification for knowledge is understood, he will develop faith everywhere in what is spoken by the crows. It is precisely through that [faith] that, by hearing the accounts of the battle between the gods and the asuras, his misconception regarding their lack of physical form will be removed.

By stating "he will abandon [the sacrifice]," Jaimini revealed his intended meaning that "the gods possess no physical form. Likewise, in that very same work, Mādhavācārya, in his commentary on the *Parāśara-smṛti*, mocked those who follow Jaimini’s view: "Out of fear of establishing the existence of a Lord (Īśvara), they have reached the conclusion that the Veda and the Śāstras lack authority; by what means of knowledge is Jaimini, the author of the Sūtras, himself established? Here, the phrase "establishing the Lord" (*īśasiddhi*) is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the establishment of the gods' corporeal forms and so forth as well.

The analysis of the compound is as follows: "devatā-vigrahau" means the deity and the body; that which has these two as its beginning (ādi) is the term "devatā-vigrahādi. By the word "ādi," there is the inclusion of their bestowing of fruits and so forth. By the word "devatā," there is the inclusion of deities such as Indra and others who are distinct from Śabda-brahman. The meaning of Mādhavācārya’s statement is that [the opponent objects] out of fear for the establishment of the Lord (Īśvara), the deity, His body, and their bestowing of fruits and so forth. By this, it is stated that, according to their view, the Veda and other scriptures that establish the Lord and the rest are not authoritative.

Furthermore, since there is an absence of a creator god, a deity, or a physical form in that context, the statement "because Jaimini also accepts this" (*jaiminināpyaṅkīkārāt*), made while asserting Jaimini’s intention, contradicts one's own earlier text.

If it is argued that there is no contradiction because the *Mañjūṣā* on the section concerning the *vṛtti* (mental function) intends to show that Jaimini—who received direct instruction—accepted the embodied form (*vigraha*) and other attributes of the deity, whereas the *Mañjūṣā* passage situated in the section on the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) describes the intention of Jaimini who did not receive such instruction, we reply: To fully comprehend the mental function of Jaimini occurring after he had received his instruction, the Blessed Lord alone, as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of all, is capable; none other than Him is so capable, and among those, people like us possess only limited knowledge.

Indeed, the established position of his doctrine must be understood through his own system alone, and not by means of another method. For this very reason, those who expound the tenets of various teachers cite the very words of those teachers as the authoritative source. Even Nāgeśa, in his exposition of the Jaiminīya-sūtras, formulated the essential points of that doctrine solely on their basis. By what authority, O long-lived one, can it be determined that the sūtra cited by him was composed later?

From the *Mañjūṣā* commentary on that very section concerning the meaning of the optative (*liṅ*), one can state that Jaimini composed the *Pūrvatantra* even before [the *Mahābhāṣya*] was taught. Otherwise, in the absence of any means to fully comprehend his intention—such as the lack of introductory remarks like "this is the underlying thought" (*ayam āśayaḥ*)—how could the description of his purport be consistent? For it is by knowing his purport through his own words that his intention must be described; enough of this excessive detail.
Śrīkhaṇḍadeva and others are knowers of the meaning of the *Pūrvatantra*.
But having reflected upon the treatises composed by Pārthasārathi Miśra and others...
They reached the conclusion that the deity has no physical form and so forth;
however, the sage Jaimini did not explicitly state the existence of a physical form and the like.
Therefore, let the wise, free from envy and other such flaws, understand that the determination made by Nāgeśa is not approved by him.

Regarding the investigation into the meaning of the suffix *mayaṭ*: in the analysis of the meaning of the rule *tatprakṛtavacane mayaṭ* (Pāṇini 5.4.21), with the intention of demonstrating that Brahman is devoid of attributes (*nirdharmaka*), [the author argues] that in such passages as "Brahman is *ānandamaya*" and "Brahman is *cinmaya*," this very same *mayaṭ* is used; therein, abundance, attributelessness, or conventional reality (*āvyavahārika*)—which is uncontradicted—is the meaning, because of the scriptural teaching of its infinity (*anantatva*). Likewise, in cases such as *prāṇamaya*, this very same *mayaṭ* is used, since there is no justification for it having the sense of a modification (*vikāra*).

In the *Mañjūṣā*, Nāgeśa demonstrated—either by way of the meaning or the literal wording—that the suffix *mayaṭ* heard in both the two *vallīs* and in the *śuddhi-mantra* signifies "abundance" (*prācurya*), by means of a passage that is either a paraphrase or a restatement of the *Vṛtti* text ending with the words "by the author of the *Vṛtti*" (*vṛttikṛtā*). He argued that there is no contradiction because, even in the *śuddhi-mantra*, purity consists in the destruction of the covering of the lower [levels].

In this regard, the investigation is as follows: having refuted the opinion of the Vṛttikāra with the statement beginning, "But this must be said," on the grounds that there is no direct logical possibility for one afflicted by modification [to be Brahman], [the author] argues that Śaṅkarācārya’s established conclusion in the *Ānandamayādhikaraṇa*—that the suffix *mayaṭ* in the word *ānandamaya* denotes a modification—is not correct. Furthermore, the statement in Śaṅkara’s Bhāṣya that "*mayaṭ* denotes a modification" is questionable, because according to Pāṇini’s sūtra *dvyacaśchandasi* (4.3.150), the suffix *mayaṭ* is prescribed to denote a modification only after a stem consisting of two syllables in the Vedic language (*chandas*).

The *Manoramā* text—which aims to describe the five-fold means, such as the rejection of sūtras not mentioned in the *Bhāṣya* and so forth, in order to refute the objection raised by certain grammarians that [the suffix *ghañ*] is not applicable because the word *ānanda* consists of three syllables—clearly states that another text with this same intent is incorrect.
Herein, it is argued that Brahman’s being devoid of attributes (*nirdharmakatva*) is untenable, as there is a lack of evidence for it. [Objection: But surely [it is said]:
"The one God is hidden in all beings, all-pervading, the inner self of all beings."
The overseer of karma, the abode of all beings, the witness, the conscious one, absolute and devoid of qualities.

If it is argued that the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad (6.11) is the authoritative source, and since it states "and [He is] devoid of qualities" (*nirguṇaḥ*), the term *nirguṇa* means "devoid of attributes" (*dharma-rahita*), we say no. This is because there is no evidence for abandoning the literal meaning of the word *guṇa*—namely, the qualities such as *sattva* and so on which are denoted by that term—and instead adopting the non-literal sense of "attributes in general. Nor can it be said that the word *guṇa* refers to "possessing functions" (*vṛttimat*) and thus denotes attributes in general; for there is no evidence for resorting to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) when the primary meaning is not contradicted.
As it is said: "[The Self] appears through the qualities of all the senses, yet is devoid of all the senses."
"In unattached yet supporting all, devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*) yet the experiencer of qualities" (Gītā 13.14).

In the commentary on this verse, Śrī Śaṅkarācārya explains the word *nirguṇa* as "devoid of the qualities such as *sattva*," and since that same meaning is appropriate here as well, if the word *nirguṇa* were to have the meaning stated by Nāgeśa, then the prescription of manifold qualities in passages such as "the one God... would be rendered purposeless.

Nor should it be argued that there is no redundancy because the connection occurs through the relationship of subject and predicate—where that which possesses qualities such as oneness is [the subject] "nirguṇa" (without qualities)—and thus, since the preceding terms are merely reiterative (anuvādaka), they are not useless; for if that were so, one could equally say that oneness and the other qualities are being enjoined by way of reiterating the state of being without qualities (nirguṇatva), and thus your desired conclusion would not be established.

Nor should it be argued that such an interpretation is improper according to the maxim that "the statement of the subject (*uddeśya*) comes first, and that of the predicate (*vidheya*) follows"; for, as seen in the rules *apṛkta ekāl pratyayaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.2.41) and *samarthaḥ padavidhiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.1), where the predicate is stated first, that restriction is not universal.

Furthermore, because of the hearing of the particle *ca* used as a conjunction, it is difficult to establish even a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) through the relationship of subject and predicate; for there can be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the properties of oneness and so forth and their absence. Therefore, the interpretation we have demonstrated is indeed superior. Nor does this contradict the following verse: "Obeisance to the peaceful, the terrible, and the deluded;
to the one whose activity is subtle; to the undifferentiated and the equal; and obeisance to the mass of knowledge. (Bhāgavata 8.3.12)

Thus, it should not be said that the Lord’s lack of attributes (*nirdharmakatva*) is established by the statement in the *Bhāgavata*, "to the one who is without distinction" (*nirviśeṣāya*), because its meaning is "to the one who is formless" (*nirākārāya*). Its purport is that, even though He possesses forms such as Vāsudeva and others which bestow tranquility and so forth, He is devoid of modifications produced by qualities (*guṇa*), unlike the individual soul (*jīva*). This qualifying term is pregnant with a reason; for this very reason, it is stated "for the sake of equality" (*sāmyāya*). The purport is that He is equal everywhere. Furthermore, the very statement "to the peaceful one" (*śāntāya*) is the authority for the aforementioned meaning of "to the one without distinction."

For how could the statement that peace (śama) consists in being devoid of all attributes (nirdharmakatva) be consistent? Scriptural and traditional texts (śruti-smṛti) of this kind are to be explained in exactly this way. In the Śrīdharīya commentary, however, having read "to the one whose nature is the qualities" (guṇadharmiṇe), it is explained as "one who conforms to the attributes such as sattva and so forth."

However, the claim that "there is a state of being non-contradictory only in a conventional sense" is not tenable, because such a meaning is not heard in the sacred scripture (*śruti*). If you assert that reality exists even without the word [denoting it], then what discerning person would have faith in a meaning that is non-verbal? Furthermore, since qualities such as truthfulness are taught by that very scripture, they too would consequently fall into the category of the merely conventional; thus, one could even say that Brahman lacks truthfulness.

The conception that among things understood from a single statement, one is ultimately real (*pāramārthika*) while the other is conventionally real (*vyāvahārika*), cannot be established without a stronger means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Since the absence of attributes (*nirdharmakatva*) in abundance would mean that, in the context of the conventional, distinctions such as attributes do not exist in reality within Brahman, it would follow that even bliss (*ānanda*) does not exist. Therefore, the recourse to Nāgeśa’s view is futile.

Indeed, when wishing to indicate an excellence of quality (*guṇātiśaya*) in the subject at hand, wise authors resort to the suffix *mayaṭ* in its abundant usage. Now, this is the inherent nature of *mayaṭ*: that in a case where it has a different substratum (*svavyadhikaraṇa*), a smallness of light (*prakāśālpatva*) is perceived in something other than itself. In some instances, however, it conveys a smallness of its own kind within its own substratum (*svādhikaraṇa*), as in "the sun consists of light" (*prakāśamayaḥ savitā*); here, a smallness of light is perceived in something other than the sun.

In some instances, however, the suffix *mayaṭ* conveys the smallness of that which is of a different class from itself within its own substratum; for example, in the case of *annamaya*, it is understood that "food is abundant, while that other than it is small. The application of these suffixes is determined according to the authority of the specific textual usage. Regarding the present case of *ānandamaya*, since there is no evidence for the existence of suffering—which is of a different class from bliss—within Brahman, the suffix *mayaṭ* must be explained as conveying the smallness of bliss in relation to a conscious being other than Brahman. Thus, authoritative teachers maintain that this does not establish the qualitylessness (*nirdharmakatva*) of Brahman.

Regarding the inquiry as to whether the term "Vṛttikṛt" (the author of the commentary) here refers to the well-known Bodhāyana or some other person, some say: "Bodhāyana cannot be intended here, because it is stated here that Brahman is devoid of attributes (nirdharmaka) and characterized by abundance (prācurya)."

However, we ascertain from the words of the venerable Śrī Rāmānuja Muni—namely, "The ancient teachers abridged the extensive commentary on the Brahma-sūtras composed by the venerable Bodhāyana; following that, we shall explain the words of the sūtras"—that Bodhāyana did not accept either the qualitylessness (*nirdharmakatva*) of Brahman or the non-ultimate reality of its indestructibility as taught in such scriptural passages as "Truth" (*satyam*). Thus we conclude.

Although one might argue that the sūtra "Because [cognition] exists when there is a body for the self" (Brahmasūtra 3.3.55)—which Śaṅkara’s Bhāṣya states was set aside by the venerable Upavarṣa in the first Tantra with the remark, "Since this very point arises in the discussion of the existence of the self, we shall explain it in the Śārīraka"—refers here to the venerable Vṛttikāra named Upavarṣa, who was the brother of [Śabarasvāmin], nevertheless, there is no evidence for his assertion that Brahman is devoid of attributes (nirdharmaka).

If it be asked who might be the author of the commentary (*vṛtti*) on this [work], one should understand that it was either some scholar similar to him, or indeed this very person (Nāgeśa). This is made clear by the explanation of the term *kalā* in the section on the secondary suffixes denoting deities (*devatātaddhita*), which states: "by the followers of the Guru in the *Vyāsasūtravṛtti*. From this, we infer that Nāgeśa also composed a commentary on the *Brahmasūtra*.

The *Śāṅkara-bhāṣya*, however, citing the rule "the suffix *mayaṭ* is used in the sense of a modification" (*vikāre mayaṭ*), proceeds with the intention that the restriction "in Vedic [usage] for a word consisting of two syllables" (*dvyacaś chandasi*) is merely general. The *Manoramā*, on the other hand, has proceeded according to its own whims and does not delight the minds of the learned; by this, the *Bodhinī* and other works following the *Manoramā* are also explained.

Regarding this *kalā*, the meaning of the sūtra is that because of the abundance of words ending in *mayaṭ* [denoting "abundance"] in the passage beginning with "of the speaker" (*vaktuḥ*), this word is also employed as an *atyantasvārthika* (purely self-referential) form ending in *maḍ*, in order to ensure the application of a single grammatical category. This has been stated by the venerable teacher [Madhusūdana Sarasvatī] in his *Induśekhara* on the *Vyāsasūtra*, based on the fact that the rule *tatprakṛtavacane* allows for the formation of purely self-referential forms through the separation (*yogavibhāga*) of the word *tat*.

In this regard, the following must be stated: regarding the section beginning with the "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*), the question arises whether the one "consisting of bliss" is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) or the individual soul (*jīva*). Having established the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) in the first Sūtra that it is the Supreme Self due to the repeated use of the word *brahman*, an objection is raised that because the word *ānandamaya* ends in the suffix *-maya* in the sense of a modification (*vikāra*), it cannot denote the Supreme Self. In response to this, the Author of the Sūtras states in Sūtra 1.1.13, "Because of the word denoting a modification," that the Supreme Self alone is what is denoted by that word, as it ends in the suffix *-maya* in the sense of abundance (*prācurya*). All the teachers [agree] on this point.

In this very way they describe the meaning of the sūtra. Furthermore, the intention of the authors of the sūtras and other authorities in establishing the application of the *maḍat* suffix as being purely *svārthika* (denotative of its own meaning) is not obtainable through the literal constraints of the words [of the sūtra]. Moreover, there is the burden of abandoning the recurrence of the already established *sādhya* portion and instead supplying a different *sādhya* portion. Furthermore, in the sūtra *tatprakṛta*, a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule) for the word *tat* is not seen in the Bhāṣya.

If Nāgeśa were to claim that the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) not seen in the *Bhāṣya* lacks authoritative status, how could his demonstration of the formation of the suffix *mayaṭ* as being purely *svārthika* (denoting its own meaning) based on such a division, as well as his description of the meaning of this particular *vraja-sūtra* rooted therein, be justified?

Furthermore, if one assumes that the suffix *mayaṭ* is used here in its primary sense (*svārthe*), it would violate the natural force of the word "prācuryāt" (due to abundance). For by that [suffix], an excellence of bliss in Brahman is understood; and this excellence has been clearly established in the *Ānandavallī*, the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*, and elsewhere, as has been skillfully demonstrated in the commentaries and other works by the venerable Ācāryas such as Śaṅkara. Since one could have simply said "svārthāt" for the sake of brevity, the use of "prācuryāt" would be redundant—enough of this. In the two *vallīs*, the *mayaṭ* in the *śuddhi-mantra* denotes abundance.
The supreme Brahman is without distinction; it is abundance and the emptiness of all dharmas.
Thus, scholars know that the statement of Nāgeśa is devoid of authoritative evidence;
being unapproved by the author of the Bhāṣya, it should not be respected by wise people.
Regarding the investigation of ignorance (*avidyā*):

In the first chapter of his *Mañjūṣā*, Nāgeśa, while elucidating the non-duality of Brahman through the passage beginning with "The phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is likewise" and ending with "Enough of this digression," states that there is a certain entity called *māyā* which acts as an auxiliary cause for Brahman in the creation of the phenomenal world, and that it consists of the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*). For this very reason, the world is illusory (*māyika*).

Ignorance (*avidyā*), however, is produced by that [Brahman] and is not beginningless; this is the view of the venerable Śaṅkarācāryas as well. For nothing other than Brahman can possibly be unborn, since in the Sūtra "But on account of the general [rule]" (Brahma-sūtra 3.2.32), which denies the beginninglessness of any entity in general other than Brahman—based on the scriptural passage "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone"—it is understood that the beginninglessness of ignorance is not accepted.

Furthermore, since no question or answer regarding ignorance (*avidyā*) as being "beginningless" (*anādi*) is found in the *Bhāṣya*, it is not accepted by the *Bhāṣya*. Moreover, having raised the following objections—that if beginningless ignorance were the cause, one would be accepting an unauthoritative plurality, that the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) of everything having Brahman as its sole cause would be violated, and that non-duality (*advaita*) would be lost—it is argued that the state of ignorance as a beginningless entity and the world's having that as its cause are untenable.

Regarding this: [the statement] "Because no question or answer concerning this subject is found, that [beginninglessness] is not accepted by the Bhāṣya" refers to the words of the venerable authors of the *Bhāmatī*, who state, "This [superimposition], imagined through an indeterminable and beginningless ignorance (*avidyā*), is established as being beginningless. [Furthermore,] there are the words of the authors of the *Pañcapādikā-vivaraṇa* stating that in the inference establishing ignorance, a qualification such as "prior to its own prior absence" must be supplied; and the words of the author of the *Vārttika* stating, "The beginninglessness of superimposition consists in its lack of a prior limit (*prākkoṭi*)," provided that it is of the nature of a beginningless entity.

The statement of Citsukhācārya, "The nature of ignorance is that which is to be removed by knowledge"; the statement of the most venerable followers of the venerable Śaṅkara’s school, "The individual soul (jīva), the Lord (īśa), the pure consciousness (viśuddhā cit), the distinction between the individual soul and the Lord, ignorance (avidyā), and its connection with consciousness"; the statement of those belonging to that same group, "This entire world is a manifestation of beginningless ignorance (anādyavidyā)"; their exertion in establishing the existence of beginningless ignorance; and [their claims] such as "caused by the ontological category of ignorance, which is the root cause" and "caused by false cognition (mithyājñāna)."

It is indicated that the commentaries of Ānandagiri and others on the *Adhyāsa-bhāṣya* are rooted in a failure to understand the true meaning of Śrī Śaṅkara’s commentary. Furthermore, the statement in the *Adhyāsa-bhāṣya*—"Thus, this beginningless and endless natural superimposition (*adhyāsa*)"—is contradicted by the *Sūtra-bhāṣya* on *Samanvaya* Sūtra 1.1.4, which states, "For there is no birth other than Brahman. This is because [Śaṅkara] thereby negates the beginninglessness of anything other than Brahman. [He defines it as: "Superimposition (*adhyāsa*) is the cognition of 'that' in what is 'not-that'; the learned..."

Since the commentary (*bhāṣya*) states, "They consider it to be ignorance," it expresses that there is no difference in meaning between ignorance (*avidyā*) and superimposition (*adhyāsa*); therefore, the purport of this commentary is that ignorance is beginningless (*anādi*).

Regarding this, some say: because of the statement "by way of what follows from what was already mentioned" (*prasaktānuprasaktyā*), because no rule of Pāṇini is cited, and because a statement from the *Paramārthasāra* is quoted, it is understood that this exposition is not in accordance with the system of Pāṇini, but rather in accordance with the opinion of the author of the *Paramārthasāra*. Furthermore, in that [work], it is not stated that there is no beginningless entity other than Brahman.

However, the Lord—who is beyond the beginningless primordial nature (*prakṛti*), being supreme, distinct, and designated by such names as Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, Vāsudeva, Upendra, Hari, and so forth—is the Supreme Brahman; through His own power (*svaśakti*), which is His very nature and is denoted by terms such as *prakṛti*, *māyā*, and *vibhūti*, He creates the manifold and diverse phenomenal world (*prapañca*).

And that power (*śakti*) is beginningless, dependent on Viṣṇu, insentient, and for that very reason not independent; it is the auxiliary cause of Viṣṇu in the creation of the world and so forth. Thus, it has been established that knowledge of Nārāyaṇa is the means to liberation. Furthermore, by the verse beginning "Of the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) which is beyond [the senses]" and the subsequent verse "Inhering as its own nature" (*svabhāvabhūtā*), the beginninglessness of *māyā* is stated; for in Rāghavānandamuni’s commentary on the term "independence" (*svātantryam*), beginninglessness is mentioned, and the intent of the root text itself lies therein.
The purport of the verse is that the eternality of *prakṛti* (primordial nature) is also established by the force of the meaning [of the text].

Now, if it is objected that a real entity called "ignorance" (*avidyā*), which is beginningless and of the nature of a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*), lacks scriptural authority, we say no; for its existence is established by such authoritative means as, "Asleep through beginningless *māyā*," and so forth. Nor should it be argued that if it were beginningless, the established doctrine that everything has Brahman as its sole cause would be undermined; for the status of having Brahman as its cause is logically consistent even with something whose existence is dependent on another. Furthermore, there is no loss of non-duality (*advaita*), because unlike *prāgabhāva* (prior non-existence), this ignorance is seen to perish and thus lacks infinity; the fault [of losing non-duality] applies only to the existence of a substance that is both beginningless and endless.

Alternatively, this fault would apply if there were another entity possessing the same level of reality (*samānasattāka*). However, it is understood from the *Siddhāntaleśasaṃgrahavyākhyāna* and other sources that since ignorance (*avidyā*), though beginningless, does not possess a reality equal to that of Brahman, there is no room for this objection. Māyā, which consists of beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and is composed of the three qualities (*triguṇā*), is what is taught by the scriptural text, "the one unborn" (*ajāmekām*). Even you, who maintain that the world has Brahman as its sole material cause, must speak in exactly this way.

Otherwise, if Māyā were a cooperative cause (sahakārin), there would be a violation of the principle that Brahman alone is the sole cause. If it were produced, it would contradict the scriptural text stating "She is unborn" (ajā), since that text declares her to be unproduced. Furthermore, once her beginninglessness is established by scripture, the fault of the loss of non-duality (advaitahāni) would fall upon your own position as well.

Nor should it be argued that there is no fault because the scriptural statement means "unborn in this particular kalpa," for since this scripture exists in every kalpa, it is possible to interpret its meaning there as well as "unborn in this kalpa," which would establish its very beginninglessness. Furthermore, if Māyā were not the auxiliary cause, the statement that the world is illusory (māyika) would be inconsistent.

Regarding the commentary (*bhāṣya*) which states, "Indeed, there can be no unborn [entity] apart from Brahman," those who know its tradition hold that there is no fault, for the meaning is that there is no independent unborn entity apart from Him. For this very reason, in the *Śāṅkara Gītā-bhāṣya*, on the occasion of explaining the verse, "Know both Prakṛti and Puruṣa to be indeed beginningless" (Gītā 13.19), it is stated: "The lordship of the Lord would be untenable."

Although primordial nature (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa) are beginningless, they possess an existence dependent upon the Lord (īśvara), because the Lord is the master of all; thus, His status as the Lord is established—this is the sense [of the verse]. This has been clarified in the *Gūḍhārthadīpikā* and in Śrīdhara’s commentary (*Śrīdharīya*) on the occasion of describing the meaning of that verse.

Furthermore, regarding the establishment of non-duality (*advaitasiddhi*) within the doctrine of creation upon perception (*dṛṣṭisṛṣṭivāda*), there arises a contradiction with the statement of the ancients, "The individual soul (*jīva*), the Lord (*īśa*), and pure consciousness (*viśuddhā cit*)," since all things would be created. Anticipating the objection that this contradicts the teaching that the six categories beginning with the *jīva* are beginningless—on the grounds that they are unproduced—it is resolved by stating that the acceptance of "creation upon perception" applies only to creations other than those that are beginningless. This is made clear in that very same doctrine [the *Advaitasiddhi*] with the words, "Because the distinction between the *jīva* and Brahman is beginningless. Moreover, in that same work, during the investigation into whether ignorance (*avidyā*) resides in pure consciousness alone, it is likewise stated regarding the *jīva*.

It has been stated that the relationship between the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) and the reflection (*bimba*) is beginningless, because its beginninglessness is logically established; thus, the beginninglessness of the relationship distinct from Brahman, as well as that of the individual soul (*jīva*), has been declared. For this very reason, the beginninglessness of the inner self (*pratyagātman*) was stated by the teacher Pañcapāda in his *Pañcapādikā* on the *Adhyāsa-bhāṣya*: "And that inner self is established as beginningless; therefore, the beginninglessness of its naturalness [in relation to the adjunct] is established by implication. Furthermore:
"To Viṣṇu, the Lord of Prajāpati, the infinite and unconquered, the cause of both Pradhāna and Puruṣa, which are themselves effects and yet unborn."
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, the unmanifest consisting of the three qualities has arisen;
O Brahmin, that unmanifest dissolves into the Puruṣa who is devoid of qualities.
There is no beginning of the self; the succession of fields is beginningless.
So too are primordial nature (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa), as well as the field and the knower of the field (kṣetrajña).
Having dissolved the gross into the instrument, the instrument into its cause, that cause into what is devoid of both cause and instrument—
in this manner, having dissolved [all things], the practitioners of yoga enter that wherein [all] resides.
We bow to you, O Hari, who are the dense mass of the awakening of the wise.
Thus, the arguments presented in the *Mañjūṣā* regarding the produced nature (*janyatva*) of ignorance (*avidyā*) do not bear upon that point.

To explain: in the first [verse], by the statement "of the two unborn" (*ajayoḥ*), the beginninglessness of both Pradhāna and Puruṣa is stated. As for the phrase "of those which have become effects" (*kāryabhūtayoḥ*), its meaning is "of those which have manifested"; for it can be said that these two also manifest, according to the direction stated by Nāgeśa that "Māyā emerges from Īśvara. In the second [verse], the statement "the unmanifest was produced" (*avyaktam utpannam*) likewise means only that it "manifested. In the third and fourth [verses], the term *kṣetra* refers to the body, which is an effect of Prakṛti.

Just as Nāgeśa stated that the dissolution of *māyā* into the Lord (*īśvara*) is merely a specific type of relation, so too other authorities maintain that the dissolution of the causal material nature (*prakṛti*) into Hari is likewise a specific type of relational connection. Therefore, consider how these [authorities] can serve as proofs for the stated position. Furthermore, even if one accepts that the Lord creates by means of the assistance of beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā*), the fact that the phenomenal world has a single cause is established simply by the Lord's independence from any other separate entity.

Furthermore, from Nāgeśa’s statement in this very section—that "only the interpretation I have provided is appropriate for the scriptural passages of the aforementioned type"—it appears that the application of scripture by those who maintain its beginninglessness is of a different nature.

Furthermore, in the *Śāṅkara-bhāṣya* on the *Brahma-sūtra* (2.1.12), the section concerning partiality and cruelty (*vaiṣamyanairghuṇya*), it is established that there exists a beginningless entity other than Brahman which serves as the cause of creation. Moreover, in the *Kalpataru* commentary on the *Devatādhikaraṇa*, it is stated: "In this context, Vācaspati holds that ignorance (*avidyā*) is of the nature of a beginningless positive entity (*anādibhāvātmā*), distinct from error or mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), as illustrated by the example of the frog. Thus, it is asserted that for Vācaspati, ignorance is an eternal, positive reality.

In this context, the meaning of "according to them" (tatreha) is "in the opinion of the followers of Śrī Śaṅkara"; that there is no reason for restricting [the application] to the section on deities (*devatādhikaraṇa*) was established in the preceding section.

If it is argued that, since "being produced" (*janyatva*) is accepted as "having an existence dependent on another," then because space (*viyat*) and so forth are also admitted to have such a nature, their being produced is easily stated; thus, the effort to prove the production of space and so forth is redundant, leading to the undesirable consequence that the *Viyyadhikaraṇa* (the section concerning space) would not arise— To this we reply: Since the production of space is heard in such passages as "From the Self, space [was born]," the doctrine of its non-production is contrary to the Śruti. Therefore, it is necessary to establish its production in order to demonstrate this. This is because the production of ignorance (*avidyā*) is not heard of anywhere [in the Śruti].

By the hearing of the word "beginningless" (*anādi*) in the phrase "by beginningless *māyā*," and by the hearing of Brahman’s status as the controller of all, this [view] is thus accepted. More on this should be seen in the Advaita treatises. Furthermore, Nāgeśa’s statement—that "there exists an eternal, beginningless entity consisting of the auspicious and inauspicious karma of living beings which is the cause of rebirth"—is contrary to the Vyāsa-sūtra: "If it is argued that there is no karma because of the non-differentiation [of the world], we say no, because of its beginninglessness" (Brahma-sūtra 2.1.36). This is because that sūtra establishes that "there exists some kind of beginningless entity."

The objection raised in the *Mañjūṣā*—that the statement regarding the beginningless nature of ignorance (*avidyā*) contradicts the Sūtra, "But as long as there is no modification, there is differentiation, as in the world" (Brahma-sūtra 2.3.8), which indicates that being an effect is pervaded by difference and thereby implies that like space (*ākāśa*), ignorance likewise lacks such [beginninglessness] (i.e., is not an effect)—is also not correct. This is because the inquiry in that Sūtra pertains specifically to the origination of the gross elements such as space; it does not concern whether or not Brahman possesses any difference defined by something else, given that Brahman is devoid of attributes (*nirdharmaka*). Thus, there is no contradiction.

Regarding the claim that "it [Brahman] is produced," that is to be questioned; for according to the view of one who asserts that Brahman is devoid of attributes (*nirdharmaka*), even the attribute of being a counter-correlative (*pratiyogitva*) cannot exist in Brahman, since the difference of pure Brahman from ignorance (*avidyā*) exists. This contradicts his own statement that "the status of being an effect follows. Consequently, it could easily be said that Brahman also possesses difference as determined by something else, which would result in the undesirable consequence (*āpāta*) that Brahman itself is an effect.

Furthermore, it appears that he intends here to refute the beginninglessness of ignorance (*avidyā*), either because he has not consulted the works such as the *Bhāmatī*, *Kalpataru*, and *Parimala* on the sūtra "But [the world] extends as far as there is modification" (*yāvadvikāraṃ tu*), or because he wishes to demonstrate that what was stated therein is inconsistent.

For in that Sūtra, the *Bhāmatī* states the reason: "because [the Self] is distinct while being non-different from Brahman"; and in the *Kalpataru*, it is stated that by the phrase "in ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth," there is an inclusion of other entities such as the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), which were mentioned in the statement "six [categories] are beginningless for us. By means of these three works, it is established that the beginninglessness of ignorance and the rest is the view approved by the author of the *Bhāṣya*.

For Miśra and others would never propound a meaning that is not intended by the author of the Bhāṣya; moreover, the beginninglessness of ignorance (avidyā) and the rest has been stated here and there in the Bhāṣya itself. Therefore, Nāgeśa’s statement that "it is not approved by the Bhāṣya" is indeed to be questioned.

By this, both Ānandagiri’s commentary on the *Adhyāsa-bhāṣya*—which states, "it is a superimposition based on a previously accumulated [impression]" (*saṃbhṛṣṭādhyāsa*)—and the commentary of others on the same *Adhyāsa-bhāṣya*—which states, "the meaning is that it is caused by the positive entity in the form of ignorance (*avidyā*), which is the root cause" (*mūlakāraṇāvidyārūpabhāvapadārthanimittaka*)—are restated; and the refutation of those views beginning with "that is not so" (*tanna*) and so forth should also be considered [as already addressed], because the beginninglessness of ignorance (*avidyānāditva*) has been stated to be the consensus of the *Bhāṣya*.

It is quite evident to those with the vision of the *Mañjūṣā* that this [author] interprets the syllables of the sūtras—whose meanings have already been elucidated by great teachers—in a different way. An example of this is found in the sūtra: "There would be an abandonment of the proposition because there is no distinction from words" (*Brahma-sūtra* 2.3.7). Instead of making a *praśleṣa* (elision/junction) of the letter 'a', he provides an explanation as if it were "there would be an abandonment of the proposition" (*pratijñā-bhaṅgaḥ*). Then, by interpreting the fragment of the sūtra as being intent on establishing an abandonment of the proposition, he joins it with a *praśleṣa* of the letter 'a' to read it as "non-abandonment" (*ahāniḥ*), meaning "the non-obstruction of the proposition."

Nāgeśa indicates that his own commentary on the Sūtras is superior to the commentary composed by Śrī Śaṅkarācārya; although there is no difference in the result whether the letter *a* is elided or not, it should be understood that his purpose is merely to demonstrate his scholarly pride in being the one capable of correctly construing the very syllables of the Sūtras. In this manner, he has provided a unique interpretation of many Sūtras, directing them toward the specific meanings he himself intends.

And this [point] is to be understood from the work titled *Etatkṛtavyāsasūtrendu* (The Moon of Vyāsa’s Aphorisms composed by him). This exposition of non-dual Brahman (*brahmādvaita*) undertaken in the *Mañjūṣā* is intended solely to demonstrate that, regarding the determination of the true nature of the category of ignorance (*avidyā*), the Advaitins have indeed committed an error; such is the meaning for those who are experts in the nuances of the words. Nāgeśa Paṇḍita states that according to Śaṅkara, ignorance consists of the form of delusion and its latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), and not as an beginningless positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*).
The followers of the venerable Śaṅkara’s doctrine maintain that this [view] is not tenable, because it contradicts the many texts of the teachers of the Advaita school.
Regarding the investigation into the doctrine of indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatva*):

You have refuted the position of the non-dualist teachers who follow the venerable Śaṅkarācārya—who accept the existence of indeterminable objects such as the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell—by first establishing in the *Mañjūṣā* that the twofold phenomenal world is illusory (*māyika*), and then stating, "By the word 'only' (*mātra*) in the phrase 'mere illusion' (*māyāmātra'), he [the author of the Brahma-sūtras] also rejects the doctrine of the indeterminable production [of effects]," and so forth. To this, we offer the following rebuttal.

Since the refutation depends upon extracting the two opposing views, that [view] is first summarized: therein, in the *Bhāmatī*—a commentary on the *Adhyāsa-bhāṣya*—there is the passage from the work of Miśra stating, "The water of a mirage and the like is neither real, nor unreal, nor even non-existent-non-unreal (but rather) indefinable (*anirvacanīya*)," as well as similar passages from other Advaita teachers; and in the *Advaitasiddhi*, within the section defining the characteristic of indefinability in the doctrine of ignorance (*ajñānavāda*), there is the statement: "In being distinct from the unreal (*asadvilakṣaṇatve*)..."

Upon a careful consideration of the text, "And when there is the state of being different from the real (sat), there is the state of being different from both the real and the unreal (sadasat)," the following is the established position in the Advaita school: objects are of three kinds—the real (sat), the unreal (asat), and the indeterminable (anirvacanīya). Among these, the real is Brahman; the unreal is things such as a rabbit's horn; and the indeterminable consists of nacre-silver and the world. Of these, the first two do not originate, whereas the third possesses origination; thus, the state of being different from both the real and the unreal constitutes indeterminability. This is the actual status of things according to the Advaitins.

In the view of Nāgeśa, however, reality is of only two kinds: existent (*sat*) and non-existent (*asat*). Among these, Brahman is the existent, while everything other than Brahman is the non-existent. This [non-existent] includes the waking world-appearance (*jāgrat-prapañca*), dream-objects, shell-silver (*śukti-rajata*), and rabbit-horns (*śaśa-viṣāṇa*). Furthermore, "indefinability" (*anirvacanīyatva*) is that nature which cannot be defined as either existent or non-existent. However, the definition of indefinability favored by the venerable Advaita teachers such as Śaṅkara is not tenable, nor is it approved by Vyāsa, the author of the Sūtras;
for the established position is that [the world is] "mere illusion" (*māyā-mātra*), as indicated by the use of the word "mere" (*mātra*).

In this regard, the following objection—that the definition of "indefinability" (anirvacanīyatva) favored by the Advaitins, namely "being different from both the existent and the non-existent," is untenable because if it is different from the existent it must be non-existent, and if it is different from the non-existent it must be existent, resulting in the failure to establish any entity that is not encompassed by either existence or non-existence—is incorrect; for this same defect applies to Nāgeśa’s position as well, according to the maxim: "The fault which is equal for both parties, or the remedy which is likewise equal."

To explain: Nāgeśa, who asserts that the world is non-existent (*asat*), must be asked: Do you consider the world to be non-existent like the horn of a hare (*śaśaviṣāṇa*) and so forth, or do you consider it to be something other than Brahman, which is the denotation of the term "existent" (*sat*)? It cannot be the first, because the world possesses causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) and thus lacks equality with the horn of a hare. Nor can it be the second, because the difference between Brahman and the world is accepted by everyone, and there is no undesirable consequence for anyone [in this view].

And thus, O Brahma, you have effectively admitted the distinction between the world and a rabbit’s horn; consequently, since there is an absence of the distinctness from both [existence and non-existence] that is agreed upon by the Advaitins following the venerable Śaṅkara, the fault exposed against them in their own system falls equally upon your view as well. Furthermore, if the world were non-existent, your statement that "it is impossible to define it as non-existent" would be self-contradictory, because that very statement constitutes its definition.

Furthermore, since it is impossible to define [the world] as non-existent, the claim that "existence precedes" does not establish the non-existence of the world. As for the argument that the world’s nature as mere illusion (*māyāmātra*) is established by the sūtras *tadananyatvam* and *māyāmātram*, that too is incorrect. We shall demonstrate in the subsequent sections that neither of those two sūtras yields such a conclusion, nor does the word *mātra* carry the sense of "mere" (*kevala*).

To demonstrate that even the venerable Śrī Śaṅkarācāryas agree with one's own conception, the commentary beginning with "imagined by ignorance" (*avidyāyāḥ kalpitā*) should be explained in this very way. The meaning of the commentary beginning with "inseparable from the Lord, yet indefinable" (*īśvarasyātmabhūte anirvacanīye*) is also precisely this.

By stating, "Other passages of this kind in the Bhāṣya are also to be explained in exactly this manner," and so forth—thereby describing the meaning of certain Bhāṣya statements as being directed toward their own desired conclusions and asserting that "it is exactly thus" in those cases—they criticize the commentaries on that Bhāṣya by the former teachers and their like. The Advaitins who have taken refuge at the feet of the [true] Teacher would not tolerate even that, because the meaning stated by them is not approved by the original Teacher, the author of the Bhāṣya, and because it lacks logical consistency.

In this regard, an investigation into the correctness or incorrectness of Nāgeśa’s commentary and that of the ancient commentators has not been undertaken for fear of making the work too voluminous. Furthermore, it is clear from the texts of the Advaitins that an indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*) entity must be accepted because otherwise the phenomena of appearance (*khyāti*) and sublation (*bādha*) would be inexplicable. Even Rāghavānanda Muni, the commentator on the *Paramārthasāra*, asserts that the world is indeed other than both existent and non-existent.

This, however, must be understood: since Śrī Vyāsa, Pāṇini, and Patañjali did not state that the world is non-existent (*asat*) and so forth, this non-existence and the like were not intended by Vyāsa and the others; for they stated, "They [regard] it as unreal and without foundation" (Gītā). The conventional usage of the world’s being "indescribable" (*anirvācya*), however, is due to its possessing non-natural attributes that are distinct from the objects of speech and mind, which serve as the causes for rejection or acceptance.
Thus, the world’s existence is like that of Brahman, not its non-existence like that of a hare’s horn.
Therefore, its being something other than both [existence and non-existence] is logical and does not contradict the scriptures.
Therefore, the refutation of what was thus stated by the teachers of the Advaita school,
as composed by Paṇḍita Nāgeśa, does not please the hearts of the learned.

Regarding the refutation of the claim that the world is illusory (*māyika*) based on the agreement with the *Tadananyatva* Sūtra: As for what was stated in the *Mañjūṣā*, namely, "Although the illusory nature (*māyāmātratva*) of the waking world is also declared by the Sūtra, 'Its non-difference [from Brahman] is established on account of the words concerning its being a mere beginning' (Brahma-sūtra 2.1.14)," they reply here: The illusory nature of the world is not declared by that Sūtra, because there is no word with such a meaning in it; furthermore, the statement of "non-difference" can be said to indicate only identity, as in the expression "the face is the moon."

Furthermore, since even in the statements of the proposition and the illustration beginning with "By which the unheard becomes heard" and "A mere modification of speech" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.4–5), no word signifying an illusory object is heard, the reality of the world is not established by those two either. Nor should it be argued that the very statement of non-difference (*ananyatva*)—which indicates the absence of substantiality in the phenomenal world (*prapañca*)—also implies its illusoriness; for [the opponent] asserts that such experience and so forth are perceived in the world.

Furthermore, since the phenomenal world consisting of jars, cloths, and so forth is insentient, while Brahman is sentient, it is impossible for the sentient and the insentient to be non-different; therefore, it must be said that the statement [of non-difference] intends to convey the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) of the effect with its cause. This invariable concomitance is established by the authority of scripture and tradition, such as: "Having created that, He entered into it" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6) and "Pervading this entire universe, I stand with one part as the world" (Bhagavad Gītā 10.42).
Moreover, it is established by the witness of all that all modifications, such as jars and bowls, do not originate from a single lump of clay.

The meaning of the scripture, however, is this: by the knowledge of one—the Lord—even an object that is unperceived or unknown becomes perceived—that is, it becomes known through similarity. Here, the property that causes the similarity is *sattva* (being). The "modification" (*vikāra*)—the entire collection of effects such as jars, bowls, and so forth—is a "mere verbal handle" (*vācārambhaṇa*), meaning it is designated by various distinct words through the organ of speech. Furthermore, all things such as jars have the name "clay" (*mṛttikā*) as well; because they are modifications of clay, they are real (*satya*) or substantial.

The point is this: although jars, bowls, and the like are designated by different words due to their differences in form, they are nonetheless recognized as being denoted by words expressing their constituent material, because that material quality and its portion persist even in the effect. Since the contact with the constituent material exists in the effect as well, the great poet Śrī Harṣa also says:
"We worship the stalks of the golden lotuses of the celestial river [Gaṅgā], whose hands are like the tips of lotus stalks;
for the excellence of the body conforms to the food, since the effect inherits the qualities from its cause."

(Naiṣadha 3.17). The meaning of the verse is clear. Alternatively, "unheard" (*aśruta*) means devoid of the fruit of hearing; by that which is heard—the Supreme Self—even what was previously unheard becomes "heard," that is, productive of its fruit. Hearing and so forth do not lead to fruit from the mere ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*) alone, but they become fruitful through the hearing and so forth of the Supreme Self. Since the knowledge of the world is the cause for knowing the Lordship of the world once Brahman is known, the point is that the knowledge of the world becomes fruitful through the knowledge of the Lord.

When an object such as a jar, which is an effect of clay, is known to be clay, one gains the certainty that curd or other substances placed therein will not incur defects such as sourness; consequently, the inclination to place curd or similar items in it arises.

Furthermore, by this proposition and example, it is understood only that there exists some object to be known other than Īśvara, but not that nothing else exists. If the intention were the non-existence of any other knowable object, then the integrity of the words "unperceived" (*avijñātam*) and so forth would be violated; for your desired conclusion—that "by merely saying 'not heard,' etc., [it follows] that speech alone is undertaken, that there is mere reliance on speech, and that no reality whatsoever exists"—is not obtained through the standard rules of interpretation (*akṣara-maryādā*).

Furthermore, the non-difference of the effect [from the cause] applies only to cases of material causality (*pariṇāmikāraṇa*), and not to cases of instrumental causality (*nimittakāraṇa*). We have already stated previously that God is the instrumental cause of the world; therefore, it is logical that the intended meaning of the statement regarding non-difference is precisely as we have explained. By this, the claim that "He creates the entire world as an illusion under the influence of the karma of those respective living beings" is also refuted, because there is no evidence for the world being of the nature of an illusion.

Since there were no living beings (other than Īśvara) prior to creation, the phrase "by the power of the karma of living beings" is not tenable. Furthermore, since error in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is a property (*dharma*), its existence without a substratum (*āśraya*) is difficult to establish. Nor can Īśvara be the substratum, because, being devoid of attributes (*nirdharmaka*) and possessing only true knowledge, error is impossible for Him. Moreover, according to the view of one who maintains the oneness of the Self, there is no living being other than Īśvara existing prior to creation; thus, it cannot be said that there is a substratum for error.

Consequently, in the absence of a substratum (*āśraya*), the existence of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is untenable. And as the venerable Śaṅkarācārya stated in the Sūtra, "There is no being, because it is not perceived" (*na bhāvo'nupalabdheḥ*, Brahma-sūtra 2.2.30): "Furthermore, what is called a latent impression is a specific kind of refinement (*saṃskāra*). And a refinement is not possible without a substratum, since this is observed to be the case in the world. Therefore, it is impossible to assert that any entity whatsoever is illusory (*māyika*).

Nor should it be said that Brahman alone is the locus of ignorance in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) by virtue of the relationship of superimposition (*adhyāsa*); for since superimposition is of the nature of a false attribution (*āropa*), and that which is superimposed is false, it follows that there is no delusion (*bhrama*) in Brahman at all, and thus its agency is untenable. Furthermore, it is difficult to maintain that the state of being colored by latent impressions exists at the time of the original creation (*ādisṛṣṭi*). Nor can it be argued that in that case, the impressions belonging to previous births are grasped; for if that were so, it would follow that those impressions are beginningless (*anādi*).

This is because it is impossible to speak in such a manner while simultaneously negating other things that are non-different from Brahman. Furthermore, if the world were non-different from Brahman, it would follow that the world is real and conscious. Even the illustration of the lump of clay has as its purport merely the cognition of the effects of clay—such as pots—as being clay, for we do not hear [in the scripture] that they are "known" [as consciousness]. This is because there is no reason to abandon a meaning that is explicitly stated in the text and to adopt a meaning that is not so stated.

By this, the claim that the entire collection of objects of enjoyment is "great" (*bṛhattva*) because of the citation of the *Śruti* regarding the "enjoyer and the enjoyed" is also to be considered. The designation of "greatness" in the *Śruti*, however, is according to the principle of dependence, like the expression "the king's kingdom. Otherwise, there would follow the absurdity of even insentient objects of enjoyment being sentient. Furthermore:
"They say the world is unreal, without foundation, and without a Lord;
born of mutual interaction, what else is it but caused by desire?"

"Grasping this view, those of ruined souls and small intellects, performers of fierce deeds and enemies of the world, exert themselves for its destruction. (Gītā 16.8–9). This contradicts the statement of the Gītā. [The opponent argues: "Only those of demonic nature say that the world is unreal; this is precisely what is meant by their being 'enemies of the world' in the Gītā. To explain their true nature, [the author] says:
Asuras do not understand the path of engagement nor the path of withdrawal;
neither shame, nor generosity, nor truth exists among them. (Gītā 16.7)

By this, the Blessed One’s intention is that for those who maintain the unreality of the world, there is a lack of knowledge regarding dharma—the engagement in and withdrawal from activities such as ritual purity, conduct, truthful speech, and the means to attain worldly prosperity and the supreme good—which constitutes their very nature. Śrī Śaṅkarācārya stated the meaning of the Gītā: "Those who say the world is unreal are speakers of falsehood and practitioners of illusion. This divine Śruti also clearly declares that the Blessed One creates objects according to their true nature: "The Seer, the Wise One, encompassing all" (Īśa Upaniṣad 8).

Furthermore, describing the purport of this Sūtra as being that the world is illusory (*māyika*) contradicts many of the topical discussions (*adhikaraṇas*) in the first quarter of the third chapter [of the *Brahma-sūtras*], specifically the section beginning with: "In the transition between [bodies], it moves enveloped, because of the descriptions of eating and so forth" (*tadantarapratipattau raṃhati saṃpariṣvaktaḥ praśnanirūpaṇābhyām*, Brahma-sūtra 3.1.1). For in that context, it is stated that the world has as its material cause (*upādāna*) entities other than Māyā, such as the elements (*bhūta*) and the like.

"Do you know how creatures depart from here? Do you know how they return again? Do you know the divergence of the two paths—the path of the gods and the path of the fathers? Do you know how, at the fifth oblation, they come to be called 'men'? (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.3). Thus, in the scripture of the Chandogas, it is declared that the elements of consciousness themselves are the cause for the production of the body. Likewise, it is heard in the second Brāhmaṇa of the eighth [Adhyāya] in the Vājasaneyi [Saṃhitā].

In his *Paramārthasāra-vyākhyāna*, the sage Rāghavānanda established the non-difference of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) from Brahman during the commentary on the first verse, stating: "Because the Supreme [Brahman] is the cause of the phenomenal world's existence.
Now, [one might ask]: Is there non-duality of existence, non-duality of action, non-duality of substance, and likewise non-duality of the Self?
"By abiding here through his own experience, the sage shakes off the three [qualities] which are his own kin" (BhāgP 7.15).

Thus, one should not be deluded into thinking that the world's illusory nature (*māyikatva*) is established by the Lord Bādarāyaṇa stating that "everything is the Self. Rather, according to the *Bhāgavata*, one should contemplate: (1) *bhāvādvaita*, which is the non-difference between cause and effect consisting of the forms of the Lord existing therein; (2) *kriyādvaita*, which is that the worship of other deities is not to be performed; and (3) *dravyādvaita*, which is the state of the self and other entities being non-different from the Supreme Being.
