By meditating in this way, one does not reach the three states such as waking and so forth, and thus becomes liberated; this is the implied meaning. Furthermore, an interpretation that takes this [verse] to mean the identity of essential nature (*svarūpa-ekya*) should be considered. The intention of these subsequent verses, which explain the meaning of this *śloka*, is precisely this; it does not, however, intend the identity of cause and effect. The scriptural passage, "Having created that, He entered into that very thing," indicates the existence of the Lord within the effects.

The Blessed Lord, the author of the Sūtras, also affirms the existence of Brahman—even with respect to ether and the other elements—in order to establish that their effects, such as air and so forth, have Brahman as their cause, by means of the aphorism: "And because [the scripture] speaks of ether and the rest as having [Brahman] as their cause, just as it has been declared" (Brahma-sūtra 1.4.15). For this very reason, it has been stated by the learned: "An element, the presiding deity of that element, and the inner controller whose body is that [element]."

If it be objected that other teachers have not described the purport of the Sūtras in this way, we reply: all teachers must accept this point in order to preserve the Vedic doctrine that Brahman alone is the cause of all. And this is the Vedic doctrine: for the Śrutis such as "from which indeed these beings [arise]," "from the Self, space was produced," and "He created fire," declare that everything, beginning with space, has Brahman as its cause.

Passages such as "Having created that, he entered into that very thing" indicate Brahman's entry into all things being created; furthermore, the venerable author of the Sūtras establishes in the aphorism "From which the origin, etc., of this [world proceed]" that everything perceived is caused by Brahman.

In the sūtra "By way of being the cause," Śrī Śaṅkarācārya also determines that everything has Brahman as its sole cause, stating: "In some places the first creation of ether is heard of, in some places of fire, and in some places of water; thus, although there is a discrepancy regarding the order of the created things, there is no discrepancy regarding the Creator, because in all cases the creation is said to proceed from the Lord alone. Such is the purport of the Śruti regarding the fact that everything has Brahman as its cause.

If the nature of the Lord does not exist within the created entities such as space (*ākāśa*) and the rest, then how could fire and other elements be the creation of the Lord? Furthermore, how could there be no contradiction regarding the Creator? And how could the Śrauta Siddhānta and the Siddhānta of the Sūtrakāra be reconciled? Reflect upon this! Therefore, the statement of the scholar Nāgeśa—that the world is declared to be non-different from Him by the *tadananyatva* Sūtra—is simply untenable.
Since such a word for that meaning does not exist in either the Śruti or the Sūtra,
the wise do not indeed praise that meaning as being based on scripture (aśābda).
Regarding the investigation of the *māyāmātra* sūtra (*Māṇḍūkya Kārikā* 3.2.3):

as for the citation of that sūtra here to establish that one's own dream is illusory (*māyika*), that too is to be considered, because that sūtra does not have that as its intended meaning (*tātparya*). For instance, in that context, the word *māyā* refers to the Lord’s diverse power (*vicitra-śakti*), as in:
"O Blessed One, you alone are this [universe] through your own *māyā*."
Having created the entire universe, beginning with the Mahat-tattva, by means of the three qualities through His illusory power (māyā),
and having entered it, the Puruṣa shines manifold within those unreal qualities, like fire within pieces of wood. (Bhāgavata 4.9.7)

In this context, since it has been stated that "māyā" is the designation for the diverse power (*vicitrā īśvara-śaktiḥ*) of the Lord, the word *nirmāṇa*—used in the explanation of the supreme reality (*paramārtha-sāra*)—is derived from the root *mā* with the suffix *traṇ* in the sense of "object" (*karman*), according to the *Uṇādi* sūtra "from *hi*, *yā*, *mā*, *śru*, *bhās*, and *bhas*, [the suffix] *traṇ*. By the force of the subject passages (*viṣaya-vākya*) such as "There are no chariots there, yet there are chariots" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 4.3.10), the phrase "chariots and so forth" is to be supplied. Furthermore, the term *nirmātāram* ("the creator") is to be understood as being in the accusative case, and thus transformed into the instrumental form *nirmātrā*.

The meaning is this: by the Creator, the Supreme Lord, one's own heaven and so forth are created as mere illusion (*māyāmātra*) through His diverse power; for their essential nature is entirely unmanifest, because—unlike waking objects—their essential nature is unmanifest in its totality due to not occurring in all places and times, yet it possesses a manifest appearance.

The meaning is this: the Lord creates dream-objects that are fit for experience solely by the person who is the seer of the dream; and the variety of His power consists in the production of such objects. Alternatively—the term *māyā* refers to the will of the Lord (*īśvarīyecchā*).
It is called *mahāmāyā*, *avidyā*, *mohanī*, *prakṛti*, *vāsanā*, and so forth; O Infinite One, it is said to be Your very will.

Thus, since *prakṛti* is read among the synonyms for the Lord’s will (*bhagavadicchā*) in the authoritative texts cited by the learned—given that it is described as *māyā* in the Śruti: “One should know Māyā to be that *prakṛti*, but the Great Lord is the wielder of Māyā” (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad)—the word *mātra* in the compound [of the Sūtra] ends in the suffix *traṇ* with the sense of the object. The meaning of the Sūtra is: "The elephant and so forth produced from himself by the Supreme Self through His will. The remainder is as before. Furthermore, the use of the word *māyā* in the sense of "will" is found even in the work of the great poet Bhāravi, in the *Kirātārjunīya*:
"Then [he saw] the eternal [palace] of the sky-dwellers, radiant with its own *māyā*-created mansion and blazing jewels..."
"Desiring to abandon the city of forests, which was adorned with gate-towers (*gopura*) the color of Indra’s bow, they left it behind.

(8.1) Thus [it is said]. Mallinātha explains "by their own *māyā*" as "by the particularity of their own will. The connection is that they abandoned the city, which was beautified by gate-towers having a color similar to Indra’s bow—the rainbow. This is because it has been established regarding creation in general that "the mere will of the Lord is creation" (*Māṇḍūkya-kārikā*).

Or, let it be that the state of *māyā* refers to latent impressions (*vāsanā*); nevertheless, because that which is created by it is real, it possesses causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), just like the objects of the waking state. For this very reason, just as in the waking state, the emission of the final constituent (*caramadhātu*) can occur in a dream through union with a woman or similar circumstances. That vision is indicative, and while it is real in its own form, the object seen is unreal; therefore, the emission of the final constituent and so forth, which are accomplished through the very nature of seeing a woman, persist even in the waking state.

In the *Bhāmatī* on the sūtra "And because there is a difference between the two," the disparity between the two cases has been made clear: namely, that [the desires] such as garlands, ointments, and tooth-marks, which are accomplished by women, do not persist [after death]. For this very reason, the great sages—remembering that even the touching of another's wife in a dream is a cause of sin—prescribe expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*) to avoid the possibility of such faults, and they prescribe specific expiations for both the members of the [four] orders (*varṇin*) and for ascetics (*yatīn*).

For this very reason—in the definition of the person who has conquered his senses (*jitendriya-puruṣa*), namely "even in a dream there is no intimacy with another's wife"—the absence of talk regarding one's own wife or the wives of others has been included. If one's own wife were non-existent, then the traditional teaching that the violation of another's wife is a cause of sin, as well as the prescription of penance for it, would be rendered meaningless.

Furthermore, it is established by the experience of all that those learned in Āyurveda perform the treatment of a disease by means of the discharge of semen in a dream; for if a dream were non-existent, no disease would arise from it, since it would lack causal efficacy (*arthakriyākāritva*), and thus the administration of its treatment would be futile. [As it is said: "That semen of mine which today has fallen upon the earth, which has flowed into the plants, and which into the waters—that very thing I take back again."

"May there be long life and luster" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 1.1.24). It should be understood that the statement regarding the re-taking of semen spilled through negligence and the description of its fruit is not inconsistent; this is a *śruti* (Vedic revelation). Such is the distinction between waking and dreaming states: while all things in the waking state are of short duration, those in the dream state are likewise only of brief duration. As the great poet Kālidāsa and others have said: "Was it a mere illusion, or a delusion of the mind, or perhaps the exhaustion of merit whose fruit was yet to come? It has vanished before my very eyes, like the precipices at the edge of one's desires. (Śakuntalā 6.10)

Thus, since the distinction between a dream-object and an illusory object has been demonstrated, and since in common worldly experience these two are treated as distinct, it is incorrect to claim that a dream-object is illusory. By this, the argument of one who seeks to establish the illusoriness of the waking world—namely, that "the world is for us merely a long dream" because of such an intention—is refuted; for the very nature of a dream-object's illusoriness is difficult to define.

Furthermore, since the difference between the objects of the dream state and the waking state has been demonstrated by the sūtra, "And because of the difference [in nature], it is not like a dream" (Brahma-sūtra 2.2.29), it is impossible to assert that waking objects are illusory (*māyika*) on the basis of the dream analogy according to the view of Vyāsa. Moreover, this difference has been established by Śrī Śaṅkarācārya and others: "My mind was exhausted by sleep; therefore, this delusion arose," and also: "The perception of a dream is merely memory."

"An error of perception has arisen," and furthermore, by such statements as, "This dream-vision is memory, whereas waking-vision is perception," and so forth; and by others who have said, "Dream-vision has sleep and the like as its cause, but waking-vision is not of that nature"; and by yet others who have stated that the dream-example is not appropriate due to the difference in properties, such as the presence of sublation in the form of "This is a dream, not waking," and so on. Other teachers have likewise said this;
for in the sūtra *māyāmātram*, there is indeed an indicator of the power of Hari’s will (*harīcchā-śakti*).
Therefore, the dream object is not illusory in the same way that the state of illusion is.
Even if it were denoted by latent impressions (*vāsanā*), the dream-object would not be illusory (*māyika*); for that latent impression is real. Therefore, what was stated by Nāgeśa is not tenable.
An investigation into the meaning of the verse beginning with "nāsadrūpā": Here, in the *Mañjūṣā* (1.pa), it is stated:
"Māyā is not of the nature of non-existence, nor is it of the nature of existence, nor is it of the nature of both."
Therefore, it should be known as inexpressible, illusory in nature, and eternal.

Having thus explained the statement from the *Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa* as referring to the *māyā* intended by [the author] himself, and having accepted that which was prohibited by it—namely, the nature of being both existent and non-existent—he anticipates a contradiction regarding that reality. To resolve this, he maintains that "existence" (*sattva*) is superimposed, whereas in the ultimate sense (*paramārthatas*), it is unreal; to provide authority for this, he cites the verse from Manu: "That which is the unmanifest cause, eternal, consisting of existence and non-existence" (Manu 1.11), and therein explains the meaning of the word "existent" (*sat*) as "superimposed existence."

And as for that [interpretation]—considering that statement to be primary and secondary, and taking the example of the statement "the unmanifest is the cause" (*avyaktaṃ kāraṇam*) as a proof, thinking: "The subtle ignorance denoted by the word 'unmanifest' is, at the time of worldly transaction, the cause of gross ignorance; therefore, it is that very [ignorance] which is designated as the cause"—both of these points are to be examined. For in that regard, Kullūkabhaṭṭa and others have explained it thus: "'Sat' means having the nature of existence because it is established in the Vedānta; 'ayata' means beyond the range of perception and other means of knowledge."

Furthermore, this verse—beginning with "The waters are *nārā*" (1.10)—is intended to determine the attributes of the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa, such as his being the agent of the creation of the aggregate of effects, as indicated in the preceding verse. Since he is knowable solely through the Śruti, the existence and non-existence previously mentioned are logically established.

If it is argued, "But we do not think so; rather, this verse is intended solely for the purpose of defining the nature of ignorance (avidyā)," let us set aside such a presumption on your part; it would not suffice to establish the true meaning of the scripture. For the verse is indeed devoted to propounding the attributes of Nārāyaṇa. This is evident from the latter half of the verse, which states, "The person created by Him is celebrated in the world as His own self," where the phrase "created by Him" (tadvisṛṣṭa) declares that the causal Brahman was created by Nārāyaṇa.

Now, it is not pleasing to the mind to claim that the Brahman denoted by the term "Unmanifest" (avyakta) is said by him [the author] to be created by ignorance (avidyā); for, being insentient, ignorance cannot possibly be the agent of creation. Indeed, scripture and other authorities, while precluding the agency of the insentient Pradhāna, establish through the repetition of the verb that Nārāyaṇa alone is the agent.

The wise understand that passages such as "He who created Brahmā in the beginning" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad) and "Therefore, this [is] indeed Brahmā" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad) specifically declare that Nārāyaṇa alone created Brahmā. Furthermore, the cited statement from the *Nāradīya Purāṇa* must serve as authoritative evidence for the view of the followers of Śrī Śaṅkarācārya, which maintains that [the world] is beginningless, of the nature of primordial ignorance (*māyā*), and of an indefinable character distinct from both existence and non-existence.

But this is not the case regarding the nature of *māyā* as conceived by Nāgeśa, for therein it is stated: "It is eternal, not of a dual nature, and indefinable (*anirvācyā*). Therefore, Nāgeśa throws his efforts in vain and commits an offense against the great masters. As for the claim that the unmanifest (*avyakta*) is *pradhāna*, its source—the commentary on this very verse—is itself to be questioned, because it contradicts the context; the glorification of the majesty of Nārāyaṇa is what has been commenced. This statement is no authority for the *māyā* favored by Nāgeśa;
rather, it would be authoritative only for that which is accepted by the teachers of Advaita.
It should be understood that regarding the object which is beginningless ignorance and characterized by ineffability,
[terms such as] "eternal" and so forth are used because they are heard from the Supreme [Scripture].
An investigation into the meaning of the verse beginning with *ṛte'rtham*:

"That which appears apart from an object, yet does not appear within the Self, [is that which is perceived] as the illusion (*māyā*) consisting of one's own intended latent impressions (*vāsanā*), serving as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)."
One should know that to be the illusion of the self, just like an appearance or just like darkness.

Having cited the verse from Bhāgavata Purāṇa 2.9.33, the explanation of its meaning— namely, "That which is perceived within the self and that which is not perceived, being of the nature of perception and non-perception, one should know it to be the *māyā* of the self, because *māyā* is precisely the manifestation of unreal objects"— is to be considered.

Because of the question regarding the essential nature of *māyā* in the verse, "By means of the application of His own *māyā*" (2.9.26), because its status as the instrument of creation is stated in such passages as, "The Lord emitted golden virility threefold by means of *māyā*" (Bhāgavata 2.10.13), and because of the employment of the term *māyā* in the subsequent verses, that which is denoted here by the word *māyā* is the entity that veils the knowledge dependent upon the Lord, which is the instrument for the creation of the universe and so forth.

This verse expresses its efficacy; this is the meaning: because (*yataḥ*), even without an object (*ṛte 'rtham*—that is, even in its absence), something might be perceived; and that which exists [in the self] would not be perceived—that is, it would not appear—as non-existence (*asattvam*) while being present, nor as difference, dependence, and so forth, while existing within the self. Therefore, one should know *māyā*—the reality that is the means for such erroneous knowledge and ignorance—to be what is denoted by the term *māyā*.

The analogy is that "appearance" (*ābhāsa*) refers to a cognition whose object is a non-existent thing, while "darkness" (*tamas*) refers to the non-cognition of an existent object. Regarding "appearance," there is the case of the two moons; as for "darkness," it is Rāhu situated in the midst of the orb of light. That Māyā functions as a remover of knowledge regarding objects as they truly exist was stated by the Blessed One himself: "Those whose knowledge has been stolen away by Māyā" (Gītā 7.15). Even such Māyā is withdrawn through realization of the Blessed One, as stated by the Blessed One himself: "This divine illusion" (Gītā 7.14).

This verse has been explained in many ways in the commentaries on the *Bhāgavata*. It is argued that this very *māyā*, by deluding those who have forgotten the Blessed Lord (*bhagavadvimuṣān*) and causing them to be devoid of discrimination between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, makes them perform what should not be done and causes them to be born in evil wombs; thus it is the cause of worldly creation (*sṛṣṭihetu*). Furthermore, since the word *māyā* has multiple meanings and is observed to be used for the power (*śakti*) of the Lord as well, it is easy to say that this verse is intended to demonstrate His sovereign capacity. [Otherwise] the verse beginning with "without an object" (*ṛte'rthaṃ yat*) would not be authoritative. Let the nature of *māyā* according to Nāgeśa’s consensus be set forth.
Refutation of the Unity of Sound:

Regarding what was stated by Nāgeśa in the first chapter of the *Mañjūṣā*, after defining the expressive word (*vācaka-śabda*), concerning its unity—this must be considered: when the venerable author of the *Bhāṣya* was determining the subject matter and purpose of this Pāṇinian science, he said, "Now begins the instruction of words (*atha śabdānuśāsanam*). Of which words? Of both worldly and Vedic words."

Thus, because it is stated that the word, which is the subject of the treatise, is manifold, its oneness is not tenable. Nor should it be argued that the Bhāṣya intends [oneness] by referring to the multiplicity of manifestors (*vyañjaka*); for in the system of Nāgeśa, since only the *sphoṭa*—the denoter (*vācaka*)—is real, and the manifestors distinct from it are unreal, it would be improper to define the unreal as the subject matter at the beginning of the work.

Nor should it be argued that the commentary on the *Sārūpyasūtra*—which states, "A single Indra, when invoked in a hundred sacrifices, is present everywhere simultaneously"—serves as proof for the unity of the expressive word (*vācaka-śabda*). This is because that commentary intends to establish the unity of the specific word "Indra," and not the non-existence of other words such as "pot" (*ghaṭa*) or "cloth" (*paṭa*). Furthermore, this [point] was stated in accordance with Kaiyaṭa’s *Udyota* on the rule *itīndravat*, following the interpretation that the term is an *avyayībhāva* compound used in the sense of "the manifestation of the word."

In fact, even if the word *indra* there refers to its literal meaning, it is easily possible to reconcile it with the context. As for the clarification of that point: in the *Devatādhikaraṇa* of the *Uttaramīmāṃsā*, although a deity possesses a physical form (*vigraha*), due to a particular capacity (*sāmarthyaviśeṣa*), only a single Indra can be simultaneously present everywhere; or else, the deity Indra, remaining in one place alone, attends to the oblations being offered by various [worshippers] all at once, just as acts such as salutation, when offered by many people, reach a single person simultaneously.

The meaning of the *Bhāṣya* should be understood according to the direction stated by the venerable Śrī Śaṅkarācārya: "They go toward the preceptors and others who are standing. Since it is said in the *Bhāṣya*, "Indra is called," and because in the world an invocation is generally observed to concern only a conscious being, it is appropriate that the purport of the *Bhāṣya* lies precisely in this sense. Otherwise, he would have simply said, "the word 'Indra' is uttered.

Now, if one objects that when the meaning of the *Bhāṣya* is explained in this way, the word *iti* is redundant, we reply: no; the word *iti* is not useless, as it is a distinct word intended to convey the specific subject matter already mentioned.

Furthermore, regarding the comprehension of words, one might think that a word-for-word recitation (*pratipadapāṭha*) must be performed; to this he says: "This word-for-word recitation is not a means for the comprehension of words. For it is heard in the *Mahābhāṣya* on the *Paspaśāhnika*, citing a traditional scripture (*śruti*), that "Bṛhaspati taught Indra the complete study of words (*śabdapārāyaṇa*) consisting of words stated word-for-word for a thousand divine years, yet he did not reach the end. However, the mention of Bṛhaspati is not pleasing to those who follow authoritative tradition (*prāmāṇika*). Even a powerful being is not capable of denying an uncontradicted meaning established by scripture.

In the *Bhāṣya* on the rule for *anvākhyāna*, it is stated: "For those [sounds] that are employed, there must be phonemes (*varṇa*) that are eternal, immutable, and free from loss, addition, or modification. Furthermore, in the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra *dādā ādyāntau*, there is the use of the plural form "in words that are employed" (*prayuktānāṃ śabdeṣu*). These serve as proofs for the multiplicity of eternal expressive words (*vācaka-śabda*). However, in the *Bhāṣya* beginning with "by which, when uttered," the singular number in the phrase "that is the word" (*sa śabdaḥ*) refers to the genus (*jāti*).

If, according to the direction of Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "by which," there were only one single word [as the object of instruction], then the science itself would be unnecessary to begin, according to the maxim: "A single illustrative example does not justify the commencement of a grammatical rule. Nor should it be argued that "the science is an instruction regarding the *sphoṭa* by way of instructing its manifestors (*vyañjaka*), and since there are many such manifestors, there is no fault"; for such a view has not been stated by the author of the Bhāṣya or others.

Because these [entities] are imagined (*kalpita*), just like [the terms] "it brings" (*ānayati*) or "it turns" (*vaṭṭayati*), the [notion of] "instruction regarding the *sphoṭa*" has been cast aside; for since the *sphoṭa* itself—which would have to be distinct from well-known words—is unestablished, any investigation into its unity and so forth is like counting the petals on a flower in the sky. If it is argued that it is not logical to say a treatise should not be commenced simply because its subject matter is a single entity—since we observe the commencement of treatises such as the *Vedānta* despite the unity of Brahman—we reply: there is a lack of parity between this case and the example cited.

Although Brahman is one, since there exist many qualities when it is being investigated, the commencement of the scripture (*śāstra*) for the purpose of investigating them is justified. However, for the proponent of *sphoṭa*, who maintains its oneness and accepts its qualitylessness (*nirdharmakatva*), the commencement of the scripture is useless because there is an absence of qualities to be investigated within that partless entity (*akhaṇḍa*). Nor should it be argued that Brahman is also partless; for the Great Sage, in commencing the Vedānta scripture, did not accept the partlessness of Brahman.

Furthermore, even by the teacher Pāṇini, the indivisibility (*akhaṇḍatva*) of either the *brahma* or the *sphoṭa* was never stated anywhere. This has been demonstrated previously on the occasion of refuting the indivisibility of words and so forth. Now, one might object: "Is this [argument] intended for the position held in the commentary on the two sūtras—that at the beginning of creation there is the production of phonemes (*varṇa*) and so forth, and at dissolution there is their destruction; and that it is only the words heard in actual usage that are expressive? For in the sūtra [Pāṇini 3.1.91], he teaches another word through this sequence: first the base (*prakṛti*), then the suffix beginning with *val* (the *ārdhadhātuka* affix), and after that the augment *iṭ*."

Regarding the commentary which demonstrates the third method for establishing that the name "Agama" (tradition/scripture) is indeed an *ādeśa* (substitute), stating: "In whatever [form] the cognition of its tradition arises," [the meaning is as follows]: In this view, just as there is instruction regarding unreal *prakṛtis* (bases) and *pratyayas* (suffixes), there is likewise the derivation of a real expressive word (*vācaka-pada*). Since nothing other than the *sphoṭa* possesses reality, even intermediate aggregates such as *iti* and so forth are unreal; thus, the purpose is to bring about the cognition of the expressive word by means of making those [aggregates] known. Alternatively, [it means] that he teaches only as much as he is able to teach in a general manner.

Because this would lead to the contingency of contradicting the earlier Bhāṣya which states, "By that [suffix], this [base] attains a distinct word-form (*śabdāntara*) as a composite whole through its qualification. Furthermore, by adopting the Bhāṣya statement "a distinct word-form as a composite," the *Uddyota* explains: "It is distinct from *tavya* and others, such as *itavya* and so on. Thus, according to Nāgeśa’s underlying intention, even in the earlier Bhāṣya, only the word *kalpataḥ* is the subject matter of the grammatical rule. Alternatively, since the two alternative views (*pakṣadvaya*) presented in the Bhāṣya according to Nāgeśa’s interpretation share the same subject matter, there would be the contingency of the subsequent Bhāṣya beginning with "Or rather" (*athavā*) being unnecessary.

Furthermore, by adopting Kaiyaṭa’s statement, "The word is eternal," and explaining it as "the meaning is that which is produced by grammar," [the view] that the imagined [meaning] alone is directly taught is established; for there is no attainment of the idea that "by that [grammar], the denoter is made known. Consequently, since both positions share the same object, the distinction between the two positions—namely, that in one case the imagined [meaning] is directly taught, while in the other the denoter is taught as an indivisible whole—is rendered inconsistent. According to the direction stated by Nāgeśa, in both positions, it is indeed the imagined [meaning] alone [that is taught].

Thinking that the view [of the opponent]—that there is direct cognition (*sākṣādbodhana*) due to the acquisition [of the suffix]—is not acceptable to Pāṇini, he states another alternative with "Or rather" (*athavā*). And this [view] belongs to the proponent (*siddhāntin*), according to the *Uddyota*. In the *Bhāṣya*, the word "this" (*ayam*) in the phrase "by him, this" (*tenāyam*) refers to the cognizer (*boddhṛ*). Furthermore, this very position is the one stated under the rule *dādhā ghu* (P. 1.1.20); by this [rule], when there is the occasion for the notion of *tavya*, the notion of *itavya* should be applied. Consequently, it should be understood that a word such as *bhavitavya*, qualified by that [suffix], is the expressive signifier (*vācaka*). This is what must be understood.

And this [first case] concerns the intermediate student (*madhyamādhikārika*). Alternatively, the second position—that "or"—concerns the most excellent student who is skilled in reasoning and refutation (*ūhāpoha-kuśala-uttamādhikārika*). This is the meaning of the commentary: by this sequence—by this order—he, namely Pāṇini, teaches—instructs—another word, that is, a denotative term. The sense is that the most excellent student, through the mere instruction of roots (*prakṛti*) and so forth, and by his own intuitive insight (*pratibhā*) alone, even without the instruction of intermediate groups, comprehends every specific aggregate belonging to the science of grammar.

Furthermore, upon a careful examination of the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "In the case of eternal [sounds]," it appears that plurality alone is appropriate for the expressive word (*vācaka-śabda*). Indeed, the unity of the expressive word is not accepted by the Bhāṣya. Having thus scrutinized the Bhāṣya, wise people maintain this view.

Furthermore, the non-scriptural status of the *sphoṭa* must be accepted on the basis of the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭa*) during the stage of analytical derivation (*prakriyā*); however, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthadaśā*), it is said:
"In a word, phonemes do not exist, nor do constituent parts exist in sentences."

"According to the direction stated in the *Vākyapadīya*—namely, 'there is no absolute distinction whatsoever between words and a sentence'—where would there be occasion for this prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) for those who maintain the doctrine of *sphoṭa*? This is indicated by the statement "according to the direction stated in the *Vākyapadīya*" in the *Kaustubha* on the remainder of the rule *eoṅ*. Furthermore, the fact that Bhartr̥hari’s own words are the very foundation for the doctrine of *sphoṭa*, rather than the words of the Three Sages (Pāṇini, Kātyāyana, and Patañjali), is shown by the statement "it has been established in detail in the *Vākyapadīya*" in Kaiyaṭa’s commentary (*bhāṣyapradīpa*) on the *Vaspaśāhnika*.

Since Kaiyaṭa and others have explicitly stated this, and since no Pāṇinian sūtra is cited as an example, those who claim that "Sphoṭa is not accepted by the Three Sages" are correct; enough with further elaboration. Regarding the authority for Sphoṭa, a statement of Hari has been cited in the works of Kaiyaṭa and others, but there is no such statement from Pāṇini himself; therefore, it is considered non-archaic (anārṣa).

Regarding the refutation of the indivisibility of the word (*vācaka*): As for what was stated in the *Mañjūṣā* (p. 1)—namely, having asserted that "words are indeed indivisible," one then says "this too" and quotes the *Sātra-bhāṣya* as "beginning and end"—that is untenable. This is because, in many sūtras such as *aiuṇ*, the *Bhāṣya* states, "In eternal words, there must be phonemes (*varṇa*) that are fixed and immutable. Since this statement establishes that the "fixed" (*kūṭastha*) consists of a collection of phonemes, we understand that the author of the *Bhāṣya* accepts precisely the divisible nature [of words]. Furthermore, the quality of indivisibility is nowhere explicitly mentioned in the *Bhāṣya*.

In this regard, the description of the second alternative (*athavā-pakṣa*) found in the *sūtra* "ādyantau" (Pāṇini 1.1.46)—namely, that "by this and by that, there is the cognition of an indivisible denoter"—should be considered doubtful, because such a meaning cannot be obtained from that *Bhāṣya*. Furthermore, reflect on how an indivisible entity could possess denotative power, given that it must necessarily be devoid of properties (*nirdharmaka*). If it is argued that "that [property] is superimposed upon it," one should understand that this simply means "that [property] does not exist there [in reality]."

Furthermore, because the *Mañjūṣā* states that "by the word *varṇa* in the *Bhāṣya*, [one means] stems, suffixes, augments, and so forth," it is possible to assert its having parts (*sakhaṇḍatva*). Upon careful consideration of the *Bhāṣya* passage beginning with "in the eternal [sounds]" (*nityeṣu*) from the sūtra *aiuṇ*, it appears more appropriate to take the meaning of "by *varṇas*" as "by syllables" (*akṣaraiḥ*). However, in the *Kalā*, the second alternative "or rather" (*athavā*) in the *Bhāṣya*, along with the corresponding passages from Kaiyaṭa’s *Pradīpa* and Nāgeśa’s *Uddyota*, have been cited as authorities; yet, the manner in which the indivisibility (*akhaṇḍatva*) is established by them has not been demonstrated.

Furthermore, the Bhāṣya statement, "Having extracted the words from the sentence, they are explained," is a proof for the fact that words possess parts (*sakhaṇḍatva*), because extraction consists in taking one part at a time from a whole aggregate. As for the commentary by Kalā and others, which states, "'Extraction' means conceptualization; having divided [the word] through conceptualization," scholars who know the true nature of words do not consider this to be consistent with the literal sense of the text. The sūtras situated within the section on numerical indicators (*aṅkādhi-kāra*) serve as proofs for the existence of parts.
It has already been established previously that the theory of indivisibility (*akhaṇḍatva*) is not accepted by Vyāsa and other authorities.
The Bhāṣya has been shown as the authority for the view that the denoter (vācaka) is composite;
how then could the property of being a denoter exist therein [if it were] non-composite?
Refutation of the claim that the *sphoṭa* is accepted by the *Bhāṣya*:

If it is argued that the *sphoṭa* is indeed accepted by the *Bhāṣya* and is both an ancient (Ārṣa) doctrine and the view of Pāṇini—on the basis of the statement in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *taparaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.70), "The word is the *sphoṭa*; the sound (*dhvani*) is a quality of the word"—we reply as follows: In that context, the term *sphoṭa* signifies either (1) that which is manifested or revealed (*sphuṭyate*), derived from the passive sense of the root, meaning the eternal object to be manifested; or (2) that from which the meaning is revealed (*sphuṭati*), derived from the active sense, meaning the expressive signifier (*vācaka*). Therefore, by that *Bhāṣya*, the *sphoṭa* characterized by Hari, Kaiyaṭa, Dīkṣita, Nāgeśa, and others—as a secondary metaphorical designation (*lakṣitalakṣaṇa*)—is not established.

To explain: for one who maintains that phonemes (*varṇa*) are produced, just as there is a distinction between short, long, and so on based on the duration of a *mātrā* and the like, there would likewise be a distinction between individual instances of *a* and other phonemes based on their different modes of articulation (*vṛtti*), such as fast (*druta*) and so forth. Consequently, the use of the term *tapara* (referring to a long vowel) in a particular mode of articulation would serve to exclude those *a*-sounds and others belonging to other modes of articulation—just as it excludes long vowels and the like—and as a result, forms such as *ais* and *aus* would not be obtained in other modes of articulation. Having first stated this resolution in accordance with the intention of the objector—who, having raised this doubt, suggests that "in other modes of articulation, *es* and the others must be explicitly stated"—he then states the actual fact (*vastutaḥ*).

The Bhāṣyakāra, demonstrating that if phonemes (*varṇa*) were eternal, no difference in the manifestation of forms such as *a*, *i*, and so forth would be experienced due to differences in their occurrence, and thus the statement regarding *ai* and others need not be made, offered another solution with an illustration: "The phonemes remain established as accomplished entities" (*siddhāstv avasthitā varṇāḥ*). His intention was this: just as a path of fixed dimensions reached by various individuals who travel at different speeds does not change but remains of one and the same form, so too a phoneme, though uttered by speakers at different times, does not undergo any alteration.

[Objection: "Surely, since time (*adhvan*) possesses a specific, established magnitude (*parimāṇa*), there is no consequence of its being differentiated; however, phonemes (*varṇa*) are not of that nature. Therefore, this is an unequal analogy. To one who, having been told this, remains doubtful due to a lack of conviction regarding the stated point, the Commentator (Patañjali) confirms the eternity of phonemes by means of another illustration, beginning with the words "If that is so" (*evaṃ tarhi*). In this context, upon a careful examination of Kaiyaṭa’s *Pradīpa*, the *Kaustubha*, the *Uddyota*, and the *Mañjūṣā*, it is understood that the word *sphoṭa* refers to the manifested entity (*vyaṅgya*).

*Śabda* is the phoneme (*varṇa*), such as *a* and so forth; *sphoṭa* is that which is manifested (*vyaṅgya*), its essence being the eternal nature of the phonemes. *Dhvani* is the modified sound (*vaikṛtadhvani*); "modified" means being produced by causes such as indolence, and it consists of modes such as slow (*vilambita*) and so on. It is a quality of the word (*śabdaguṇa*), a property residing in each specific phoneme that is manifested immediately after the manifestation of the phoneme's own form; it is an auxiliary to the phoneme, and its essence is being the sole cause for the perception of a phoneme as qualified by its respective mode.

Therefore, that *dharma*—like shortness (*hrasvatva*) and so forth—is not a differentiator of phonemes (*varṇa*) qualified by another mode of occurrence (*vṛttyantara*). The commentary asks "How? in order to state an illustration. [The answer is] "Like the striking of a kettle-drum (*bherī*) and so forth. Here, the word *āghāta* is formed with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*). "Striking of the kettle-drum" (*bherī-āghāta*) is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*). From that, the suffix *vati* is applied in the third case-ending. "Sphoṭa" is the ellipsis. The meaning is that the *sphoṭa* becomes like the sound produced by the striking of a kettle-drum.

The meaning is as follows: just as the movement of feet in various numbers, such as one or two, does not cause a difference in the sound of a drum, so too a difference in the mode of manifestation (*vṛtti*) does not cause a difference in the individual phonetic manifestations (*varṇavyakti*) such as the letter *a*. This is because it is experienced by those who know the true nature of sound. Here, although there is a disparity between the example and the illustrated case regarding their impermanence, they stand in the relationship of example and illustrated case simply by virtue of being objects of a single kind of perception.

He states the intended meaning of the illustrative sentence in the *Bhāṣya* with the words "tadyathā" (for example). Regarding "bherīghāta" (the striking of a drum): here, the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*) according to the rule [Pāṇini 3.2.1], resulting in a *upapada* compound. Regarding "āhatya" (having struck): the word "while hearing the sound" is to be supplied as the remainder of the sense. The literal meaning is clear. Regarding "sphoṭa" in the *Bhāṣya*: since this is part of the illustration, the phrase beginning with "athāpi" (even though) follows. The meaning is: "even though heard by a person whose nature is to move away from the vicinity of the seed."

The *sphoṭa* is indeed of that very duration—specifically characterized by the measure of time belonging to the striking moment of the contact between the drum and the stick—as expressed in the phrase "it becomes audible," and so forth. To the question, "How can the sound possess such an extent? the *Bhāṣya* replies: "caused by the *dhvani*. This means: produced by a specific effort residing in the person, and brought about by a heterogeneous property of the sound denoted by the term *dhvani*, which arises from a particularly firm contact of the teeth and palate.

Unable to tolerate the difficulty of applying [the example] as a mere remainder of the illustration (*dṛṣṭāntaśeṣatva*), Kaiyaṭa states that this is the presentation of the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*)—namely, that "the *sphoṭa* is exactly that much"—in this alternative view, beginning with the words "In this case, thus," and so forth. "Thus, like the sound of a drum (*bherīśabda*)," [it means] the *sphoṭa*—even the phoneme *a* and so on—is "exactly that much," meaning it exists precisely as qualified by shortness (*hrasvatva*) and other properties belonging to the time of its production (*utpatti-kālika*) or manifestation (*abhivyakti-kālika*). The sense is that there is no difference therein. He says "resonance" (*dhvani*) because the *vṛtti* in the *Bhāṣya* does not imply a difference. "Vṛddhi" means "length" (*hrasvatva*).

This [mention of "smallness"] is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of "greatness" (*mahattva*) and so forth; the intended meaning (*tātparya*) is that greatness and the like are produced by sounds (*dhvani*) uttered slowly, not slowly, or rapidly. However, Nāgeśa states in the *Mañjūṣā* and *Uddyota*: "The *sphoṭa* exists even in the sound of a drum; therefore, this sentence refers to both the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the thing illustrated (*dārṣṭāntika*). According to his view, one must supply the words "just as... so too" (*yathā-tathā*) and apply the *bhāṣya* sentence by repeating it.

The author of the *Bhāṣya*, the foremost among those who know the true nature of word and meaning, has established through his own experience [the eternity of phonemes (*varṇanityatva*)], yet he speaks of them as "sounds" (*dhvani*) out of consideration for his students.
Sound and *sphoṭa* belong to words; indeed, sound is perceived as being either slight or great for some [words], both of which exist by their very nature.

The meaning of this is as follows: *dhvani* is the manifesting word (*vyañjaka-śabda*), and *sphoṭa* is the manifested word (*vyaṅgya-śabda*). "Small" and "great" are specific types of *dhvani*; these two—smallness and greatness—consist in their producing a cognition that is either delayed or immediate. "Of such a kind" means belonging to words; *dhvani* here refers to the modified sound (*vaikṛta-dhvani*), which is perceived—that is, known. To provide proof for the fact that *dhvani* is related to the word by being the cause of its perception, he states "both" (*ubhayam*) when the two kinds of words mentioned exist.

Both the state of being manifested (*vyaṅgyatva*) and the state of being a manifestor (*vyañjakatva*) [belong to sound] by its very nature—that is, by its own form (*svarūpeṇa*). Since sound possesses such a nature, there is no dependence upon other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in that regard. The intention is that it nevertheless becomes an object of the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of yogis. Regarding this, he states the established rule: "Of some," etc. The phrase "both of those" is to be supplied. The meaning is as follows: for certain articulated sounds (*vyakta-śabda*), both of those—the state of being manifested and the state of being a manifestor—apply; however, for unarticulated sounds (*avyakta*), it is only resonance (*dhvani*) itself.

This same explanation is provided in the *Kaustubha* regarding the *Bhāṣya* and other texts. Consequently, in the *Bhāṣya* and the *Kārikā*, the word *sphoṭa* means "that which is manifested" (*vyaṅgya*); it is derived from the root *sphuṭ* with the suffix *ghañ* in the passive sense (*karmaṇi*), according to the rule of "diversity of application" (*bāhulakāt*). The essential point here is this: this *Bhāṣya* is undertaken to demonstrate that even when there is a difference in mode (*vṛtti-bheda*), there is no difference in the phoneme (*varṇa*) itself—since the phoneme is eternal—even when a difference in manifestation is urged by one who maintains that phonemes are produced effects. It does not, however, aim to establish that the signifier (*vācaka*) is a distinct *sphoṭa*.

Alternatively, the *Bhāṣya* on the *sūtra* "eoṅ" (Pāṇini 1.1.2), which states, "Or rather, only the *sphoṭa* is indicated from both sides; thus, by the sound *ra*, [the sound] *la* occurs," is engaged in the discussion of whether a portion of a phoneme (*varṇaikadeśa*) is included or not. It proceeds to dispel the doubt regarding the failure of the substitution of *la* in words such as *klṛpta* under the view that it is not included; therefore, it is not conducive to establishing the *sphoṭa* as intended by Hari and others.

And its meaning is as follows: in both cases, by the rule "raḥ la," there is merely the *sphoṭa*—that is, merely a common property shared by both independent phonemes (*varṇa*) and parts of phonemes (*varṇaikadeśa*). Such a property resides in either the letter *ra* or the letter *la*, or in a part of those similar letters, or in both; it is the cause for the appearance of both in a single form. However, it is not the cause for their being grasped by a word that denotes an independent phoneme. For this very reason, he will state later: "the hearing of *la* occurs in place of the hearing of *ra*."

The author of the Sūtras, the Teacher, explains [this] by way of specific instances. Having stated this, he states the resulting conclusion: "Because of the hearing of *ra*" (*ra-śruteḥ*). Where there is the hearing (*śruti*)—that is, the act of listening (*śravaṇa*)—of *ra*, that is "the hearing of *ra*"; [the compound] belongs to such a case. The analysis of "the hearing of *la*" (*la-śruti*) is exactly the same. Alternatively, the suffix *ktin* in "hearing" (*śruti*) is used in the passive sense, meaning "that which is being heard."

The term *raḥ* is a bahuvrīhi compound meaning "that in which the sound *r* is heard"; thus, it refers to the locus where the sound *r* is being heard. Consequently, the specific meaning is that for that which possesses the appearance of *r*, there occurs a substitute (*ādeśa*) consisting of the appearance of *l*. Because the two roots *kṛp* and *it* possess the property of having the appearance of *r*, they respectively receive the substitutes *kalp* and *klap*, since both the phoneme and its parts possess the properties that cause the appearance of *r*.

For this very reason, they say that here the word *sphoṭa* refers to the property (*dharma*) that produces manifestation, based on the etymology: "that from which the word (*śabda*) bursts forth (*sphuṭati*) or unfolds. Kaiyaṭa, however, states that *sphoṭa* is the universal (*sāmānya*) manifested by the *repha* and *lakāra*, whether they are included within the phonemes or not. In the *Kaustubha* as well, while explaining the remainder of the rule *eoṅ* and the rule *kṛporola*, Dīkṣita—who asserts that "the genus (*jāti*), common to both independent and non-independent [sounds], is intended to be expressed in both the subject and the predicate"—has clarified precisely this meaning of Kaiyaṭa.

Nāgeśa, however, argues that since there is no evidence for the existence of such a genus (*jāti*), even the Bhāṣyakāra—who states, "while one should have said 'of the *ra*-genus,' [he says] 'because of the hearing of the *ra*'"—does not accept the existence of such a genus. Furthermore, if one were to admit a genus common to both [the *ra* and *ṣa*] based on inference, this would lead to the conclusion that the rule applies only to the view that a letter consists of parts (*ekadeśa-grahaṇa-pakṣa*). This would contradict the intent of the Bhāṣya, which begins with the view that the letter is not grasped as a whole (*agrahaṇa-pakṣa*). Moreover, it contradicts the statement in the rule *raṣābhyām* (Pāṇini 8.4.1) that "this letter is distinct, like Narasiṃha," which implies it is a unique entity.

Having demonstrated the contradiction with the *Sūtra* and *Kaiyaṭa*, he explains the meaning of the Bhāṣya passage "on account of the non-hearing of 'ra'" (*raśruteḥ*) by stating that, due to the total absence of a real 'ra' in some cases, there occurs an appearance of the letter 'la' within the *sphoṭa* which possesses the semblance of 'ra'.

On this point, the following must be said: It has been stated more than once previously that the view of Nāgeśa—who asserts the falsity (*mithyātva*) of everything other than Brahman on the grounds that it constitutes the mode of error—is not accepted by Pāṇini and others; therefore, in the system of Pāṇini and his followers, the *repha* (the sound *r*) and so forth do indeed exist as real entities. For this very reason, the Blessed One [Patañjali] stated, "because of the hearing of the *ra*" (*raśruteḥ*); otherwise, he would have simply said, "of the appearance" (*avabhāsasya*), and so on.

"In the *Sāra*, the author of the *Sāra* states: 'Even though everything is illusory (*māyika*), it is not non-existent like the horn of a hare. And in the remainder of the commentary on the verse beginning with 'Therefore, like the five sheaths (*pañcakośa*)', he says: 'Nor can there be an awakening to the real *sphoṭa* through an unreal conceptualization of base and suffix; for its unreality will be established later, since even the division into base and suffix is illusory, just like the five sheaths.'"

For it has been stated by the author of the *Darpaṇa* on that very point: "There is no falsity [of the world] like that of an absolutely non-existent thing, such as a hare's horn"; thus, since illusory objects lack absolute non-existence, phonemes, their aggregates, words, and so forth, likewise lack non-existence. By this, the statement of Tājī, who claims that everything other than Brahman is illusory and therefore non-existent, is refuted.

Nor should it be said that he did not state that the world is non-existent; for after establishing the non-existence of things such as the silver in a shell (*śukti-rajata*) both externally and in its own location, he states in the *Mañjūṣā*: "The phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is exactly like this, because the world is described in the scripture by way of examples such as a mirage. This is because the non-existence of the water in a mirage was established in the preceding text, and thus the non-existence of the world is also stated by him. In his view, there is indeed no distinction between a rabbit's horn and illusory silver.

Since he stated during the refutation of the view that "the indescribable is distinct from both the existent and the non-existent" that "a real entity serving as the locus of the distinction between the existent and the non-existent is unestablished," if the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell and the like were merely a specific instance of a rabbit's horn and such, then—given that the entity serving as the locus of the two-fold distinction would exist—the refutation of the definition of the indescribable favored by the Advaitins would be inconsistent. Furthermore, just as in the case of the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, the statement that it "appears" here is untenable, because no sublationary cognition arises.

It should not be argued that this [interpretation] is subsumed under the "apprehension" (grahaṇa) view alone, and thus the contradiction with the initial statement remains as before; for there is a distinction: in the case of apprehension, there is the cognition of identity (*tattva*), whereas in the case of non-apprehension, there is the cognition of similarity (*sādṛśya*). Since apprehension of a similar entity cannot occur without a primary [entity] being present, the author of the Sūtra in the rule *kṛpo ro la* does not intend merely to indicate the primary individual (*mukhyavyakti*), but rather to indicate the property of the grasper (*grāhakadharma*) which applies to both the primary individual and its similar counterpart. Therefore, the intention of the Bhāṣya is that there is apprehension of both.

If words did not possess phonemes (*varṇa*), then the treatise that instructs on correctness (*sādhutva*) by means of the analogy of the "line-drawn gavaya" (*rekhāgavayanyāya*)—within the position that words are eternal (*nityatvapakṣa*)—would be inconsistent with the usage of the learned. For its meaning is as follows: just as a gavaya is made known through the configuration and arrangement of the lines [depicting] a gavaya, so too is the eternal word "cow" (*gavādiśabda*) made known through the arrangement of the partial manifestations (*rekhā*) of the phonemes such as *ga* residing in the eternal word.

This is what must be understood: since in the form *edhi* (the second person singular of the imperative) derived from the root *as*, no letter belonging to the verbal root *as* is perceived—just as [no letter of the root] is perceived in the position of the line (*rekhā*)—by that same logic, it is not tenable that "the scripture is the instructor. Therefore, the commentary (*uddyota*) on the rule *ādyantau* is not tenable.

In the sentence of grammatical derivation (*prakriyāvākya*), that which is produced after the operation of the rules (*śāstrapravṛtti*)—which stands in the place of the *repha* (the letter *r*) and the *sthāna* (the substitute)—is understood by that [word] to be the word *edha*, which is eternal and expressive of the meaning "fuel. This is because the letters situated in the place of the *repha* and the *sthāna* are perceived therein. By that same logic, it is proper to say that the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*) is the instructor. Nor should it be argued that this [word] is a different, partless phoneme (*varṇāntara*), just as the nature of Nṛsiṃha is not pervaded by the natures of "man" and "lion" taken separately; for even if it were a different phoneme, there is no evidence for its being partless. Indeed, although Nṛsiṃha is not delimited by [the separate categories of] "man-ness" and so forth, he does not possess partlessness.

By the author of the *Sūtras*, who prescribes specific grammatical operations such as prolation (*pluta*) in the rules "The first half-mora of that [vowel] is acute" (*Pāṇini* 1.2.32) and "In the case of an *ec* vowel that is not a *pragṛhya*, when followed by a vowel, the first half becomes *ā* and the second becomes *i* or *u*" (*Pāṇini* 8.2.107); and by the author of the *Bhāṣya*, who states "And because the latter part of the *ai* and *au* vowels is greater," and who deliberated on whether parts of letters are included or excluded by the term "letter"—all of this is done by accepting that letters possess constituent parts (*sāvayavatva*). Therefore, these [letters] do not lack parts (*niravayavatva*).

The unreality of the cognition of "wholeness" (*samudāyatva*) in that collection, as well as the reliance on the existence of parts therein, is rooted in error; this is demonstrated by the following analysis using the example: "There are no parts in phonemes":
"In words there are no phonemes, and in sentences there are no parts;
there is no absolute distinction whatsoever between a sentence and its constituent words."

Thus, the claim in the *Vākyapadīya* that words and sentences are partless (*niravayavatva*) is groundless. This is because the *Mahābhāṣya*, in the passage beginning with "In the case of eternal words," states that words in the form of sentences and words must consist of phonemes (*varṇa*), thereby indicating that their possession of parts is the intention of the author of the *Bhāṣya*. Nor should it be argued that the *Bhāṣya* concerns the manifesting agents (*vyañjaka*) while the *Vākyapadīya* concerns the *sphoṭa*; for the nature of a *sphoṭa* as something distinct [from phonemes] is not established in the *Bhāṣya*.

How could the *Vākyapadīya*, which establishes its meaning without the assistance of commentaries and the like, be acceptable to the followers of Pāṇini? Nor should it be argued that because [the word] possesses parts, it must be produced and therefore words are not eternal; for we do not observe that the primordial nature (*mūlaprakṛti*), which consists of the three qualities (*triguṇa*) and possesses parts, is itself produced. Furthermore, on the view that words are eternal, there is no occasion for the objection regarding the non-establishment of the whole (*samudāya*).

Furthermore, grammatical operations based on the status of being at the end of a word (*pada*), the beginning of a word, or the internal structure of a suffix (*pratyaya*) are established by rules such as *padāntasya* (Pā. 8.4.37), *sātpadādyoḥ* (Pā. 8.3.111), *ṣaḥ pratyayasya* (Pā. 1.3.6), and *iṇaḥ ṣīdhvaṃluṅliṭāṃ dhoṅkāt* (Pā. 8.3.78). Likewise, operations based on the status of being a subsequent member of a compound (*uttarapada*), the preceding member (*pūrvapada*), or having a single vowel (*ekāj*) in the subsequent member are established by rules such as *aluguttarapade* (Pā. 6.3.1), *uttarapadasya* (Pā. 7.3.10), *ekājuttarapade ṇaḥ* (Pā. 8.4.12), *pūrvadāt* (Pā. 8.3.106), and *hṛdbhagasindhvante pūrvapadasya ca* (Pā. 7.3.19).

By prescribing compound formation through rules such as *taddhitārthottarapadasamāhāre ca* (Pāṇini 2.1.51) and by enjoining grammatical operations based on the preceding and following members of a compound, the author of the Sūtras has demonstrated that even words and sentences possess constituent parts; therefore, the assertion that they are partless is certainly not the intention of the Teacher who founded this science. Consequently, that [assertion] should not be respected by those who rely on authoritative means of knowledge. Furthermore, this is supported by the Bhāṣya: "There is no partlessness of phonemes and so forth in words."

In this context, the phrase "in words" (*śabdeṣu*) means "in words consisting of phonemes, words, and sentences. By this, the statement made by Kaiyaṭa regarding the *Samartha-sūtra*—namely, that "in reality, [words] are indeed partless and are analyzed (*anvākhyāyante*) solely on the basis of an unreal fiction"—is refuted. This is because the existence of parts in eternal words is established by the statement in the *Bhāṣya*, "In eternal words, there must be phonemes," and because it would be impossible to define a science (*śāstra*) as one that teaches an unreal object.

The learned declare that a scripture (*śāstra*) is indeed a collection of words that produces true knowledge regarding reality (*tattva*). Furthermore, if one teaches what is false, those who abide by it will never attain the truth; just as those desiring to go to a desired city, if instructed on a wrong path, will wander only there and never reach the city.

Furthermore, in the *Samartha-sūtra*, Nāgeśa refuted both the partlessness (*niravayavatva*) and the meaninglessness (*nairarthakya*) of words. However, some [opponents], by way of presenting a counter-argument, state in their text: "There is no evidence for the meaninglessness of the perceived parts or for the partlessness of the whole; as for eternality (*nityatva*), it can be asserted merely on the basis of being unproduced (*aniṣpādyatva*). By this, it is indicated that there is no rule that eternality and having parts necessarily exist in mutual exclusion.
Moreover, the term *sphoṭa* occurs in the *Bhāṣya* under the rules *e-oṅ* and *ataḥ kṛ-kami-kaṃsa-kumbha-pātra-kuśākarṇīṣv anyatarasyām*.
But in the first [case], that word "tat" (that) refers to the Dharma, according to that sūtra and its commentary.
In the second [chapter], it is determined that the eternal word (*nityaśabda*), distinct from the *sphoṭa*, is the expressive agent; therefore, what was stated in the *Mañjūṣā* is not tenable.
Therefore, [the passage] from the Bhāṣya is not a proof for the establishment of the sphoṭa as being equal to Brahman;
thus it was spoken by one who has taken refuge at the lotus feet of those who know the Bhāṣya.
Refutation of the Bhāgavata’s Agreement with the Sphoṭa Theory:
Now, it may be argued that the Blessed Vyāsa, in the *Bhāgavata*, states:
"He who hears this *sphoṭa* while the sense of hearing is dormant and perceives the void..."

If it is argued that the *sphoṭa* is the view accepted by great sages such as Vyāsa, because of the statement: "That by which speech is manifested, whose manifestation is in space, belongs to the Self" (12.6.5), we reply: the word *sphoṭa* is derived from the root *sphuṭ* with the suffix *ghañ*, meaning "that from which the meaning bursts forth" (*apādāna*) or "that by which the meaning is burst forth" (*karaṇa*), and is thus a synonym for the signifier (*vācaka*). Alternatively, since there is a reference to "this *sphoṭa*" in relation to the previously mentioned *praṇava* consisting of three syllables, it is a synonym for the *praṇava*.

Alternatively, since it will be stated in the second half of the verse that "by which speech is manifested," the syllable *praṇava* is called *sphoṭa* by virtue of being the manifestor of the Vedas and so forth; therefore, in that context, the word *sphoṭa* means "the manifestor. As for the meaning of the verse: That Supreme Self, whose vision is directed toward the void (*śūnyadṛk*)—meaning possessing knowledge even when the void exists, i.e., when the auditory faculty is inactive—perceives this *sphoṭa*, the sound that denotes itself, while the ear is asleep, that is, while the sense organ of hearing is devoid of function.

To the question "Of what nature is the *praṇava*?", he says: "By which... By which *praṇava*, speech—all the Vedas—[is manifested]; of which *praṇava*, in the space of the Self—the space of the heart of the Supreme Self, according to Śrīdhara Ācārya; the sense is that the Supreme Self alone hears this, and no other.

Regarding the *saṃhitā* reading, "suptaḥ śroteva śūnyadṛk," Vijayadhvajācārya explains it as follows: "Suptaḥ" means one who has attained the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*). "Śūnyadṛk" means one who sees the "Void" (*śūnya*), which is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*); thus, he is so called. One who possesses direct realization of Brahman (*brahmāparokṣī*)—that is, a knower of Brahman (*brahmajñānī*)—while being in that state of sleep, hears the *sphoṭa* just like the Supreme Self. The underlying meaning is that both the Supreme Self and the knower of Brahman are the hearers of the *sphoṭa*. Here, this should be understood: in the fourth chapter of the first book (*skanda*), the sequence for the acquisition of the Vedas and other scriptures is described in summary.
"By how many ways were the Vedas divided by the high-souled teachers of the Veda, such as Vyāsa’s disciples, Paiṅgi and the others? O gentle one, explain this to us."

By such passages as Bhāgavata 12.6.1, which describe in detail the creation of the phenomenal world of sound (*śabda-prapañca*), it is established that from the heart-space of Lord Nārāyaṇa—who had formed the resolve, "Let me create"—there first appeared, by His mere will, a certain *nāda* resembling the resonance of a bell.

From that *nāda*, through the manifestation of the traditional collection of syllables (*akṣara-samāmnāya*) and so forth, all the Vedas were manifested; and that *praṇava* is the designator of Nārāyaṇa, as described in such passages as: "That by which speech is manifested is the direct designator of Brahman, the Supreme Self, from His own abode."

Nor should it be argued that because the term "Parameṣṭhin" is used there, and because the lexicon states "Parameṣṭhin is the Grandfather (Pitāmaha)," it must refer exclusively to the four-faced Brahmā; for since the word "Parameṣṭhin" denotes the Supreme Self (Paramātman), and given the established doctrine that everything has Brahman as its cause, it is more appropriate to understand it as referring to the Supreme Brahman. The term *parameṣṭhī* is derived from the root *sthā* with the suffix *ini*, meaning "one who stands in the highest place."

Nor should it be said that this [Nāda] is within the range of everyone’s direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) simply because the Blessed One previously stated, "It is perceived through the cessation of the functions [of the mind]. For such a statement was made from the perspective of a yogi; indeed, by the power of yoga, yogis are capable of perceiving even that [Nāda] as if it were before their eyes.

Alternatively, the mention of an illustration is intended to show that the Nāda which manifests the *praṇava* is perceived just as we perceive a particular sound when our ears are covered. This is according to the convention (*samaya*) of all Tantric practitioners, who hold that "the supramundane must be understood by means of mundane illustrations."

Furthermore, upon a close examination of the *Bhāgavata*, it is understood that the sphoṭa known as Praṇava is manifested by a sound (*nāda*) that is not within the range of any sensory perception; however, the Grammarians (Vaiyākaraṇas) maintain that it is manifested by the *vaikharī* sound, which is perceivable by the ears of others. Thus, because the subject matter of the *Bhāgavata* differs [from that of the Grammarians], this [teaching] of the *Bhāgavata* is not in accord with their [view].

By this, the following is refuted: [the claim] that because the Lord Vyāsa stated in the *Sāṃkhyakārikā*—“That by which the three states, which are the functional operations of the *guṇas*, are sustained”—that the *sphoṭa* is the material cause (*upādāna*) of both the proliferation of names and forms (*nāmarūpa-prapañca*), since he described the creation of the three states (*bhāvas*) such as *sattva* and the other *guṇas* (i.e., the manifold of forms), we too have spoken accordingly. This is rejected because the *sphoṭa* mentioned in the Lord’s statement regarding the *praṇava* is different from the *sphoṭa* you intend.

Furthermore, among the fourfold states of *nāda* distinguished as *parā*, *paśyantī*, *madhyamā*, and *vaikharī*, it is established by scriptural authority that *parā* is *śabdabrahman* because it is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the manifold universe consisting of both word and meaning—as stated in the passage: "From Prakṛti, who is of the nature of *bindu* and dominated by the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), there arose *parā*, which is *śabdabrahman*, the cause of words, meanings, and objects. Since the *sphoṭa* manifested by *vaikharī* is of the nature of an effect, it cannot be the cause; moreover, its status as *brahman* has not been asserted.

Nor should it be said that Nāgeśa has stated the causality of the *sphoṭa* on the grounds that "since the single *sphoṭa*, which is of the nature of the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*), is the material cause of both the word and its meaning, it is the cause of both those effects"; for in that context, the traditional scholars have explained the term *sphoṭa* as being synonymous with *parā* (the supreme speech). It is for this very reason that the citation of the authority, "of that which is primarily characterized by the power of action" (*kriyāśaktipradhānasya*), becomes consistent.

The supreme speech alone is the authority, because of the statement regarding its being the "ocean of sound" (*śabdabrahman*); furthermore, because in the passage "the functions of the qualities," the manifestation of the three *vyāhṛtis* is mentioned. Moreover, since the treatise begins with the investigation of the expansion of names and subsequently shows the investigation of the expansion of names such as the Vedas, to introduce the creation of the expansion of forms in the middle would contradict the initial context. If the creation of forms were intended here, then one should have described it either at the beginning or at the end.

Because of such scriptural and traditional texts as "From the Self, space was produced" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2), "It thought: 'May I be many, may I grow forth'; It sent forth fire" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.3), "In the beginning, He created water alone," and "Water is called *nārā*"—all of which are intent upon the creation of the manifold world of forms—and because the creation of the manifold world of forms beginning with space is not described as proceeding from the syllable *praṇava*, it is impossible for the *praṇava* to be the cause of the manifold world of diverse forms.

Wherever the creation of the manifold world of forms is heard of or remembered as proceeding from the Praṇava, it should be understood that the creation of the Supreme Self, who is denoted by the Praṇava, alone is being described.

Nor should it be argued that the statement by the venerable Bādarāyaṇa in the sūtra, "And [it is] not so, because of the origination from the Word, as is known from perception and inference" (Brahma Sūtra 1.3.28), which declares that even the manifold of forms originates from the Word, proves that the previously mentioned status of the *sphoṭa* as the creator of the world is logical; for in that context, although the literal meaning of the phrase "because of origination from that" is "because of the production of Indra and others from the Word," the intended sense is that the Word serves as the reminder of the forms (*ākṛti*) of the objects to be created.

Desiring to create, Prajāpati first attends to Vedic words such as "Indra" and so forth; repeatedly recollecting the specific forms (*ākṛti*) signified by those words, he creates Indras and others characterized by those very forms. Thus, the author of the Sūtras has demonstrated that the word itself serves as a cooperative cause (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*). Consequently, there is no contradiction with the established doctrine—set forth in the Sūtra "From which [proceed] the origin and so forth of this [world]" (Brahmasūtra 1.1.2)—that everything has Brahman as its cause.

This is clear from Śaṅkara’s commentary on the Sūtra, "If it be said that [the world] is sound, no" (*śabda iti cet na*). Nor should it be argued that there is no contradiction with our stated doctrine because the *sphoṭa* is also an effect of Brahman and is thus Brahman; for we do not maintain that everything which is an effect of Brahman is itself Brahman, nor is there any evidence that the *sphoṭa*, as a general category of effects of Brahman, possesses the same causality as Brahman, since there is no proof that the *sphoṭa* is the cause of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*).

Nor should it be said that by the phrase "non-difference from that" (*tadananyatvam*), the non-difference of the effect from its cause is being asserted; for this has already been resolved by the fact that non-difference exists only through the absence of manifestation (*avibhāva*) and not by way of essential nature (*svarūpataḥ*), since it is therefore impossible for the *sphoṭa* to be eternal. The *sphoṭa* propounded in the *Bhāgavata* is distinct from the *sphoṭa* accepted by Hari (Vyāsa) and others. Therefore, the *Bhāgavata-smṛti* cannot be an authoritative means of knowledge regarding its existence.
Regarding the subject of *sphoṭa*, the refutation of the Naiyāyika position is as follows:

It is well known that the Naiyāyikas maintain, "There is a conventional relationship (*saṃketa*) between words and word-meanings, but not between a sentence and the sentence-meaning; rather, that [sentence-meaning] arises through the power of the sentence itself—which is unprecedented—by means of the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) consisting in the co-occurrence of other words. However, the *sphoṭa*, whose distinct nature has been described by those who consider themselves Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*), certainly does exist. Thus they say.

In the first chapter of the *Mañjūṣākṛti*, the author explains the intention of the *Bhāṣya* through a passage beginning with "And for the sake of knowing the convention (*samaya*)" and ending with "the view that the sentence-sphoṭa is not accepted by the Naiyāyikas is refuted. Having thus described the intent of the *Bhāṣya*, he shows that it is stated quite clearly that, just as in the case of words, there is a divine convention (*aiśvara-samaya*) even regarding sentences; therefore, the Naiyāyikas also accept both the expressive power (*śakti*) and the sphoṭa in the sentence.

In order to demonstrate that even the Naiyāyikas are favorable to his own position, he asserts that the object of knowledge (*prameya*) not accepted by them is actually the intended meaning (*tātparya-viṣaya*) of their system. Regarding this, the *Bhāṣya* states: "Grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) is the exposition of speech characterized by words for the sake of knowing the conventions (*samaya*); it is the characterization of the meaning of speech characterized by sentences. By this [statement], the learned should investigate how, either explicitly or implicitly, the potency of the sentence (*vākya-śakti*) and the *sphoṭa* are obtained according to their doctrine.

Furthermore, in that context (*Dvādaśāranayacakra*, 2.1.56), the reading "for the sake of maintaining the convention" (*samayapālanārtham*)... "the meaning is the definition" (*arthaḥ saṃkṣepaḥ*) is observed. Therein, grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) is that which makes known the correctness of words; "meaning" (*artha*) is their collection; and "definition" (*lakṣaṇa*) is the differentiator—that which distinguishes correct speech from pseudo-sentences, or that which makes known the correctness of a sentence through its uncontradicted meaning. To that end, the commentators on that [text] have said: [grammar is for the sake of maintaining the convention].

Furthermore, how can it be consistent to claim that the *sphoṭa* is accepted by the Naiyāyikas, given that the *Muktāvalī*, in its section on sound (*śabdakhaṇḍa*), refutes the view that the *sphoṭa* is manifested by the phonemes through the very same means that manifest them; and given that Jaṭantu Bhaṭṭa, while elucidating the intent of the *Nyāyasūtra-bhāṣya-vārtika-tātparya-ṭīkā* and other works in the sixth chapter of the *Nyāyamañjarī*, refuted the doctrine of an additional *sphoṭa* by stating, "This theory is rootless, akin to a city of Gandharvas"?

And know this: it is an expression of a meaning that was neither stated nor intended by him. By this, [it is clear that] relying on the reading "arthalakṣaṇam" alone, the connection of the word *vyākaraṇa* here [is incorrect]. Consequently, the interpretation beginning with "it is that which makes known the capacity of speech in the form of a sentence to produce the cognition of meaning" is based solely on a failure to examine the Nyāya-bhāṣya and its commentaries.
By this, let it be clearly understood that Nāgeśa, having even fabricated an alternative reading of the text, speaks according to his own single whim; thus, he is unrestrained.
The Sphoṭa has been refuted by the logicians as being akin to a city of Gandharvas; consider how it could possibly be accepted as their own view.
The refutation of [theories such as] the "Greatness" (*bṛhattva*) of the *sphoṭa*:

First, the *sphoṭa* is threefold, distinguished as that of the phoneme (*varṇa*), the word (*pada*), and the sentence (*vākya*). These, in turn, are twofold through the distinction between genus (*jāti*) and individual (*vyakti*), thus resulting in six types. With the further division into the indivisible word-*sphoṭa* (*akhaṇḍapadasphoṭa*) and the indivisible sentence-*sphoṭa* (*akhaṇḍavākyasphoṭa*), there are eight. Among these, according to the statement of Hari: "The established position of the doctrine is that the sentence-*sphoṭa* remains at the ultimate limit," the sentence-*sphoṭa* is primary; even therein, the genus-*sphoṭa* (*jātisphoṭa*) is the most primary. "Existence itself, being differentiated among cows and so forth due to the difference of its correlates... [is the basis for this].
It is called "jāti" (the universal); in it all words are established.
They declare that [Being] to be the meaning of the nominal stem and the meaning of the verbal root;
it is eternal, it is the Great Self, and they say that suffixes such as *tva* and *tal* denote it.
Thus, from the summary of the meaning of Hari’s verses:
"In every individual object, there exist two parts, the real and the unreal.
That which is real therein is the universal (jāti); the individuals are considered to be unreal. (70)

Explaining this through the following verse, Dīkṣita states: "In every individual object, there exists a certain pervasive existence (*sattā*) denoted by the term 'genus' (*jāti*). And that existence is Brahman itself, according to the scriptural statement: 'All this is indeed the Self. The word *tasya* (of that) is a synonym for *sattā*. This existence denoted by the term 'genus' resides both in the word and in its referent. In this regard, the unity of the word is established due to parsimony (*lāghava*). As it has been said:

'Just as [parsimony] is observed in the case of the genus being the denotable (*śakya*), let it be seen that parsimony applies to its being the denotative (*śakta*) as well. Or, the distinction among phonemes is merely adventitious (*aupādhika*), like the difference between high and low pitches.'"

Thus, it is said: "In this way—since Brahman itself, as delimited by its various individual manifestations (*vyakti*), is the universal (*jāti*), and there is no real entity existing apart from Brahman, the oneness of the Self (*ātmaikatva*) is established. Consequently, for one engaged in the investigation of words, proficiency regarding the Upaniṣadic Brahman arises, like finding a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*) while setting out to search for a cowrie shell. Thus did [the author] describe the supreme purpose of studying the science of grammar (*vyākaraṇa-śāstra*) in the first chapter of the *Kaustubha*.

Regarding this, they say: one must first investigate why great masters such as Śaṅkarācārya and others, while commenting [on the scriptures], established that knowledge of Brahman is the means to liberation, rather than abandoning such a great purpose as the investigation of words.
