Their intention, however, was this: those who have studied the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (*vedāṅga*), whose internal defects have been shaken off by ritual action (*karman*) and other means, and whose internal organs are purified, become possessed of the knowledge of Brahman through the meditation on the Self enjoined by such scriptural passages as "The Self, indeed, my dear," and—by the grace of the Supreme Lord—having abandoned the body, they become liberated, and not by any other means.
But surely...
Two kinds of Brahman are to be known: the Brahman of sound and that which is supreme. One who is proficient in the Brahman of sound attains the supreme Brahman.

If it is argued that, since the attainment of liberation in the form of the realization of Brahman is mentioned while the investigation of the word (*śabda*) is underway, what was stated in the *Kaustubha* is correct—this is not so. For whether in the Śruti or the Smṛti, the phrase "the Supreme Brahman" has the sense of "the Veda," and its intended meaning is that the one intent upon investigating the meaning of the Veda attains Brahman. It is for this very reason that the statement that even the Supreme Brahman is "to be known" (*vedya*) in the passage "and that which is beyond" is consistent. By this, the claim that this statement is proof for the existence of *sphoṭa* is refuted.

Nor should it be argued that the author of the *Bhāṣya*, while determining the incidental purpose of the treatise, has already stated that liberation is the fruit of the inquiry into words—since he established through the verses "four horns" (*catvāri śṛṅgāḥ*) and "like groats" (*saktumiva*) that the knowledge of correct words results in equality with Mahādeva and union with Brahman (*brahmasāyujya*), as these two states (equality and union) alone constitute liberation.

By the two sūtras, "Yoga is its designator, the *praṇava*" and "Reflection upon its meaning," Patañjali establishes that the *praṇava* is the designator of Īśvara, and that reflection on Īśvara—characterized by the qualities expounded by the *praṇava*—is the means to liberation. His intent here is not that liberation results from the mere knowledge of the word, but rather that through the knowledge of the word, there arises a state of purity of mind (*sāmya*), which serves as a preparatory refinement for the inquiry into the meaning of the Vedas, the means to the knowledge of Brahman.

This is because the intention of the Bhāṣya is that such is the purport of the Śruti. For this very reason, the scriptural accounts of Nārada and Śvetaketu—who had studied all the Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs—being told that they were "knowers of names only, not knowers of the Self" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.2), as well as their subsequent request for instruction on the Self, "May the Blessed One indeed tell me that" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.4), become consistent.

If the realization of the Self were established through the knowledge of words alone, then, since both [the seeker and the teacher] would have studied grammar, the realization of Brahman would follow from the mere investigation of words; consequently, the scriptural mention of its absence and the prayer for it would be inconsistent. For this very reason, the *Bhāṣya* states that grammar is merely an auxiliary (*aṅga*), saying, "Among the auxiliaries, grammar is the principal. The meaning of this is that it is a means for the investigation of the meaning of the Vedas.

For this very reason, after stating that grammar is an *aparavidyā* (inferior knowledge), the *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad* declares that there is another, the *parabrahmavidyā* (knowledge of the supreme Brahman), in the passage beginning: "Two knowledges are to be known: the higher and the lower" (Muṇḍaka 1.1.4). For this same reason, the production of the knowledge of Brahman in Sanaka and others through the interpretation of the *Māheśvara-sūtras*—beginning with *aiuṇ*—as being directed toward Brahman is fruitful; otherwise, since the knowledge of Brahman would be impossible for them through the mere investigation of words via Pāṇini’s grammar (which is rooted in the *Māheśvara-sūtras*), that [interpretation] would be useless. Furthermore, it is also not tenable that the *sphoṭa* is Brahman.

In the view of the proponents of *sphoṭa*, since there is no entity other than *sphoṭa* and it is non-existent [apart from that], the conclusion that "Brahman does not exist" follows; thus, they fall within the category of atheistic doctrines (*nirīśvaravāda*), while the status of *sphoṭa* itself is established as Brahman. However, in the doctrine of Brahman (*brahmavāda*), because anything other than Brahman—even *sphoṭa*—would necessarily be non-existent, its establishment as Brahman is not possible. Consequently, one must reflect that since "all this is indeed the Self," the reality of *sphoṭa* is also the reality of the Self.

By this, one should also reflect upon what was stated in the *Mañjūṣā*—repeating the text of others—that "no distinction whatsoever is defined in the Lord (*īśvara*), because He is of the nature of all things. This is because there is no evidence for the Lord being of the nature of all things. Nor should it be said that the doctrine is simply that the *sphoṭa* is Brahman; for there is a lack of authoritative proof, such as scripture, for such a meaning. Furthermore, it is not so stated in the *Bhāṣya* and other works. [As it is said: "Not at all, not at all; the root *kṛñ* (in the sense of 'making') does not apply here. Liberation is not attained through those who are proficient in grammar and the like.
"One who is well-versed in the Brahman of Sound (*śabdabrahman*) would not be well-versed in the Supreme [Brahman] if he were to remain there."
"His labor is fruitless, like that of one who guards a barren cow" (Bhāgavata 11.11.18).

Because experts have determined that one who delights merely in the analysis of words lacks the knowledge of Brahman, liberation, and the means thereto, those who know the higher and lower truths and the masters of the commentaries do not respect what has been stated [by others] regarding the Kaustubha and other such works.

The *sphoṭa* itself is a point of contention because it is not accepted by many. Kaiyaṭa, however, states that the *bhāṣya* intends the *sphoṭa* when he says: "In some places he speaks of the *varṇasphoṭa*, in some places the *padasphoṭa*, in some places the *vākyasphoṭa*, and in some places the *jātisphoṭa*. Yet, such an interpretation of the intended meaning is entirely inconsistent with the actual words of those respective passages of the *bhāṣya*.

Furthermore, if the nature of the *sphoṭa*, its status as the signifier (*vācaka*), and its identity with Brahman were intended by the author of the Bhāṣya, then just as the author of the Bhāṣya established the meaningfulness of phonemes (*varṇa*) and other properties through detailed investigation in such passages as, "But are these phonemes meaningful, or are they meaningless? Is word (*śabda*) eternal, or is it non-eternal?", he would likewise have begun with the question, "But is the manifestor (*dhvani*) the signifier, or is it the *sphoṭa*? and then [established] the *sphoṭa*'s...

Having established everything such as denotative power (*vācakatva*) and so forth, one should have established that liberation (*apavarga*) results from the knowledge of that; yet he did not establish it in that way. Therefore, we consider that what was stated by Kaustubha and others is not in accord with the *Bhāṣya* and other authoritative works.

Regarding the objection stated by Nāgeśa—that "in this view [of the Advaitins], because the universal (*jāti*) is impermanent, because there is no evidence for the existence of a universal without a substratum, and because the destruction of the universal is heard in the statement 'that which was the fiery nature of fire has departed' (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.3.6)"—all of that applies equally even to his own position as a proponent of the *jāti*-sphoṭa. Furthermore, in the view of the Advaitins, what loss is there if the universal is impermanent? For the author of the Bhāṣya did not state that the universal is impermanent.

Since Śaṅkarācārya stated in the Sūtra "If it be said that [the word] refers to the individual, no; because the form is eternal" (Brahma-sūtra 1.3.17) that the universal (*jāti*) is eternal—given that there is no contradiction regarding words such as "cow" even while individuals are being produced—it is incorrect to say that "in the Advaitins' view, the universal is non-eternal."

In the view of the ancient proponents of the *jātisphoṭa* theory, since the universal (*jāti*) is of the nature of Brahman and is therefore eternal, its cessation is impossible; thus, the cessation mentioned in the Śruti text "it has departed" (*apāgāt*, Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.4.1) does not refer to the universal itself, but rather to its being subject to linguistic usage (*padavyavahāryatva*). Therefore, the criticism raised by the modern [proponents] is not correct. The author of the *Kaustubha* maintains that the *sphoṭa* is Brahman; therefore, through the investigation of it, one attains the vision of Brahman, and the person also attains liberation.
Therefore, it is not appropriate that he did not cite the words of the Sage regarding that matter,
since they would be contradictory to the Brahma-mīmāṃsā, the supreme Śrutis, and so forth.
Therefore, this is not approved by the knowers of Brahman, nor even by Pāṇini;
thus it is determined by those people who are skilled in the investigation of Brahman.

Refutation of the Universal-Sphoṭa (jātisphoṭa) as accepted by Nāgeśa: "The universal-sphoṭa alone is the ultimate established doctrine. A universal (jāti) is a property that generates a cognition of a recurring form; for it to be logically established as having that definition, and for the apprehension of a recurring potency to be established, there must be an infinity of sphoṭas due to the distinctions consisting in the coloring by various times and various phonemes. Just as for those who maintain the oneness of the self, the status of 'selfhood' (ātmatva) is maintained as a universal despite the multiplicity of selves caused by limiting adjuncts (upādhi), so too its status as a universal is due to its subsistence in those [individual sphoṭas]. When that [universal] is delimited by limiting adjuncts, it becomes the individual-sphoṭa (vyaktisphoṭa)."

"Nāgeśa [states] that if it is characterized by its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), it is the *jāti-sphoṭa*. To this, the following must be said: the *sphoṭa* has been established with great effort; is it the *jāti*, or something else? In the first case, according to the view of the Advaitins, since the *jāti* is impermanent and there is no evidence for the existence of a *jāti* without a substratum (*āśraya*), the refutation stated by him against the opponent applies equally to his own position. In the second case, however, the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that it is the *jāti-sphoṭa* would be violated.

The example "like the difference between selves for Advaitins" is inappropriate. In their view, the self is a substance (*dravya*), and therefore the existence of a universal (*jāti*) therein is logical. However, since the *sphoṭa* established in Nāgeśa’s system is not accepted as a universal, it is impossible to admit a universal therein, according to the technical maxim: "A universal is not admitted in a universal. Furthermore, in common experience, such a cognition arises through a recurring property residing in the object of cognition (*bodhya*), and not through a similar property residing in the signifier (*bodhaka*).

Therefore, the laborious effort to postulate an infinite *sphoṭa* based on adventitious conditions (*upādhi*) is indeed fruitless. Furthermore, if the connection with the condition were eternal, then because the distinction between *sphoṭas* and their being the substratum of the aforementioned properties would also be eternal, the unity and indivisibility of the *sphoṭa* would be destroyed. If, however, it were occasional, there would be a lack of a substratum (*āśrayāsiddhi*) for the universal (*jāti*) consisting of those aforementioned properties.

Furthermore, if one were to conceive it in this way, since the universal residing in the *sphoṭa* itself would be what conveys the meaning, the meaningfulness of the *sphoṭa*—which is established as distinct from the phonemes (*varṇa*) and so forth, manifested by the *vaikharī* speech, and existing in the intermediate state (*madhyamā-nāda*)—would not be proven; thus, the previously stated principle that "the *sphoṭa* possesses meaning" would have to be reconsidered. Nor should it be argued that there is no room for the aforementioned fault because the difference in that very *sphoṭa* is merely adventitious (*aupādhika*), and its status as a genus (*jātitva*) consists in its subsisting in different individual instances; for such a conception lacks support from the *Bhāṣya* and other authoritative sources.

In the view of one who asserts that the "imagined" (*kalpita*) is the real entity (*satva*), the universal (*jāti*) previously mentioned cannot be established, because the distinction between individual instances (*vyakti-bheda*) and their subsistence therein (*tadvṛttitva*) are non-existent. Furthermore, since everything other than the *sphoṭa* is false (non-existent), it is difficult to find the full collection of causal factors (*samagrī-sampad*) that would produce an infinity of *sphoṭas*. In this position, one must even seek the indirect glance of Paraharika regarding the systematic arrangement of the *sphoṭa*.

For those striving to establish categories not supported by the *Bhāṣya* and other authoritative texts, any discussion regarding the parsimony (*lāghava*) or complexity (*gaurava*) of adopting such a position is merely a hollow clamor; enough said.
It is only through the coloring of time (*kāla-varṇa-anurāga*) that an infinity of *sphoṭas* is postulated.
The nature of *sphoṭa* exists therein; therefore, it is called a "universal" (*jāti*).
No authority for such an assumption is seen in the Bhāṣya or other works;
therefore, the learned hold that Nāgeśa’s statement is not tenable.

In the *Pātañjala-bhāṣya*, the nature of the *sphoṭa*—which is distinct and different from those words well-known in the world as denoters—is not described; rather, the eternality (*nityatva*) of words is established here and there. Therefore, we consider that the eternality of denoters was indeed intended by Pāṇini and the author of the *Bhāṣya*. Furthermore, this doctrine of *sphoṭa* was refuted by the Sāṃkhya teachers through the aphorism: "Sound is not of the nature of *sphoṭa*, because of its being perceived and not being perceived," and by the teacher named Upavarṣa, who followed them.

Furthermore, [this is established] by the venerable Śaṅkarācārya and his followers in the *Devatādhikaraṇa* (8) of the *Brahmasūtra-bhāṣya*; by Kumārilabhaṭṭa in the *Tantravārttika*; by Pārthasārathimiśra in the *Śāstradīpikā*, in the fifth section (*adhikaraṇa*) on the "Eternity of Words" (*Autpattika*, 1.1); by Jayantabhaṭṭa in the *Nyāyamañjarī* (6.ā.); by Viśvanātha in the *Muktāvalī*, in the section on words (*śabdakhaṇḍa*); and by the venerable Rāmānuja Muni and his followers in the *Bhāṣya*, its commentaries, the *Śrutaprakāśikā*, and the *Tattvaṭīkā*.

In the *Jijñāsādhikaraṇa* [of his own work], in the *Tattvamuktākalāpa*, and in the *Jijñāsādhikaraṇasudhā* and *Tattvanirṇayaṭīkā* by the illustrious Lord Jayatīrtha, the master of ascetics, the doctrine of *sphoṭa* has been refuted in many ways. It should not be argued that our teacher’s established doctrine can be abandoned merely because it has been critiqued by others; for since it is not mentioned in the *Bhāṣya* and other such works, and because it is un-Pāṇinian, it would follow that it is not the teacher’s established doctrine. As it is said: "When there is a conflict between two authorities, the word of the majority prevails; when the numbers are equal, the word of those with superior qualities; and when there is a conflict even among those of superior qualities, the word of those who possess the highest excellence is to be accepted" (*Yājñavalkyasmṛti-vyavahārādhyāya* 78).

This is because, according to the principle of established precedent (*vyavasthāpaka-nyāya*), since there are many who do not accept *sphoṭa* and because their word alone is authoritative due to its being a quality (*guṇitva*), [the view of those who accept it is not primary]. As for the claim that *sphoṭa* is approved by Vyāsa—on the grounds that Yādavaprakāśa explained the verse "born from the syllable of Brahman" (*Gītā* 3.15) such that the word *brahma* refers to *sphoṭa* and the word *akṣara* refers to its manifestor—and that it is likewise approved by Pāṇini—that is not so.

In this context, by the word *brahma*, the *sphoṭa* is not stated to be the cause of action anywhere, since the object that is the cause of action is understood through the term *karma*. Here, "action" (*karma*) refers to the activity of the officiating priests and the sacrificer; "Brahman" (*brahma*) refers to the Veda, according to Śaṅkara’s commentary, or to primordial nature (*prakṛti*), according to Rāmānuja’s explanation—and by others as well, it is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) itself, as in:
"Non-violence, equanimity, contentment, austerity, charity, fame, and infamy—these various states of beings arise from Me alone" (Gītā 10.5).

Thus, because the *Gītā* declares that actions such as giving originate solely from the Supreme Self (Paramātman), and because of this interpretation, the assertion of Yādavaprakāśa is not to be respected. Nor should it be argued that the existence of the *sphoṭa* is established by the statement in the *Harivaṃśa*, "You are the letter 'a' among letters; you are the *sphoṭa* residing in the phonemes," for by that [statement], the *sphoṭa* as conceived by Nāgeśa and others is not proven. To explain: "residing in the phonemes" (*varṇasaṃśrayaḥ*) means "consisting of them"; "the *sphoṭa*" refers to the property of being the signifier (*vācakatva*), and that [property] is You.

The meaning is "dependent on you. This is because the statement is intended to convey a grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—like the expression "the king is the kingdom"—and thus lacks the status of a valid authority for establishing the existence of a *sphoṭa* distinct from that described by Nāgeśa and others. Nor should it be argued that the *Śruti* passage beginning with "subtle, inseparable from its object in essence," and the *Mahābhārata* passage beginning with "O Goddess, between the *prāṇa* and *apāna*," serve as authority for that [distinct *sphoṭa*], as this was already addressed in the *Mañjūṣā* within the discussion on *śakti* (4.20).

Since these two [passages from] Śruti and Smṛti are not cited in the Bhāṣya and other such works, they lack authority regarding the point stated; for this very reason, Nāgeśa stated: "Śruti and Smṛti are clear in the work of Hari. And for this same reason, it is stated in the *Bhaṭṭadīpikā* (1.3.11 a): "This is contrary to Śruti. Since the word *sphoṭa* is not heard in Śruti and Smṛti, it is difficult to maintain that those two have the *sphoṭa* as their intended meaning.

The meaning of the scriptural passage is as follows: that speech—the Vedic word—which existed as one prior to its division; which was established within the Self, being solely devoted to the Supreme Self; which possesses manifold forms and many branches; which is subtle because it is infinite and thus difficult to comprehend; which, in its true sense, has its reality not yet fully disclosed and is closely bound [to the Self]; which flows abundantly, bestowing desired objects—that speech, like some other [speech] dedicated to the propitiation of another deity...

The meaning is as follows: others, who are ignorant of the true reality (*tattvārtha*), "know"—that is, they understand—by means of statements from the *Mahābhārata* such as "The Vedas have Nārāyaṇa as their supreme goal" (Śāntiparvan 357.77), that the Veda has been determined to have Nārāyaṇa as its ultimate purport; yet, being ignorant of the corroborative expansions (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) found in the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, and ignorant of the indicators of purport such as the introductory passages (*upakrama*), they believe it refers to other deities as they appear [on the surface]. The intended purport of the *Mahābhārata* statements is simply that there is a conventional usage of words based on their connection to various respective locations, such as the navel (*nābhi*). Therefore, neither the Śruti nor the *Mahābhārata* has the *sphoṭa* as its ultimate purport.
Nowhere in the Bhāṣya has this sphoṭa been established by the author of the Bhāṣya;
moreover, this doctrine of sphoṭa has been thoroughly refuted by many teachers.
The Śruti and Smṛti are not authoritative in this matter, because the word "sphoṭa" is not heard therein;
therefore, what was stated by Kaiyaṭa, Bhaṭṭoji, and Nāgeśa is not correct.
Refutation of the Inconsistency in the Critique of Sphoṭa:
Now, one might object that this [theory] of *sphoṭa* is un-Pāṇinian; indeed, the author himself has made this clear in his concluding summary:
"The grammarian Nāgeśa [upholds] the doctrine of the sage Sphoṭāyana."
Having thus adorned it, he said: "May Śiva be pleased with Umā through this."

If you say: "By stating 'thus I have merely extracted the essence of Sphoṭāyana’s doctrine from the *Annambhāṣya*,' your engagement here is fruitless and based on not having read his work from beginning to end"—to this we reply: It was precisely after examining his entire work that we proceeded with this [treatise].

Thus, even though it is introduced in that manner, Nāgeśa’s intention—that this *sphoṭa* is also accepted by Pāṇini—is revealed by the general designation "the established doctrine of the Grammarians" (*vaiyākaraṇasiddhānta*) at the outset, by the citation of various statements from the *Mahābhāṣya*, and by the explanation of the term "Grammarians" (*vaiyākaraṇa*) as "Pāṇini and others" along with illustrative examples in the *Kalā*.

The concluding statement, however, intends merely to indicate that the doctrine of *sphoṭa* was first conceived by the sage Sphoṭāyana. If Nāgeśa had intended it to belong to Pāṇini, he would not have cited the sentences from the Mahābhāṣya.

As for the evidence that the Sphoṭa was first conceived by him (Sphoṭāyana), it is simply the statement in the *Śekhara* on the rule *avaṅ sphoṭāyanasya* (Pāṇini 6.1.123): "The name 'Sphoṭāyana' is etymologically significant, meaning that this sage had the Sphoṭa as his refuge (*ayana*), that is, as its object of exposition. If one then asks, "Why did the author [of the Laghu-śabdendu-śekhara] not cite his own words regarding the Sphoṭa as authoritative evidence?"—one must ask Nāgeśa himself for the resolution of this objection.

However, regarding the alternative reading *sphoṭāyanasya*, one must consult Nāgeśa himself for the resolution. In the case of the reading *sphoṭāyanasya*, the suffix *phak* is applied to the nominal stem *sphoṭa* by the rule *naḍādibhyaḥ phak* (Pāṇini 4.1.99). In this view, it should be understood that there was another sage named Sphoṭāyana who was a rememberer (*smartṛ*) of Sphoṭa, according to Nāgeśa’s statement: "the opinion of the sage Sphoṭāyana."

Alternatively—by adding the suffix *añ* to the word *Sphoṭāyana* according to the rule for the *bidādi* group (Pāṇini 4.1.104), since *bidādi* is an *ākṛtigaṇa*; as for the etymology, it has already been stated. Thus, this effort is made to dispel the doubt that [the author] might be a follower of Pāṇini, which arises from the consistency between the introduction and the conclusion. For there is a doubt as to whether [the author] is a follower of Pāṇini or not, because of the initial general reference and also because of the examples cited in the Bhāṣya.
Therefore, my activity directed toward avoiding those [faults] is fruitful;
the concluding statement, moreover, serves to indicate that this [work] originated from him.

An investigation into *śakti* (potency): *Śakti* is the will of God (*īśvara*) that "this meaning is to be understood from this word. The Naiyāyikas designate this very [will] as *saṃketa* (convention), while others call it *abhidhāyakatva* (denotative capacity). It is rooted in this alone that the relationship between word and meaning is characterized as that of the signifier and the signified, or as the state of being the cognizer and the cognized, and as the denoter and the denoted; such is the usage in the technical treatises (*śāstra*). In this regard, the Mīmāṃsakas maintain that *śakti* resides in the genus (*jāti*) and in the meaning as connected with the action (*kāryānvita*).

The Naiyāyikas maintain that [the word's denotation] is an object delimited by a universal (*jāti*) which is not yet related [to other factors]. The Vaiyākaraṇas hold that it is sometimes the universal and sometimes the individual (*vyakti*). Nāgeśa, however, says that it is even sometimes the related [object]. The learned authorities state that the meaning is only the related one. Kauṇḍabhaṭṭa, in his *Padārthadīpikā*, states: "According to the Vedāntins, the power (*śakti*) of words resides in the related [meaning]. Examples of the evidence for these views are to be found in their respective treatises.

And in this regard, they say that the usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*), which is the crest-jewel among those who determine linguistic capacity (*śaktigrāhaka*), is the authoritative means (*māna*) for the theory of "denotation of the related" (*anvitābhidhāna*), as it is highly agreed upon. For instance: after hearing the sentence "Bring the cow" and so forth uttered by an elder who is the instigator (*prayojaka*), a child standing nearby observes the activity performed by the elder who is the prompted agent (*prayojya*). Having inferred that "this prompted agent has grasped a linguistic capacity (*śakti*) for the cow as being related to the act of bringing," he first grasps the capacity of the word "cow" (*go*) as referring to a cow related to the act of bringing, [and subsequently] [grasps the capacity of the word "bind" in the sentence] "Bind the cow."

Thus, having heard another sentence such as "Bring the cow," and observing the activity of an elderly man of middle age engaged in the act of tying up a cow, one grasps the word’s capacity as being connected with the act of tying—due to the omission of the portion concerning bringing—and understands that in the referent "cow" and so forth, there exists a fitness for connection with something other than what is unsuitable. Consequently, upon hearing non-verbalized sentences such as "cow," "jar," or "cloth," because there is no word therein expressive of an action, even though a specific action is not heard, one grasps the capacity of the word "cow" and so forth as denoting a cow and so forth as connected with something else that is suitable for connection. Therefore, by this reasoning, it is logical that words denote meanings already connected (anvitārtha-vācakatva).

Among the three—the primary power-possessor (*śaktigraha*), its object, and the connection between the action and its qualifiers—when the two forms, namely the action and its qualifier, are excluded according to the aforementioned method, there exists the cause consisting in the non-hearing of words expressive of distinct actions; yet, regarding the exclusion of the factor of connection (*anvaya*), there is no such cause.

When it is said, "Bring the jar," is it a blue one or a red one that is to be brought? When it is said, "Bring the blue [thing]," is it a blue jar or a red one that is to be brought? When it is said, "Bring the blue [jar]," is it a jar or a cloth? When it is said, "Bring the beautiful [thing]," is it a person or a jar? When it is said, "Bring Devadatta," is he a learned man or an unlearned man, a Brahmin or a non-Brahmin? When it is said, "Devadatta," what does he do? When it is said, "He cooks," who...?

Thus, the arising of such an inquiry (*jijñāsā*) confirms the theory of *anvitābhidhāna* (the expression of meanings as already connected). For if the meaning were not expressed as being already connected (*anvita*), such an inquiry would never have arisen. Furthermore, there is here the support of the *Mahābhāṣya* on the sūtra "kāraka" (*Pāṇini 1.4.23*). To explain: the *Bhāṣya* states, "The designation [of *kāraka*] is according to its literal meaning (*anvartha-saṃjñā*), so that it may be understood that 'it performs action (*karoti*)' is a *kāraka*. On this, Kaiyaṭa comments: "Action alone is understood from the word as that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*); the designation *kāraka* belongs to that which brings about the accomplishment of the action."

The *Udyota* states: "Since it is the action (*kriyā*) alone that is understood as the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) by means of the word, the sense is that when a term denoting a factor of action (*kāraka*) requires a related correlate for its own meaning, that very action is what becomes connected [to it]. Alternatively, the *Bhāṣya* says: "Or rather, as long as one might say 'in the action,' so long does the term 'factor of action' (*kāraka*) apply. The *Udyota* explains: "For it is that [action] which brings about the agents and so forth, endowing them with specific designations, as well as their status as objects and their very nature as producers."

In this context, when there is an expectancy for a correlate (*saṃbandhin*), that very [correlate] is connected; as stated by Uddyota, "The state of being an object (*viṣayatva*) is the state of being a generator (*janakatva*)," and according to the Bhāṣya which aims to demonstrate the linguistic derivation (*vyutpatti*) of words denoting action and factors of action (*kāraka*), words signifying action and factors of action possess meanings that are inherently related. Therefore, they denote meanings that generate a fixed mutual expectancy, and thus they are capable of expressing meanings already connected (*anvitārtha*). By this analogy, it can be asserted that all words are of such a nature, since expectancy exists everywhere.

This has been established previously. The capacity to denote an object that generates an expectancy for another object related through positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is "the denotation of a related meaning" (*anvitārthavācakatva*). Consequently, it should be understood that the theory of the denotation of the related (*anvitābhidhāna*) receives support from the *Bhāṣya* and other authorities. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Mañjūṣā*: "In some cases, words indeed bring about the cognition of their own meanings as related to others—as in 'Enter the house' (*praviśa paṇḍīm*), etc.—because at the time of grasping the power of the whole, the powers of the constituent parts are also grasped as being produced in tandem."

The meaning of the *Mañjūṣā* is that the apprehension of the expressive power (*śakti*) of words occurs with respect to a qualified object through sentences such as "Enter the house" and "Eat the ball of rice. In the *Udyota*, the same explanation is provided for "Enter the ball of rice" and other such examples found in the rule *igyaṇaḥ saṃprasāraṇam*. Thus, they maintain that the view supported by the *Bhāṣya* is that the expressive power of words resides in an object connected with something else that is fit [to be so connected]. It should be understood that the two faults—redundancy (as in the case of "two Brāhmaṇas") and the repetition of cognition—are easily avoided.

In this regard, the view that "the capacity to convey meaning" (*pratyāyakatva*) is *śakti* is the position accepted by the authors of the Bhāṣya. This is because, in the *Paspaśā* section, while defining the nature of a word (*śabda*) through the definition "that which, when uttered, brings about the cognition of things possessing a hump, a tail, hooves, a dewlap, and horns is a word," the author of the Bhāṣya also defines the very nature of *śakti* as "the capacity to convey meaning" (*arthapratyāyakatva*). Thus, he establishes that being a word consists in being a generator of the cognition of meaning, and that *śakti* is precisely this capacity to convey meaning.

By this, it is stated that the relationship between word and meaning is the relation of the signifier and the signified (*pratyāyaka-pratyāyyabhāva*). Furthermore, that relationship is eternal, because the *Vārttika* and the *Bhāṣya*—in the statement "the relationship between word and meaning is established" (*siddhe śabdārthasaṃbandhe*)—make known the eternality of the word, the meaning, and their relationship.

From the commentary by Pārthasārathi Miśra on the word *autpattika* in the sūtra "But the relationship between a word and its meaning is innate" (*Jaimini Sūtra*), which states, "The eternality of the relationship between words and their referents is expressed by the word *autpattika*," it should be understood that the eternality of those respective relationships was also intended by Jaimini and others.

In this context, the meaning of the term *autpattika* is "co-temporal with the manifestation of the word"; that is, there is only the manifestation of the word as qualified by its power of denotation (*bodhakatva-śakti*). Consequently, the intention of the *Bhāṣya* and other texts is that the relationship between word and meaning is indeed innate (*svābhāvika*). Many teachers hold this very view, for this is the position established in the *Bhāṣya* regarding the "relationship" (*saṃbandha*), since no other [type of] relationship is mentioned in the *Bhāṣya*, and because from the *Bhāṣya* statement—"that which, when uttered, brings about the comprehension of the meaning"—it is understood that the relationship is simply the capacity to convey the meaning (*arthapratyāyakatva*).

These very [ideas]—namely, the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of word, object, and cognition upon one another as stated in the *Yoga-sūtra-bhāṣya* and its commentaries on the Vibhūti-pāda, beginning with "due to the mutual superimposition of word, object, and cognition" (3.17)—cannot be accepted by grammarians (*śābdika*), because it is not mentioned in the *Mahābhāṣya*.

It should be noted that, because Vācaspati stated in his *Yogabhāṣya* that "the cognition of a single form is conditioned by convention (*saṃketa*) and not real," the identity between those two is not actual; furthermore, since he stated therein that the cognition of a single form is not real, the identity based upon it is likewise unreal. Moreover, in the *Nyāyamañjarī*, during the investigation into the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*), the status of identity as a relation (*saṃbandha*) is refuted. For further detail, see the *Darpaṇa* commentary on the *Sāra* in the section on *Śaktivāda*.

And this will be discussed somewhat later in this very work, in the investigation of the manifestation of words within verbal cognition (*śābda*). Expressions such as "Hear this meaning" (*arthaṃ śṛṇu*) must be explained through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Bhartṛhari also maintains that the relationship between words and their capacity to convey meaning is innate; we shall establish this through his own definitive verse (*kārikā*). For it is said: "That assistance which exists there, its property is inferred therein.
This is the power even of powers; this is the quality even of qualities."
Just as the capacity of the sense organs for their respective objects is beginningless,
so too is the relationship between words and their meanings a beginningless capacity.

"Like the relationship between mother and son based on the consciousness of fitness for the *samaya* [initiation] and so forth, in a word denoting a relation (*sambandha*), the relation is the fitness; fitness is [itself] a fitness.

This is the meaning: where there is a relation—which is of the nature of a service—there a property (*dharma*) consisting of the capacity to produce an effect is inferred. That relation is the power even of powers—that is, it is the power that stimulates the capacities for producing effects.

Just as a lamp, although possessing the capacity to illuminate an object, illuminates that object only through its connection with it, so too a word, although possessing an innate power, brings an object to mind only when it is connected to that object. Regarding this connection, Nāgeśa maintains that it is the superimposition of identity (*tādātmyādhyāsa*), while others hold that it is beginningless linguistic usage (*anādivyavahāra*) and the like.

Just as the sense organs—the eyes and so forth—possess an innate, beginningless capacity (*yogyatā*) or specific power (*sāmarthya*) to produce cognitions of their respective objects such as color-form, so too is the relation with objects beginningless. This capacity, which is the inherent property that delimits the capacity to generate cognition, is natural (*svābhāvika*). For this very reason, it is stated in the *Śabdaratna* on the *sarūpa-sūtra*: "Otherwise, a capacity that already exists cannot be established even by a thousand treatises on *ekaśeṣa*."

By this it is stated that the capacity of words to produce the cognition of meaning exists inherently (*svataḥ*), and is not produced by human efforts such as convention (*saṃketa*). Rather, human effort serves merely as an indicator of a power that already exists.

Regarding the term "relation" (*saṃbandha*)—that is, the "relatum-word" (*saṃbandhi-śabda*), [which is] qualified by the relation consisting in the capacity to convey meaning—with respect to "fitness" (*yogyatā*)—that is, with respect to the defining property (*avacchedaka-dharma*) of being a generator of cognition (in other words, that which determines it)—the "relation" is [one such as] *saṃketa* (convention) and so forth. "Fitness" means worthiness; the meaning is that this exists in the relation between word and object. The sense is that the relation itself is the inferent of the beginningless relation of the word’s capacity to convey the object, which resides in the word.

The cognition of fitness (*yogyatā*)—that is, the knowledge of the fitness of the relationship—and from convention (*samaya*), which is the linguistic usage of people like us. He provides an example with the words "mother" and so forth; the meaning is clear. Although differences in interpretation (*yojanā*) of these verses are seen in ancient and modern texts, the underlying intent is the same: that the power of conveying meaning is inherent (*svābhāvikī*), whereas the divine convention (*īśvara-saṃketa*) and so forth are merely its inferential indicators.

In this regard, in his *Śaktivāda* within the *Bhūṣaṇa*, Kauṇḍabhaṭṭa indicates that it is not tenable by restating the view of certain teachers and repeating their refutation. This passage of refutation, as restated by him, is as follows: "Since there is deviation—because in some cases the knowledge of convention (*saṃketa*) is the cause [of word-meaning cognition] and in others the knowledge of power (*śakti*)—not even one of these two would be such a cause. For us, however, the knowledge of that [power] is the cause precisely in its form as 'conventionality' (*saṃketatva*), so there is no deviation; and this is common to both divine convention and [human] convention."

Nor [can it be argued that] "let that [capacity] belong only to those like us, since it conforms to the necessity of specific powers, excellence, and so forth, for it is the Lord alone who is postulated as such"—because even you must admit that He is the grasper of that capacity in the context of the worldly process of creation and so on; and because you too must admit that the will of the Lord, established for both parties, is the grasper of that capacity; and because it is more cumbersome (gaurava) to postulate a distinct capacity while discarding the will of the Lord, which is established for both.

And since "correctness" (*sādhutva*) consists in being that which has been designated by such a divine convention, and its determination is derived from grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), grammar is not useless. Thus, in every respect, it is improper to postulate a distinct ontological category (*padārthāntara*); this is the summary. Therefore, the followers of the Naiyāyikas maintain that power (*śakti*) is simply the will of God.

Regarding this, the illustrious followers of Jayatīrtha state: the claim that in some cases the knowledge of convention (*saṃketa*) and in others the knowledge of power (*śakti*) is the cause [of verbal cognition] is not the established doctrine (*rāddhānta*) of the illustrious Jayatīrthas; rather, in all cases, cognition arises through innate power (*svābhāvikī śakti*), while convention is merely its indicator (*anumāpaka*). Therefore, there is no room for the aforementioned mutual deviation (*vyatireka-vyabhicāra*). For this very reason, it was stated by them in the *Paddhati* that even the relationship between words and their referents (*padārtha-sambandha*) is indeed innate.

Taking the phrase "and in the case of *sudhā* [the word for nectar], by its very nature" as the point of reference, it is stated that "[it is] indeed by its own inherent nature. The intention is that even in the worldly transaction of creation and so forth, the convention established by God (*īśvara-saṃketa*) merely serves as an indicator of the inherent power; thus, at that time, the word does not possess the capacity to convey meaning through its own independence. This has been clarified by those same authors in the *Nyāyasudhā* with the subsequent passage beginning with "Or rather" (*athavā*).

If it is asked, "In that case, why was it said: 'We do not claim that a word never possesses the capacity to convey meaning through convention; rather, in some cases there is comprehension through an innate power (*svābhāvikī śakti*), and in others through convention'?"—listen: this is a restatement of the Mīmāṃsaka's response to the objection raised by the Naiyāyika. As for the avoidance of the suspected deviation (*vyabhicāra*), it can be very easily resolved by you yourself—who accept the two modes of operation (*vṛtti*) consisting of *śakti* and *lakṣaṇā*—by introducing the qualification of the cause (*kāraṇaviśiṣṭya*) into the scope of the delimiting condition of the effect (*kāryatāvacchedakakoṭi*) and by incorporating the property of "occurring immediately after" (*svottaratva*).

If it is argued that in the texts belonging to that [school], the word *yava* is seen to be used figuratively (*gauṇatva*) for *priyaṅgu* rather than being a conventional designation (*saṃketa*), we reply: even the practice of calling it "figurative" occurs only after the conclusion of the *Yavavarāhi-Adhikaraṇa* has been established; prior to that, the intention of the Mīmāṃsakas is that the word *yava* indeed possesses a conventional designation for *priyaṅgu*.

Otherwise, since there would be no equality of status between the two forms of consensus, the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) itself could not arise; consequently, the section concerning *yava* and *varāha* would fail to arise. As for the discussion of parsimony (*lāghava*) and prolixity (*gaurava*), it is merely a "dry clamor," because the usage of Mlecchas has existed for a long time, and we do not observe the application of the term "secondary" (*gauṇa*) to them in common parlance; thus it was said that [their usage] is based on convention (*saṃketa*).

The form of God’s will is: "May this [word] become the indicator of this word-meaning. In that context, since the state of being an indicator appears as its object, it is perceived that there exists an indicatorship consisting of a natural relation distinct from [God’s] will; therefore, one must admit that a distinct *śakti* (potency) indeed exists. Consequently, the view of the venerable Jayatīrtha and other teachers alone is correct. However, the claim that "correctness (*sādhutva*) consists in being designated by God" is not tenable.

Because technical designations such as *ti*, *ghu*, and *bha* created by modern humans would lack correctness (*sādhutva*) due to their not being created by God, [one might object]. If it were said that "correctness consists in being conventional" (*saṃketitatva*), then even words like *gāvī* and so forth would incur correctness, since they too are conventional words. Therefore, one must state that correctness is a specific property (*dharma-viśeṣa*) distinct from being conventional—one manifested by the science of grammar (*vyākaraṇa-śāstra*) and serving as the cause for spiritual prosperity—or that it is simply non-corruption (*anapabhraṣṭatva*). Thus, being conventional and correctness are indeed different.

Thus, let the wise understand that this refutation of Jayatīrtha’s work—which follows its own follower—and Kauṇḍabhaṭṭa’s subsequent endorsement of it through his commentary, is based on a failure to perceive Jayatīrtha’s later text beginning with "athavā" and other treatises.
The capacity to convey meaning is the power of a word, and that too is held to be innate; that convention is merely its manifestor—this is the view accepted by many.
This very opinion is also held by the venerable sage Jayatīrtha;
yet one who considers himself a knower of logic, being ignorant of his intention, refutes this as follows:
And Kauṇḍabhaṭṭa rejoices because he merely restates the objection;
therefore, both of these should be known as superficial observers.
An Examination of Indication (Lakṣaṇā):

Now, it might be argued that grammarians are unable to maintain the consistency of linguistic usage through indication (*lakṣaṇā*), because this Nāgeśa, in his two *Mañjūṣās*, having accepted the convention that "all words denote all meanings," admitted that the word *gaṅgā* possesses primary denotative power (*śakti*) even with respect to the riverbank, and thereby rejected the function of indication. The authors of the *Bhūṣaṇa* and its commentary, the *Tatsat*, likewise reject that function. Nor should it be said that the convention "all words denote all meanings" is not approved by the author of the *Mahābhāṣya*.

It can be said that this principle is accepted in the *Vṛddhi-āhnika* of the *Mahābhāṣya*, as evidenced by the question, "Why does the substitution of *ku* not occur? For instance, while Kaiyaṭa, in explaining the intent of that question, stated the reason for the worldly nature of words such as *aij*—which serves as the basis for their being the subject matter of the grammatical treatise—in the passage beginning with "A word possessing multiple powers," he set forth the reason consisting of the eternity of the relationship between word and meaning; whereas Nāgeśa, in determining the intent of the *Pradīpa*, stated [the reason] as "because of the acceptance that all words are denoters of all meanings."

How is the doubt—that a single word can possess multiple powers of denotation—refuted? Consequently, we conclude that this position is supported by the Bhāṣya, as it is stated thus in both the *Pradīpa* and *Udyota* during the occasion of describing the intention of the question in the Bhāṣya. And thus, since even in cases of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) the matter is resolved through primary denotation (*śakti*) alone, there is no occurrence of a separate function of indication.

If this is argued, they say here: "The capacity of all [words] to denote all objects is certainly not established by universal experience; therefore, the reason stated in the passage beginning with 'because of multiple powers' (*anekaśakteḥ*) is not capable of proving their status as worldly (*laukikatva*). For this very reason, Kaiyaṭa states another reason, namely 'because of being an imitation' (*anukaraṇatvāt*) or 'because of being a genus' (*jātitvāt*). The sentence 'Even in the view that new designations are created' (*apūrvāḥ saṃjñāḥ kriyante iti pakṣe’pi*) has been cited in the *Udyota*. The phrase 'because of being a genus' (*jātitvāt*) refers to the three-fold position."

In this view, whether pro-per names (*saṃjñāśabda*) are included within genus-words (*jātiśabda*) or whether they possess a unique status (*apūrvatva*) is one point of deliberation. Furthermore, whether there is a multiplicity of powers (*anekaśaktitva*) or an eternity (*anāditva*) [of the relationship between word and meaning] is another point of deliberation. Moreover, since the possession of multiple powers is established even by the mere admission of polysemy—as in the case of words such as *hari*—the acceptance that "all words denote all meanings" is not necessary; therefore, at this stage, there is no support from the Bhāṣya for this position.

Furthermore, if the position that "all [words] denote all meanings" is adopted, then it could be argued that even those meanings being manifested are apprehended solely through [denotative] power (*śakti*); thus, the function of manifestation (*vyañjanāvṛtti*) would be rendered obsolete. This is not a desirable conclusion, because it has been established in the *Mañjūṣā* (Prakriyā-prakāśa) that the function of manifestation must necessarily be resorted to.

This is because it is the consensus of many authors of treatises—such as Mammaṭabhaṭṭa and others—who composed the *Kāvyaprakāśa*, as well as of the *ālaṅkārikas* (poetic theorists), who established the division of functions beginning with "denotation" (*abhidhā*), "indication" (*lakṣaṇā*), and so forth. Not only do others agree on this point, but even the authors of the *bhāṣyas* (commentaries) concur.

For instance, regarding the expression "how [can] Tuṣajakasya be called *patnī*?"—where it is explained that "*patnī* is used in the sense of 'like a wife' (*patnīva patnī*) because of a comparison"—the authors of the Bhāṣya, by citing the rule *patyur nayo yajñasaṃyoge* (Pāṇini 4.1.33), demonstrate that the word *patnī*, which primarily denotes a wife in connection with a sacrifice, applies to the wives of outcasts (*vṛṣala*) and others through similarity. By thus showing the application of words like *siṃha* to a boy (*māṇavaka*) and so forth through four distinct modes, they clearly consider the function of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to be entirely separate [from metaphorical identification]. Understand this, for it is evident to the learned.

Furthermore, it is stated in the *Yogavācaspatya* that "all words are capable of denoting all meanings" (Mañjūṣā 4.15). This is because of the statement in the *Mañjūṣā*: "The relationship between all objects and all words is accessible only to the knowledge of a yogi," and because of the statement in the *Paribhāṣenduśekhara*: "The acceptance that 'all [words] denote all meanings' is from the perspective of a yogi, not from our perspective. Therefore, it cannot be said that for people like us, the cognition of a riverbank (*tīra*) and so forth through words such as *gaṅgā* occurs by means of primary denotative power (*śakti*).

Since this has been stated almost entirely by Nāgeśa himself, we must certainly resort to the function of *lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication). Furthermore, even for those who accept the principle that "all words denote all meanings," their intention is simply that a word denotes various objects as delimited by distinct *śakyatāvacchedakas* (determinants of denotability), just like words such as *akṣa* or *hari*. Thus, one must say that the word *gaṅgā* conveys the current in its capacity as a current (*pravāhatvena*), and conveys the bank in its capacity as a bank (*tīratvena*); it is not the case, however, that it conveys the bank by means of an imposed current-ness (*āropitapravāhatvena*).

That being the case, it would be pointless to employ the unfamiliar term *gaṅgā* while abandoning the well-known term *tīra*. Nor can it be argued that because the intended qualities such as coolness are not perceived from the word *tīra*, "Gangahood" is superimposed upon the bank, and that through the mediation of this superimposed property (*āropitadharmapuraskāreṇa*), the perception of coolness, purifying power, and so forth arises regarding the hamlet when the bank is understood from the word *gaṅgā*. This is because your excessive desire for the principle that "all words denote all things" cannot be fulfilled by this [theory], and furthermore, because if one accepts such a superimposition (*āropa*), it ultimately results in nothing other than *lakṣaṇā* (indication).

Furthermore, for one who maintains that the bank (*tīra*) and so forth are understood through primary denotation (*śakti*), the purpose of "superimposition" (*āropa*)—as seen in the analogy "the wife is like a wife" (*patnīva patnī*), the statement in the *Bhāṣya* that [the meaning] occurs "in four ways," and the superimposition of the delimitors of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) such as proximity—is difficult to establish. Indeed, those who argue that word-meanings are conveyed by primary denotation in common usage do not resort to properties such as proximity as the basis (*nimitta*) for such understanding.

Furthermore: "What more need be said? Since the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtras 'pratyayaḥ', 'paraśca', and 'puṃyogāt' establishes that there is a lack of grammatical correctness (*asādhutva*)—even by way of secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*)—for those suffixes (*pratyaya*) and other words which are taught by the *Śāstra* for a certain meaning when they are used for another meaning, or for their own meaning when used for others; therefore, Nāgeśa’s systematic arrangement made in the *Śekhara* on the sūtra 'yena vidhiḥ' would be undermined if all [words] were to have all meanings."

Furthermore, because the rule *tadasyāstyasmin* (Pāṇini 5.2.94) mentions two meanings—*asya* ("of this") and *asmin* ("in this")—it is not the intention of the author of the Sūtras that "all [suffixes] denote all meanings. If that were his intention, then even when a suffix is prescribed for only one of those two meanings, forms such as *gomān* would denote all meanings; yet it is not the intention of the author of the Sūtras that "all [suffixes] denote all meanings. If that were his intention, then even when a suffix is prescribed for only one of those two meanings, forms such as *gomān*... [would denote all meanings].

Since the word *sarvārta* can be said to possess both meanings by virtue of its conventional usage (*samaya*), there is no purpose in employing both [the primary and secondary senses]. Consequently, in order to justify such usages as *gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ* ("a hamlet on the Ganges"), grammarians must necessarily resort to the function of indication (*lakṣaṇā*). For this very reason, the linguistic practice of grammarians—such as "the words *raghu* and *yadu* have indication (*lakṣaṇā*) with respect to their descendants, but not indication in the case of the nominal suffix"—is naturally consistent. By this, the intended meaning is that in such instances, one is dealing with a non-standard (or unestablished) denotative power (*śakti*).

The maxim of the primary and the secondary (*gauṇamukhyanyāya*) also concerns what is well-known (*prasiddha*) and what is not well-known (*aprasiddha*). To assume that the usage of terms such as "by means of indication" (*lakṣaṇayā*) follows the system of another school is indeed a strained interpretation. Consequently, it appears that the claim that there is no function of indication (*lakṣaṇāvṛtti*) is certainly not intended by the authors of the Sūtras and the Bhāṣya. Regarding the view that there is no indication, the wise who investigate the Mahābhāṣya state: "This is by no means the opinion of the authors of the Bhāṣya."

**Refutation of the Pervasiveness of Universals such as Cowness:** Regarding what was stated in the *Mañjūṣā*: "Even though all universals are pervasive, because word-meanings possess diverse potencies (*vicitra-śaktitva*), a particular word-meaning manifests only a certain universal," and so forth—by which it was asserted that universals such as cowness (*gotva*) are pervasive—the underlying intention (*āśaya*) is as follows: Because cowness and the like are pervasive, a horse-individual (*aśva-vyakti*) manifests only horseness (*aśvatva*) and not cowness; likewise, a cow-individual manifests only cowness and not horseness. Thus, through words such as "cow" (*go*), there is no cognition of horses and the like. This is because the word "cow" (*gopa-da*)... [is restricted to its own specific object].

[The word] possesses the capacity to produce the cognition of the mere universal *gotva* (cowness) as established in common worldly usage through its own denoted function; it does not, however, possess the power to produce the cognition of *aśvatva* (horseness) and so forth. In the commentary (*vyākhyāna*), it is stated that this is "due to the nature of the limiting adjunct" (*upādhisvabhāvāt*). In that regard, one must consider what constitutes that limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).

Regarding this, they say: no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is found for the claim that universals such as "cowness" (*gotva*) are all-pervasive (*vyāpaka*); rather, it is only the eternity (*nityatā*) of the universal that has been stated, not its pervasiveness. If it is argued: "Since Brahman alone is established by valid cognition, all entities are but powers (*śakti*) of Brahman and not distinct from it—as stated in the *Mañjūṣā* that all things are of the nature of Brahman's power—and since that [Brahman] is pervasive, it is thereby established that cowness and the like, which are of that same nature, are also pervasive," we reply: No.

In the view of Nāgeśa, who maintains that Brahman is devoid of attributes (*nirdharmaka*), it is impossible for the capacity (*śakti*) to belong to Him. Furthermore, as has been established previously, Vyāsa, Pāṇini, and Patañjali do not advocate non-duality (*abhedavāda*); thus, the doctrine that all entities are of the nature of Brahman’s power (*brahma-śakti-rūpa*) and that they are non-different from Brahman (*brahmānanyatva*) is not accepted by this triad of sages. By this, the explanation stating "of the genus 'cow-ness,' which is of the nature of Brahman’s existence" (*brahma-sattā-rūpāyā gotva-jāteḥ*) and so forth is also refuted.

In the systems of the three sages who maintain the existence of distinctions (*bhedavādin*), there is an absence of the nature of being Brahman in *gotva* (cowness) and the like; for one who maintains that [Brahman] is devoid of attributes (*nirdharmaka*), it is difficult to establish that being (*sattā*) is Brahman. Here, by the statement "because Brahman alone is established by valid means of knowledge" (*pramāṇasiddhatayā*), it should be understood that the claim that all entities other than Brahman, as well as universals such as *gotva*, are of the nature of Brahman’s power (*brahmaśakti*) is likewise unproven.

From the *Sarpasāhnika-bhāṣya*, which states: "That which is non-different among different things, and uncut among cut things, is called 'form' (*ākṛti*"); and from the *Sarūpa-sūtra-bhāṣya*, which states: "Or rather, because of the denotation of form; for when 'cow' is said, no specific distinction [such as] 'white' or 'blue' is understood"—one obtains precisely this meaning: that the property in the form of *gotva* (cowness) and so forth, which serves as the delimitor of the referent (*padārthatāvacchedaka*) of each respective word and is perceived as the delimitor of the denotable capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), is what is expressed by the word "genus" (*jāti*). This is the sense derived from those two *bhāṣyas*.

Because pervasiveness is not obtained. If you consider that pervasiveness belongs to the property of "cowness" (*gotva*), then, like "knowability" (*prameyatva*) and other such properties, cowness—being pervasive—would not be the delimitor of the denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) of the word "cow. Since it is impossible for a pervasive property to serve as a delimitor, some property recognized by all learned people must be established as the delimitor of the denotative capacity of the word "cow" in order to avoid over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Furthermore, that [position] is not easily established. The statement in the *Mañjūṣā-vyākhyā* regarding the illusory transformation (*vivarta*) of "cowness" and so forth into the Great Creator; the statement in the *Dhātvartha-mañjūṣā* and in the *Uddyota* on the *bhūvādi-sūtra* by Nāgeśa, namely, "the illusory transformations in the form of action belonging to Brahman—the cause of the world—whose nature is existence (*sattā*), through the assistance of *māyā*"; and such assertions must be considered with caution. Thus, because it was not stated by the three sages [Patañjali, Kātyāyana, and Pāṇini], how can a collection of doctrines not accepted by Pāṇini and others be worthy of being designated as the "established tenets of the Grammarians" (*vaiyākaraṇasiddhānta*)?

Because the meaning [of the term *bhāva*] is not described in this way in the *Niruktabhāṣya* or the *Mahābhāṣya* regarding the *Nirukta* statement "there are six modifications of *bhāva*"; because Kaiyaṭa explains it simply as "the state (*bhāva*) is action (*kriyā*)"; and because it is appropriate that the word *bhāva* in this statement—which aims to explain the different types of *bhāva* from the portion of the previously introduced statement, "verbs have action as their primary meaning, while nouns have substance as their primary meaning"—should be explained precisely as "action" (*kriyā*), especially in the context of the *bhūvādi* sūtra where roots such as *asti* (to be) and others are treated.

The intention of Patañjali is that the sixfold divisions—beginning with "birth" (*janman*)—to be described later, constitute the meaning of the word *bhāva* occurring in the statement cited to establish [the status of] action as a denoter of activity; for there is no evidence that existence (*sattā*), which is the state of being designated by the term "action" residing solely in the category of substance (*padārtha*) characterized by self-maintenance (*ātmadhāraṇa*) and serving as the cause for the conventional usage "existent as long as the substance lasts," is an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) of Brahman according to Patañjali’s system. Regarding Brahman in Patañjali’s view...

And because there is an absence of the status of being a *vivarta* cause [of speech]. Now, if it is argued that since it is stated later in the *Mañjūṣā*, "by the author of its commentary," all of this is approved by the commentator on the *Nirukta*, we say no. For in the *Niruktabhāṣya* itself, neither a sentence with such a sequence nor another sentence with this same meaning is observed; therefore, we do not trust that this is approved by the author of that commentary. Some, however, state that the meaning of the word is that there are six modifications (*vikāra*) of entities—objects such as jars and cloths. Consequently, because it would entail the pervasiveness of all universals (*jāti*), this is indeed un-Pāṇinian.

However, this must be noted: those subjects discussed here in the *Mañjūṣā*, such as the *sphoṭa* and its unity, as well as the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca-mithyātva*) and so forth, are all neither Pāṇinian nor Bādarāyaṇian. This is because no statements with such meanings are found in the works of Pāṇini or Bādarāyaṇa; furthermore, the exposition of the falsity of the world and other such views contradicts the formal proposition (pratijñā) that these are "the established tenets of the Grammarians" (*vaiyākaraṇa-siddhānta*), since the falsity of the phenomenal world and similar doctrines do not constitute the established tenets of the Grammarians.

What need is there for further elaboration? The very statement by the author of the work, "In some places it has been written according to the *Ādhānika* treatise" (Mañjarī 1), reveals that those [topics] described do not conform to Pāṇini’s system. This is because, from that statement, it is understood that the subjects were not described in accordance with the works of the ancient teachers. Enough said on this point. Furthermore, regarding the omnipresence (*vyāpitva*) of universals such as "cowness" (*gotva*) and their being the power (*śakti*) of Brahman, no evidence is found in the *Bhāṣya* for the view that all entities (*bhāva*) are of the nature of Brahman.
Regarding the subject of the sphoṭa and the falsity of the phenomenal world (prapañca-mithyātva),
neither the word of Pāṇini nor the statement of Vyāḍi is observed [to apply].
Therefore, the wise who take refuge at the feet of Vyāsa and others declare that all of this is not the intended meaning of Vyāsa and Pāṇini.

It is well known that the Naiyāyikas maintain that in every verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), there is no manifestation of the word itself. Nevertheless, having established that the word does manifest in verbal cognition, [the author] cites the consensus of Gautama by stating: "And because Gautama, in his definition of perception—'Perception is knowledge arising from the contact of a sense-organ with its object, which is non-verbalizable (*avyapadeśya*), non-erroneous, and of a determinate nature' (Nyāyasūtra 1.1.4)—by employing the qualifier 'non-verbalizable,' has accepted the manifestation of the word in verbal cognition."

In the *Mañjūṣā* (*Pra.pa.* 32.20), this should be considered: here, in this sūtra, the term "avyapadeśyam" (indescribable) means "not verbal" (*aśābdam*). At the time of the direct perception of an object, a word does not operate; a word does not produce a cognition of an object that has become the content of that direct perception. Therefore, that [cognition] is non-verbal. However, at the time of verbal comprehension, a word operates; by bringing the object that is its own content to mind, it produces that [verbal cognition]. Therefore, in that case, it possesses the nature of being verbal (*śābdatva*).

However, the intended meaning of that qualification is that [the cognition] does not have sound as its object; this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the Nyāya system, which is obtained from the sūtras and the Bhāṣya. To explain: therein, the Bhāṣya—devoted to investigating the function of the qualifier *avyapadeśya* (non-verbal)—states: "Verily, words are names for objects; through them, there is comprehension of the object. And from the comprehension of the object, there is worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*). In this regard, the knowledge of an object produced from the contact of the sense-organ with the object occurs as 'it is color' or 'it is taste,' and so forth."

Form, taste, and sound are the designations for objects; by means of these, cognition is designated—namely, one cognizes "this is form," or one cognizes "this is taste. Since [cognition] being designated by a word as a name would result in it being verbal (śābda), he says: "inexpressible" (avyapadeśyam). That cognition of an object which occurs when the relationship between word and meaning has not been employed (i.e., is unknown) is not designated by a word as its name; nor is it designated by a word as its name even when the relationship between word and meaning has been grasped, such that one knows: "this word is the name of this object."

But when that object is grasped, it does not differ from the previous cognition of the object; the cognition of that object remains exactly as it was. However, for that cognition of the object, there is no other synonymous word by which it might be designated for the sake of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*). Nor can there be linguistic usage with something that is not itself cognized. Therefore, the object to be known is indicated by means of a naming word (*saṃjñā-śabda*) functioning as an instrument (*karaṇa*), as in: "the cognition of color," or "the cognition of taste."

Thus, at the time of the cognition of the object, that denotative word is not operative; however, it is operative at the time of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*). Therefore, the cognition of the object produced by the contact of the sense-organ with the object is "without words" (*aśabda*). Here, the portion ending with *yāvadartham* constitutes the statement of the prima facie objection (*samādāna*), while the portion beginning with *yāvadartham* and ending with *yāvadavadhāraṇe* constitutes the resolution (*samādhāna*). The compound *yāvadartham* is an indeclinable compound (*avyayībhāva*) formed according to the rule *yāvadavadhāraṇe*.

The analysis of the compound is "as many as are the meanings" (*yāvanto'rthāḥ*). The underlying point is this: because of the identity (*tādātmya*) between word and meaning, in every instance where a meaning is cognized, there is the manifestation of that meaning as conjoined with its expressive word. Consequently, just as in verbal cognition (*śābda*), where the status of being verbal (*śābdatva*) arises because the meaning conjoined with the word appears as the object (*viṣaya*), so too in perception (*pratyakṣa*), since the object qualified by the word appears [as the object], it would possess the status of being verbal by virtue of having a word as its object.
If one asks, "Let it be so; what loss is there for us?"—the answer is that it would not constitute a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

The intention of the *Samādhānagrantha* is as follows: word and meaning are in reality distinct. It cannot be said that there is an identity between them, nor that such identity is superimposed upon them, because there is no resulting effect [from such a view]. Therefore, in no cognition whatsoever does there appear an object conjoined with a word, but rather the object alone, for it is experienced exactly in that way.

If it is objected that, in this case, because the [object] appears as verbal (*śābda*), it would not be designated as "verbal" (*śābda*), we reply: being a verbal object (*śabdaviṣayakatva*) is not the determinant for such a designation; rather, it is being an object presented by words (*śabdopasthāpitārthaviṣayakatva*). Since that [latter condition] exists there, it is so designated. Thus, in perception (*pratyakṣa*), the object is merely the thing in contact with the sense organ, and not a thing presented by words (or connected with words).

Therefore, since it does not possess the nature of verbal testimony (*śābdatva*), its status as a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) is well-established. This point was stated by the author of the Bhāṣya himself when he said: "At the time of the manifestation of the object, that word of the designation (*samākhyā-śabda*) is not employed; however, at the time of conventional usage (*vyavahāra-kāle*), it is employed. And thus, the claim that Gautama and others agree with the view that [this cognition] has the nature of verbal testimony within the realm of verbal testimony is not tenable.

By this—namely, by citing the passage from Vācaspati Miśra’s commentary on the *Bhāṣya* which states that "verbalness (*śābdatva*) consists precisely in having a verbal object for perception, and not in being produced by words"—the claim that "having a verbal object" is what Vācaspati intended by "verbal cognition" (*śābda*) is refuted.

Furthermore, since both of those texts are devoted to describing the nature of the subterranean waters (*audakāśaya*) and thus lack the status of being definitive philosophical treatises (*siddhāntagrantha*), Vācaspati has extensively refuted the identity of word and meaning (*śabdārthatādātmya*) in this very sūtra within the *Nyāyavārtikatātparyaṭīkā*; moreover, this [identity] is not accepted by the Naiyāyikas themselves.

Merely because it is stated that "the word [as a means of knowledge] does not have [the object] as its object in perception," why must that [object] be admitted in verbal cognition? Gautama, moreover, never spoke with such a loud voice anywhere that "it appears in verbal cognition. Jayanta Bhaṭṭa, the crest-jewel of Naiyāyikas, in the *Nyāyamañjarī* (1.ā.), while explaining the purpose of the term *avyapadeśya*, and in other sections as well, rejects the position that the word exists in verbal cognition. Therefore, how could this [position] be considered the intention of Gautama?

Furthermore, since it is stated that "the individual, the configuration, and the universal are the word-meanings" (*Gau.Sū.* 2.2.68), and because sound (*śabda*) is not included among these three, the claim that its manifestation in verbal cognition occurs as something outside the scope of word-function (*padavṛtti*)—as agreed upon by Gautama—is not tenable. It is not Gautama’s established doctrine that sound is also an object of word-function; rather, this is the view of Bhartṛhari, who stated: "It is both the object of knowledge and the knower."

However, the authors of the philosophical treatises do not consider it correct that there is a manifestation (*bhāna*) in verbal cognition even of that which is not an object of the linguistic function (*vṛtti*). If there were a manifestation even of what is not an object of the linguistic function, then upon being told "bring the jar," there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that space (*ākāśa*), which is presented through the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), would also manifest in the verbal cognition.

Furthermore, the grammarians' tenet that "in verbal cognition there is the manifestation of the word" (*śābde śabdabhānam*) is itself non-Vedic (*anārṣa*), since they do not cite the words of sages such as Pāṇini, but instead quote as their authority the non-Vedic statement from the *Vākyapadīya*: "There is no cognition in the world that does not follow from the accompaniment of a word. Consequently, for the wise, determining the intention of the sages by relying on a tenet that is non-Vedic is not pleasing to the mind. If it is argued that because a word is remembered through its meaning, that remembered word manifests in the verbal cognition, we say: no.

For it might follow that even place, time, and persons would appear [in verbal cognition], since they too can be remembered at some time. Furthermore, the position that [the word] appears as something inferred (*unnītabhānapakṣa*) has been rejected by Nāgeśa in his *Mañjuṣā* (p. 1), citing Dinakarī’s *Śabdakhaṇḍa*, which states: "That position is not accepted by everyone. Moreover, such a hypothesis would contradict the words of Gautama. Therefore, Nāgeśa’s statement—that "Gautama accepts the appearance of the word in verbal cognition"—is not tenable. Furthermore, in cases of imitation (*anukaraṇa*) and in the case of technical names (*saṃjñā*), it is not appropriate to assume the word itself [to be the object of cognition] in that manner.
The inclusion of the qualification "inexpressibility" (*avyapadeśyatva*) regarding perception is because that [perception] is expressed by means of words that are associated with the object's form.
This serves to dispel the doubt that it would merely be verbal in nature;
therefore, by means of that [scripture], the establishment of his desired object will certainly not occur.
Gautama did not explicitly state that sound appears within sound;
nor did the authors of the Bhāṣya and others say so. Therefore, that is not their view.
An Examination of the Fact that the Manifestation of the Word in Cognition is Not Accepted by the Three Sages:

Furthermore, the claim that "the word manifests in verbal cognition as well as in other types of cognition," which is stated in the *Mañjūṣā* and other works, is not accepted by the three sages (*munitraya*), because they have not stated it so. Now, one might argue that the rule *svaṃ rūpam* (Pāṇini 1.1.68) and its commentary (*bhāṣya*) are authoritative on this point, since the author of the *Udyota* explains the *bhāṣya* on that rule—namely, "And his comprehension [of the meaning] is preceded by the word"—as "the comprehension of the meaning has the word as its qualifier. And indeed, there is the state of having the word as a qualifier.

If it is argued that this means "having sound as its qualifier" (śabdaprakārakatvam), and that just as potness (ghaṭatva) and so forth possess the status of qualifiers, sounds likewise possess that status, such that every cognition has sound as its qualifier—this being the meaning [of the Bhāṣya] and in agreement with the three sages (Patañjali, Kātyāyana, and Pāṇini)—we say no. This is because that meaning is not obtained through the literal force of the words in that Bhāṣya, and because Kaiyaṭa has not explained the Bhāṣya in that manner. If one asks, "What then is the meaning of the Bhāṣya? it is said: The meaning of the Bhāṣya is that "the hearer's comprehension of the object is preceded by the knowledge of the word."

For instance, it is universally acknowledged by all the world that the comprehension of an object is preceded by the knowledge of the word. Furthermore, when a word has been employed and understood, one gives a reply such as, "The object is known; we shall perform the action according to the injunction. Therefore, in accordance with worldly linguistic usage, words like *rāja* and *śvaśura* mentioned in rules such as *rāja-śvaśurād-yat* (Pāṇini 4.1.137) and *agneḥ ḍhak* (Pāṇini 4.2.33), just like words such as *paśu*, *apatya*, and *devatā*, are directed solely toward the meaning (*arthapara*).

Furthermore, regarding the technical operations (*kārya*) prescribed by the treatise, since suffixes such as *yat* and others apply after a nominal stem (*pratipadika*), and because there is a commonality among words denoting "king" (*rājan*) and so forth, the suffix *yat* and others would consequently apply [to all of them]. Nor should it be argued that, by virtue of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), only the word "king" (*rājan*) and its synonyms—which are present as the cause—is grasped and not any other [synonym], for there is no evidence (*pramāṇa*) to rely upon such a principle.

Therefore, in order to dispel the doubt that it is impossible to say "only its own form (*svarūpa*) is grasped," Pāṇini begins the rule *svaṃ rūpam*. Its meaning is as follows: in cases such as *rāja-śvaśurāt* [Pāṇ. 4.1.137], regarding the word *rājan* which has been extended by the suffix *ic*, its own (*svam*)—that is, its form (*rūpam*) as qualified by its own specific meaning—is what is intended.

The nature of the word consists of sounds composed of phonemes similar to those specific phonemes that constitute the uttered sound. Here, the term *saṃjñā* (name) refers to the word to be understood; the word *pada* is used in the accusative case with the suffix *aṅ*; and the word *sva* (own) means its own referent. The word *rūpa* (form) refers to a word characterized by a particular sequence [of phonemes], because such is obtained from the Bhāṣya. And thus—the implication is that in rules such as *rāja-śvaśurāt*, the application of *yat* and other suffixes occurs only from words like *rājan* when they possess meaning, and not from the suffixes *in* and so on, nor from meaningless elements; in this way, the *arthavat-paribhāṣā* (the maxim that a meaningful element is significant) is established by this very [principle].

Alternatively, this is the view of the Vārttika-bhāṣya: it is universally accepted that the cognition of a word is the cause for the presentation of its meaning.
