Consequently, since a word known as the cause for the presentation of the meaning is proximate, there is no reason to abandon it and grasp another word that is remote; thus, because there is no reason to abandon the word "rāja" (king) and grasp other synonymous terms that are remote, the understanding arises from the very word "rāja" etc., which is presented as the cause.

When the formation of *yad* and other suffixes begins to operate, Kātyāyana and Patañjali maintain that the very non-observation of *yad* and other suffixes after words such as *in* and others serves as the proof for the principle of proximity (*pratyāsatti*); thus, they hold that this particular rule need not be commenced. Accordingly, it is stated in the Vārttika and Bhāṣya: "Or rather, there is no comprehension of meaning preceded by the word; therefore, there is the exclusion of the meaning"—this is the Vārttika.

"Or rather, this purpose does not exist. Why? Because the comprehension of an object is preceded by the word; therefore, it is preceded by the word even when someone is called by name. And when that name is not perceived by him, he asks, 'What did you say?'—for his comprehension is preceded by the word," so says the Bhāṣya.

This is the meaning: the purpose of the word *etad* in this context is to exclude [the application of] technical designations (*saṃjñā*) [or, alternatively, to exclude synonyms and the like]. Taking the word *hu* in the Vārttika to indicate what is well-known in the world, he states that by way of a positive example: "For [the cognition of] an object is preceded by the word. This means that it is established in the world that the comprehension of an object is preceded by the knowledge of the word. Regarding the stated point, he states the negative example (*vyatireka*): "Therefore... He explains its meaning with the words: "That which is not... (i.e., that which is new).

The meaning is this: when a person in the world, being called by someone, does not properly perceive the sound uttered by the person calling him, he inquires, "What did you say? By this, the negative example (*vyatireka-dṛṣṭānta*) is stated—that in the absence of the cognition of the word, there is no comprehension of the object. The word "iti" here functions as a particle of conclusion; thus, because of the existence of these positive and negative examples, the sense is established. For this hearer, "comprehension" (*saṃpratyaya*) refers to the arising of the cognition of the object.

"And preceded by word" means precisely "preceded by the cognition of the word. The very fact that [cognition] is preceded by the cognition of the word, which was asserted [in the sūtra], has been restated here. On this basis, the claim that the Bhāṣya intends to provide another argument by means of the qualification "of the word" is to be considered doubtful; for such a meaning cannot be obtained from the literal sense of the words. This is because, just as the author of the Bhāṣya established that the cognition of an object is preceded by the cognition of the word, it is improper to assume such a meaning [for the present passage] when he has not provided any justification for the qualification "of the word."

Nor should it be argued that one must accept the manifestation of a word as a qualifier (*prakāratayā bhāna*) because from expressions such as "ghaṭaḥ kalaśaḥ" (the pot is a jar) there arises a cognition of non-difference; otherwise, such a cognition would not occur due to the absence of a difference between the delimiting properties (*avacchedaka-dharma*). This is because of the linguistic rule (*vyutpatti*) that "a difference between those properties is the cause for a cognition of non-difference delimited by those properties, with respect to the relation of being the delimitation of the subject-property (*dharmitāvacchedakatā-sambandha*). For [if this were necessary], the cognition would be impossible in cases such as "kākaḥ kākaḥ pikaḥ pikaḥ" (a crow is a crow, a cuckoo is a cuckoo).

Nor should it be said that the consequence of [the need for] secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is a fault; for it has been stated in the *Mañjūṣā* and other works that, according to the grammarians' view, there is no such thing as secondary indication at all.

Furthermore, the theory that words manifest [their meanings] in verbal cognition (*śābda-bhāna-vāda*) has been refuted in detail within the *Śaktivāda* section of the *Darpaṇa* commentary on the *Sāra*, beginning with the words "here they say" (*atra vadanti*). Moreover, in the view of this proponent of the non-difference between the two (the word and its meaning), since both appear as one and the same, how could the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣya-viśeṣaṇa-bhāva*) be established? Furthermore, since it was established at the outset of the *Mañjūṣā* that "while their difference is real, their non-difference is superimposed," even non-difference is not real.

How can an unreal non-difference serve as the determiner of the object, given that it is only the object conjoined with the word that appears? Furthermore, even if one person has such a determination (*adhyavasāya*) regarding those two [the word and the object], it cannot be said that others will have such a cognition based on that person's determination; for there is no restrictive rule that because one person is mistaken, others must necessarily be so as well.

Furthermore, with respect to appearing as a qualifier (*prakāratayā bhānam*), the cause is the apprehension (*upasthiti*) produced by a function (*vṛtti*) assigned to a word, and not the cognition of identity (*abhedabuddhi*). This is well-established: in cases other than those involving both technical names (*saṃjñā*) and imitations (*anukaraṇa*), there is no status as an object of apprehension produced by a function for a word.

Furthermore, since the non-difference of word and meaning is refuted by Śaṅkarācārya in the *Brahma-sūtra* 1.3.33 (*bhāvaṃ tu bādarāyaṇaḥ*) with the statement, "The mere word cannot be the nature of the object because of the difference between word and meaning," and since it was likewise refuted by Vācaspatimiśra in the *Brahma-sūtra* 1.3.10 (*akṣaramambarāntadhṛteḥ*) with the argument, "Non-difference between word and meaning is not tenable due to the difference in their essential natures, the difference in their means [of cognition], and the difference in their causal efficiency," such non-difference is not supported by reason.

In the *Śaktivāda*, the theory of the non-difference between word and meaning (*śabdārthayor abhedavādaḥ*) has been refuted in many ways by [the author] with the words, "But that is not correct," and so forth. Furthermore, in the dialogue between Nārada and Sanatkumāra, it is stated: "I am indeed a knower of mantras, but not a knower of the Self; whatever you have studied here is merely name" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 7.1.3). Since the Lord of the Vedas has thus taught that even Nārada—who was a knower of all the sciences including the Ṛgveda and others—lacked knowledge of the Self, the difference between word and meaning is established by the Śruti itself.

The identity (*tādātmya*) between the word and its referent is contradicted by scripture. If there were such an identity, then it could be said that when the knowledge of the word arises, the knowledge of the Self also arises; consequently, the statement "he does not know the Self" and the restrictive expression "this is merely a name" would be inconsistent. Furthermore, it is clear to everyone—even according to the arguments of Nāgeśa and others—that this [identity] does not exist, as they maintain that "non-difference is merely superimposed."

If it is argued that the identity (*tādātmya*) of word and object is necessary for the justification of the *Praśastabhāṣya*—"What is that which possesses a dewlap... that is the word"—and that otherwise the question and conclusion—"The object in the form of a horn, that is the word"—would be untenable, we say no.

Since we observe in the world the use of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in expressions such as "this is a cow" and "this is white," one might suppose that there is identity (*tādātmya*) between those two; however, this commentary—being in the form of a question and its restatement—is not intended to establish identity between word and meaning. Furthermore, even by the explanatory passage providing the resolution, "No, he says: that which is called 'substance' [is the referent]," it is precisely the cognition of identity that is being precluded.

Consequently, the commentator (the Bhāṣyakṛt) has dispelled the questioner’s delusion regarding identity (*tādātmya*). It should be understood that the purport of the section beginning with "If, then... (*yatarhi*)—which consists of a series of questions and answers—is precisely this: the Bhāṣyakṛt does not accept an identity between word and meaning. In common usage, such as in the expressions "This is a cow" (*gaur ayam*) or "This is white" (*śuklo 'yam*), the meaning is simply "this is the denotatum of the word *go*" or "this is the denotatum of the word *śukla*," and not that "it is non-different from the word *go*. Furthermore, as stated in the *Mañjūṣā*: "The sun rises copper-red and sets copper-red;
in prosperity and in adversity, the great remain uniform in nature."

Regarding this, [the opponent claims]: "The author of the *Prakāśa* states that such a cognition does not arise without the word 'tāmra,' because the cognition has the word as its qualifier. This is not correct, for the sentence beginning with "the word 'tāmra'" is not even found there; furthermore, the meaning "cognition having the word as its qualifier" cannot be obtained from the *Prakāśa* text in that passage.

For instance, regarding that [point], there is the following statement: "But in that case, if one were to say, 'It is precisely this red object that sets,' then that very same meaning, which was already conveyed by another word, appears as if it were a different meaning and thereby obstructs comprehension. The word *sthagayati* means "it blocks" (*niruṇaddhi*). It does not produce comprehension instantaneously. And "blocking" consists in the non-production of a presentation due to a lack of confidence. For this very reason, the commentary on the *Pradīpa* explains the phrase from the *Prakāśa* as "it would intervene in the comprehension" (*pratītiṃ vyavadadhīta*).

The intended meaning regarding the lamp (*prakāśa*) and the light (*pradīpa*) is as follows: Just as a particular meaning, having been conveyed by a specific word in a preceding sentence, is conveyed by that very same word in a subsequent sentence and thus becomes an object of immediate cognition—whereas that same meaning, when conveyed by a different word, does not do so, but rather involves a delay because it is perceived as if it were something else—the delay occurs because the cognition "this is that very same meaning" arises only after the cessation of the initial [mis]perception.

The use of another word is the cause for the perception of difference, while the knowledge of synonymy is the cause for its cessation; thus, unable to endure delay, the poet employed that very same word again.

For this very reason, both [the author and the commentator] employed the words *eva* and *eva*. If the author of the *Prakāśa* had intended for the word to function as a qualifier (*prakāraka*), then, given that the word *rakta* is used and its quality appears as a qualifier, the meaning would be distinct; consequently, the statement "it is that very same [thing]" (*sa eva*) and the statement "as if it were something else" (*anya iva*) would be inconsistent, because the difference [between the two cases] would be evident due to the difference in qualifiers. Furthermore, the absence of intensity (*utseka*) and lack of intensity (*anutseka*) is the cause of the single form, not the status of being a qualifier of a word.

The wise declare that the single-mindedness of the great—namely, the total absence of pride and the like in both prosperity and adversity—is the defining characteristic of a Mahāpuruṣa. Furthermore, if one accepts that a cognition possesses the property of having multiple word-forms as its qualifier (*padaprakārakatva*), then the statement that "repetition" (*punarukti*) is a defect does not hold together; for authors such as the *Kāvyaprakāśa*-composer maintain that repetition occurs only when another word with the same meaning is employed.

If the status of a word as a qualifier (*prakāratva*) is accepted in the manner stated by Nāgeśa, then—since the meaning differs due to the difference in its delimiters (*avacchedaka*)—the absence of synonymy (*samānārthakatva*) would not result in that being a fault. Furthermore, the maxim widely accepted by many, namely "that which has already been expressed need not be used" (*uktārthānām aprayogaḥ*), would become devoid of scope; for if each respective word were a qualifier, the meanings would differ, and thus a word whose meaning has already been expressed (*uktārthaka-śabda*) would be virtually non-existent.

By this, the statement in the *Sūtraśekhara* on the rule *svaṃ rūpam*—"of the word *rājan*, which appears as the qualifier (*prakāra*) in the cognition produced by that [word]"—as well as the statement in the *Mañjūṣā* during the investigation of the meaning of the ablative case—"because there is only the object qualified by the word"—and the similar assertions of other grammarians, are all to be considered doubtful, since they lack a foundational statement (*mūlavacana*) expressing such a meaning.

If it is argued that—since awareness lacks the word as its qualifier (prakāra)—there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of an after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) such as "the word *kalaśa*" for one who has grasped the word-potency (*śakti*) of the word *ghaṭa*, because the referent of the word is one and the same; whereas if the word were the qualifier, there would be no such consequence because of the difference between the referents of the words *ghaṭa* and *kalaśa*—we reply: Just as the arising of awareness from synonymous words is prevented by incorporating the condition of "being immediately followed by itself" (*svāvyavahitottaratva*), so too can such an after-cognition be easily prevented.

Furthermore, for one who has grasped the word-potency (*śakti*) of the word "ghaṭa," there never occurs at any time, in the moment immediately following that, a subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) in the form "kalaśa" (jar). This is because the grasping of the potency of that specific word is a cause for such a reflective awareness, and in the present case, that [cause] is absent.

If it is argued that since the *Ratnagrantha* on the rule *kṛttaddhita* states that "even a word is meaningful when it is the object of a grammatical operation" (*vṛttiviṣaya*), and thus asserts that a word itself can be the denotatum (*śakya*), it is logical for that word also to appear as a qualifier (*prakāra*), because it is necessary for whatever is presented as the denotatum to appear in some way as the meaning; we reply: no, for the meaning of that passage is that in cases of imitation (*anukaraṇa*), the word itself is the denotatum.

Furthermore, if a word were to appear as a qualifier (*prakāra*), then because there would necessarily be no apprehension of the difference between the respective meanings and their respective words as qualifiers, there would be no such thing as a "word having the same meaning. Consequently, the *Vārttika*—"even for those [words] that have the same meaning, provided they are distinct"—along with its commentary (*bhāṣya*), as well as the *Manoramā* and other works which demonstrate how the meaning of the *Vārttika* is obtained through the very letters of the *Sūtra*, would be rendered untenable. Moreover, it is said: "There is no cognition in the world that is devoid of the accompaniment of words;
every cognition appears as if permeated by speech."
Just as light possesses two powers— namely, the power of being perceived and the power of making things perceptible—
so too do these two exist separately in all words.

However, one should discern that such statements as "the words of Hari" (Harīvacana) are not the words of the three sages (Trimunivacana), and thus are non-Vedic (*anārṣa*). Since it is stated in the *Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya* that "as in the words of Hari," it is understood that the state of being permeated by words (*śabdānuviddhatva*) is real. As for the restrictive interpretation of the term "only permeated" (*anuviddhameva*) regarding the aesthetic flavor (*kalā*), that is indeed questionable; for such an interpretation lacks the support of the *Bhāṣya* and other authoritative works. Therefore, it cannot be maintained that verbal cognition (*śābda*) has words as its qualifying mode (*prakāraka*).

The illustration of light is intended merely to show that the nature of being perceived exists in the case of imitation, while the nature of being an imitator exists elsewhere; it does not intend to imply that both exist simultaneously in a single locus. Thus is its purport.

Furthermore, regarding the sūtra *svaṃ rūpam*, Kaiyaṭa—having taken the portion of the Bhāṣya beginning with "the object associated with mantras and the like," and having taken the portion beginning with "and association belongs only to that which is permeated by the word"—explained it as: "The sense is that such [an object] does not exist, according to the statement of Hari. Then, he interpreted the intention of the Bhāṣya differently, stating: "Others say that 'being associated' means being associated by virtue of being capable of being denoted by that [word]."

In this regard, the following should be noted: by citing the statement of Hari as authority for the meaning stated by Kaiyaṭa, and then describing a different intention (*bhāvāntara*) in the Bhāṣya due to a lack of confidence in that meaning, it is effectively asserted that "pervasion by words" (*śabdānuviddhatva*) is not intended by the three Munis. In doing so, one must consider whether the author of the Mañjūṣā—having established in the *Śaktivāda* section of the *Sābda* chapter that pervasion by words applies to all suffixes (*pratyaya*)—is thereby making the Bhāṣya inconsistent. The Bhāṣyakāra did not say, "The word appears in the cognition. Furthermore, the statement "There is no cognition [of an object] without [the presence of] a word" is not a teaching of Pāṇini.
Therefore, one who asserts that there is an appearance of words within verbal cognition in accordance with that [view] would not deserve any reckoning among the followers of Pāṇini.
The refutation of the view that words possess a non-conceptual nature regarding their referents:

Here, in the *Mañjūṣā*, it is stated in the section concerning the reality of things (*vastutattva*)—specifically regarding the meaning of nominal stems—that because conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is impossible [with respect to the ultimate], the presentation of various positions such as "one, two, three, four, or five" in relation to a thing indicates that these are not ultimately real, being intended merely for the sake of establishing conventional usage (*vyavahāra*). Thus, the unreality of things is shown.

To this it is replied: "In such a Lord Bhava, whose existence has been established through experience since the beginning of *saṃsāra*, how could there be any doubt? Thus Udayanācārya, at the commencement of his work *Kusumāñjali*, after restating various alternative views, says:
"He whom the Sāṃkhyas worship as *Sāṃkhya*, the Vedāntins as *Brahman*, the Buddhists as *Buddha*, and those skilled in logic (*pramāṇakuśala*) as the 'Agent' (*kartṛ*)."
May that Hari, the Lord of the three worlds— whom the followers of the Jaina teaching call the Arhat and whom the Mīmāṃsakas call Karma— grant you your desired fruit.

Thus, by way of a brief restatement of the fact that Hari is the subject of such attributes as being Śiva, made by a certain crest-jewel among learned poets; by the arising of conceptual alternatives such as "qualified" (*saguṇa*) or "unqualified" (*nirguṇa*) regarding Brahman—which is the ultimate reality—for those desiring to know Brahman; by the arising of alternatives such as "Is this a post or a person? regarding an object present before one in the world; and by the authors of the treatises (*śāstra*) delineating conceptual alternatives as a subordinate part of their effort to establish the intended meaning as their own final conclusion (*siddhānta*), the author of the Sūtras, Pāṇini, [said]: *ava...*

By the mention of the names of ancient teachers in rules such as *sphoṭāyanasya* (Pāṇini 6.1.123), by indicating various alternative views regarding grammatical operations such as elision (*ava-hādi*), by the presentation of both the positions of injunction (*vidhi*) and restriction (*niyama*) in the Bhāṣya on *vipratiṣedhe paraṃ kāryam* (Pāṇini 1.4.2), by the prescription of heavy or light punishments and expiations in the Dharmaśāstras according to differences in time, place, age, and condition, and by the presentation of the alternatives of rice (*vrīhi*) and barley (*yava*), or the taking and not taking of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup, in the Pūrva-mīmāṃsā;

It is well known to all that it is the established style of the authors of treatises to present various alternatives and diverse positions on a single subject in order to test the validity of their own system; for instance, in medical science, by demonstrating multiple treatments for a single disease, and in the *Gītā*, in the twelfth chapter, by presenting numerous means such as devotion to the Lord (*bhagavaccittatva*) which accomplishes grace from the Lord capable of delivering one across the ocean of worldly existence. Thus, the presentation of options and various sides regarding a single topic is intended for the refinement of one's own doctrine.

In that case, the experience of the non-existence of certain things would not arise for anyone; and since unreal objects are unfit for investigation, the very treatise devoted to their investigation would be rendered useless. Indeed, one does not observe in the world any prudent person who, acting with foresight, would proceed to investigate an unreal thing such as a rabbit's horn.

One might object: "Since the absence of [the notions of] singularity and so forth pertains to the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*), it resides in that [meaning] and not in denotative capacity (*vācakatva*); therefore, because it does not reside in the subject (*pakṣavṛttitvābhāva*), it cannot serve as a probans for proving the unreality of denotative capacity—why then was this fault not stated? This objection should not be raised.

It can be answered that, upon the conclusion of the dilemma—namely, whether denotative capacity, in its relation to the object determined by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), is determined by one object or by two objects—it is impossible to establish that conceptual construction resides in denotative capacity; thus, that fault was not mentioned.

This is the meaning: in the aforementioned instances—such as in the mention of the attribute of being "dark" in the phrase "some imagined it to be a mark" (*aṅkaṃ ke'pi śaśaṅkire*); in the ritualistic discourse of the Mīmāṃsakas regarding karma and Brahman, such as "Does the word *agni* in 'one offers the *agnihotra*' refer to the name of a rite, or does it denote the deity Agni? Is the word *ākāśa* (ether) intended for the well-known physical ether, or for the Supreme Self?"; and in common worldly usage, such as "Is it a post or a person?"—in all these cases, with respect to anything whatsoever...

Since the knowledge of unreality does not arise regarding an object until after [its existence] has been established, conceptualization and the like do not prove that an object is unreal. Furthermore, the authors of the scriptures do not propound an unreal meaning within their respective treatises; rather, in various places, the intellect of the wise arises with the thought that no other alternative is possible in the given context.

Even Śrī Vyāsa and Pāṇini did not state an unreal meaning anywhere in their independent works; therefore, the claim that Vyāsa and Pāṇini spoke of only an illusory (māyika) meaning is not to be trusted by authoritative persons—enough said.
In the world, the cognition of non-existence does not arise with respect to objects of conceptual construction;
therefore, conceptual construction cannot establish the non-existence of real entities.
Therefore, those who know the reality of things say that regarding a single object,
one cannot be capable of imagining both its conceptual construction and its non-existence simultaneously.
Regarding the refutation of the claim that the words of the seers (*ṛṣi*) are not ultimately real:

if it is asserted in the *Mañjūṣā*—"Even though the vision of the seers concerns reality, because practical transaction (*vyavahāra*) is impossible with a thing that is [merely] real, they act in various ways during the course of worldly transaction as if they had not seen reality; therefore, one should not consider the truth of words and word-meanings even on the basis of their speech"—one should be satisfied by understanding the literal meaning of this through the very explanations provided by its [the Mañjūṣā's] own author.

From this, everyone is able to understand that Nāgeśa considers all the works of the Ṛṣis (*ārṣa-grantha*) to be expositions of non-ultimate reality (*apāramārthika-vastu*). This being the nature of the works of the Ṛṣis themselves, what need is there to mention the compositions of human authors (*pauruṣeya-grantha*)? And thus, his position is that even all those [human] works are indeed non-ultimate.

To this it is replied: if the term "darśana" (philosophical system) here were taken to mean "knowledge," then because those [systems] would establish objects contrary to what has been known, the treatise [containing them] would lack authority (*aprāmāṇya*) due to its not being rooted in a reliable person (*āpta*). On the other hand, if by that term one were to refer to the scripture itself, then it would be contradictory for a single philosophical system to have as its object both a reality that is the true nature of things and an object that is not so.

Nor should it be argued that there is no contradiction because the purport of those texts is that Brahman alone is real while everything other than it is unreal; for such a statement is not found in those respective systems of philosophy (*darśana*). In any system where Brahman is propounded, it is not established therein that the means of knowledge for perceiving anything other than Brahman are unreal. Furthermore, in systems such as those of Jaimini and others, there is no exposition of Brahman at all. Thus, such a division is untenable. Therefore, everything propounded in all the scriptures is indeed [real] for that [system].

Furthermore, [this applies] to the *smṛtis* composed by sages such as Manu and Yājñavalkya; to the two *itihāsas*, the glorious *Rāmāyaṇa* and *Mahābhārata*; to the *purāṇas* such as the glorious *Bhāgavata*; to the *kalpasūtras* composed by great seers such as Baudhāyana, Āpastamba, Kātyāyana, Āśvalāyana, and Gobhila; to the Sāṃkhya, Yoga, and other systems composed by Kapila, Patañjali, and others; to the *Vākyapadīya*; to the work *Paramārthasāra*; to the *Caraka-saṃhitā*; and to Patañjali’s *Mahābhāṣya*.

It is truly remarkable that, having established the fact that the words of various great sages and commentators on their respective texts—who follow those very traditions—do not convey the true meaning, he nevertheless cites passages from such Smṛti works as the *Bhārata*, *Bhāgavata*, *Harivaṃśa*, and *Mānava* as authoritative evidence for proving his desired doctrine of the *sphoṭa* and other categories, thereby establishing the entire range of objects of knowledge such as the *sphoṭa*.

This is what must be understood: by the same logic, my own treatise would also be a propounder of what is not ultimate reality (*apāramārthika*). If it were certain that my treatise was rooted in a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that does not reveal reality (*atattvāvedaka*), how could a sense of its authority arise in the minds of discerning people? Or how could there be confidence in my words, the conviction of my being a reliable authority (*āpta*), the perception of my own work as something to be adopted, or how could the best of scholars, my fellow monastics, [accept me] in the midst of the assembly?

The assembly of scholars would read [the texts] without even considering whether they were composed by him; thus, the virtuous conclude that "this person spoke in such a manner. If all the words of the sages (*ṛṣi*) were to convey non-ultimate meanings and the sages themselves were untruthful speakers, then how could the ultimate reality of Brahmā and the others be established according to this view? One must consider the following: if the treatises expounding the *Brahmasphoṭa*, as well as the *Paramārthasāra* which teaches the unity of the Self, and works such as the *Caraka-saṃhitā*, were likewise [non-ultimate], then how could the ultimate reality of Brahmā and the rest be proven?
[In this system,] the word of the sages concerns illusory objects, and the sages are untruthful speakers.
By speaking thus, through the power of the words of this speaker of untruth, this—
How can this established meaning in the form of *sphoṭa* be considered authoritative?
This "scholar" merely defiles the assembly of the best of sages.
Thus, by wise people who take refuge in the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), this should be well-reflected upon:
how was it that he was counted among the ranks of scholars by the learned in the midst of the assembly?
The refutation of the claim that great scholars are mistaken:

Here, in the *Mañjūṣā*, by the passage stating, "It should be understood that in the treatises of the Neo-Naiyāyikas, the investigation into the meanings of roots and suffixes is due to the delusion of their reality, because their internal organs are permeated by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of grammar," [it is asserted] that Pāṇini and others are opponents of the non-real meanings of roots and suffixes; and that the authors of works such as the *Maṇi* and the *Dīdhiti*—namely Gaṅgeśa Upādhyāya, Raghunātha Bhaṭṭācārya, and others—who proceeded to investigate those meanings based upon that [grammar], are themselves mistaken.

By stating "those [words] ending in case-suffixes" (*tad eva vibhaktyantāḥ*) and "the referent of a word consists of the individual, the form, and the genus" (*padam vyaktyākṛtijātayaḥ padārthaḥ*), Gautama has indeed implied the unreality of the meanings of stems and suffixes; yet, by not explicitly stating their unreality in his own work, Nāgeśa reveals both their lack of confidence in what their own teacher said and their ignorance regarding the intended meaning of that statement. Furthermore, by demonstrating the manner in which the meaning of the *vārttika* is obtained through the *ghañ* suffix in the sense of an instrument in the rule *upadeśe 'janunāsikaḥ*, as well as the expression of the meanings of stems and suffixes, Nāgeśa indicates the fallibility even of the authors of the *bhāṣya* and others.

On this point, it must be said: in the sūtra *vṛddhir ādaic*, the venerable author of the Bhāṣya, having set aside the positions regarding the restriction of usage and so forth, informs Vararuci—who was composing a section on technical designations (*saṃjñā*)—that "the relationship between a designation and the designated is established by implication alone. He states: "The Teacher, who is the embodiment of authority, with darbha grass as his ritual purifier in hand, seated in a pure place facing east, composed the sūtras with great effort; therein, it is impossible to utter even a single meaningless syllable."

Furthermore, by saying "What more need be said regarding this Sūtra?", [the author] indicates through the term *pramāṇabhūta* that the Teacher possesses qualities such as speaking in accordance with reality and the absence of defects such as being a deceiver; through the phrase *darbhapavitrapāṇi*, his supreme orthodoxy (*paramāstikatva*); through the phrase *mahatā prayatnena*, the absence of defects consisting of states such as insanity and the lack of mental distraction due to preoccupation with other tasks; and [he shows] that the treatise possesses great purpose because it was composed by a teacher endowed with the aforementioned qualities, according to the manner stated at the outset.

To counter that argument, while demonstrating that this sūtra must necessarily be accepted by all, he reveals the intention of the author of the sūtras—the venerable Ācārya—and thereby dispels the suspicion of its meaninglessness: "This sūtra is not useless like the phrase 'ten pomegranates, six cakes,' etc.; therefore, since other [possible] meanings for the term *vṛddhi* are impossible, and because of the use of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the sentence-meaning results in the conclusion that 'the vowels *ā*, *ai*, and *au* are designated as *vṛddhi*. Thus he refuted the doubt regarding the sūtra's lack of purpose.
Who indeed would be capable of asserting that such a Pāṇinian treatise teaches unreal matters?

In this very same way, all the great sages (*maharṣis*), their followers, and other teachers—such as Āpastamba and others—teach the real Śrauta and Smārta duties with supreme benevolence toward living beings for the sake of attaining the ultimate goals mentioned in the scriptures, such as Brāhmaṇahood, by means of statements like, "Now, therefore, we shall explain the duties pertaining to conventional conduct," and "Now, therefore, we shall explain the New and Full Moon sacrifices. All people know this very well from the words of those respective commentators.

Those great sages and their respective Kalpas, being those for whom the Word is the sole authority (*śabdapramāṇaka*), would never at any time speak of an unreal object as if it were real. Nāgeśa, however—his mind defiled by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) born from the incessant study of non-scriptural works such as the *Vākyapadīya* and the *Paramārthasāra*—is unrestrained; he is truly deluded himself, yet honored by deluded people, as he declares all the words of the great sages to be propounders of unreal objects and asserts that those who establish the subject matter in accordance with them are mistaken.

Indeed, no one in the world who acts with foresight is seen to exert great effort to establish an unreal object. Nor is any discerning person seen in the world to practice asceticism for a long time, desiring the favor of the Supreme Self through the means of such [unreal things]. Furthermore, no wise person in the world is ever seen to contemplate an unreal object, such as a hare's horn, as being real.

"Now, sir, do you really say this? Is it not well known to the whole world that magicians worship and strive especially for the sake of minor deities in order to display objects that are unreal, and that they perform incantations directed toward them? To this it is replied: It has already been established that the teacher Pañcaśikha maintains that an object displayed by a magician is not unreal.

Other teachers also maintain that its lack of substantiality consists merely in its short duration, not in its being unreal. Furthermore, some hold that since people eat fruits and other things brought and given by a magician through a specific power acquired by the grace of a deity propitiated by him, it possesses causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), and thus it is not unreal.

Furthermore, it is incorrect for Nāgeśa to claim that name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is unreal, because another Śruti passage states: "Name-and-form are real; by these two this vital breath (*prāṇa*) is covered; the vital breaths are indeed real, and in them this [Brahman] is real. Since this other Śruti declares the reality of the entire category of transformations—the manifold world of name-and-form—which is distinct from Brahman, Nāgeśa’s position is untenable. Nor is this Śruti merely an incidental citation; in the *Mañjūṣā*, he has cited the words of Gautama and others in various places as authoritative evidence, thereby indicating that their status is established by this very [text].

By such expressions as "it resounds" (*dhvanayati*) and "resounded" (*dhvanitam*), and by describing that the intention (*tātparya*) of Gautama and others is precisely that the reality of things is non-existent according to the principle of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya-maryādā*), it is clear that there is no explicit statement in their own treatises to the effect that the intention regarding the reality of things is such [i.e., non-existent]. Therefore, it is not tenable to claim that the unreality of the meanings of roots and suffixes is "resounded" [by them]; rather, this should be understood by determining the meaning of their sūtras exactly as they are.

Let us examine this. For the sequence of the aphorisms is as follows: "A word (*pada*) consists of those [phonemes] ending in an inflectional suffix" (Nyāya Sūtra 1.2.60), and "There is doubt [regarding the meaning of a word] because of the figurative application [of the term 'word'] to the individual, the form, and the genus" (1.2.61). Here, having investigated the eternality or non-eternality of phonemes (*varṇa*) by means of the preceding section, these two sūtras are introduced for the purpose of defining the nature of a word and its denotative power. Be it the eternality or non-eternality of phonemes, it is words alone that are employed in common usage to convey meaning.

Regarding the inquiry as to what its definition is, the intent of the first sūtra is that "a word ending in a nominal suffix (subanta) and a word ending in a verbal suffix (tiṅanta) constitute a pada. Regarding the second [sūtra], experts in its commentary state that its intent is to resolve the doubt—arising from the need to determine whether universals (jāti) and so forth are denoted—as to whether everything is denoted in every case, or only some of them.

And in this regard, it is said: according to observation, phonemes (*varṇa*), ending in case-terminations, become recognized as words (*pada*). For that purpose, "proximity" (*saṃnidhi*) is the occurrence of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*); when the individual (*vyakti*), the form (*ākṛti*), and the genus (*jāti*) exist in an inseparable connection, the word "cow" (*gaur*) is employed. In that case, it is not known whether any one of these is the word-meaning, or all of them.

In this regard, let the wise discern that the unreality (*avāstavatva*) of that which is afflicted by *prakṛti* has been suggested (*dhvanita*) through both the Sūtra and the Bhāṣya. Nor can it be argued that because the word "vikṛtāḥ" means "having undergone modification," the unreality of the general category of modifications follows; for there is no such tenet among the Naiyāyikas, and the meaning of that text must be described strictly according to their own established doctrine. Otherwise, how could that meaning be considered intended by Gautama? In fact, its true meaning is that they are characterized by specific effects (*kārya*), such as the vowel *au*, which are prescribed by the Śāstra.

If one were to engage in inquiry with the notion that the meanings of bases and suffixes possess ontological reality, one would be mistaken; and if one were mistaken, then the author of the Bhāṣya would also be mistaken.
Even you, while engaging in that investigation, have become truly deluded;
for you have composed this based upon the words of one who was deluded.
Consider how this established doctrine could possibly be worthy of being adopted;
know that your labor will be as fruitless as moonlight in a forest.
Regarding the practice of the *Pāñcarātra*,
as it was stated in the *Mañjūṣā* during the investigation into the meaning of the secondary nominal suffixes (*taddhita*) used in the aforementioned sense:
"But for those living beings who are extremely defiled [and thus] [excluded] from the path of the Veda..."
The paths such as the Pāñcarātra and others are beneficial only for a limited time.

Thus, on the occasion of explaining the statement in the *Sūtrasaṃhitā*—namely, that for those who have fallen away from the Vedic path and are exceedingly defiled, the Pāñcarātra and other systems are their path—it is argued that their authority is established according to the distinction of qualified recipients (*adhikāribheda*), like the *udutta-anudutta* oblation. To this it is replied: This [work] is non-Pāṇinian, because such a rule of meaning is not found in Pāṇini’s grammar, nor is such an arrangement seen in the *Bhāṣya*. Furthermore, the venerable Vyāsa himself, in the *Śāntiparvan* of the *Mahābhārata*, states:
"The Lord himself is the speaker of the entire Pāñcarātra;
O King, those who know the Pāñcarātra are devoted to its proper sequence."
"Having attained exclusive devotion (*ekāntabhāva*), they indeed enter Hari.

By such statements, the speaker of the *Pāñcarātra* is the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa himself; and he establishes that those who are established in His path—being His single-minded devotees (*ekāntabhakta*) and having become vessels for unsurpassed, supreme love for the Blessed One—attain their desired fruit. Furthermore, this is demonstrated through the narration of history (*itihāsa*), showing how Uparicara and others, being pure-souled and devoted to the path of the Vedas, attained their cherished fruits by following the *Sāttvata* (i.e., *Pāñcarātra*) injunction and worshipping the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa.
Having heard this, Rudra spoke it again to the Goddess;
for then the Goddess Sarasvatī, instructed by Nārāyaṇa,
entered all those sages out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.

By such statements as *Bhāradvāja-śāstra* 3.43, which define Brahmā and others as both speakers and listeners, [the author] has clearly stated that ascetic great sages who know the Vedas are qualified for the Pāñcarātra through the grace of the Supreme Self. In this regard, whose voice would even venture to say that Brahmā and others, as well as Uparicara and his peers, were impure or devoid of the Vedas?

If, anywhere, a statement is seen claiming that this Tantra lacks qualification, it should be understood as intended for delusion; the underlying purpose is to ensure that the wicked do not engage with it.

If it is argued that the statement, "Having not obtained the supreme good in the four Vedas, Śāṇḍilya mastered this scripture," implies a lack of regard for the Vedas, and that through this censure of the Vedas the Pāñcarātra is understood to have inferior eligibility—this is replied as follows: Here, the statement regarding the non-attainment of the supreme good does not imply a disregard for the Vedas; rather, even for one who has studied all the Vedas, the fruit is not attained by that alone.
Instead, the Pāñcarātra must be known as that which fulfills the meaning of the Vedas, because it is unsurpassed.
Furthermore, this *Gītā* is its summary; therefore, there is nothing equal to it anywhere.
Thus it is said in the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa:
"I am indeed visible through the Veda, the Pāñcarātra, devotion, and sacrifice;
otherwise, I am not visible even in hundreds of millions of years."

Thus, according to the direction stated in the *Vārāha-purāṇa*, it is understood that the attainment of the fruit occurs only through Vedic practice accompanied by the study of the *Pāñcarātra*. Therefore, it cannot be said that a censure of the Vedas is perceived here; rather, following the maxim "for there is no censure," the objection raised in the scripture is intended merely to dispel doubt.

(Prapañcasāra 43) "He spoke this Sāvitra-Aṅgiras to him"—this instruction of the Sāvitra-vidyā to Bhāradvāja, son of Atri, does not imply a censure of all the Vedas, nor was it explained in that manner by the commentators (*bhāṣyakāra*s). Furthermore, in the seventh book of the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*, in the dialogue between Nārada and Sanatkumāra, although he heard that he had not attained the highest good in its entirety—including the limbs (*aṅga*s) and the secret doctrines (*rahasya*)—no censure of the study of the Vedas and so forth is implied there either; neither did the commentators or the teachers explain it thus. Moreover: "Composed on the great mountain Meru, it is equal to the four Vedas."
It is honored by the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, as well as by the Atharva-Āṅgirasa hymns.
This is the Great Upaniṣad, endowed with the four Vedas,
expounded according to the conclusions of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, and proclaimed as the Pāñcarātra.
In the Śāntiparvan of the Mahābhārata, beginning with the passage "Sung from the mouth of Nārāyaṇa... (348), it is stated that the Pāñcarātra, together with all the Vedas, was composed by the sages:
"For just as all [the Vedas] are authoritative, so too is that supreme scripture."
"This instruction of mine shall indeed be authoritative" (344.41).

Since this declares the authority of the Pāñcarātra just as it does for other objects created by the Blessed One, it is unreasonable to maintain that the Pāñcarātra lacks authority because it is not rooted in the Vedas, or that it lacks authority because it is intended for those of inferior qualification, by relying on a statement that contradicts the *Bhārata*—which is remembered as the "fifth Veda"—and which asserts: "The *Bhārata* is the fifth Veda."

Just as there is a lack of authority for Smṛti texts that contradict the Vedas, it has been determined in the *Mañjūṣā* that those who adhere to the path of the Sūtras in contradiction with the *Bhārata* are ineligible for Vedic rites; likewise, the determination regarding eligibility for Tantric rites in the *Tattvakaustubha*, Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita’s determination regarding eligibility for those who have fallen from their caste (*patitādhikāra*) and his determination regarding heresy (*pāṣaṇḍitva*) in the *Tattvakaustubha*—and other such determinations made by others—are not to be respected.

This is because Brahmā and others—such as Uparicara and his peers—who are designated in the *Bhārata* as being qualified [for Vedic rites], as well as Śāṇḍilya, have not fallen from their status through contact with women and the like; and because, as preeminent devotees of Vāsudeva, they cannot be considered heretics (*pāṣaṇḍin*). Furthermore, the venerable Śaṅkarācārya, in his commentary on the four aphorisms beginning with "Because of the impossibility of origination" (*Brahma-sūtra* 2.2.42), which aim to refute the Pāñcarātra, did not cite the words of the *Sūta* and other such texts as corroborative authorities (*upabṛṃhaṇa*), and there remains doubt regarding their authority.

Alternatively, understand that those people who, having produced a firm conviction regarding the lack of authority in the great scripture of the Pāñcarātra among those hostile to Nārāyaṇa and his devotees, have set out to prevent its practice—these are the Smṛtis which proclaim the non-authority of the Pāñcarātra.
As for the statement: "My sacrifice is threefold: Vaidika, Tāntrika, and Miśra."
One should worship me according to the very same procedure intended for those three.
Regarding this verse from the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* (11.27.7), it is stated in the *Tantrādhikāra-nirṇaya* concerning mixed worship (*miśrapūjā*) that:

"Outcastes (*patita*), Brahmins, and others are indeed qualified for mixed worship; for those engaged in performing expiation (*prāyaścitta*), there is a reinstatement of the Vedic mantras employed in the *tantra*, just as there is a reinstatement of the qualification for the *saṃdhyā-vandana*. Here, the following must be considered: Is this outcaste one who has performed the expiation, or one who has not?

[The first case is] not [possible], because for him (the Śūdra), since his eligibility for actions appropriate to his own caste and stage of life is established, his inclination would necessarily be directed toward Vedic worship alone; thus, there is no possibility of his inclination being directed toward a mixed [form of worship]. Nor is the second [case possible], because he lacks eligibility for that worship, and consequently does not engage in it.

Although the performance of the *saṃdhyāvandana* is established by the analogy of the *saṃdhyāvandana* for the sake of achieving fitness for performing the prescribed acts of expiation (*prāyaścitta*), worship is not included among the duties of the twice-born (*dvijāti*). This is because, according to the definition of loss of caste (*pātitya*) as "falling away from the duties of the twice-born," worship is not attained; furthermore, unlike the injunctions for expiation, there is no specific injunction for worship stating, "the fallen one should perform worship."

On the contrary, in the section on penance (*prāyaścitta*) in the *Mitākṣarā*, under the commentary on verse 43, "The one with a skull" (*śiraḥkapālī*), it is stated that there is indeed a loss of duties: "For the twice-born, [the duties are] study, sacrifice, and knowledge; for the Brāhmaṇa, additionally teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and receiving gifts. This refers to the loss of those duties of the twice-born which constitute the limbs of the performance of vows (*vratacaryā*). Here, the word "sacrifice" (*ijyā*) refers to the worship of deities beginning with the *agnihotra* and ending with the propitiation of the Lord.

As for what was also stated—that because the initiation (*upanayana*), the study of the Vedas (*āpana*), and so forth are mentioned in the *Nibandhas* as existing in other *kalpas*, and because their eligibility for the mixed worship (*miśrapūjana*) is declared in the *Āgamas*, [therefore women have such eligibility]—that is exceedingly crude. For since women who have undergone initiation possess the eligibility for the recitation of Vedic mantras and the like, it is possible for them to engage in Vedic worship itself. Furthermore, no prohibition is observed stating that "even for women who have undergone initiation, there is no eligibility for the Vedic worship of Hari."

And thus, the statement regarding the three-fold knowledge (traividya) would not be redundant. Nor should it be argued that even if the subject matter concerns the three castes (traivarṇika), the redundancy of the classification remains the same, on the grounds that all of them possess the qualification for the Vedas and are entitled to Vedic worship. This is because the purpose is not redundant, as its intent is to teach that worship must necessarily be performed—whether in brief or in detail—in accordance with the time, place, and condition [of the practitioner].

Since it is heard that there is a transgression (*pratyavāya*) in failing to perform the worship of the Blessed One, and since that [worship] must necessarily be performed in order to avoid such transgression, the intended meaning is that when one lacks the time or other resources to perform Vedic worship, a concise *miśra-pūjā* (mixed worship) should be performed. To make it clear that the meaning stated by Tīkṣita is not accepted by Vyāsa, we shall cite the very verses from the *Bhāgavata*: Uddhava said:
"O Lord, explain the *kriyā-yoga*, which is the means of worshipping You—how the *sāttvatas* worship You, O Bull among the *Sāttvatas*."
The sages—
the blessed Nārada, Vyāsa, and the teacher Aṅgiras— repeatedly declare this to be the supreme good for human beings.
That which the unborn Lord spoke has issued forth from your lotus-like mouth;
the Lord Bhava [Śiva] likewise spoke it to his sons, headed by Bhṛgu, and to the Goddess.
O giver of honor, I consider this to be approved by all castes and stages of life, and the highest among all that leads to spiritual welfare, even for women and Śūdras.
O Lord of the Lord of the Universe, O lotus-petal-eyed one, tell this which liberates from the bonds of karma to a devotee who is devoted to you.
The Blessed Lord said: O Uddhava, I shall describe to you in brief, according to their sequence, the infinite path of the ritualistic section (karmakāṇḍa) of this [Veda].
My sacrifice is threefold: Vedic, Tantric, and mixed.
One should worship me according to whichever of these three rites one desires.

Thus [it is said]. This is its meaning: among the three types of persons (*makā*), a faultless member of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*) should worship me according to the desired method (by means of one or another form of worship). From the previous statement, "and approved by all castes and stages of life," the term *traivarṇika* is obtained as the agent; from the mention of "to the devotee" (*bhaktāya*) and so forth, and from the word "pure" (*śuci*) which is to be explained, the sense of "faultless" (*nirdoṣa*) is also obtained.

In this regard, the intention of the root text is not that because one who has fallen [from caste] (patita) is not mentioned among the classes of qualified persons (adhikāri-varga) in the first chapter, such a person lacks the qualification for worship here. For neither Śrīdhara and others, nor the commentators themselves, have established as a settled conclusion (siddhānta) that one who has fallen is qualified for the Miśra [form of worship]. Indeed, Dīkṣita and others, out of hatred for Viṣṇu and the Vaiṣṇavas, falsely attribute the status of being qualified for those who have fallen to the Pāñcarātra system, thereby describing the authoritative texts (pramāṇas) in a distorted manner.

Furthermore, since the *Sāntiparvan* of the fifth Veda known as the *Bhārata*, in chapters numbered 343, 358, and 359—which establish the origin and purpose of the *Pāñcarātra*—it is stated that [the followers of this system] possess the highest qualification (*uttamādhikārikatva*), the conclusions reached by Nāgeśa Dīkṣita and others are contrary to the Vedas. Even though women, Śūdras, and others are included within the category of those qualified for practice, they are not entitled to perform the three types of direct worship (*sākṣāt-trividha-pūjā*).

However, in that regard, women—just as during the conclusion of a vow (*vratodyāpana*) and similar occasions—should themselves make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) and have the entire worship performed through a Brahmin, accompanied by Vedic mantras; by that much alone they obtain the fruit appropriate for them. Some maintain that Śūdras are entitled to the worship of Hari by reciting Puranic mantras. But the author of the *Nirṇayasindhu* holds that even in that case there is no entitlement for a Śūdra, and that even the Puranic mantra must be recited by Brahmins.

Some maintain that because they have the authority for the recitation of names, they ought to perform worship preceded by the utterance of those names; this applies equally to women as well. In all three types of propitiation, since there is the application of Vedic mantras and the eight-syllabled mantra, that scripture indeed begins with the worship of the syllable *oṃ* and its tone.
In that regard, it has been proclaimed by the sages wherever that Compassionate One resides.

Thus, by the statement in the *Mahābhārata* regarding its being joined with the syllable *oṃ*, and because it is equal to the Veda, the intended meaning of the passages concerning eligibility (*adhikāra*) is that—just as in the Veda—women and *śūdras* lack direct eligibility for the worship of the Lord there as well, and therefore it must be performed through the mediation of a Brahmin; this has been explained in detail elsewhere, so let it suffice here.
Those who are impure and devoid of the Vedas are eligible for the *Pāñcarātra*.
Thus, this conclusion is contradicted by the fifth [alternative].
"Therefore, one should avoid that [work] by means of the Veda known as the *Bhārata*";
thus say those who are well-versed in the meaning of authoritative sources such as the *Bhārata*.
"The twice-born who has fallen [into sin] becomes eligible for worship in the mixed [caste]"—
this determination regarding initiation is rooted in hatred toward Hari.
Now, as for the conclusion:

the great seers—high-souled beings of venerable and diverse conduct, recipients of the supreme grace of the Supreme Self, free from greed, desirous of dharma, longing for the highest good of all living beings, regarding the welfare of others as their own purpose, and wishing to uplift others—instruct people by making them understand the true nature of dharma and adharma, which yield the fruits of heaven, liberation, and hell, respectively; they thus engage people in dharma and turn them away from adharma.

The worldly practice of the venerable teachers who are experts in their respective Tantras prevails. In this regard, the worshipful great sage and teacher Pāṇini, while teaching the actual meanings of roots and suffixes, stated that the meaning [of the word] is unreal (*avāstava*) within the dharma consisting of the usage of words; whereas other learned persons, however, harbor the delusion of its reality. This has been skillfully demonstrated previously, and thus Nāgeśa’s interpretation is indeed not to be disregarded.

According to the grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇas*), words are indeed eternal; and according to the system of certain other teachers as well, the constituent parts of roots (*prakṛti*) and suffixes (*pratyaya*) existing therein are likewise real and eternal, for they were precisely demonstrated by Pāṇini—how then could they be unreal?

The doctrine of the unreality of the phenomenal world (*prapañca-asatyatva-vāda*) set forth in the *Añjūṣā* is neither connected with this treatise (*śāstra*), nor is it accepted by the teacher Pāṇini, as no statement to that effect is found in his grammar (*tantra*). Nor is it intended by the author of the *Bhāṣya*, since such a thing is not stated in the *Bhāṣya*. Furthermore, since no unreality of any entity whatsoever is mentioned in the Sāṃkhya system, and since the author of the *Bhāṣya* was a Sāṃkhya teacher, it would be inappropriate for him to conceive of entities as being merely illusory (*māyāmaya*) according to that system.

Even the venerable Vyāsa does not hold the view that the world is unreal, for it is not stated as such in his own works such as the Mahābhārata; on the contrary, because he censures those who claim the world is unreal in the verse from the Gītā, "Unreal and without foundation" (16.8), the most eminent scholars among the knowers of Brahman maintain that his position is that the world is indeed real, as has been elaborated upon.

All three of these teachers maintain that Vāsudeva is the supreme being and the presiding authority over all, and they intend to express the real, fundamental distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme Self (paramātman), rather than their identity or the non-reality of their difference.

This has been described. Furthermore, it has been established that the scriptural statements do not have the intention of conveying identity. In some cases, even the following word-interpretation can be made: in the phrase "tat tvam asi" (That thou art), the word *tat* is derived from the root *tan* with the suffix *kvip* in the sense of an agent (*kartari*), or with the suffix *vic*; it is masculine, and by the rule "sor halṅyādi lopaḥ," the case-ending *s* is elided; because it is used in a secondary sense (*gauṇatvāt*), it does not receive the designation of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) and so forth.

Due to its being an archaic form (*ārṣatva*), there is the *kvip* suffix for the habitual action (*ācāra*) even from the root *bal*; or else, from the root *halan* (to move), there is the *kvip* suffix for the habitual action. Since it is possible to resolve the matter by assuming that only those specific usages where a fault would otherwise arise are not denotative (*anabhidhāna*), there is no evidence for assuming a general absence of such faults. Consequently, the meaning is: "You are one whose conduct is similar to the conduct of the Self as agent. The intended sense is: "Like the Self, you too are free from all defects. And thus, this [verse] does not intend to express identity.

In the passage "one who knows the *brahman* becomes, as it were, the *brahman*," the particle *eva* has the sense of "as it were" (*iva*). Thus, the meaning is "becomes, as it were, the *brahman*. Similarly, in such passages as "One contending [in battle] should sacrifice a dwarf dedicated to Viṣṇu; having become, as it were, Viṣṇu, he conquers these worlds" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 2.1.3.16), the phrase "Viṣṇu indeed" (*viṣṇureva*) means "Viṣṇu, as it were" (*viṣṇuriva*). Therefore, this [text] also does not have identity as its intended meaning.

"Brahman, the knower of Brahman attains the Supreme; Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite; he who knows It as hidden in the cave of the heart, in the highest ether, enjoys all things for the duration of his life and, upon departing, attains the world of Brahman, from which he does not return again" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.15.1); and "He who knows this thus, having shaken off evil, becomes established in the infinite, supreme heavenly world" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 4.1). In such passages, there is the attainment of the world of Brahman by the knower of Brahman, as well as the experience of all desires together with Brahman.
It is being established that identity with Brahman is not [the meaning], and therefore the oneness of the self is not what is intended by the Śruti.

If it is asked, "For what reason should the sense of 'as if' (*iva*) in the vision be accepted?"—it is said: if the purport of the sentence were solely the attainment of the state of Viṣṇu, then since such attainment is of the nature of liberation (*mukti*), it would be redundant to speak of attaining a world that is a means to ephemeral worldly happiness after liberation; furthermore, there would be a violation of the natural force of the *ktvā* suffix. This is because, upon examining the context of the passage, one gains the understanding that the fruit of the sacrifice under discussion is indeed the attainment of that world.

It is illogical to conceive of this as the fruit of ritual action (*karma*) for the sake of attaining the state of Viṣṇu. If one were to conceive it thus out of recklessness, it would contradict the established doctrine that liberation is to be accomplished through the knowledge imparted by all the Teachers (*ācāryas*). Furthermore, by the word "striving" (*spardhamāna*), there is the sense of desiring to overcome others; from this, it is understood that such a person is qualified for ritual action (*karma*), and not for liberation, since the scriptures determine that only those who are "peaceful, self-controlled," and so forth, are qualified for liberation (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.23).

Furthermore, if the intended meaning were solely the attainment of the status of Viṣṇu, then the statement would be satisfied merely by saying "he becomes Viṣṇu" itself; therefore, one must maintain that the sentence culminates in similarity alone, and thus the word must be accepted as having the sense of "as it were" (iva). And by stating this similarity, it should be understood that the performer of the Vaiṣṇava sacrifice—who is competing with other men—attains a prowess equal to that of Viṣṇu, who is the means for conquering the worlds.

We learn from those foremost among the knowers of Brahman that the Lord Vāsudeva, the master of all, who is to be propitiated through all ritual actions, being well-pleased and bestowing the fruits desired by his surrendered devotees, gladdens them in both this world and the next; and we understand from the Vedas, Itihāsas, and other sources that there are many such Vaiṣṇavas, objects of the Lord’s compassion, who, having taken refuge, experience happiness in both worlds.

In this regard, there are great kings such as Nahuṣa and Ambarīṣa, and Dhruva, Prahlāda, Pāñcālī, Rukmī, Rāvaṇa, Vibhīṣaṇa, and others serve as examples. By this it should be understood that age, caste, and so forth are not the causes for receiving grace; rather, it is devotion (*bhakti*) and surrender (*prapatti*). In this matter, not even a single person has obtained the fruit by contemplating, "You and I are one and the same"; rather, Hari is the Lord of all, and He is to be known through taking refuge in Him and by hearing of His deeds and so forth.

Even today, it is established by the personal experience of everyone that people who worship the Blessed One in temples and other places do not realize, "I am one with You. We understand from the Itihāsas and other sources that Hiraṇyakaśipu and others, whose minds were awakened to the idea of themselves being the Lord of the Universe, spoke as if they had lost their senses.

Therefore, considering that the notion of oneness is not correct, the devotees (bhāgavatas) abandon the thought of identity and take refuge in the Lord as their protector— perceiving Him through qualities such as His sovereignty over all— and perceive themselves as His servants and those to be protected. O Infinite One, may I forcibly become one among the great ones of pure heart who constantly offer devotion unto You.
"By which [means] may I, intoxicated by drinking the nectar of the stories of Your qualities, swiftly carry across this ocean of worldly existence, so vast and full of calamities? (Bhāgavata 4.9.11).
O Lord, O Kesava, remover of the distress of those who have sought refuge, grant me Your grace!
"O Acyuta, protect me further with your glance! (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.20.16).
"O Nātha, O Lord of Ramā, O Lord of Vraja, O destroyer of distress! O Janārdana, lift me up from this ocean of Kuru-suffering! (Mahābhārata, Śāntiparvan 10.46).
He who protects the one who has sought refuge from that which pursues him with fierce speed,
and who protects the terrified refugee from whatever fear he fears.
"Death pursues one relentlessly; let us take refuge in Him. (Bhagavadgītā 8.2.33) "I am the younger brother of Rāvaṇa, and I have been insulted by him."
Having come for refuge to you, the protector of all beings, he has abandoned both his sons and his wife and sought refuge with Rāghava. (Rāmāyaṇa, Yuddhakāṇḍa 19.4, 5)
"Announce me quickly to the high-souled Raghava, the refuge of all the world, that Vibhishana has arrived."

In accordance with the direction stated in the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* and other texts—such as, "Thus Dhruva and others, having taken refuge in Vāsudeva, became supremely happy"—it should be understood from the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* and similar sources that other devotees likewise, having gone for refuge to the Blessed One, experienced happiness both in this world and the next. The Blessed Vāsudeva himself says:
"Those people who worship Me, thinking of no other..."

For those who are constantly devoted to Me, I provide for their well-being and security. To one who has surrendered even once and pleads, "I am yours," I grant fearlessness from all beings; this is My vow.

Understanding that, according to the direction stated [in the *Rāmāyaṇa* 18.33–34], he has taken a vow to protect his devotees who have sought refuge as his attendants, and concluding—on the basis of such scriptural statements as "A person who has a teacher knows" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad*)—that only the knowledge taught by a teacher is the means for attaining both indirect and direct realization, those who know the tradition, having learned the true science from a teacher and investigating that knowledge through study at the appropriate time, daily gratify Vāsudeva, the Lord of Śrī, by serving him; and having approached that Refuge-seeker for shelter, they take refuge in him.

May the virtuous—those followers of Pāṇini, those who take refuge in Vāsudeva, and those who know Brahman—experience the bliss of sovereign dominion in both this world and the next, attained through His compassionate side-glances; and may we take refuge in Śrīmannārāyaṇa, the Lord of Śrī. May there be peace!
"He who, having no other refuge, takes refuge in Vāsudeva with devotion—Him this Lord of the World, the Supreme Person known through the Vedas, protects."
In the Kali age, in the year measured by the Vedas (4), the oceans (4), the sky (0), and the arrows (5)— that is, 4405—
this was composed by the learned Śrī Setumādhava, born in the lineage of Ātreya.
This work, titled *Bhāvanirṇaya*, composed by Vyāsa and Pāṇini, has reached completion through the grace of the venerable Guru, Lord Hari.
Thus [ends the work] by the follower of the doctrines of the illustrious Pūrṇaprajña, the ornament of the lineage of the illustrious Āryācāryas,
the great preceptor Śrī Muṣṇa Vyākaraṇa Subbarāyācārya’s son,
who attained clarity in the science of words (Śabdabrahmavidyā) through the service of the lotus feet of his illustrious father.

This work, titled *Śrīvyāsapāṇinibhāvanirṇaya*, composed by Vyākaraṇasetumādhavācārya— who is adorned with such titles as Vidyāmārtaṇḍa, Śrīmadhvasiddhāntabhūṣaṇa, and Mahāmahopādhyāya— is hereby completed.
May this be offered unto Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
